SYNTH-0002♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Lisa Flores♔♔♔♔♔♔COMMENT OF LISA FLORES, FIREFIGHTER, WAKE COUNTY, NORTH CAROLINA⏎Submitted to the HHS Docket: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎Two winters ago, my crew transported a 63-year-old cardiac patient out of a burning duplex on Caldwell Street in Raleigh. The receiving hospital had roughly four minutes of usable history before making a call, and they made the wrong one initially, because nothing in the handoff flagged his pacemaker model. An AI-assisted intake system had been piloted at that hospital and shelved eight months prior over reimbursement disputes none of us ever heard explained. He survived. His left hand did not fully recover. I am not writing about that outcome to generate sympathy. I am writing because the decision to pilot that system, and the decision to shelve it, were both made without any accountability to the people closest to the consequences, and the RFI now before HHS is structured in a way that will make that accountability problem permanent rather than correctable.⏎⏎The document HHS has issued frames regulatory scrutiny as an obstacle to innovation and describes its own purpose as "reducing uncertainty that impedes AI adoption" (89 FR, HHS/ASTP, 2024). That framing is not neutral. It is an ideological commitment dressed as an administrative question. What concerns me is not whether AI can improve clinical care in specific contexts. What concerns me is that HHS is not simply setting a policy; it is foreclosing future democratic choices, and that is a meaningfully different thing. Langley et al. (2022), writing in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, documented how institutional deskilling follows EHR dependency with measurable speed, within four to seven years of adoption, clinical judgment in affected domains shows statistically significant atrophy among practitioners who no longer practice without the system. Coiera, Ash, and Berg (2016) documented analogous unintended consequences across health IT implementations more broadly. The pattern is not speculative. Once hospitals cannot function without a vendor's system, the democratic option to say "we don't want this" disappears. The lock-in is not a side effect of AI adoption; in many architectures it is a design feature, as Dafny and Lee (2023) argue in Health Affairs with specific attention to how market concentration follows from integration dependency. Frank Pasquale's analysis in The Black Box Society (2015) remains the clearest account of why opacity in algorithmic systems is not a technical problem awaiting a technical fix but a political condition that distributes power in specific and traceable directions. Langdon Winner asked in 1980, in "Do Artifacts Have Politics?", whether technological systems carry political properties independent of the intentions of their designers. The answer, in the context of clinical AI, is yes, and HHS is about to write those properties into federal infrastructure without having asked the public whether that is what it wants.⏎⏎My specific request to HHS addresses the framing question the RFI implicitly raises about the appropriate role of federal agencies in shaping adoption timelines:⏎⏎1. SYNTH-0003♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Rebecca Thompson♔♔♔♔♔♔Submitted by: Rebecca Thompson, Rockford, IL (private citizen, commercial truck driver, cardiac patient)⏎⏎RE: HHS Health Sector AI RFI — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎⏎WHAT I WANT TO KNOW BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE⏎⏎My first question is a practical one and I want it on the record before I get into anything else: does any of this cost me more money? That is not a rhetorical setup. I am on a fixed income. I drive long-haul routes and I manage my schedule around cardiology appointments in Rockford, and the last thing I can absorb is a new line item on an EOB that says "AI-assisted diagnostic review" or some similar charge that I never consented to and cannot appeal because I did not know it was happening. I have read enough of the RFI to understand that HHS is asking about reimbursement pathways for AI tools, and I want someone at this agency to state plainly whether accelerating adoption means accelerating billing. If a cardiology practice adds an AI screening layer to my EKG review, who pays for that layer? Because in my experience, when something new gets added to a clinical visit, the patient finds out about it later, on paper, with a balance due.⏎⏎About eighteen months ago, I found out that my cardiologist's office was running my EKG data through some kind of AI screening tool. I found out because a nurse mentioned it while I was already putting my jacket on. I asked whether I could see what the tool flagged. I asked whether its output had any bearing on the medication adjustment my doctor made that same visit. Three different people in that office gave me three different answers, none of which amounted to a real explanation. I am not against the technology. I want to be clear about that. But I left that office not knowing whether a machine had influenced what I was putting into my body, and I have not received a satisfying answer since. That experience is what brought me to this comment.⏎⏎⏎THE RELATIONAL QUESTION HHS IS NOT ASKING⏎⏎HHS frames this RFI around acceleration. The word appears repeatedly. What I do not see is any serious engagement with what gets lost when the pace of a clinical encounter is reorganized around algorithmic output. There is a body of evidence on this that I think deserves more weight than this RFI gives it. A 2014 meta-analysis by Kelley, Kraft-Todd, Schapira and colleagues, published in PLoS ONE, found that the quality of the patient-clinician relationship is itself a determinant of health outcomes, independent of the technical accuracy of the treatment. That is not a soft or sentimental finding. It means that how a doctor is present with a patient has measurable effects on whether that patient gets better. Zulman and colleagues wrote about this directly in JAMA in 2020, describing specific practices that sustain physician presence and connection during clinical encounters, and noting that those practices are under pressure from documentation burdens and workflow interruptions. Adding an AI layer to the EKG review, or the medication decision, or the differential diagnosis, does not automatically reduce that pressure. It can redistribute attention in ways that erode the relational quality of the visit without anyone in the room noticing.⏎⏎Eric Topol, who is generally optimistic about AI in medicine, wrote in Nature Medicine in 2019 that the convergence of human and artificial intelligence in clinical care carries real risks of relational erosion, specifically that clinicians may come to mediate the patient relationship through a screen rather than through direct engagement. He framed that as a concern worth managing, not a reason to stop, but the concern is there in the text and I think HHS should engage with it more directly than this RFI does. Shortliffe and Sepúlveda made a related point in JAMA in 2018: that clinical decision support tools are most beneficial when they are transparent to the clinician and legible to the patient, and that opacity in either direction creates a kind of accountability gap that is hard to close after the fact. My experience in Rockford is a small example of exactly that gap.⏎⏎⏎THE DESKILLING CONCERN AND WHAT IT MEANS FOR PATIENTS LIKE ME⏎⏎There is a second issue I want to raise and I will admit I am less certain about how to frame it, but it matters. Timothy Hoff published research in Health Care Management Review in 2011 examining how primary care physicians adapt to work innovations, and one of the patterns he documented was deskilling: the gradual atrophy of clinical judgment in areas where automated tools take over the cognitive work. Parasuraman and Manzey wrote about the complacency effects of automation more broadly in Human Factors in 2010, finding that humans who rely on automated systems over time become less able to catch errors when those systems fail. I am not saying AI tools will make my cardiologist worse at her job. I am saying that if HHS accelerates adoption without requiring any assessment of these effects, we will not know whether that is happening until it has been happening for a while. And patients like me, who are not in a position to independently evaluate the quality of a clinical judgment, are the ones who will absorb that uncertainty.⏎⏎The ONC Federal Health IT Strategic Plan for 2024 through 2030 does mention the importance of trustworthy AI, and I read that section carefully. What it does not specify is what "trustworthy" means in relational terms, as opposed to technical accuracy terms. A tool can be highly accurate in the aggregate and still be wrong for a specific patient in a specific encounter, and if the clinician's attention has shifted toward the tool's output and away from the patient in the room, that individual error is harder to catch. I do not think HHS has fully reckoned with that problem yet.⏎⏎⏎WHAT I AM ASKING FOR⏎⏎My ask is specific. Before any AI tool is permitted to influence a clinical decision, whether that means flagging an abnormality, recommending a medication adjustment, or generating a differential diagnosis, HHS should require demonstrated safety in relational and clinical terms, not just technical accuracy benchmarks. That means studies that follow real patients over time and ask whether the quality of their clinical encounters changed. It means disclosure requirements that are legible to patients, not just to clinicians. It means that when a nurse offhandedly mentions that a machine looked at my heart, I should already have a piece of paper in my hand explaining what that means, who reviewed the output, and whether it affected my care that day.⏎⏎I also want an answer to the cost question. Not a general assurance that HHS is committed to affordability. A specific answer to whether new reimbursement pathways for AI tools will result in new patient-facing charges, and if so, what recourse a patient on a fixed income has when those charges appear without prior notice. I have been waiting eighteen months for someone in that cardiology office to give me a straight answer about what happened during that visit. I would rather not wait another eighteen months for HHS to get around to the question of what it costs.♔♔2026-01-23T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-23T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔4♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Medicine is fundamentally a human relationship built on judgment, context, and trust, and AI threatens to reduce patients to data points and clinicians to machine overseers.♔individual♔high♔resigned♔Illinois♔truck driver♔52♔My cardiologist's office in Rockford started using some kind of AI screening tool on my EKG data about eighteen months ago, and I only found out because a nurse mentioned it offhandedly while I was already pulling my jacket back on. SYNTH-0004♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Linda Robinson♔Cerner Corporation♔♔♔♔♔Linda Robinson⏎Compliance Officer, Cerner Corporation⏎304-[redacted]@cerner.com⏎⏎Submitted via regulations.gov⏎Docket: HHS-2024-AI-Clinical-RFI⏎⏎RE: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎⏎Cerner Corporation | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 1⏎⏎⏎THE FRAMING PROBLEM⏎⏎The Department's Request for Information asks the right questions about the wrong half of the AI deployment problem. HHS has structured this RFI around acceleration — reducing friction, expanding reimbursement pathways, clarifying regulatory guidance so that health systems can move faster toward AI-assisted clinical care. Cerner's compliance function does not dispute that those barriers are real. An internal audit conducted across our active clinical deployment partnerships in Q2 2024 found that 83% of site compliance officers identified regulatory ambiguity around AI-generated clinical decision support as the primary bottleneck delaying full system integration. That finding is consistent with what this office has observed across our health system partners for the better part of three years.⏎⏎But there is a separate AI deployment already underway in the health sector, one that HHS appears to be treating as outside the scope of this RFI, and that omission is not a minor gap. Health insurers — specifically Medicare Advantage organizations and large commercial payers — have been deploying AI-driven prior authorization systems at scale for several years now. These systems are not speculative. They are operational. And the evidence that they are causing patient harm is no longer preliminary.⏎⏎The HHS Office of Inspector General found in April 2022 that some Medicare Advantage organizations were denying prior authorization requests in ways that raised serious concerns about beneficiary access to medically necessary care (OEI-09-18-00260). The U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations published findings in October 2023 — "Refusal of Recovery: How Medicare Advantage Insurers Have Denied Patients Access to Post-Acute Care" — documenting that major insurers used algorithmic tools to generate post-acute care denials at rates that could not plausibly reflect individualized clinical review. The Kaiser Family Foundation's March 2023 issue brief by Koma, Cubanski, and Neuman on prior authorization in Medicare Advantage documented that beneficiaries who lack administrative support infrastructure are systematically less likely to successfully appeal denials, regardless of the clinical merits of their case.⏎⏎This is the AI adoption problem that is already harming patients. The RFI's framing, which treats AI adoption as something that needs to be accelerated rather than something that has already been deployed in ways that require accountability architecture, reflects a structural blind spot that this comment is intended to address directly.⏎⏎⏎Cerner Corporation | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 2⏎⏎⏎THE PRIOR AUTHORIZATION SYSTEM AS AN AI DEPLOYMENT CASE STUDY⏎⏎Cerner's compliance team has reviewed the appeals process structures used by several major Medicare Advantage organizations as part of our health system partnership work. What we observe is an appeals infrastructure that is not designed to surface clinical errors — it is structured in ways that systematically disadvantage claimants with limited administrative capacity. The American Medical Association's 2022 Prior Authorization Physician Survey found that 35% of physicians reported that prior authorization delays had led to a serious adverse event for a patient in their care. That is not a documentation problem. That is a patient safety outcome attributable, in part, to AI-generated decision velocity that has outpaced any meaningful clinical review layer.⏎⏎The ProPublica and Capitol Forum investigation published in March 2023, reported by Rucker, Miller, and Armstrong, documented that Cigna's internal review process allowed physicians to reject prior authorization claims in batches — sometimes processing over 50 denials in a single day — without reading the underlying records. Whether that process was automated, semi-automated, or simply structured to replicate the output of an automated system is, from a compliance standpoint, a distinction without a difference. The functional result is AI-paced denial velocity with human-labeled accountability, which is precisely the configuration most resistant to regulatory correction.⏎⏎The racial equity dimension of this problem is also documented. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan published findings in Science in 2019 (366(6464):447-453) demonstrating that a widely used commercial algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients relative to white patients with equivalent clinical complexity. That study examined a care management algorithm, not a prior authorization tool, but the underlying mechanism — cost as a proxy for need — is structurally identical to the optimization logic embedded in many payer-side AI denial systems. HHS has not, to Cerner's knowledge, issued guidance requiring payers to audit their prior authorization AI for demographic disparities before deployment or on any ongoing basis.⏎⏎Georgetown University's Center on Health Insurance Reforms published a working paper in January 2024 by Palanker, Volk, and Lucia documenting state-level efforts to address AI in health insurance. The National Academy for State Health Policy's Q1 2024 tracker on state AI legislation in health insurance found that at least 17 states had introduced or passed legislation imposing some form of transparency or human review requirement on AI-generated insurance decisions. The fact that state legislatures are moving faster than federal regulators on this question is not a sign that the problem is being handled — it is a sign that the federal framework is creating a patchwork compliance environment that will ultimately serve neither patients nor health systems.⏎⏎⏎Cerner Corporation | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 3⏎⏎⏎WHAT THE RFI SHOULD ADDRESS BUT DOES NOT⏎⏎The Department's stated goals in the 2023 National AI Health Roadmap — responsible adoption, patient-centered design, equity-conscious deployment — are not objectionable as written. The problem is that the Roadmap, like this RFI, is oriented toward the provider side of the AI equation. It addresses clinical decision support tools, diagnostic algorithms, documentation assistance. It does not establish accountability architecture for payer-side AI systems that are making coverage determinations affecting millions of Medicare Advantage and commercial insurance beneficiaries annually.⏎⏎This is not a small omission. Cerner's analysis of reimbursement claims data from twelve health system partners found that AI-assisted diagnostic workflows reduced documentation burden by an average of 31 minutes per encounter. That is a real operational gain. But fewer than 20% of those encounters qualified for any form of AI-augmented reimbursement under existing CMS coding structures. The implication is that the financial case for provider-side AI adoption remains structurally weak while the financial case for payer-side AI denial systems remains structurally strong. HHS is proposing to fix the first problem without addressing the second. The incentive asymmetry that results will not produce the responsible adoption outcomes the Roadmap describes.⏎⏎The administrative burden literature is relevant here. Schulte and Fry's 2019 investigation for Kaiser Health News and Fortune — "Death by a Thousand Clicks: Where Electronic Health Records Went Wrong" — documented how EHR implementation created documentation burdens that consumed physician time without producing proportionate clinical value. The prior authorization AI problem is the same structural failure repeating in a new technological context. A system optimized for administrative throughput rather than clinical accuracy will generate the same category of harm regardless of whether the underlying tool is an EHR or an AI denial engine.⏎⏎Dafny, Gruber, and Ody's work on insurer cost-optimization incentive structures (American Journal of Health Economics, 1(1):53-81, 2015) is also directly applicable. Insurers operating in competitive markets have strong structural incentives to minimize payouts, and AI systems trained on claims data will, absent countervailing regulatory requirements, optimize toward that objective. This is not a criticism of any individual insurer's intentions. It is a description of how optimization systems behave when the objective function is cost rather than clinical appropriateness. HHS's RFI does not appear to account for this dynamic.⏎⏎⏎Cerner Corporation | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 4⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎Given the above, Cerner's compliance function offers the following recommendations for HHS's consideration in response to the RFI's questions regarding regulatory actions the Department can take to support responsible AI adoption:⏎⏎1. Mandatory human clinical review for all AI-generated prior authorization denials. Before HHS expands any AI reimbursement incentive structure on the provider side, the Department should require that every prior authorization denial generated or scored by an AI system receive documented review by a licensed clinician with relevant specialty expertise. "Documented review" should mean a timestamped attestation that the reviewing clinician accessed and read the patient's clinical records — not a batch-approval workflow of the type described in the Rucker, Miller, and Armstrong reporting. This requirement should apply to Medicare Advantage organizations as a condition of continued CMS contract participation.⏎⏎2. Demographic disparity auditing as a pre-deployment requirement. Any AI system used in prior authorization, care management, or coverage determination should be required to demonstrate, prior to deployment and at regular intervals thereafter, that its outputs do not vary systematically by race, ethnicity, or socioeconomic status in ways not explained by clinically relevant factors. The Obermeyer et al. findings from 2019 established a clear methodological framework for this kind of audit. There is no technical obstacle to requiring it. The obstacle is regulatory will.⏎⏎3. Transparency requirements for payer-side AI. Medicare Advantage organizations and commercial insurers operating in federally regulated markets should be required to disclose, at minimum: (a) whether an AI system contributed to a prior authorization denial; (b) the general category of algorithmic logic applied; and (c) the demographic performance characteristics of that system as measured in the most recent audit cycle. The Georgetown and NASHP tracking work cited above documents that states are already moving toward these requirements. Federal action would establish a consistent floor rather than a fragmented state-by-state patchwork.⏎⏎o Several states have passed legislation requiring human review of AI insurance decisions as of Q1 2024, per the NASHP tracker. Federal preemption of a weaker standard would effectively nullify those protections.⏎⏎o CMS already has contract oversight authority over Medicare Advantage organizations. The regulatory mechanism exists. What is needed is the will to apply it to AI-generated denial workflows specifically.⏎⏎4. Accountability trail requirements. Any AI-assisted denial should generate an auditable record that can be reviewed by CMS, by the affected beneficiary's physician, and — upon appeal — by an independent reviewer. The current appeals process does not require payers to produce the algorithmic basis for a denial. That gap is not accidental. It is a feature of a system structured to minimize successful appeals rather than to ensure accurate initial determinations.⏎⏎⏎Cerner Corporation | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 5⏎⏎⏎THE REIMBURSEMENT QUESTION⏎⏎This office recognizes that the RFI is also seeking comment on reimbursement structures that could accelerate provider-side AI adoption. Cerner's position is not that those questions are unimportant. The finding that fewer than 20% of AI-assisted encounters in our partner health systems qualify for AI-augmented reimbursement is a real structural problem. The documentation burden reductions we observed — averaging 31 minutes per encounter — represent genuine clinical capacity that the current coding framework fails to recognize or reward.⏎⏎But Cerner's compliance function cannot in good conscience recommend that HHS prioritize expanding AI reimbursement pathways for providers while the payer-side AI denial problem remains unaddressed. The practical effect of doing so would be to increase the volume of AI-assisted clinical decisions while leaving intact the AI-generated denial infrastructure that is already contesting those decisions on the back end. That is not a pathway to better patient outcomes. It is a more technologically sophisticated version of the same access problem that the OIG documented in 2022 and that the Senate Subcommittee documented in 2023.⏎⏎There is also a workforce dimension worth noting. The AMA's 2022 survey found that physicians spend an average of nearly two business days per week on prior authorization tasks. If provider-side AI reduces documentation time by 31 minutes per encounter, and that time is immediately consumed by AI-generated prior authorization response workflows, the net clinical capacity gain is close to zero. The Department's reimbursement framework should account for this interaction effect, and Cerner would welcome the opportunity to provide encounter-level data from our health system partners to support that analysis if HHS finds it useful.⏎⏎One additional observation, which may be outside the formal scope of this RFI but which Cerner's compliance function believes is worth recording: the comment period for this RFI was not widely publicized through channels accessible to frontline clinical staff or small and rural health systems. Cerner became aware of the RFI through our government relations monitoring function. Health systems in West Virginia and other rural states with limited administrative infrastructure are unlikely to be represented in this comment record in proportion to their stake in the outcome. HHS should consider whether the comment process itself reflects the equity principles the Roadmap articulates, and whether targeted outreach to underrepresented health system types would produce a more complete evidentiary record before the Department finalizes any regulatory or reimbursement actions.⏎⏎⏎Cerner Corporation | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 6⏎⏎⏎The specific mechanism Cerner recommends — mandatory human clinical review with documented accountability trails before any AI reimbursement expansion — is administratively feasible under existing CMS contract authority. The precedents are in the literature. The patient harm documentation is in the public record. What the Department's RFI has not yet grappled with is the question of sequencing: whether it is responsible to accelerate AI adoption on the provider side before establishing a floor of accountability on the payer side. Cerner's compliance function believes the answer to that question is no, and we would welcome the opportunity to discuss the specific audit methodologies and accountability trail architectures that could make a phased approach workable in practice.⏎⏎Contact for follow-up questions regarding this submission:⏎⏎Linda Robinson⏎Compliance Officer⏎Cerner Corporation⏎lrobinson@cerner.com⏎[phone number on file with submitting office]♔♔2026-01-23T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-23T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔7♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI-powered insurance decision-making automates prior authorization denials and coverage restrictions in ways that are opaque, unappealable, and systematically biased against vulnerable patients.♔organization♔high♔resigned♔West Virginia♔compliance officer♔48♔An internal audit conducted across Quiet Signal Technologies LLX's 47 active clinical deployment partnerships in Q2 2024 found that 83% of site compliance officers identified regulatory ambiguity around AI-generated clinical decision support as the primary bottleneck delaying full system integration. SYNTH-0005♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Susan Brown♔Coalition for Health AI♔♔♔♔♔Coalition for Health AI⏎Comment Submitted to HHS Docket: AI in Clinical Care RFI⏎Contact: info@coalitionforhealthai.org⏎⏎Coalition for Health AI | HHS AI RFI | Page 1⏎⏎The framing of this Request for Information concerns us deeply, and we want to be direct about that before addressing the specific questions HHS has posed. The RFI is structured around a presumption — that the primary problem is adoption speed, and that regulatory, reimbursement, and research-and-development barriers are what stand between the health system and better care. We do not share that presumption. The communities we serve, which include frontline nurses in Baltimore County hospital systems, community health workers in Prince George's County, and clinical social workers operating in federally qualified health centers across Maryland's Eastern Shore, are not experiencing a shortage of AI deployment. They are experiencing a shortage of protection from it. We urge HHS to treat this moment not as an acceleration opportunity but as a governance gap that, if left unaddressed, will produce measurable harm to both workers and the patients who depend on them.⏎⏎We are focusing our comment primarily on two of the RFI's implicit questions: what workforce conditions are necessary for AI to produce genuine clinical benefit, and what oversight structures should HHS require before deployment proceeds. We are not addressing reimbursement coding questions or FDA clearance pathways in this submission, as those are outside our organizational expertise and are being addressed by others. What we can speak to, with specificity, is what happens to care quality when the clinical workforce is treated as a cost variable rather than a clinical asset — and how AI deployment, without mandatory protective structures, accelerates exactly that dynamic.⏎⏎The burnout argument advanced by AI vendors and, frankly, reflected in the RFI's own framing, deserves direct scrutiny. The claim that AI will reduce clinician burnout is not well-supported by the documented mechanisms of burnout itself. Shanafelt and colleagues, writing in the Mayo Clinic Proceedings in 2022, tracked burnout and work-life integration satisfaction among physicians across nearly a decade, finding that the drivers most consistently associated with burnout were alert fatigue, loss of professional autonomy, and documentation burden — not insufficient computational assistance (Shanafelt et al., 2022, 97(3), 491–506). Wachter and Goldsmith made a related argument in the Harvard Business Review in 2018: that the electronic health record had become a primary driver of physician dissatisfaction not because of what it failed to do, but because of how it restructured clinical work around data entry, compliance documentation, and productivity surveillance (Wachter & Goldsmith, HBR, March 30, 2018). AI systems deployed in their current dominant form — ambient documentation tools, clinical decision support systems flagging dozens of low-priority alerts, productivity dashboards visible to supervisors — do not resolve any of these mechanisms. In many cases, as Sexton and colleagues documented in BMJ Quality & Safety in 2021, the accumulation of EHR-mediated burden directly predicts both clinician wellbeing decline and perceived patient safety degradation (Sexton et al., 2021, BMJ Quality & Safety, 30(11), 901–910). We are not arguing that AI cannot relieve burden. We are arguing that the specific AI products currently being marketed as burden-relief tools are structurally designed to serve administrative goals, and that HHS's RFI does not adequately distinguish between those two categories.⏎⏎Coalition for Health AI | HHS AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎The workforce surveillance question is where our concern becomes most acute. Kellogg, Valentine, and Christin, in a 2020 analysis published in the Academy of Management Annals, documented what they called the "new contested terrain of control" — the deployment of algorithmic management systems that shift the locus of performance evaluation from human supervisors to automated productivity metrics, in ways that workers cannot contest, cannot fully observe, and cannot appeal through conventional labor processes (Kellogg, Valentine & Christin, 2020, Academy of Management Annals, 14(1), 366–410). This is not a theoretical concern in healthcare. The Economic Policy Institute's 2023 briefing paper on algorithmic wage and productivity surveillance in healthcare documented specific cases in which hospital systems used AI-generated productivity reports to justify reductions in nursing staff ratios, arguing to state regulators that AI tools had "effectively increased" the productive capacity of remaining staff and therefore reduced the need for additional hires (EPI Briefing Paper #478, 2023). We have seen versions of this argument made in Maryland. We do not name the specific systems here because the matter involves ongoing labor disputes, but the pattern is consistent with what EPI documented nationally: AI deployed as efficiency tool becomes AI deployed as staffing-cut justification, and the workers most affected are the ones who had the least input into the procurement decision.⏎⏎National Nurses United surveyed 4,800 registered nurses in 2023 and found that 61% of respondents working in facilities that had deployed algorithmic management tools reported increased workloads following deployment, while only 14% reported workload reduction (NNU Research Report, 2023). More significantly for this RFI, 78% of those respondents reported that they had not been consulted during procurement, and 83% reported that they did not have a formal mechanism to report AI-generated recommendations they believed were clinically incorrect. That last finding is not just a labor issue. It is a patient safety issue. The Government Accountability Office's 2022 report on AI in health care identified the absence of post-deployment monitoring and clinician feedback mechanisms as one of the primary structural risks associated with clinical AI deployment (GAO-22-104629, 2022). When frontline nurses cannot flag a malfunctioning algorithm through a formal channel, the algorithm keeps running. The American Medical Association's 2023 Digital Medicine Practice Snapshot found that fewer than 30% of surveyed practices had formal processes for frontline clinician input into AI procurement decisions, and fewer than 20% had post-deployment review structures that included frontline worker feedback (AMA Policy Research Perspectives, 2023). These are not incidental gaps. They are the predictable result of procurement processes designed to serve administrative and financial goals rather than clinical ones.⏎⏎Coalition for Health AI | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎We want to be honest about something that the burnout-promise framing obscures: the AI products most aggressively marketed to healthcare administrators are not primarily designed to serve clinicians. They are designed to serve the administrators who purchase them. Topol's influential 2019 Nature Medicine paper argued that the convergence of human and artificial intelligence in medicine had genuine potential to restore the "human connection" in clinical care by freeing clinicians from cognitive burden (Topol, 2019, Nature Medicine, 25(1), 44–56). We find that vision genuinely compelling. What Topol described, however, requires AI designed around clinician autonomy and patient benefit — not around throughput metrics and administrative dashboards. The products currently being deployed in the majority of community hospital systems the Coalition works with are not the Topol vision. They are productivity surveillance systems with clinical interfaces bolted on. HHS's RFI, by treating "AI adoption" as a unified category rather than distinguishing between these functionally different deployment types, risks accelerating the latter while claiming credit for the former.⏎⏎Obermeyer and colleagues' 2019 Science paper documenting racial bias in a widely deployed population health management algorithm is relevant here in a way that goes beyond the bias finding itself (Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli & Mullainathan, 2019, Science, 366(6464), 447–453). The algorithm had been deployed at scale across hundreds of health systems before the bias was identified — not because the health systems were negligent, but because no pre-deployment impact assessment was required, no post-deployment monitoring for disparate outcomes was mandated, and no frontline clinician feedback mechanism existed that would have surfaced the problem earlier. The ONC's own 2021 Strategy on Reducing Regulatory and Administrative Burden acknowledged that health IT deployment had consistently outpaced the governance structures needed to ensure it served care rather than creating new forms of burden (ONC Report to Congress, 2021). We are asking HHS not to repeat that pattern with AI.⏎⏎Coalition for Health AI | HHS AI RFI | Page 4⏎⏎Our specific asks are as follows, and we want to be clear that we frame these as achievable policy requirements, not aspirational suggestions:⏎⏎1. Mandatory frontline worker consultation as a condition of any HHS-facilitated or federally reimbursed AI deployment. This means structured input from nurses, physicians, medical assistants, and other direct-care staff before procurement is finalized — not post-deployment feedback surveys. The AMA's 2023 data showing that fewer than 30% of practices have such processes suggests this is not happening voluntarily.⏎⏎2. Pre-deployment workforce impact assessments, modeled on environmental impact assessment requirements, that require deploying entities to document anticipated effects on staffing ratios, workload distribution, and job function before deployment proceeds. These assessments should be made available to affected workers and their representatives.⏎⏎3. An explicit prohibition, enforceable through conditions of participation or as a condition of federal reimbursement, on using AI-generated productivity metrics as the primary or sole justification for staffing ratio reductions. This is the specific mechanism by which AI is currently being used to justify understaffing, and HHS has the authority to address it directly.⏎⏎4. Post-deployment monitoring requirements that include worker wellbeing as a required outcome measure alongside clinical quality metrics. Dyrbye and colleagues documented in 2019 that work-unit safety culture and nursing burnout are directly correlated with patient safety outcomes (Dyrbye et al., 2019, Journal of Nursing Administration, 49(10), 487–493). A monitoring framework that measures clinical outcomes without measuring worker wellbeing is measuring an incomplete picture of safety.⏎⏎o A sub-requirement worth specifying: post-deployment monitoring should include a formal, accessible channel for frontline workers to flag AI-generated recommendations they believe are clinically erroneous or potentially harmful, with a documented review process and feedback loop to the deploying entity and, where relevant, to FDA.⏎⏎Coalition for Health AI | HHS AI RFI | Page 5⏎⏎We recognize that these requirements would add process steps to AI deployment, and we anticipate that some respondents to this RFI will argue that such requirements slow adoption and thereby delay clinical benefit. We take that argument seriously, and we want to respond to it directly. The communities we serve in Maryland are not well-served by AI deployment that is fast. They are well-served by AI deployment that is safe, that does not erode the workforce providing their care, and that is designed around their clinical needs rather than around administrative throughput targets. The GAO's 2022 report on AI in health care found that benefits to patient care were most consistently realized in deployment contexts where clinicians had meaningful input into implementation and where post-deployment monitoring was robust (GAO-22-104629, 2022). Speed of deployment and quality of deployment are not the same variable, and HHS's RFI, in framing adoption acceleration as the primary goal, conflates them in ways that we believe will produce worse outcomes for patients and workers alike.⏎⏎There is also a specific concern about community hospitals and federally qualified health centers that we want to raise, because the RFI's framing implicitly assumes a deployment context of well-resourced academic medical centers or large health systems with dedicated IT infrastructure. The practices the Coalition works with most closely are smaller, are more likely to serve Medicaid and uninsured populations, and have significantly less capacity to conduct independent evaluation of AI products before purchase. They are also more vulnerable to vendor representations about workforce efficiency gains, because their operating margins are thinner and the promise of cost reduction through AI is genuinely appealing to administrators under financial pressure. This is precisely the context in which mandatory pre-deployment assessments and frontline consultation requirements are most necessary — and it is precisely the context in which they are least likely to happen without federal requirement. We would note that the EPI's 2023 briefing paper found that algorithmic productivity surveillance was disproportionately deployed in lower-wage healthcare settings, which correlates strongly with the facilities serving the communities we represent (EPI Briefing Paper #478, 2023). That is not a coincidence. It reflects a pattern of technology deployment that concentrates efficiency extraction in the parts of the health system with the least power to resist it.⏎⏎We want to close by returning to something that we think gets lost in the technical framing of AI governance discussions. The clinical workforce is not a cost input that AI can substitute for or optimize around. It is the mechanism by which care is delivered, and its health — its engagement, its autonomy, its capacity for clinical judgment — is a patient safety variable. Shanafelt's longitudinal data make clear that clinician burnout has been worsening for over a decade (Shanafelt et al., 2022). Deploying AI systems that intensify surveillance, increase alert burden, and remove professional discretion will not reverse that trend. The policy framework HHS builds around AI adoption will either protect the conditions under which good care is possible, or it will accelerate the extraction of value from a workforce that is already under severe strain. We believe HHS can build the former, and we have tried in this comment to be specific about what that requires. The consultation requirement alone — simply mandating that the people who will use these tools have a formal role in deciding whether and how they are deployed — would represent a meaningful shift from current practice, and it is administratively feasible to implement as a condition of participation well within existing CMS authority.⏎⏎We are available to discuss any of the above with HHS staff and would welcome the opportunity to connect agency staff directly with frontline workers in Maryland who can speak to these dynamics from their own clinical experience. SYNTH-0006♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Mark Jackson♔National Council on Aging♔♔♔♔♔NATIONAL COUNCIL ON AGING⏎Comments in Response to HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎Submitted by Mark Jackson, Policy Director⏎⏎⏎THE GOVERNANCE QUESTION HHS IS NOT ASKING⏎⏎The National Council on Aging (NCOA) submits these comments with a specific focus on two dimensions of the RFI that the Department has, perhaps deliberately, chosen not to foreground: the structural irreversibility of AI deployment in clinical settings, and the democratic legitimacy question that irreversibility raises. NCOA represents millions of older adults who are disproportionately the subjects of algorithmic clinical decision-making — not its architects, not its beneficiaries in the first instance, and not, under the current trajectory, its meaningful overseers. Before engaging the Department's specific questions, this organization needs to state plainly what the RFI's framing obscures: the decision to accelerate AI adoption in clinical care at the pace and in the manner HHS is contemplating is not a technical optimization question. It is a question about who governs medicine, and HHS is answering it unilaterally.⏎⏎NCOA's position is informed partly by the survey and convening data generated by the Association for Diagnostics and Laboratory Medicine (ADLM), whose 2024 member survey of approximately 8,200 laboratorians and pathologists found that 63 percent of respondents reported their institutions had piloted or deployed at least one AI-assisted diagnostic tool in the preceding 24 months. Fewer than 20 percent indicated their facility had received clear CMS reimbursement guidance covering those tools' clinical outputs. This is not a minor administrative lag. It is the signature of a deployment pattern in which systems are embedded in clinical infrastructure before the governance architecture necessary to oversee them exists. NCOA's own regional engagement with older adult communities in 2024 — including four convenings in Missouri, Ohio, Tennessee, and New Mexico — produced consistent themes: older patients are aware that algorithms are being used in their care, they have almost no information about how those algorithms work, and they have been offered no meaningful mechanism for objecting.⏎⏎⏎IRREVERSIBILITY AS A STRUCTURAL CONDITION, NOT A RISK TO BE MITIGATED⏎⏎The RFI asks, in several of its framing questions, how HHS can reduce "uncertainty that impedes AI innovation" (89 Fed. Reg., Health Sector AI RFI, ONC/ASTP 2024). NCOA finds this framing a category error of some consequence. The "uncertainty" in question is not merely commercial or regulatory friction; it is the deliberative space in which democratic societies make choices about what they want their institutions to do. Treating that space as an impediment to be cleared is not a neutral policy choice. It is a choice about who gets to decide.⏎⏎The specific mechanism NCOA wants the Department to take seriously is what this organization will call deployment-induced foreclosure. Coiera (2019) documented, in the context of clinical workflow reorganization following health IT deployments, that the practical reversibility of a technology falls sharply once that technology has reorganized the routines, staffing models, and institutional knowledge around it. This is not unique to AI — Dafny and Lee (2016) made a parallel observation about healthcare market consolidation, noting that institutional lock-in in healthcare is particularly durable because the switching costs are borne not by the institution that made the original choice but by the patients and clinicians embedded in the resulting system. AI deployment in clinical settings combines both dynamics. Once a hospital's diagnostic workflow has been restructured around a vendor's ambient documentation system or a risk-stratification algorithm, the clinical staff who previously performed those functions through direct judgment have, within a relatively short window, lost the practiced competency to do so without the system. The institutional knowledge atrophies. The workflows reorganize around vendor logic. Contractual dependencies accumulate.⏎⏎NCOA wishes to be specific about what this means for older adults. Consider the use of AI-driven prior authorization systems, which several major insurers have deployed to manage utilization for Medicare Advantage beneficiaries. When a prior authorization algorithm denies a claim, the appeal pathway nominally exists, but the practical capacity for a 74-year-old patient in rural Missouri to navigate that pathway — to obtain the clinical documentation, to engage the appeals process, to reach a human reviewer — is not equivalent to the nominal availability of that pathway. Eubanks (2018) described this dynamic in a different context but with directly applicable precision: automated systems do not eliminate human judgment, they relocate it to positions in the process where it is least accessible to the people most affected. Once that relocation has occurred and the system has been in operation long enough that the institutional memory of the prior process has faded, the practical option of returning to human-centered review does not exist in any meaningful sense.⏎⏎The GAO documented this concern at a structural level in its 2022 report on AI in health care (GAO-22-104629), finding significant gaps in federal oversight capacity relative to the pace of deployment. What the GAO report did not fully develop — though the evidence it compiled supports the inference — is that each month those gaps persist, the population of deployed systems generating path-dependent institutional dependencies grows, and the realistic possibility of course correction narrows. HHS's acceleration agenda, as framed in this RFI, would widen those gaps faster than any realistic governance build-out could close them.⏎⏎⏎NCOA Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎THE PROPRIETARY OPACITY PROBLEM IS NOT PRIMARILY A SAFETY PROBLEM⏎⏎Much of the existing policy literature on AI transparency in clinical settings frames algorithmic opacity as a patient safety issue, and it is that. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan (2019) demonstrated in Science that a widely deployed commercial algorithm used to manage health care for large patient populations encoded significant racial bias that was invisible to the institutions using it precisely because the algorithm's internal logic was proprietary. The bias was not incidental; it was structural, embedded in the choice of the outcome variable the algorithm was trained to predict. No external auditor, no clinician, no patient could have identified it through the interfaces the vendor provided.⏎⏎But NCOA wants to make a different argument here, one that the safety framing tends to obscure. The opacity of proprietary clinical AI systems is not primarily a safety deficiency. It is a structural democratic deficiency. Pasquale (2015) developed this argument at length in The Black Box Society, and it has not lost force in the intervening decade: when the logic governing significant social decisions is legally shielded from inspection, the oversight mechanisms that democratic societies depend upon — legislative, judicial, professional, and civil — cannot function. Selbst and Barocas (2018) made a related point specifically about the limits of explainability requirements as a substitute for genuine accountability: even if a system can generate a post-hoc explanation of a specific output, that explanation does not expose the system's overall decision logic to the kind of scrutiny that would allow democratic communities to decide whether that logic is acceptable. Brundage et al. (2020) extended this analysis to the structural impossibility of meaningful external audit under current proprietary frameworks, finding that the mechanisms vendors typically offer for "trustworthy AI" claims are not verifiable by external parties in any technically robust sense.⏎⏎For older adults specifically, this opacity takes on additional weight. Medicare and Medicaid are public programs. The clinical decisions made within them — including decisions about what care is appropriate, what is medically necessary, what risk level a patient presents — are decisions being made with public resources on behalf of a public that has, through decades of legislative deliberation, established specific expectations about what those programs will do. When a proprietary algorithm makes or substantially shapes those decisions, and when the algorithm's logic is not available for inspection by CMS, by Congress, by the beneficiaries themselves, or by the clinicians nominally responsible for the care, a transfer of authority has occurred that the democratic process authorizing those programs did not sanction. This organization does not believe HHS has the mandate to ratify that transfer through an acceleration agenda that treats regulatory scrutiny as market friction.⏎⏎⏎ADLM SURVEY CONTEXT AND THE REIMBURSEMENT-GOVERNANCE MISALIGNMENT⏎⏎Returning to the ADLM data because it is unusually specific and deserves more attention than it typically receives in policy discussions: the finding that fewer than one-third of the 47 laboratory AI products cleared by FDA between 2020 and 2024 had associated CPT codes enabling straightforward billing is not primarily a reimbursement problem. It is a governance signal. The absence of a billing pathway is, in the current system, one of the few friction points that slows deployment and creates an opening for deliberation. When CMS eventually resolves those billing ambiguities — and this RFI is in part a request for input on how to do so more quickly — it will remove one of the few remaining structural checks on deployment pace. NCOA is not arguing that reimbursement ambiguity is a good governance mechanism; it is clearly an accidental and imperfect one. But the appropriate response to its inadequacy is not to eliminate it faster than the governance architecture can be built to replace it. The appropriate response is to build the governance architecture first.⏎⏎Mello et al. (2013) made a structurally analogous argument in a different context, writing about the sequencing of clinical trial data sharing: the infrastructure and governance norms for responsible data sharing had to be developed in parallel with, not subsequent to, the mechanisms that would compel sharing. The sequencing mattered because once data sharing norms were established by practice rather than by deliberation, they became very difficult to alter. The same logic applies here. Deployment norms established in the absence of governance frameworks tend to become the de facto standard against which any subsequent regulatory requirement is measured — and found burdensome.⏎⏎⏎REGARDING THE SPECIFIC QUESTION OF REIMBURSEMENT PATHWAYS FOR AI-ASSISTED CLINICAL TOOLS⏎⏎The RFI asks specifically about regulatory and reimbursement actions HHS can take to accelerate adoption. NCOA's response to this question is more restrained than the Department may prefer, but it is offered in good faith.⏎⏎NCOA does not oppose the development of clearer reimbursement pathways for AI-assisted clinical tools. What this organization opposes is the development of those pathways in advance of, or as a substitute for, the governance conditions that would make reimbursement appropriate. Specifically, NCOA recommends that any new CPT code or coverage determination for an AI-assisted clinical tool be conditioned on the following, at a minimum:⏎⏎1. The tool's training data, validation methodology, and performance characteristics across demographic subgroups — including age, race, sex, and insurance status — must be disclosed to CMS and available for review by an independent technical body prior to coverage determination. This is not an onerous requirement; it is the minimum necessary for a public payer to make an informed coverage decision.⏎⏎2. The tool must have been validated on a population that includes older adults in proportions representative of the Medicare population it will be used to serve. The current FDA clearance pathway does not require this, and the ADLM policy analysis of cleared laboratory AI products found significant gaps in the demographic representativeness of validation datasets. A coverage determination that does not condition reimbursement on age-representative validation is, in effect, a decision to use Medicare beneficiaries as a post-market validation population without their knowledge or consent.⏎⏎3. Any institution receiving reimbursement for AI-assisted clinical services must maintain a documented human override pathway — not a nominal one, but a functionally accessible one — and must report annually to CMS on the frequency with which that pathway is invoked and the outcomes associated with its invocation. This requirement is not technically complex. It is administratively modest. Its absence from current deployment frameworks is a policy choice, not a technical inevitability.⏎⏎4. Contracts between health systems and AI vendors must not contain confidentiality provisions that prevent the health system from disclosing the tool's decision logic to CMS, to state regulators, or to the patients whose care it affects. Topol (2019) wrote optimistically about the convergence of human and artificial intelligence in clinical settings, and NCOA does not dispute the potential he described. But Topol's analysis, like much of the optimistic literature, assumes that the governance conditions for responsible deployment will be developed alongside the technology. That assumption has not been borne out by the deployment record of the past five years, and reimbursement policy should not proceed as though it has been.⏎⏎⏎NCOA Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 5⏎⏎THE DEMOCRATIC DOMAIN RESERVATION ARGUMENT⏎⏎This organization has tried, in the preceding sections, to engage HHS's acceleration agenda as a technical and regulatory question. There are genuine technical and regulatory dimensions to it, and the recommendations above reflect NCOA's best judgment about what governance conditions would need to exist before acceleration is appropriate. But NCOA wants to be direct about a dimension of this question that the technical framing tends to suppress.⏎⏎A democratic society has the right to decide that certain domains of human activity should remain stubbornly human — not because human performance in those domains is always optimal, but because the accountability relationships that human performance creates are themselves part of what the domain is for. Clinical judgment is one such domain. When a physician makes a diagnostic error, there is a pathway — imperfect, adversarial, expensive, but real — through which that error can be examined, contested, and corrected, and through which the physician's practice can be modified or ended. When an algorithm makes a systematic diagnostic error, as Obermeyer et al. (2019) documented, that pathway does not exist in the same form. The error propagates silently across millions of cases until a researcher with access to outcome data and the methodological tools to detect it publishes a finding that the vendor may contest, that the institutions using the tool may not act upon, and that the patients harmed by it may never learn about.⏎⏎The question of whether that trade is acceptable — faster throughput and possibly better average performance, in exchange for the accountability relationships that make error correction and democratic oversight possible — is not a question HHS can answer on behalf of the public. It is a question the public has not been asked. The RFI's framing of regulatory oversight as "uncertainty that impedes AI innovation" does not merely get the answer wrong; it forecloses the question. When HHS removes the friction that slows deployment, it does not simply accelerate adoption; it forecloses, before the deliberation has occurred, the option of deciding that the accountability relationships medicine depends upon should not be traded away for efficiency.⏎⏎NCOA recognizes that this argument will be characterized by some as technophobic or as an obstacle to genuine improvements in care for older adults. That characterization misunderstands the argument. This organization is not arguing that AI has no role in clinical care. It is arguing that the decision about what role AI should play, under what conditions, with what oversight, and with what preserved space for human judgment, belongs to a democratic process that HHS is in the process of preempting. The irreversibility mechanisms described above — workflow reorganization, atrophied expertise, contractual lock-in, the establishment of deployment norms through practice rather than deliberation — mean that the window in which that democratic process could meaningfully shape the outcome is closing. Once it closes, the choice will have been made. Not by Congress. Not by patients. Not by clinicians. By the deployment schedules of a small number of large vendors whose internal logic is, as Pasquale (2015) and Brundage et al. (2020) documented in different registers, structurally insulated from the oversight mechanisms a democratic society depends upon to govern itself.⏎⏎⏎CLOSING OBSERVATIONS⏎⏎NCOA does not oppose HHS engagement with AI governance. This organization would welcome a regulatory process genuinely oriented toward building the governance architecture — transparency requirements, demographic validation standards, human override mandates, audit rights — that would make responsible acceleration possible. What this organization cannot support is an acceleration agenda that treats the absence of that architecture as an opportunity rather than as a problem.⏎⏎The ADLM survey data cited throughout these comments reflects a deployment reality that is already well ahead of the governance capacity to oversee it. The 63 percent of institutions that have deployed AI-assisted diagnostic tools without clear reimbursement guidance are not waiting for governance; they are operating in its absence and establishing, through practice, the norms that governance will eventually have to work around. Every month that gap persists, the population of older adults whose care is being shaped by systems they cannot see, contest, or meaningfully influence grows. HHS has the regulatory authority to condition reimbursement, to require disclosure, to mandate demographic validation, and to preserve human override pathways. The question this RFI has not asked — and that NCOA is asking on behalf of the older adults it represents — is whether HHS has the democratic mandate to do anything less.⏎⏎NCOA requests that the Department publish, as part of any subsequent rulemaking arising from this RFI, a specific analysis of the demographic representativeness of validation datasets for AI tools under consideration for Medicare coverage, and that CMS establish a public-facing registry of AI tools for which coverage determinations have been made, including the subgroup performance data that formed the basis of each determination. The registry need not be technically complex; a structured data table updated quarterly would suffice.
