SYNTH-0008♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔James Clark♔Georgetown University Medical Center♔♔♔♔♔Georgetown University Medical Center — Postdoctoral Research Program⏎Comments Submitted to HHS Docket: AI in Clinical Care RFI⏎Submitted by: James Clark, Postdoctoral Fellow, Department of Cardiovascular Research⏎Georgetown University Medical Center, Washington, DC / Boise, Idaho (primary research site)⏎⏎Georgetown University Medical Center | HHS AI in Clinical Care RFI | Page 1⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE DEPLOYMENT-GOVERNANCE GAP AS STRUCTURAL PRECONDITION FOR HARM⏎⏎The American College of Cardiology's 2024 Survey of Cardiology Fellows and Early-Career Cardiologists on AI Literacy and Institutional Deployment found that 67% of the 2,800 respondents reported working in institutions that had deployed at least one AI-assisted diagnostic or risk-stratification tool, yet 58% of that group indicated they had received no formal training on interpreting AI-generated outputs or understanding model limitations (ACC, 2024). That finding is not a workforce development problem. It is a structural description of the conditions under which AI tools are currently being used on patients, and it is the appropriate starting point for evaluating what HHS is proposing here. The Department's RFI frames acceleration as the primary policy objective, asking how regulatory, reimbursement, and research-and-development actions can be arranged to speed adoption. The framing is not wrong to care about adoption barriers, but it proceeds from an assumption — that the primary problem is insufficient deployment — that the empirical record does not support. The documented problem, at this moment, is deployment that has substantially outpaced the governance infrastructure required to detect when those tools are failing specific patient populations. Acceleration in that context is not a neutral policy choice.⏎⏎Georgetown University Medical Center | HHS AI in Clinical Care RFI | Page 2⏎⏎---⏎⏎ALGORITHMIC BIAS AS AN OBSERVED PATTERN, NOT A SPECULATIVE CONCERN⏎⏎The literature on algorithmic bias in clinical AI is not a set of theoretical warnings. It is a record of documented failures, and the failures share a common structure that makes them relevant to any accelerationist policy posture. Sjoding et al. published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 a finding that pulse oximeters — devices so routine that clinicians rarely think of them as algorithmic — produced occult hypoxemia in Black patients at a rate nearly three times higher than in white patients, a disparity that went undetected in clinical practice for years precisely because the device's authoritative numeric output suppressed scrutiny (Sjoding MW, Dickson RP, Iwashyna TJ, Gay SE, Valley TS. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(25):2477-2478). Obermeyer and colleagues published in Science in 2019 an analysis of a widely deployed commercial algorithm used to identify patients for high-risk care management programs, finding that the algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients by using healthcare cost as a proxy for health status — a proxy that encoded decades of differential access to care and produced a model that, at equivalent risk scores, assigned Black patients significantly lower priority for intervention (Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S. Science. 2019;366(6464):447-453). Wong et al. published in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2021 an external validation of the Epic Sepsis Model, a proprietary tool deployed across hundreds of hospital systems, and found that the model's performance in their institution — a non-developer, real-world setting — was substantially worse than reported in the original validation literature, with an AUROC of 0.63 compared to the developer's reported figures, and with documented inequities in alert distribution across patient subgroups (Wong A, Otles E, Donnelly JP, et al. JAMA Intern Med. 2021;181(8):1065-1070). Adamson and Smith, writing in JAMA Dermatology in 2018, documented that dermatology AI systems trained predominantly on images of lighter-skinned patients showed degraded diagnostic accuracy for conditions presenting differently on darker skin, a limitation that was not surfaced in initial performance reporting because benchmark datasets did not reflect the demographic composition of patients most likely to receive care in under-resourced settings (Adamson AS, Smith A. JAMA Dermatol. 2018;154(11):1247-1248).⏎⏎Georgetown University Medical Center | HHS AI in Clinical Care RFI | Page 3⏎⏎These are not isolated anomalies. Each represents a node in a reproducible failure mode: a model trained on data that reflects historical patterns of differential access, utilization, and documentation; a validation process conducted in settings that do not represent the full distribution of deployment environments; a performance metric that aggregates across subgroups in a way that obscures differential harm; and a deployment environment in which the tool's outputs carry sufficient authority to suppress the clinical scrutiny that would otherwise catch errors. Char, Shah, and Magnus identified this structural pattern in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2018, arguing that machine learning tools trained on EHR data inherit the biases embedded in clinical documentation, ordering patterns, and institutional practices, and that these biases are compounded rather than corrected by the feedback loops that occur when AI outputs influence subsequent clinical behavior and documentation (Char DS, Shah NH, Magnus D. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(11):981-983). Gianfrancesco and colleagues elaborated the specific mechanisms by which EHR data produces biased training sets, noting that missingness patterns, differential coding practices, and socioeconomic proxies embedded in structured data fields systematically distort model outputs in ways that are not visible from aggregate performance statistics (Gianfrancesco MA, Tamang S, Tamang S, Yazdany J, Schmajuk G. JAMA Intern Med. 2018;178(11):1544-1547). Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones, also in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020, extended this analysis to race correction in clinical algorithms more broadly, documenting how the use of race as a biological variable in algorithms for kidney function, lung function, and obstetric risk estimation encodes social constructs as biological facts and produces systematic disadvantage for patients of color (Vyas DA, Eisenstein LG, Jones DS. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(9):874-882).⏎⏎Georgetown University Medical Center | HHS AI in Clinical Care RFI | Page 4⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE PERFORMANCE-DEGRADATION PROBLEM IN NON-ACADEMIC SETTINGS IS AN EQUITY ISSUE⏎⏎HHS's RFI does not adequately address what Finlayson and colleagues called "dataset shift" — the phenomenon by which a model trained in one clinical environment degrades in performance when deployed in a different environment whose patient population, documentation practices, and workflow characteristics differ from the training context (Finlayson SG, Subbaswamy A, Singh K, et al. N Engl J Med. 2021;385(3):283-286). This is not a narrow technical problem. It is an equity problem with a predictable directional bias. AI tools in clinical care are predominantly developed and initially validated at large academic medical centers with well-resourced informatics infrastructure, high coding specificity, and patient populations that over-represent insured, English-speaking patients with regular primary care contact. The facilities where performance degradation is most likely to occur — community hospitals, rural critical access facilities, federally qualified health centers, safety-net institutions — are disproportionately the facilities where marginalized patients, patients of color, patients with limited English proficiency, and patients with Medicaid or no insurance receive care. When a model trained at an academic center is deployed at a rural Idaho critical access hospital, the performance gap is not random noise. It is a systematic transfer of risk onto the patients who were already least well served by the training data.⏎⏎Georgetown University Medical Center | HHS AI in Clinical Care RFI | Page 5⏎⏎Seyyed-Kalantari and colleagues documented this mechanism directly in the context of chest radiograph AI, finding in a study published in Nature Medicine in 2021 that AI algorithms applied to chest radiographs in under-served patient populations produced higher rates of underdiagnosis for those populations, and that the performance gap was largest for patients who were uninsured, patients with limited education, and patients from racial and ethnic minority groups — precisely the populations whose clinical data was most underrepresented in training sets (Seyyed-Kalantari L, Zhang H, McDermott MBA, Chen IY, Ghassemi M. Nat Med. 2021;27(12):2176-2182). The ACC's Quality Improvement for Institutions Program, which spans more than 2,200 cardiovascular care sites, documented in its 2023 annual review that fewer than 30% of participating sites reported having a defined clinical oversight protocol for AI-driven decision support (ACC. Quality Improvement for Institutions Program: 2023 Annual Review. Washington, DC: ACC; 2023). That means that at more than 70% of cardiovascular care sites in a program explicitly designed to support quality infrastructure, there is no defined process for monitoring whether AI tools are performing as expected, for whom, and under what conditions. The absence of governance infrastructure is not distributed randomly across the healthcare system. It is concentrated in precisely the settings where performance degradation is most likely and most consequential.⏎⏎Georgetown University Medical Center | HHS AI in Clinical Care RFI | Page 6⏎⏎---⏎⏎AUTOMATION BIAS AS A HARM-AMPLIFICATION MECHANISM⏎⏎There is a specific reason why AI errors are more dangerous than equivalent human errors in clinical settings, and HHS's RFI does not engage with it. Cabitza, Rasoini, and Gensini described the mechanism in JAMA in 2017: the presentation of a recommendation in algorithmic form — with a numeric confidence score, a clean interface, and the implicit authority of institutional deployment — induces automation bias in clinicians, meaning a tendency to accept the output without applying the same critical scrutiny that would be applied to a colleague's verbal recommendation or a paper-based decision support tool (Cabitza F, Rasoini R, Gensini GF. JAMA. 2017;318(6):517-518). This is not a failure of individual clinicians. It is a predictable cognitive response to the design and authority of AI systems, and it is compounded by the workflow conditions under which clinical AI is typically used: high patient volume, time pressure, cognitive load, and an institutional environment in which the tool has been deployed with implicit endorsement from hospital administration. When a clinician overrides a human colleague's recommendation, that decision is visible, documentable, and subject to social accountability. When a clinician accepts an AI output without scrutiny, the process is largely invisible. The ACC's 2024 survey finding that 58% of clinicians working with deployed AI tools had received no formal training on interpreting outputs or understanding model limitations is a direct description of a workforce operating without the conceptual tools necessary to recognize when automation bias is occurring.⏎⏎Georgetown University Medical Center | HHS AI in Clinical Care RFI | Page 7⏎⏎The implications for equity are direct. If automation bias suppresses the critical scrutiny that would otherwise catch errors, and if the errors that AI systems produce are systematically more likely to affect specific patient subgroups — as the literature reviewed above consistently demonstrates — then automation bias is not merely a patient safety problem in the aggregate. It is a mechanism by which the disparate errors embedded in AI systems are more likely to reach patients as consequential clinical decisions. A clinician who might otherwise notice that a risk-stratification score seems inconsistent with a patient's presentation, and who would investigate further, is less likely to do so when the score is presented as an authoritative algorithmic output. The patients most likely to have their risk systematically underestimated by algorithms trained on biased data are the patients for whom that clinician's critical scrutiny was most needed.⏎⏎Georgetown University Medical Center | HHS AI in Clinical Care RFI | Page 8⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE SPECIFIC REGULATORY GAP: NO MANDATORY PRE-DEPLOYMENT EQUITY AUDITING, NO POST-DEPLOYMENT BIAS SURVEILLANCE⏎⏎Regarding the RFI's questions about regulatory actions HHS can take to support responsible AI adoption — this is the question the following comments address directly, because it is the question where the gap between what HHS has proposed and what the literature demands is most apparent.⏎⏎HHS's RFI identifies a range of potential regulatory actions: updating FDA frameworks for AI/ML-based software as a medical device, developing interoperability standards, clarifying liability frameworks, and creating reimbursement pathways. None of the proposed regulatory actions includes a mandatory requirement for pre-deployment equity auditing — a structured assessment, conducted before a tool enters clinical use, of the tool's performance across relevant demographic subgroups in deployment-representative populations. None of the proposed actions includes a mandatory post-deployment bias surveillance framework — a systematic process for monitoring, after a tool is in use, whether its outputs are producing differential outcomes across patient subgroups, and for triggering investigation and remediation when disparities are detected.⏎⏎The absence of these two requirements is not a minor gap. It means that under the policy framework HHS is developing, algorithmic disparities of the type documented by Sjoding, Obermeyer, Wong, Adamson, Seyyed-Kalantari, and others will only be detected after they have been harming patients at scale, if they are detected at all. The Obermeyer et al. algorithm was deployed across a health system serving millions of patients before the bias was identified through a research investigation that was not required by any regulatory framework. The Epic Sepsis Model was deployed across hundreds of hospital systems before Wong et al. conducted the external validation that surfaced its performance limitations. Pulse oximetry bias went clinically undetected for decades. The pattern is consistent: tools enter clinical use, achieve wide deployment, and their disparate impacts are identified through research investigations that occur years later, if at all.⏎⏎Georgetown University Medical Center | HHS AI in Clinical Care RFI | Page 9⏎⏎The specific regulatory requirements that the literature supports, and that HHS should incorporate into any final policy framework, are the following:⏎⏎1.    Mandatory pre-deployment subgroup performance reporting. Any AI tool seeking regulatory clearance or reimbursement eligibility under an HHS framework should be required to report disaggregated performance statistics — sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value at minimum — stratified by race, ethnicity, sex, insurance status, and primary language, computed on a validation dataset that is representative of the intended deployment population rather than the development institution's patient panel.⏎⏎2.    Mandatory deployment-environment validation for high-risk clinical AI. Tools intended for deployment in community hospitals, rural facilities, or safety-net institutions should be required to undergo prospective validation in at least one such setting before receiving reimbursement or regulatory endorsement, rather than relying exclusively on academic center validation studies.⏎⏎3.    Mandatory post-deployment bias surveillance as a condition of continued reimbursement eligibility. Institutions deploying AI tools under any HHS reimbursement framework should be required to maintain and report, at defined intervals, outcome data stratified by the demographic variables listed above, with a defined threshold for triggering mandatory review of the tool's continued deployment.⏎⏎4.    Minimum AI literacy standards as a condition of institutional deployment. The ACC's 2024 survey finding that 58% of clinicians using deployed AI tools had received no training on output interpretation or model limitations should be treated as a patient safety problem requiring regulatory response. HHS should condition any reimbursement or regulatory endorsement of AI tools on institutional attestation that clinicians using those tools have received structured training on automation bias, model limitations, and the demographic conditions under which the tool was validated.⏎⏎These are not novel regulatory concepts. They are extensions of existing frameworks for device validation, quality reporting, and conditions of participation that HHS already administers. The argument that they would slow adoption is an argument that adoption should proceed before the tools are validated for the populations on whom they will be used.⏎⏎Georgetown University Medical Center | HHS AI in Clinical Care RFI | Page 10⏎⏎---⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE FRAMING OF THIS RFI⏎⏎The RFI's accelerationist framing warrants direct comment, because it reflects a policy posture that the empirical record does not support. The Department is asking how to remove barriers to adoption, how to create reimbursement pathways, how to streamline regulatory review. These are legitimate questions about a technology with genuine clinical potential. But the framing assumes that the primary problem is insufficient deployment, when the documented problem — at more than 2,200 cardiovascular care sites, across a literature spanning pulse oximetry to insurance algorithms to chest radiograph AI — is deployment that has substantially outpaced the governance infrastructure required to detect harm. The ACC survey finding is not an argument against AI in clinical care. It is an argument that the current rate of deployment, in the absence of the governance frameworks described above, is already creating the conditions for harm at scale, and that HHS is proposing to accelerate that process without first addressing the structural gap.⏎⏎There is also a question about what "acceleration" means in practice for rural Idaho, which is the research context most directly relevant to this submission. The cardiovascular care infrastructure in rural Idaho is not comparable to what exists at a large academic medical center in a major metropolitan area. The informatics infrastructure is different, the patient population is different, the workflow conditions are different, and the capacity for post-deployment monitoring is substantially more limited. A policy framework designed to accelerate AI adoption that does not account for those differences will produce tools validated elsewhere and deployed here without the governance infrastructure to detect when they are failing the specific patients in this context. That is not a hypothetical concern. It is a description of the current situation, documented in the ACC's 2023 institutional review.⏎⏎Georgetown University Medical Center | HHS AI in Clinical Care RFI | Page 11⏎⏎The dataset shift literature is particularly relevant in this context. Finlayson et al.'s 2021 New England Journal of Medicine analysis of clinician and dataset shift in AI documented the specific mechanisms by which a model's performance degrades as the deployment environment diverges from the training environment, and noted that the divergence is often invisible to the clinicians using the tool because the tool continues to produce outputs — it does not fail silently in the way that a broken laboratory instrument does. A tool that is producing systematically biased outputs in a rural critical access hospital looks, from the clinician's interface, identical to a tool that is performing as designed. The only way to detect the difference is through the kind of post-deployment subgroup outcome monitoring that HHS has not proposed to require.⏎⏎Georgetown University Medical Center | HHS AI in Clinical Care RFI | Page 12⏎⏎The comment does not argue that HHS should halt AI development in clinical care. The literature is clear that there are specific contexts in which AI tools have demonstrated genuine performance advantages, and the potential for AI to extend specialist-level diagnostic capability to under-resourced settings is real and worth pursuing. But the potential is only realized equitably if the deployment framework is designed to detect and correct disparate performance before it becomes embedded in clinical practice. The tools that are currently being deployed at scale were not designed with that framework in place, and the RFI does not propose to create it. What HHS is proposing is a reimbursement and regulatory structure that will make AI tools more widely available without first establishing the monitoring infrastructure that would allow the healthcare system to know whether those tools are working equitably for the patients who receive care in the settings where the governance gap is largest. That is the specific concern this comment addresses, and it is not resolved by any of the regulatory actions currently described in the⏎⏎Georgetown University Medical Center | HHS AI in Clinical Care RFI | Page 13⏎⏎[continued from previous page] — RFI's proposed framework. The ACC's Quality Improvement for Institutions data and the 2024 fellow survey together describe a system in which deployment has already outpaced governance at the institutional level. HHS's proposed acceleration would widen that gap at the national level, without the pre-deployment equity auditing or post-deployment bias surveillance requirements that would be necessary to detect the resulting harm before it becomes entrenched.⏎⏎Contact for follow-up questions regarding this submission:⏎James Clark, Postdoctoral Fellow⏎Georgetown University Medical Center⏎jclark-postdoc@gumc.georgetown.edu [address on file with submitting office]♔♔2026-01-14T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-14T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔10♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI systems in healthcare inherit and amplify racial, socioeconomic, and institutional biases from training data, and their apparent authority makes those biases harder to detect and correct than human error.♔academic_organization♔high♔resigned♔Idaho♔postdoctoral fellow♔54♔A 2024 ACC survey of 2,800 cardiology fellows and early-career cardiologists found that 67% reported working in institutions that had deployed at least one AI-assisted diagnostic or risk-stratification tool, yet 58% of that group indicated they had received no formal training on interpreting AI-generated outputs or understanding model limitations. The AI-assisted ECG monitoring system our hospital piloted in 2022 flagged him. I was the nurse who sat with him afterward. I am not writing this as someone who is afraid of these tools. I am writing as someone who watched that technology work, and who is now genuinely alarmed by what this RFI is actually asking, which is not whether AI should be adopted thoughtfully, but how quickly federal policy can be reoriented to accelerate adoption that is already, in many institutions, outpacing our ability to understand what we are embedding. Eric Topol's 2019 synthesis in Nature Medicine (15:44-56) documented real clinical promise in algorithmic pattern recognition, and I do not dispute that evidence. What I dispute is the assumption that documenting promise is sufficient grounds for the kind of systemic embedding this RFI appears to be building toward. Coiera's 2021 analysis in npj Digital Medicine (4:94) showed something that does not get enough attention in policy conversations: clinical workflow integration creates operational dependency that outlasts the original rationale for adoption. Clinicians and institutions lose the procedural memory to function without a system, not because they are lazy, but because workflows reorganize around available tools. Selbst and colleagues made a related structural point at ACM FAccT 2019 — AI systems embedded in institutional infrastructure resist correction even after documented failures, because the cost of reversal grows faster than the evidence for harm accumulates. That is not a hypothetical. I have watched it happen with far less consequential health IT decisions than the ones this RFI is contemplating.⏎⏎THE DEMOCRATIC LEGITIMACY PROBLEM⏎⏎What concerns me most is not any particular algorithm. A federal agency frames regulatory scrutiny as an obstacle to innovation rather than as a legitimate democratic function.⏎2. Adoption accelerates before accountability infrastructure exists, which the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology acknowledged explicitly in their 2023 report on AI governance in health care, finding structural gaps in the ability of current regulatory frameworks to audit proprietary clinical AI systems.⏎3. Proprietary systems whose internal logic cannot be examined by clinicians, patients, or independent regulators become load-bearing infrastructure, at which point reversal is practically foreclosed regardless of what evidence emerges.⏎4. The question of whether medicine should be organized this way is never actually put to the communities who will live with the answer.⏎⏎Sheila Jasanoff argued in The Ethics of Invention (2016) that democratic societies retain the right to decide that certain domains should remain governed by human judgment even at the cost of efficiency, and that this is a legitimate collective choice, not a failure of rational policy. I am not asking HHS to stop thinking about AI. I am asking HHS to reframe this RFI around a different question, which is not how to accelerate adoption but what democratic process should precede irreversible embedding. Robinson | Page 1⏎⏎⏎The framing of this RFI deserves to be examined before any of its specific questions are answered, because the framing is itself the problem. HHS is asking how to accelerate AI adoption in clinical care. Our institution has spent three fiscal years attempting to answer a prior question — how to deploy AI systems responsibly when no coherent federal accountability framework exists — and the data we have accumulated in that effort are not encouraging. A 2024 internal analysis conducted by our AI Governance Committee across 13 specialty service lines found that 68% of implementation delays were attributable not to technical immaturity or clinician resistance, but to unresolved federal guidance on liability attribution and reimbursement eligibility. Of 47 distinct AI model integrations attempted or completed across our health system between fiscal years 2022 and 2024, only 11 achieved sustainable operational status. That is a 77% attrition rate. Our data scientists and faculty clinicians, surveyed during the 2024 Governance Committee review, identified the absence of a unified HHS validation and accountability framework as the single greatest barrier to scaling proven tools from pilot status to standard-of-care deployment. HHS is asking us how to go faster. Our data suggest that the more urgent policy question is how to go safely, and those two questions are not the same question.⏎⏎⏎SECTION I: THE LIABILITY VACUUM IS NOT AN INCIDENTAL GAP⏎⏎The core structural problem with accelerated AI deployment in clinical settings is that existing medical malpractice doctrine, built on the premise of an identifiable human decision-maker exercising professional judgment, has no coherent mechanism to assign responsibility when an AI-assisted error occurs. Price, Gerke, and Cohen identified this problem in 2019, writing specifically about the indeterminate causation problem that arises when physician conduct is mediated by algorithmic recommendation (Price WN II, Gerke S, Cohen IG, "Potential liability for physicians using artificial intelligence," JAMA, 2019;322(18):1765–1766). What our institutional experience has since confirmed is that the problem is not merely theoretical. When our clinical decision support tools have generated recommendations that were questioned or that contributed to suboptimal care pathways, the post-hoc attribution conversations among clinicians, hospital administration, and vendors have been, to use a precise term, incoherent. Each party possesses a structurally plausible deflection narrative. The attending physician did not program the model. The hospital did not train it. The vendor did not make the clinical judgment to act on its output. Respondeat superior doctrine, which assigns liability upward through an employment relationship, does not map cleanly onto a tripartite arrangement where the critical decision is distributed across an algorithm, a deploying institution, and an end-user clinician who may not fully understand the model's basis for its recommendation.⏎⏎Gerke, Minssen, and Cohen have written extensively on this configuration, noting that the ethical and legal challenges of AI-driven healthcare are compounded precisely because the locus of decision-making becomes genuinely ambiguous when deep learning systems are in the loop (Gerke S, Minssen T, Cohen G, "Ethical and legal challenges of artificial intelligence-driven healthcare," in: Bohr A, Memarzadeh K, eds., Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare, Academic Press, 2020:295–336). Sendak and colleagues observed in their 2020 study of clinical deep learning deployment that clinicians frequently treat AI outputs as authoritative without understanding the model's internal logic, a dynamic they described using the phrase "the human body is a black box," meaning that clinicians already operate with significant epistemic uncertainty about patient physiology, and AI systems layer a second black box on top of that uncertainty without resolving the first (Sendak MP, Elish MC, Gao M, et al., "'The human body is a black box': supporting clinical decision-making with deep learning," Proc ACM FAT*, 2020:99–109). When errors occur in this double-opacity environment, the question of who had the relevant duty of care and who breached it cannot be answered by reference to any existing federal standard. HHS's RFI does not propose to answer it either. That silence is the design flaw this comment is addressing.⏎⏎⏎Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center | HHS AI RFI Comments | T. Robinson | Page 2⏎⏎⏎SECTION II: THE DEFLECTION ARCHITECTURE IS A DESIGNED FEATURE⏎⏎It would be reassuring to characterize the tripartite liability diffusion described above as an accidental regulatory gap — something that fell through the cracks of a framework designed for a different technological moment. Our reading of the current deployment landscape does not support that reassurance. The commercial incentive structure for AI vendors in the clinical space actively benefits from liability indeterminacy. Vendors negotiate contract terms that assign clinical responsibility to deploying institutions. Deploying institutions, in turn, rely on clinician professional standards as their first line of indemnification. Clinicians, for their part, can point to the vendor's model and the institution's procurement decision. The result is not a gap but a loop — a closed circuit of deflection in which harmed patients have no clear defendant and no coherent evidentiary pathway to establish causation. Doshi-Velez and colleagues at the Berkman Klein Center identified the explanation problem as central to AI accountability, arguing that legal accountability frameworks depend on the ability to reconstruct decision logic, and that most current clinical AI systems cannot provide that reconstruction in any legally meaningful form (Doshi-Velez F, Kortz M, Budish R, et al., "Accountability of AI under the law: the role of explanation," Berkman Klein Center Working Paper, 2017, https://ssrn.com/abstract=3064761). HHS's proposed acceleration of deployment would embed systems with this structural accountability deficit more deeply into clinical workflows, making post-hoc remediation correspondingly more difficult.⏎⏎Mello, Frakes, Blumenkranz, and Studdert, writing in JAMA in 2020, examined the relationship between malpractice liability structures and health care quality, and their analysis supports a concern that our institution has observed operationally: the deterrence function of malpractice liability depends on a legible connection between negligent conduct and legal consequence, and when that connection is obscured by technological intermediation, the deterrence effect degrades (Mello MM, Frakes MD, Blumenkranz E, Studdert DM, "Malpractice liability and health care quality," JAMA, 2020;323(4):352–366). Char, Shah, and Magnus, writing in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2018, made a related point about the ethical infrastructure required to make machine learning deployment responsible — arguing that implementation without accountability architecture is not cautious innovation but a transfer of risk from institutions to patients (Char DS, Shah NH, Magnus D, "Implementing machine learning in health care — addressing ethical challenges," N Engl J Med, 2018;378(11):981–983). HHS should engage seriously with this literature before characterizing its RFI as a patient-centered initiative.⏎⏎⏎SECTION III: SPECIFIC CONCERNS REGARDING THE RFI'S SCOPE AND OMISSIONS⏎⏎This comment focuses primarily on two dimensions of the RFI where the accountability deficit is most acute and where HHS's silence is most consequential.⏎⏎First, the RFI's treatment of reimbursement pathways for AI-assisted clinical services does not address the liability implications of creating financial incentives for adoption in the absence of accountability standards. When CMS or private payers reimburse AI-assisted diagnostic or treatment decisions, they are implicitly validating the clinical legitimacy of those decisions. That validation, however, does not resolve the question of who bears responsibility when the AI-assisted decision is wrong. Topol, writing in Nature Medicine in 2019, described the convergence of human and artificial intelligence in high-performance clinical settings as requiring what he called a new "cognitive partnership" between clinicians and algorithms — a partnership that presupposes institutional and legal structures capable of assigning responsibility within that partnership (Topol EJ, "High-performance medicine: the convergence of human and artificial intelligence," Nat Med, 2019;25(1):44–56). No such structures currently exist in any HHS-administered framework, and the RFI does not propose to create them.⏎⏎Second, the RFI's discussion of validation standards for clinical AI is inadequate. Cohen, Evgeniou, Gerke, and Minssen, examining the European AI strategy in Lancet Digital Health in 2020, identified prospective validation requirements as the minimum necessary condition for responsible clinical AI deployment — noting that post-market surveillance alone cannot protect patients from harms that are structurally invisible until they have already accumulated at scale (Cohen IG, Evgeniou T, Gerke S, Minssen T, "The European artificial intelligence strategy: implications and challenges for digital health," Lancet Digital Health, 2020;2(7):e376–e379). The absence of a unified HHS validation framework is not merely an administrative inconvenience. Our institution has catalogued at least 14 instances across the past three years in which commercially deployed clinical AI tools were integrated into our workflows on the basis of vendor-supplied validation studies that were not independently replicated, were conducted on patient populations that did not reflect our own demographics, or were performed on training data whose composition we could not audit. Hoffman and Podgurski, examining AI discrimination in health care, have documented how validation failures of precisely this kind produce systematic disparate harm in clinical populations that are underrepresented in training datasets (Hoffman S, Podgurski A, "Artificial intelligence and discrimination in health care," Yale J Health Policy Law Ethics, 2019;19(3):1–51). Keskinbora's analysis of medical ethics considerations in AI deployment reaches similar conclusions regarding the inadequacy of relying on vendor-supplied performance metrics as a substitute for independent clinical validation (Keskinbora KH, "Medical ethics considerations on artificial intelligence," J Clin Neurosci, 2019;64:277–282).⏎⏎⏎Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center | HHS AI RFI Comments | T. Robinson | Page 3⏎⏎⏎The specific operational consequences of these validation failures at our institution include the following:⏎⏎1. An AI-assisted sepsis prediction tool deployed in our emergency department in early 2023 produced alert fatigue rates that were not observed in the vendor's published validation cohort; the tool was withdrawn from operational use after seven months, contributing to one of the 36 failed integrations referenced above, and the institutional cost of that deployment cycle — including integration labor, clinician training, and EHR modification — exceeded $340,000 by our biostatistics team's accounting.⏎⏎2. A radiology AI tool for chest X-ray interpretation, deployed in our outpatient pulmonology service, demonstrated performance degradation in patients over age 70 that was not disclosed in the vendor's pre-deployment documentation; this was identified only through our own prospective monitoring protocol, which was not required by any federal standard but was implemented on the initiative of our AI Governance Committee.⏎⏎3. A natural language processing tool for clinical note summarization, piloted in our oncology service, produced structured outputs that attending physicians reported treating as authoritative despite the tool's documented 12% error rate on medication dosage extraction — a rate our team considers clinically unacceptable, but which no federal standard currently prohibits.⏎⏎Each of these cases illustrates the same structural problem: deployment proceeded without an enforceable federal accountability framework, errors accumulated, and the question of who bore legal and financial responsibility for the resulting clinical and institutional harms was never coherently resolved. HHS is proposing to create conditions under which this pattern occurs not at the pilot scale but at the scale of standard-of-care deployment across the U.S. health system.⏎⏎⏎SECTION IV: WHAT HHS MUST DO BEFORE ACCELERATING ADOPTION⏎⏎Our institution's position, informed by three years of direct operational experience and grounded in the literature reviewed above, is that HHS should not take any regulatory or reimbursement action to accelerate AI adoption in clinical care before the following conditions are met. This is not a suggestion. The Department has a statutory obligation to protect patients, and the current regulatory posture is inconsistent with that obligation.⏎⏎The conditions we consider minimally necessary are:⏎⏎a. A published federal framework for liability attribution in AI-assisted clinical errors, specifying the respective duties of care borne by AI vendors, deploying institutions, and clinical end-users, and providing a legally operable mechanism for establishing causation when algorithmic recommendation contributes to patient harm. The framework should not be advisory; it must be enforceable.⏎⏎b. Mandatory independent validation requirements for clinical AI tools, specifying minimum cohort size, demographic representativeness standards, and performance benchmarks, with validation conducted by parties without financial relationships with the tool's developer. The ONC's existing work on interoperability standards under the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement provides a partial model for how HHS can establish certification-style requirements (Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology, Draft Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement, HHS/ONC, 2022), but that framework does not extend to clinical AI validation and would require substantial modification to do so.⏎⏎c. A reimbursement structure that conditions payment for AI-assisted clinical services on demonstrated compliance with the validation and accountability frameworks described above, rather than creating financial incentives for adoption that outrun accountability requirements.⏎⏎Obermeyer and Lee, writing in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2017, argued that the future of medicine depends on integrating human and artificial intelligence in ways that preserve rather than erode the epistemic standards that clinical practice requires (Obermeyer Z, Lee TH, "Lost in thought — the limits of the human mind and the future of medicine," N Engl J Med, 2017;377(13):1209–1211). Our institution does not oppose AI adoption. We have invested substantially in attempting to achieve it. What we oppose is a federal posture that treats accountability infrastructure as something to be developed after deployment has occurred at scale, on the theory that the benefits of adoption justify the risks of a transitional period without enforceable standards. That theory has already cost our institution approximately $2.1 million in failed deployment cycles over three years, by our Governance Committee's accounting. It has also, in ways that our retrospective analyses cannot fully quantify, exposed patients to clinical decision support tools whose error profiles were not disclosed, whose liability implications were not resolved, and whose integration into care pathways was predicated on vendor representations that no federal body had independently verified.⏎⏎The RFI's silence on liability attribution is not a placeholder pending further regulatory development. It is a signal that HHS is prepared to accelerate deployment while leaving the accountability question to litigation — which is to say, to patients who have already been harmed. That is not a policy our institution can endorse, and the Department should not interpret the absence of widespread formal objection as evidence that the health care sector has accepted it. Our 2024 Governance Committee survey found that 84% of our faculty clinicians expressed concern about personal liability exposure from AI-assisted clinical decisions, but fewer than 20% had submitted formal comments to any federal body on the subject, because they did not believe formal comment would produce a response. This comment is submitted in the hope that belief is wrong, though our institution acknowledges the empirical basis for it is not negligible.⏎⏎One further point that does not fit cleanly into the above framework but which our biostatistics team considers important: the RFI's implicit assumption that regulatory acceleration will produce adoption at scale assumes a deployment-ready health system infrastructure that does not uniformly exist. Our own EHR environment, built on a legacy Epic configuration with significant custom modifications accumulated over eight years, creates integration constraints that no federal reimbursement incentive will resolve in the near term. The liability question and the infrastructure question are related, because health systems that cannot safely integrate AI tools will face pressure to deploy them anyway if reimbursement incentives make non-deployment financially costly — and that pressure will fall most heavily on smaller and rural institutions that lack the internal governance capacity we have at a major academic medical center. SYNTH-0014♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Edward Allen♔♔♔♔♔♔My wife Karen had a valve problem that two separate echocardiogram reads called unremarkable. A third read, assisted by imaging software at Hartford Hospital, caught it. Six weeks later she was in surgery, and her surgeon told us that if it had waited another year, the repair would have been substantially more complicated and possibly unsafe. I sat in that waiting room thinking about the twenty miles between Hartford Hospital and the smaller facility near our home in Connecticut, and what those twenty miles meant for who gets access to what technology. That arbitrariness is real, and the clinical promise of AI is real, and I don't want to pretend otherwise.⏎⏎But that is not what I want to address here.⏎⏎THE AUTOMATION OF ADMINISTRATIVE WORK⏎⏎What concerns me about this request for information is a quieter assumption running through its framing: that administrative work in healthcare is a processing problem, and that AI can process it better and faster than people can. I want to push back on that assumption directly, because I think it misunderstands what administrative healthcare workers actually do, and because the consequences of getting this wrong will fall on patients who are already vulnerable and already poorly served.⏎⏎People who do care coordination, patient navigation, prior authorization review, and benefits counseling are not doing clerical work. They are doing something closer to what Hubert and Stuart Dreyfus described in Mind Over Machine (1986) as expert pattern recognition: they are reading situations, not forms. A care coordinator at a Federally Qualified Health Center in Hartford who has worked that community for eight years knows which patients will lose Medicaid coverage during a redetermination cycle and quietly call no one about it, knows which transportation vendors are reliable in February and which ones aren't, knows that a particular patient's daughter handles the paperwork but her son makes the decisions and those two people are not speaking right now. Michael Polanyi called this kind of knowledge "tacit" precisely because it resists encoding (The Tacit Dimension, 1966). You cannot extract it into a training set. You cannot write it into a prompt. When you automate the role that carries it, you don't transfer the knowledge. You discard it.⏎⏎The efficiency argument for administrative AI is not wrong on its face. Sinsky et al. (2016, Annals of Internal Medicine, 165(11), 753-760) documented how administrative burden consumes physician time that should go to patients, and that finding is cited constantly and correctly. Understaffing is real. The documentation load is genuinely unsustainable. I understand why people look at those numbers and reach for automation. What I think the efficiency framing misses is that administrative friction in healthcare is not purely waste. Some of it is. But some of it is a checkpoint where a human being with contextual knowledge catches an error before it reaches a patient. A prior authorization reviewer who flags an inconsistency between a diagnosis code and a requested procedure, not because a rule told her to but because she has seen this physician's coding patterns for three years and something looks off, is doing something no algorithm trained on population-level claims data can replicate. When you remove that reviewer and replace her with a system optimized for throughput, you don't just speed up the process. You remove a safety layer while creating new categories of error that the system will not flag because the system does not know what it does not know.⏎⏎The evidence on automated administrative decision-making is not encouraging. The National Academy for State Health Policy's 2022 issue brief on automated Medicaid eligibility determinations documented systematic errors in multiple state implementations, including cases where automation incorrectly terminated coverage for eligible beneficiaries at scale, with errors that were invisible to program administrators until advocates started tracking individual cases. The Government Accountability Office's 2023 report on prior authorization in Medicare Advantage (GAO-23-105765) found that even under human administration, plans were approving services that should have been denied and denying services that should have been approved at rates that CMS was not adequately monitoring. That is the baseline we are proposing to automate. Obermeyer et al.'s 2019 Science paper (366(6464), 447-453) on racial bias in a widely deployed health management algorithm showed that systematic errors in automated systems are not random: they follow the contours of existing inequity, amplifying disadvantage in populations that are already underserved. Administrative AI will not be different. The errors will not distribute evenly.⏎⏎WHAT HHS SHOULD REQUIRE BEFORE ANY ADMINISTRATIVE AI DEPLOYMENT⏎⏎I want to be specific about what I am asking for, because "be careful with AI" is not a regulatory position.⏎⏎1. Pre-deployment safety demonstration: Any AI system used to make or assist in administrative decisions affecting patient access to care (prior authorization, eligibility determination, care coordination routing, benefits navigation) should be required to demonstrate accuracy and equity benchmarks against a defined patient population before deployment, not after. Post-market surveillance is insufficient for decisions that affect access to care in real time.⏎⏎2. Accountability frameworks that already exist should apply: The regulatory accountability structures in 45 C.F.R. § 164.530 and 42 C.F.R. § 431.200 et seq. cover administrative decision-making in covered entities and Medicaid programs. HHS should explicitly confirm that AI systems operating in these functions are subject to the same accountability requirements as human administrators, and should not allow vendors to disclaim liability by characterizing their tools as "decision support" when those tools are in practice making the decision.⏎⏎3. Preservation of human review capacity: Efficiency gains from administrative AI should not be used to justify reducing the workforce that performs administrative oversight. If a system automates the initial processing of prior authorization requests, a human reviewer with genuine authority to override the system's recommendation must remain in the workflow. This is not a formality. It is the difference between a safety layer and a liability disclaimer.⏎⏎4. Transparency to patients: Patients affected by automated administrative decisions should be informed that automation was involved and should have a clear, accessible process for requesting human review. This is basic procedural fairness and it is currently absent from most AI deployment frameworks I have seen discussed in this rulemaking context.⏎⏎The concern I keep coming back to is this: the patchwork logic that created the disparity I described at the beginning of this comment, where Karen's outcome depended partly on which hospital had invested in which software, is now being applied to administrative functions. But in the clinical AI context, at least there is a visible event when something goes wrong. A missed diagnosis eventually surfaces. An administrative error that terminates someone's Medicaid coverage, or routes them to the wrong care coordinator, or generates an incorrect prior authorization denial, may never surface as a discrete failure. The patient just falls through. That invisibility is not a reason to be less careful. It is a reason to be more careful, and to require demonstrated safety before deployment rather than assuming efficiency gains will outweigh harms we have not yet measured.⏎⏎I recognize that the people working on this rulemaking are trying to solve real problems. The administrative burden on the healthcare system is genuinely unsustainable. I am not arguing for preserving the status quo. I am arguing that the expertise of administrative healthcare workers, the tacit and contextual knowledge they carry, is a patient safety resource, and that treating it as overhead to be eliminated rather than capacity to be supported is a mistake that will be paid for by people who are already paying too much. The NASHP findings from 2022 should be required reading for anyone designing a deployment framework here, because those state-level Medicaid automation projects were also launched with efficiency goals and genuine good intentions, and the errors they generated were invisible until someone went looking.⏎⏎HHS should require that before any administrative AI system is deployed in a clinical care setting, the deploying entity demonstrate that human expertise has been preserved in the workflow, not just nominally but functionally, and that the system has been tested specifically for the kinds of errors that fall on♔♔2026-01-15T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-15T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔4♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Even administrative healthcare functions that appear routine require human contextual judgment that AI cannot replicate, and automating them will produce systematic errors that harm patients and workers.♔individual♔high♔supportive♔Connecticut♔customer service representative♔57♔My wife Karen's cardiologist at Hartford Hospital used an AI-assisted imaging tool to catch a borderline finding on her echocardiogram that two previous manual reads had flagged as unremarkable — within six weeks she had a valve repair that her surgeon said would have been far more complicated, possibly dangerous, had it waited another year. SYNTH-0015♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Brian Adams♔University of Chicago Center for Health and the Social Sciences♔♔♔♔♔University of Chicago Center for Health and the Social Sciences⏎Comments Submitted to HHS Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎Docket: HHS-2024-AI-RFI-Clinical-Care⏎Submitted by: Brian Adams, Research Faculty, Center for Health and the Social Sciences⏎⏎—————————————————————————————————⏎UChicago CHSS | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 1⏎—————————————————————————————————⏎⏎⏎THE POLITICAL ECONOMY OF AI ACCELERATION: MARKET CONCENTRATION, REGULATORY CAPTURE, AND THE LIMITS OF THE CURRENT FRAMING⏎⏎The Center for Health and the Social Sciences at the University of Chicago submits these comments in response to HHS's Request for Information on accelerating AI adoption in clinical care settings. These comments do not address clinical safety, algorithmic accountability, or workforce displacement — important questions that other commenters will engage more directly. This submission focuses on a narrower but consequential set of concerns: the structural economic conditions of the health AI market, and the degree to which the RFI's framing already reflects the successful prior influence of the concentrated commercial interests that HHS is ostensibly regulating.⏎⏎The concern is not that HHS is acting in bad faith. The concern is that the policy conversation has been shaped upstream of this RFI, and that the proposed instruments — reimbursement reforms, interoperability mandates, public-private partnerships — will, under present market conditions, function primarily as mechanisms for incumbent entrenchment rather than broad diffusion of beneficial technology.⏎⏎⏎MARKET CONCENTRATION AND THE STRUCTURE OF THE HEALTH AI VENDOR ECOSYSTEM⏎⏎The health AI market is not competitive in any meaningful sense. A small number of large EHR vendors and technology platform companies control the data infrastructure through which AI tools must flow to reach clinical settings, and the barriers to entry for smaller or non-commercial developers are substantial. Gans and Stern (2023) document this dynamic explicitly, describing how EHR incumbency creates compounding AI market entry barriers through proprietary data formats, certification dependencies, and switching costs that effectively foreclose competition from firms that cannot absorb the cost of multi-year integration cycles. The CHIME survey data cited in the background to this RFI — finding that 78% of health IT leaders identify interoperability gaps as a primary deployment barrier — is read by the Center as evidence of this incumbency structure, not simply as a technical problem amenable to standards-based solutions.⏎⏎The historical record on healthcare market consolidation is not encouraging here. Dafny and Lee (2016) and Beaulieu et al. (2020) have both documented how consolidation in healthcare markets tends to reduce quality while increasing cost, even when the original rationale for consolidation was efficiency-based modernization. The analogy is not perfect, but the mechanism is structurally similar: when regulatory action reduces friction for large, well-capitalized actors while nominally remaining technology-neutral, the practical effect is accelerated concentration. Adler-Milstein and Pfeifer (2017) documented precisely this dynamic in the information blocking context, where certification-based compliance requirements that appeared vendor-neutral in design produced outcomes that systematically favored large EHR vendors with dedicated regulatory affairs capacity.⏎⏎The GAO's 2022 report on AI in health care (GAO-22-104629) acknowledged that the market for clinical AI tools is characterized by significant information asymmetries between vendors and health system purchasers, but stopped short of analyzing the competitive structure implications. This Center believes that gap in the federal analytical record is consequential, and that HHS's RFI should have included explicit questions about market concentration dynamics before moving to questions about acceleration mechanisms.⏎⏎—————————————————————————————————⏎UChicago CHSS | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 2⏎—————————————————————————————————⏎⏎⏎THE RFI FRAMING AS A POLITICAL ECONOMY PROBLEM⏎⏎The structure of this RFI warrants scrutiny as an artifact of prior influence, not just as a policy document. The questions posed — how to streamline reimbursement, how to reduce regulatory burden, how to structure public-private partnerships for AI development — are questions that assume the primary problem is regulatory friction slowing beneficial technology. That framing is not neutral. It reflects a particular diagnosis of the problem, and that diagnosis happens to be the one most consistently advanced by the large technology vendors and health system associations with the greatest lobbying capacity and the most direct financial interest in regulatory acceleration.⏎⏎Stigler's foundational 1971 analysis of regulatory capture argued that the regulated industry tends to shape the regulatory agenda in its own interest, particularly in technically complex domains where the regulator depends on industry for information. The health AI context is a near-textbook case: HHS depends substantially on vendor-provided data, vendor-funded research, and vendor-staffed advisory bodies to understand the technology it is attempting to govern. Mazzucato and Collington (2023) extend this analysis to the consulting and technology sectors specifically, documenting the structural mechanisms through which private actors extract public value from government modernization initiatives while simultaneously shaping the terms on which those initiatives are designed.⏎⏎The Center is not arguing that the commercial actors involved are acting illegally or even that their interests are entirely misaligned with patient welfare. The argument is narrower: the framing of this RFI reflects prior successful influence, and that framing will determine which policy instruments are considered, which actors benefit, and which risks are treated as residual rather than central.⏎⏎Landi and Muoio (2023) documented the degree to which EHR vendor consolidation has already constrained health system procurement choices in ways that produce vendor lock-in and reduce the leverage of safety-net hospitals in particular. The reimbursement reforms contemplated in this RFI, if implemented without structural conditions, will reproduce that dynamic at the AI layer of the health IT stack. Frakt and Jha (2023) have argued more broadly that reimbursement structure reforms in health care consistently advantage actors with the administrative capacity to navigate new billing categories — and in the AI context, that means large integrated vendors, not community health centers or critical access hospitals in rural North Carolina or elsewhere.⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS REGARDING PROPOSED POLICY INSTRUMENTS⏎⏎The Center's concerns resolve into four specific analytical objections to the policy instruments under consideration, which are offered here not as a comprehensive critique but as a starting point for the kind of structural analysis this RFI should have solicited directly:⏎⏎1.  Reimbursement reforms for AI-enabled care pathways, absent market structure conditions, will function as revenue transfer mechanisms to incumbent vendors. If CMS creates new billing codes or add-on payments for AI-assisted clinical decision support without requiring open interoperability as a condition of payment eligibility, the practical effect will be to subsidize proprietary platforms. The National Academy for State Health Policy documented this risk in its 2023 issue brief on vendor lock-in and AI-enabled clinical decision support, noting that health systems that receive reimbursement incentives tied to specific AI tools face dramatically increased switching costs in subsequent procurement cycles.⏎⏎2.  Public-private partnership mechanisms, including Cooperative Research and Development Agreements (CRADAs) and data-sharing arrangements between federal health data infrastructure and commercial AI developers, require structural firewalls that are not currently contemplated in the RFI. Mazzucato and Collington (2023) describe the generic mechanism by which private actors use public-private partnership structures to gain preferential access to publicly-funded data and infrastructure, then extract rents from the resulting market position. HHS should require independent oversight of any such arrangements, with explicit conflict-of-interest provisions and public disclosure of data access terms.⏎⏎3.  Interoperability mandates, as Schulte and Fry (2019) documented extensively in the EHR context, are systematically undermined by large vendors with the political capacity to shape implementation guidance in ways that preserve de facto proprietary advantage while achieving nominal compliance. The same dynamic should be anticipated in the AI context. Interoperability requirements that are technically meaningful — requiring, for example, that AI model inputs and outputs be accessible through standardized APIs regardless of EHR platform — will face intense vendor resistance, and HHS should be prepared for that resistance to manifest in the sub-regulatory guidance process, not just in public comment.⏎⏎4.  The RFI does not ask whether the federal government should support open-source or publicly-owned AI tools as an alternative to commercial procurement. This is a significant omission. Obermeyer et al. (2019) demonstrated that a widely-deployed commercial algorithm used in population health management systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients — an outcome that the commercial vendor had limited incentive to address until public scrutiny forced the issue. The existence of publicly-owned or open-source alternatives would create competitive pressure on commercial vendors while preserving public access to model architecture and training data for independent audit.⏎⏎—————————————————————————————————⏎UChicago CHSS | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 3⏎—————————————————————————————————⏎⏎⏎RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎The Center offers the following recommendations, which follow directly from the political economy analysis above rather than from clinical or technical considerations:⏎⏎a.  HHS should commission an independent market concentration analysis of the health AI vendor ecosystem prior to finalizing any reimbursement or regulatory reforms. That analysis should examine horizontal concentration among AI developers, vertical integration between EHR vendors and AI product lines, and the degree to which existing certification and billing infrastructure creates durable incumbent advantage.⏎⏎b.  Any reimbursement reforms for AI-enabled care pathways should include open interoperability requirements as a condition of payment eligibility, with enforcement mechanisms that are not delegated to the vendor certification process.⏎⏎c.  HHS should establish structural firewalls between vendor-funded research and any standard-setting or guidance-development processes related to clinical AI. This includes restricting the participation of vendor employees and vendor-funded researchers in advisory committees that set technical standards for AI reimbursement eligibility.⏎⏎d.  HHS should issue a specific solicitation for public comment on the potential for federally-supported open-source clinical AI tools, modeled on existing precedents in genomics (e.g., the NIH's All of Us data platform) that have preserved public access to federally-funded research infrastructure.⏎⏎e.  Any CRADAs or public-private data-sharing arrangements entered into in connection with this initiative should be subject to independent oversight, with public disclosure of data access terms, revenue-sharing arrangements, and conflict-of-interest certifications for all participating parties.⏎⏎The Center recognizes that these recommendations are in some tension with the acceleration framing of the RFI itself. That tension is the point. The question of whether HHS should be accelerating AI adoption in clinical care — as opposed to ensuring that AI adoption, at whatever pace market and regulatory conditions produce, serves patient welfare rather than vendor revenue — is a prior question that this RFI does not ask. The Center believes it should have been asked, and that the failure to ask it reflects exactly the kind of upstream agenda-setting that Stigler's framework would predict.⏎⏎One additional concern that does not fit neatly into the categories above: the 14-month average delay from AI procurement to clinical deployment documented in CHIME member case studies is cited in this RFI's background materials as evidence of regulatory friction that should be reduced. A 14-month integration timeline in a market where procurement decisions are made by health IT administrators under significant vendor pressure, and where post-deployment monitoring capacity is limited, may reflect appropriate caution rather than inefficiency. PNHP does not oppose the application of computational tools to medicine. What PNHP opposes, with mounting urgency that this RFI has done nothing to diminish, is the Department's apparent intention to accelerate deployment of clinical AI systems before resolving the foundational legal question that every other accountability structure in American medicine has required as a precondition: who is responsible when the system causes harm?⏎⏎That question is not rhetorical. Medical malpractice doctrine, as it has operated for over a century, rests on the assumption that an identifiable human decision-maker exercised clinical judgment, and that this person can be held to account. When a physician delegates a decision to an AI-driven clinical decision support system, the accountability chain does not merely bend — it fractures. The clinician deflects to the tool. The hospital deflects to the vendor specification. The vendor deflects to training data or user configuration error. This is not a hypothetical future risk. Obermeyer and Emanuel documented in 375 New England Journal of Medicine 1216 (2016) that algorithmic decision-making already obscures clinical responsibility in ways traditional negligence doctrine was not designed to address. The Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability section 2 (Am. Law Inst. 1998) provides no clean doctrinal home for AI clinical tools, which are neither products in the traditional sense nor professional services. Hoffman and Podgurski, writing in 19 Yale J. Health Pol'y L. & Ethics 1 (2019), identified this liability vacuum with precision that HHS has declined to engage. The GAO reached parallel conclusions in GAO-22-104629 (Feb. 2022), finding that accountability frameworks lag AI deployment across clinical settings. None of this is new literature. The Department has had years to act.⏎⏎The documented harms are already accumulating in the administrative layer, which this RFI treats as peripheral when it is in fact a primary site of AI-driven patient harm. The HHS Office of Inspector General, in OIG Report OEI-02-23-00140 (Apr. 2024), documented the systematic misuse of automated prior authorization denial systems in Medicare Advantage — systems making consequential clinical-access decisions with no identifiable human accountable for the outcome. Existing administrative simplification rules, including 45 C.F.R. section 164.306 and 45 C.F.R. section 162.1101, impose transaction processing obligations that were written without any anticipation of AI intermediation and create zero accountability obligations for AI-driven processing nodes. Frank Pasquale's structural analysis in The Black Box Society (Harvard Univ. Press 2015) described exactly the vendor opacity and institutional lock-in that follows once AI becomes embedded in regulated industries — and that embedding is already well advanced in the prior authorization and claims adjudication infrastructure connecting payers and providers.⏎⏎⏎PNHP Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 2⏎⏎⏎The contrast with the European Union's approach is not merely instructive — it is damning.
