SYNTH-0018♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Michelle Lopez♔American Association of Nurse Practitioners♔♔♔♔♔EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎The American Association of Nurse Practitioners (AANP) submits these comments in response to HHS's Request for Information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings. AANP represents more than 355,000 nurse practitioners across the United States who collectively deliver tens of millions of patient encounters annually, including a substantial share of primary and specialty care for patients with chronic liver disease, metabolic syndrome, and other conditions for which AI-assisted clinical decision support tools are now being actively marketed. AANP urges HHS to approach this RFI with considerably more caution than its framing suggests, and to resist the institutional momentum toward deployment-first, evaluation-later policymaking that has characterized prior waves of health information technology adoption. The core argument advanced in these comments is not that AI has no role in clinical care — it plainly does, and AANP has engaged constructively with AI policy for several years — but rather that the RFI's operating assumptions systematically underweight the relational dimensions of clinical practice in ways that, if translated into reimbursement and regulatory frameworks, will produce measurable patient harm. Appendix A, which contains AANP's full registry analysis and provider survey data referenced herein, is being transmitted separately to the docket and should be considered part of this submission.⏎⏎AANP Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-OS-2024-0011 | Page 1⏎⏎The RFI uses the phrase "enhance productivity" at least four times in describing the goals of AI adoption in clinical settings. AANP wants to address that framing directly, because it is not a neutral choice of language. Productivity, in the economic sense the RFI invokes, measures output per unit of input — encounters per clinician per hour, documentation time per note, referrals generated per abnormal test result. These are not clinically irrelevant metrics, and AANP does not pretend otherwise. But when "enhance productivity" becomes the organizing aspiration for AI deployment in clinical care, it encodes a model of medicine as transaction processing rather than as relational practice, and that encoding has downstream consequences for how tools are designed, how they are reimbursed, and how their success is measured. A data from AANP's 2023 State of Liver Disease Policy Survey — conducted among 210 hepatology providers and 94 patient advocacy partners across 38 hepatology centers — found that reimbursement ambiguity and the absence of validated clinical integration frameworks were the two leading barriers to AI tool adoption, not lack of interest in the tools themselves. What providers told us, in follow-up interviews, was more textured than a survey can capture: they were worried that AI tools would be deployed to speed up encounters, not to deepen them, and that reimbursement structures would reinforce that pressure. HHS should take that concern seriously as a policy signal, not dismiss it as technophobia.⏎⏎Consider what clinical care actually looks like in a hepatology practice managing patients with early-stage fibrosis. A 52-year-old woman — AANP will call her a composite drawn from multiple provider accounts — presents with fatigue that she describes as "just tired, you know, from everything." She has had an abnormal FIB-4 result for seven months. She has not seen a hepatologist. She cannot articulate, in clinical language, that her fatigue is qualitatively different from the exhaustion of caregiving and economic stress that fills the rest of her description. The nurse practitioner in that encounter is not primarily processing data. She is reading the patient's affect, noticing that the patient's adult daughter, who came to the appointment, will not meet the clinician's eyes, registering that something in the room is not being said. The referral that follows — the one that will catch the early-stage fibrosis before it advances — comes not from an algorithmic prompt but from a clinical judgment that is inseparable from the relational attunement of that encounter. AANP's registry data, encompassing more than 47,000 patients across those same 38 centers, found that 63% of patients with early-stage fibrosis had no documented specialist encounter within 12 months of an abnormal non-invasive test result. That is a genuine care gap. But the answer to that care gap is not to replace the relational encounter with an algorithmic nudge; it is to ensure that relational encounters happen, and that clinicians have the training and time to act on what those encounters reveal.⏎⏎AANP Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-OS-2024-0011 | Page 2⏎⏎The clinical literature on the therapeutic relationship is not soft or supplementary evidence — it is a body of randomized controlled trial data that HHS should be required to engage before designing reimbursement frameworks for AI tools that mediate that relationship. Kelley and colleagues' 2014 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials published in PLOS ONE documented that the quality of the patient-clinician relationship produces measurable, independent effects on clinical outcomes — effects that are not explained away by technical quality of care or diagnostic accuracy (Kelley JM, Kraft-Todd G, Schapira L, Kossowsky J, Riess H, PLOS ONE, 2014;9(4):e94207). Hojat and colleagues found that physicians' empathy scores, measured prospectively, predicted hemoglobin A1c and LDL cholesterol control in diabetic patients independently of other clinical variables — a finding with direct implications for any AI system that reduces the relational bandwidth of the clinical encounter in the name of efficiency (Hojat M, Louis DZ, Markham FW, Wender R, Rabinowitz C, Gonnella JS, Academic Medicine, 2011;86(3):359-364). Zolnierek and DiMatteo's meta-analysis of 127 studies found that patients of physicians with stronger communication skills were 19% more likely to adhere to treatment recommendations — and that meta-analysis included studies spanning multiple decades and clinical contexts, making it one of the most robust findings in health services research (Zolnierek KB, DiMatteo MR, Medical Care, 2009;47(8):826-834). Epstein and Street have argued compellingly that patient-centered care is not a stylistic preference but a measurable mechanism through which clinical outcomes are produced, and that frameworks which treat relational quality as separable from technical quality fundamentally misunderstand how healing works (Epstein RM, Street RL Jr., Annals of Family Medicine, 2011;9(2):100-103). None of these citations appear in HHS's RFI. That is a significant gap.⏎⏎The RFI's framing also largely ignores what the automation bias literature has established about the longitudinal effects of algorithmic intermediation on clinical reasoning capacity. This is not primarily an individual clinician problem — it is an institutional and generational one, and that distinction matters enormously for policy. Parasuraman and Manzey's foundational review in Human Factors documented that automation complacency is not a character flaw in individual users but a predictable cognitive response to reliable automated systems — systems that perform well enough, often enough, that vigilant human oversight becomes cognitively costly and gradually attenuates (Parasuraman R, Manzey DH, Human Factors, 2010;52(3):381-410). Goddard and colleagues' systematic review in JAMIA confirmed that automation bias — the tendency to favor automated recommendations over independent judgment — is a consistent finding across clinical decision support deployments and is not reliably mitigated by training alone (Goddard K, Roudsari A, Wyatt JC, Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, 2012;19(1):121-127). What this means at the institutional level is that health systems that deploy AI clinical decision support (CDSS) tools at scale are not just changing how individual clinicians make individual decisions — they are changing the training environment in which the next generation of clinicians develops clinical reasoning capacity. A nurse practitioner who has spent the first several years of her practice following AI-generated care pathway recommendations for liver disease management will have built different cognitive habits than one who developed those pathways through accumulated clinical judgment. When the AI system fails — and all systems fail, as Kohn, Corrigan, and Donaldson documented with respect to every prior generation of health information technology in To Err Is Human — the clinician trained in an AI-mediated environment will have fewer independent reasoning resources to fall back on (Kohn LT, Corrigan JM, Donaldson MS, eds., To Err Is Human: Building a Safer Health System, Washington, DC: National Academies Press, 2000). HHS's RFI does not address this deskilling risk at all, and AANP considers that a serious omission.⏎⏎AANP Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-OS-2024-0011 | Page 3⏎⏎There is also an anchoring problem that the RFI's framing tends to obscure. Tversky and Kahneman's work on heuristics and biases established that numerical anchors — even arbitrary ones — systematically distort subsequent judgment (Tversky A, Kahneman D, Science, 1974;185(4157):1124-1131). In clinical contexts, an AI system that presents a risk score or a recommended care pathway before the clinician has completed her own assessment does not merely add information to the encounter — it restructures the cognitive sequence of that encounter in ways that systematically favor the algorithm's framing. Shortliffe and Sepúlveda noted in their 2018 JAMA commentary that the clinical decision support literature has not adequately grappled with the difference between tools that extend clinical reasoning and tools that substitute for it, and that the design and deployment context of CDSS tools determines which function they actually serve in practice (Shortliffe EH, Sepúlveda MJ, JAMA, 2018;320(21):2199-2200). AANP agrees, and would add that reimbursement frameworks that reward speed and throughput will reliably push deployed CDSS tools toward substitution rather than extension, regardless of what their designers intended. The incentive structure is the policy. HHS needs to understand that.⏎⏎Abraham Verghese has written with clinical precision about what is lost when the patient becomes, in his phrase, an "icon" — a data object whose representation in the electronic health record becomes more real to the clinical encounter than the person in the room (Verghese A, New England Journal of Medicine, 2008;359(26):2748-2751). AANP believes that AI-assisted clinical care, deployed under the productivity-enhancement framework the RFI advances, will accelerate that iconization. Eric Topol's influential 2019 Nature Medicine paper on the convergence of human and artificial intelligence in medicine is worth citing here precisely because of where it falls short: Topol argues that AI will "liberate" clinicians from administrative burden and restore time for human connection, but the paper's policy prescriptions — faster deployment, broader integration, reduced regulatory friction — do not actually describe mechanisms by which that liberation occurs or how it would be measured (Topol EJ, Nature Medicine, 2019;25(1):44-56). The assumption is that time freed from documentation will automatically flow back into relational care. AANP's provider survey data suggest otherwise. When clinicians in our network described their experience with existing AI documentation tools, the most common response was that the time savings were absorbed by increased patient volume expectations, not by longer or deeper individual encounters. Bickmore and Paasche-Orlow have documented that information technology deployments in health settings consistently underperform on relational outcomes because the institutional incentives surrounding them are misaligned with relational goals (Bickmore TW, Paasche-Orlow MK, American Journal of Health Behavior, 2012;36(3):367-377). That is not a technology problem. It is a policy and payment problem, and it is the problem HHS has the authority to address.⏎⏎AANP Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-OS-2024-0011 | Page 4⏎⏎AANP's specific policy recommendations, responsive to the RFI's questions regarding regulatory action and reimbursement design, are as follows:⏎⏎1. HHS should establish a moratorium on reimbursement approval for AI-assisted clinical decision support tools deployed in direct patient care contexts absent prospective evaluation data that includes both safety outcomes and relational-impact measures. "Prospective evaluation" means pre-deployment data collection, not post-market surveillance of tools already in widespread use. The 21st Century Cures Act's framework for software as a medical device provides a starting point, but it does not require relational-impact evaluation, and HHS should close that gap through rulemaking.⏎⏎2. Any reimbursement framework for AI CDSS tools developed through CMS or through value-based payment arrangements must require the collection of patient-reported experience measures (PREMs) as a condition of ongoing reimbursement. PREMs should specifically assess patients' perceptions of whether their clinician was present and attentive during the encounter, whether they felt heard, and whether the clinical interaction addressed concerns that the patient had not explicitly articulated. These are not soft metrics — they predict adherence, return-to-care rates, and downstream utilization in ways that are clinically and economically significant.⏎⏎3. HHS should commission, through AHRQ or through a dedicated funding mechanism within ONC, a research program specifically focused on the relational and deskilling dimensions of AI adoption in clinical care. This program should include longitudinal cohort studies of clinician reasoning capacity before and after AI CDSS deployment, qualitative research on patient experience of AI-mediated encounters, and health services research on whether AI-freed time in clinical practice is actually reinvested in relational care or absorbed by throughput pressure. The evidence base for relational harm from AI intermediation is currently thin not because the harm is implausible but because nobody has funded the research to document it. HHS should fund that research before deploying the tools at scale, not after.⏎⏎4. HHS should convene a formal stakeholder process — distinct from this RFI — specifically focused on the therapeutic alliance as a clinical safety variable. That process should include patient advocates, behavioral scientists, health services researchers, and front-line clinicians, and its output should be a conceptual framework for measuring relational quality that can be integrated into AI tool evaluation requirements.⏎⏎AANP Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-OS-2024-0011 | Page 5⏎⏎AANP recognizes that some of these recommendations will be characterized as obstructionist by stakeholders with commercial interests in accelerated AI deployment, and AANP wants to be clear that this characterization would be inaccurate. There are AI applications in clinical care that AANP supports and has supported actively: ambient documentation tools that reduce administrative burden without mediating clinical reasoning, population health analytics that help practices identify patients who have fallen out of care, and image analysis tools that assist specialist interpretation without displacing it. The distinctions that matter are not between "AI" and "no AI" but between deployment contexts and incentive structures that preserve relational clinical practice and those that erode it. AANP's concern is specifically with the RFI's framing, which does not make these distinctions, and with the reimbursement and regulatory infrastructure that framing would produce if left unchallenged.⏎⏎AANP Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-OS-2024-0011 | Page 6⏎⏎There is one more dimension of this issue that AANP wants to name, even though it is harder to operationalize than the recommendations above. The patients in AANP's liver disease registry — the 47,000-plus individuals whose care trajectories we have followed across 38 hepatology centers — are not, in aggregate, the patients who will benefit most from AI productivity enhancements. They are disproportionately low-income, disproportionately from communities with limited specialist access, disproportionately from groups whose medical histories include encounters with healthcare systems that did not listen to them. For those patients, the therapeutic relationship is not a nice-to-have. It is frequently the mechanism by which they stay engaged with care at all. A system that optimizes for throughput and algorithmic consistency will, in AANP's assessment, systematically underserve those patients even if its technical performance metrics look excellent. The 63% of early-stage fibrosis patients in our registry who had no documented specialist encounter within 12 months of an abnormal non-invasive test result — those patients were not lost to follow-up because the algorithm failed. They were lost because nobody called them back. Nobody sat with them and helped them understand what "fibrosis" means and why it matters and what comes next. No AI system currently on the market or in development addresses that problem. HHS's RFI, in its current form, does not either, and AANP urges the Department to revisit its framing before translating this solicitation into policy.⏎⏎For questions regarding this submission, contact the AANP Policy and Regulatory Affairs team at policy@aanp.org⏎⏎AANP Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-OS-2024-0011 | Page 7⏎⏎NOTE: Appendix A (AANP/GLI Joint Registry Analysis, 47,312 patient records, 38 hepatology centers, data through Q3 2024) and Appendix B (2023 State of Liver Disease Policy Survey, full methodology and crosstabulations) are being submitted as separate attachments. SYNTH-0019♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔James Adams♔PathAI♔♔♔♔♔Tapestryhealth Office of Compliance and Clinical Informatics⏎Comments Submitted to HHS Office of the Deputy Secretary / ASTP-ONC⏎Re: Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitted by: James Adams, Chief Compliance Officer, PathAI / Tapestryhealth Compliance Function⏎Date: January 2025⏎⏎Tapestryhealth Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 1⏎⏎MARKET CONCENTRATION AND THE POLITICAL ECONOMY OF THIS RFI⏎⏎Tapestryhealth operates across 47 affiliated clinical sites and submits these comments based on a Q1-Q4 2024 internal compliance review that produced findings we believe are directly relevant to the framing of this Request for Information (Tapestryhealth Office of Compliance and Clinical Informatics, 2024). That review found that 68% of AI-assisted decision-support tools currently deployed across our network lack audit trail documentation sufficient to satisfy existing OIG guidance on algorithmic accountability (Office of Inspector General, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, OIG-CPG-2023-04, 2023). We also found that 23% of claim denials involving AI-flagged coding recommendations during that same period were attributed specifically to insufficient documentation of model version provenance and validation status. We raise these findings not to rehearse compliance failures, but because they illuminate something about the political economy of this RFI that we think HHS needs to confront directly.⏎⏎The framing of this RFI is, at its core, a vendor-friendly document. The questions are organized around acceleration, adoption, and reimbursement modernization in ways that take for granted that the primary obstacle to beneficial AI in clinical care is regulatory friction rather than market structure. That premise is contestable, and Tapestryhealth submits that HHS should examine it carefully before proceeding. The health information technology market is structurally concentrated among a small number of large EHR vendors and AI technology incumbents whose lobbying capacity and public comment infrastructure allow them to shape regulatory frameworks in ways that entrench their market position (Gee & Bhatt, 2023, Health Affairs, 42(8), 1102-1111; Dafny & Lee, 2022, New England Journal of Medicine, 386(14), 1289-1292). We are not making a speculative claim. The Federal Trade Commission made a substantially similar observation in its October 2023 policy paper on generative AI and health data, which identified market concentration risks and regulatory gaps that have not been resolved in the intervening period (Federal Trade Commission, 2023). The RFI's emphasis on public-private partnerships and CRADA mechanisms, without any corresponding attention to how those mechanisms will be governed or who will control the resulting data and model assets, is a structural choice that will benefit large incumbents disproportionately.⏎⏎Tapestryhealth Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎REIMBURSEMENT MODERNIZATION AND LOCK-IN DYNAMICS⏎⏎Tapestryhealth's compliance analysis focuses specifically on two areas addressed in this RFI: the proposed reimbursement modernization framework and the CRADA and public-private data partnership structures. We do not address clinical safety, workforce, or liability questions in this submission, which are covered in separate filings from our clinical informatics leadership.⏎⏎On reimbursement, the concern is straightforward. The Congressional Budget Office's 2024 working paper on federal reimbursement policy and AI in clinical settings documented that distributional effects across provider types are not neutral, and that smaller and independent providers face substantially higher administrative burdens in navigating AI-related billing and coverage processes than large integrated health systems (Congressional Budget Office, CBO Working Paper 2024-07). Tapestryhealth is a mid-sized affiliated network, and our experience is consistent with that finding. The proposed reimbursement modernization, as framed in this RFI, will primarily benefit organizations that have already made large capital investments in AI infrastructure integrated with dominant EHR platforms. Adler-Milstein and Pfeifer (2022) documented that EHR switching costs are substantial enough to constitute genuine market lock-in, with hospital transition data showing that once an institution is embedded in a given vendor's infrastructure, the effective cost of switching exceeds the potential benefit in almost all scenarios (Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, 29(6), 987-996). A reimbursement framework that is operationalized through EHR-integrated workflows will replicate this dynamic at the AI layer. Underperforming AI products embedded in dominant EHR platforms will be insulated from competitive accountability because the cost of replacing them exceeds the cost of tolerating their failures.⏎⏎The American Hospital Association's March 2024 survey of health system AI procurement found that contract terms from dominant AI vendors routinely include data-use provisions that transfer substantial value from healthcare systems to technology companies, often without health system leadership fully understanding the scope of those provisions at signing (AHA Research Series, March 2024). Schulman and Richman (2023) made the same point more bluntly: the economics of healthcare AI, as currently structured, systematically displace clinical value toward vendor profit rather than patient welfare (JAMA, 329(19), 1651-1658). Tapestryhealth does not think HHS has adequately grappled with this in the RFI's framing of reimbursement modernization.⏎⏎o The proposed coverage structures do not address proprietary model opacity.⏎o There is no proposed requirement that reimbursement eligibility be conditioned on audit trail documentation meeting OIG standards.⏎o There is no mechanism to prevent reimbursement benefits from flowing to AI products that have not been validated against real-world performance benchmarks at the site of deployment.⏎o The CRADA structures described in the RFI contain no proposed conflict-of-interest standards governing what participating vendors can do with data generated through federally-subsidized partnerships.⏎⏎Tapestryhealth Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎CRADA MECHANISMS AND PROPRIETARY CAPTURE⏎⏎Maddox, Rumsfeld, and Payne (2023) examined public-private data partnerships in healthcare AI and identified a consistent pattern they described as "proprietary capture," in which nominally public partnership structures produce model assets and data derivatives that are effectively controlled by private vendors with no durable public-benefit obligations attached (npj Digital Medicine, 6(1), 44). The CRADA mechanisms described in this RFI appear to reproduce this structure without modification. HHS has not proposed any requirement that model outputs or validation datasets generated through CRADA partnerships be made available for independent audit, that participating vendors disclose the terms under which they retain rights to derivative data products, or that there be any public accountability mechanism if a CRADA-developed AI tool underperforms after deployment at scale.⏎⏎We want to be direct about what we think is happening here, because Tapestryhealth believes the compliance and governance community has an obligation to name it. Kesselheim and Avorn (2022) described a pattern in health technology policy in which the framing of a regulatory question itself constitutes a form of capture, because it defines which solutions are visible and which are not (Milbank Quarterly, 100(3), 712-738). The framing of this RFI, which takes AI acceleration as the governing objective and treats regulatory friction as the primary obstacle, makes invisible a range of policy options that would prioritize market accountability, vendor transparency, and public control of federally-subsidized data assets. Those options are not radical. They include, for example, conditioning reimbursement eligibility on public disclosure of model version history and validation status, requiring that CRADA participants submit to independent audit of model performance and data-use practices, and establishing a mandatory conflict-of-interest review process before any public-private AI data partnership is finalized. None of these appear in the RFI.⏎⏎Tapestryhealth Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 4⏎⏎SPECIFIC REQUESTS AND CONCERNS⏎⏎Tapestryhealth urges HHS to take the following actions before finalizing any acceleration policy emerging from this RFI:⏎⏎1. Commission an independent market-structure analysis of the health AI vendor landscape, with specific attention to concentration ratios, EHR integration dependencies, and switching cost dynamics, prior to finalizing any reimbursement modernization framework. This analysis should be conducted by an entity with no financial relationship to any EHR vendor or AI technology company.⏎⏎2. Impose a moratorium on new public-private AI data partnerships, including those structured through CRADA mechanisms, until HHS has established conflict-of-interest standards governing participating vendors' rights to derivative data products and independent audit requirements for model performance and data-use practices.⏎⏎3. Condition any new reimbursement eligibility for AI-assisted clinical decision support on audit trail documentation meeting the standards set out in OIG-CPG-2023-04. Our Q4 2024 internal review found that this standard is not currently met by the majority of deployed tools across our network, which means that reimbursement modernization without this condition will primarily reward vendors whose products are already embedded in large health systems, not vendors whose products actually perform.⏎⏎Our analysis is that the comment process for this RFI has been structured in a way that gives large EHR vendors and AI incumbents a structural advantage, because they have the government relations infrastructure to submit detailed, technically sophisticated comments that shape the final regulatory text. Tapestryhealth is submitting these comments in part to put into the record that mid-sized affiliated networks with serious compliance functions do not share the premise that acceleration is the correct governing objective, and that the absence of market-structure analysis in the RFI's framing is a gap that should concern HHS as much as it concerns us.⏎⏎REFERENCES⏎⏎American Hospital Association. SYNTH-0022♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Susan Mitchell♔♔♔♔♔♔ON THE QUESTION OF WORKFORCE IMPACT AND PROFESSIONAL AUTONOMY⏎⏎My colleague Rosa was working a shift at our branch in the Bronx last October when she went into cardiac arrhythmia. The ER team later told her family that an AI-assisted ECG tool had flagged the irregularity seventeen minutes before any clinician caught it independently. I have spent the months since then reading whatever I can find on clinical AI implementation, and what I keep returning to is a discomfort that the literature supports but that this RFI does not adequately name: the question of what these tools will actually be used for, inside institutions that face relentless financial pressure, is not the same question as what they are capable of doing in controlled or ideal conditions.⏎⏎HHS is asking how to accelerate AI adoption in clinical settings. I want to respond specifically to the workforce dimension of that question, because I think the Department is at risk of accelerating a technology whose measurable patient-care benefits will be captured by administrators and vendors while the costs fall on the nurses, physicians, and care coordinators who are already working under conditions that Shanafelt et al. (2022), writing in Mayo Clinic Proceedings, documented as a clinician burnout crisis that worsened significantly between 2011 and 2020, predating the pandemic entirely. The tools being marketed to hospital systems right now are marketed as burnout-reduction solutions. Bates et al. (2021) in npj Digital Medicine did find genuine evidence that AI assistance can reduce cognitive load in emergency settings. But there is a meaningful gap between reducing cognitive load and reducing headcount, and the financial incentives facing health systems will, predictably, push toward the latter. National Nurses United documented this in their 2023 policy brief on AI and the healthcare workforce: administrators receiving AI-generated productivity metrics tend to interpret them as evidence that existing staff can absorb more patients per shift, not as evidence that staff are finally getting support. That is not a speculation about bad faith. It is a structural prediction about how cost-cutting institutions respond to efficiency data, and HHS should take it seriously as a patient safety consideration, not merely a labor one.⏎⏎The second problem, which I think is actually more serious and less discussed in this RFI's framing, is algorithmic performance monitoring of clinicians themselves. Kellogg, Valentine, and Christin (2020) in the Academy of Management Annals documented in considerable detail how algorithmic control systems in workplaces systematically erode professional autonomy and discretionary judgment, and their analysis applies directly to healthcare settings where AI tools generate real-time productivity data on how long a nurse spends with each patient, how quickly a physician closes an encounter note, how a care coordinator's caseload compares to a system-generated benchmark. Arndt et al. (2017) in the Annals of Family Medicine showed that primary care physicians were already spending more than half their working hours on EHR tasks rather than direct patient care, and that EHR event log data was being used to assess their productivity in ways that did not account for complexity. Adding AI-generated performance metrics to that environment does not reduce surveillance; it intensifies it. And there is a direct causal line between that kind of surveillance and patient harm, because a clinician who is being monitored against productivity benchmarks will, rationally, spend less time with difficult or slow patients, will document to the metric rather than to the clinical picture, and will suppress the kind of open-ended observation that catches what the algorithm missed. The seventeen minutes that mattered for Rosa's recovery depended on a clinician who was paying attention in a way that no algorithm had prompted. I genuinely worry about what happens to that kind of attention when the clinician is also being scored on throughput.⏎⏎I should note that Obermeyer et al. (2019) in Science demonstrated that AI tools trained on existing healthcare data can encode and amplify racial and socioeconomic bias in ways that are not visible in aggregate performance metrics. My Bronx community is majority Black and Latino and has higher rates of poverty than the city median. The patients who are most likely to be harmed by a surveilled, understaffed, demoralized clinical workforce are the same patients who are most likely to be harmed by biased algorithmic outputs. These are compounding risks, and the ONC's own issue brief on EHR adoption and usability acknowledged that health IT implementation has historically produced uneven benefits across patient populations.⏎⏎My specific request to HHS is this: any AI procurement in federally reimbursed settings should require, as a condition of reimbursement, three things. First, mandatory structured consultation with frontline clinical workers before any AI tool is deployed in their practice environment, with documentation that their input was considered. Second, an independent staffing-impact review conducted at six and eighteen months post-deployment, with results reported to CMS. Third, a clear regulatory prohibition on using AI-generated productivity or performance data as the primary basis for staffing ratio reductions. I recognize that the third of these will be contested by health systems on operational grounds. But without it, the first two are largely procedural gestures. The financial pressure to cut staffing will find a way to use whatever data is available to justify that cut, and "the AI said our nurses are efficient" is going to be a very hard argument to rebut in the absence of an explicit rule against it.⏎⏎I'd also note that the consultation requirement would need to specify what "frontline" means in practice, because in my reading of the literature, the people who get consulted in these processes are typically charge nurses and department heads rather than the floor nurses and♔♔2026-02-08T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-08T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔3♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare will be used by employers and insurers as a mechanism for workforce surveillance, productivity extraction, staffing cuts, and the devaluation of clinical expertise rather than genuine care improvement.♔individual♔high♔supportive♔New York♔librarian♔45♔When my colleague Rosa developed a sudden cardiac arrhythmia during her lunch break at the branch last October, the ER physicians told her family afterward that an AI-assisted ECG interpretation tool had flagged the irregularity seventeen minutes before any clinician independently caught it — time that, by the cardiologist's own account, made a measurable difference in her recovery. Our health IT practice works directly with clinical operations teams who are deploying, evaluating, or declining to deploy AI-assisted tools in real patient care environments. That experience is what grounds this submission.⏎⏎Booz Allen Hamilton Comments | HHS AI RFI 2025 | Page 2⏎⏎The framing of this RFI gives us genuine pause. The Department is asking what actions it can take to accelerate AI adoption, and that framing presupposes that speed is the right variable to optimize. Booz Allen's position is that it is not. The more appropriate policy question is what conditions need to be met before AI tools are deployed at scale in clinical settings, and what regulatory architecture will ensure that deployment decisions are made by accountable humans with adequate information rather than by market pressure or reimbursement incentives alone. The RFI's acceleration framing, taken at face value, risks treating the current pace of AI adoption as a problem to be solved rather than as a reasonable response to genuine uncertainty about safety, equity, and accountability.⏎⏎This is not a theoretical concern. Booz Allen's internal benchmark study, conducted across 38,000 patient cases in oncology practice networks spanning more than 500 sites, found that interoperability gaps between EHR systems and AI inference engines were the single most frequently cited barrier to full platform utilization, reported by 68% of participating sites. The same study found that algorithm-assisted patient screening for clinical trial matching reduced median time-to-enrollment by 47% compared to manual workflows. Both findings are real. But the Department should notice what they mean together: the performance gains are real, and the structural barriers are also real, and those barriers are not primarily the result of over-regulation. They are the result of fragmented technical infrastructure, inadequate data governance, and the absence of clear accountability standards for AI-assisted clinical decisions. Removing regulatory friction without first addressing those structural conditions will not produce safe, equitable AI adoption. It will produce faster deployment of tools whose failure modes are not yet well understood, into clinical environments that are not yet equipped to catch those failures.⏎⏎Booz Allen Hamilton Comments | HHS AI RFI 2025 | Page 3⏎⏎PRECAUTIONARY DEPLOYMENT STANDARDS BEFORE ACCELERATION⏎⏎The Department should, as a threshold matter, establish preconditions for AI deployment in clinical care that must be demonstrated before any tool is eligible for reimbursement incentives or regulatory accommodation. Booz Allen recommends that HHS, working with ONC and CMS, develop a tiered risk classification framework for clinical AI tools that draws from but goes beyond the FDA's existing Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) guidance. The FDA's current framework, articulated in its 2021 action plan for AI/ML-based SaMD (86 Fed. Reg. 2987), addresses pre-market performance requirements but does not adequately specify post-market surveillance obligations or real-world equity monitoring requirements. That gap needs to close before the Department creates new incentives for adoption.⏎⏎Specifically, Booz Allen recommends the following preconditions for any AI tool deployed in clinical care settings with federal reimbursement support:⏎⏎1. Prospective performance validation on patient populations that are demographically representative of the intended deployment environment, with disaggregated results by race, ethnicity, sex, age, and insurance status. A tool that performs well on aggregate AUROC metrics may still produce systematically worse outputs for Medicaid patients or patients from underrepresented racial groups. Booz Allen has seen this pattern in multiple deployments, and it is not caught by standard pre-market validation protocols.⏎⏎2. Mandatory post-deployment monitoring at intervals no greater than 90 days, with automatic suspension triggers if model performance degrades beyond pre-specified thresholds. The clinical AI literature is clear that model drift is a real and recurring problem (see, e.g., Nestor et al., "Feature Engineering Improves Prediction of Hospital Mortality with Machine Learning," Critical Care Medicine, 2019), and current deployment practice does not consistently account for it.⏎⏎3. Clear documentation, available to treating clinicians at the point of care, of what the AI tool was trained on, what its known failure modes are, and under what circumstances its outputs should not be relied upon. This is not asking for something exotic. The ONC's 2024 Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability (HTI-1) final rule at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) already requires certain transparency disclosures for clinical decision support. Those requirements should be extended and strengthened to cover all AI tools that influence clinical decisions, not just those that meet the current CDS definition.⏎⏎4. Explicit assignment of clinical accountability to a licensed human clinician for any AI-assisted decision that affects patient diagnosis, treatment, or care pathway. The Department should be direct about this: AI tools do not make decisions. Clinicians make decisions. The regulatory architecture should make that accountability visible and enforceable, not obscure it through language about "AI-assisted" workflows that diffuses responsibility without locating it anywhere specific.⏎⏎Booz Allen Hamilton Comments | HHS AI RFI 2025 | Page 4⏎⏎THE REIMBURSEMENT QUESTION IS WHERE THIS GETS COMPLICATED⏎⏎Booz Allen wants to be honest that the reimbursement question is harder than the RFI's framing suggests, and we are not certain that any single reimbursement model gets this right. CMS has begun exploring new payment pathways for AI-assisted services, and there is genuine tension between two legitimate concerns. On one side, the absence of reimbursement pathways is a real barrier to deployment of tools that have demonstrated safety and effectiveness. Clinicians and health systems cannot sustain AI infrastructure at scale without payment support, and that is a fair point. On the other side, creating reimbursement incentives before precautionary standards are in place will accelerate adoption for financial reasons rather than clinical ones, and the history of health IT incentive programs -- including the HITECH Act's Meaningful Use program, which drove EHR adoption at a pace that outran usability and interoperability standards -- should give the Department pause.⏎⏎Booz Allen Hamilton Comments | HHS AI RFI 2025 | Page 5⏎⏎Booz Allen's recommendation is that CMS delay the creation of AI-specific reimbursement codes or add-on payments under the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule until the precautionary deployment standards described above are in place and operational. The sequencing matters. If reimbursement incentives arrive first, market dynamics will drive adoption regardless of whether the safety and accountability infrastructure exists. The Department has seen this movie before. The Office of Inspector General's 2023 report on EHR-related fraud (OIG Report OEI-01-20-00510) documented how incentive-driven adoption created compliance vulnerabilities that are still being worked through years later. The AI context is different in some respects but the underlying dynamic -- incentives driving adoption faster than governance can keep pace -- is the same.⏎⏎There is a separate concern about AI in insurance and prior authorization decisions that Booz Allen believes the Department should address directly and separately from the clinical care context. The use of AI tools by payers to automate prior authorization denials has been documented extensively (see, e.g., the Senate Finance Committee's June 2023 report on prior authorization in Medicare Advantage), and it raises accountability questions that are categorically different from AI tools that support clinician decision-making. A physician using an AI screening tool to identify clinical trial candidates retains clinical judgment and can override or disregard the AI's output. A beneficiary whose prior authorization request is denied by an automated system has no equivalent check unless the appeals process is functional and accessible. Booz Allen urges HHS to treat these two contexts as requiring distinct regulatory frameworks, and to resist any tendency to allow the positive use cases in clinical care to provide cover for problematic uses in coverage and payment administration.⏎⏎Booz Allen Hamilton Comments | HHS AI RFI 2025 | Page 6⏎⏎INTEROPERABILITY AS A PREREQUISITE, NOT AN AFTERTHOUGHT⏎⏎The 68% figure cited above -- the share of oncology sites in Booz Allen's benchmark study that identified EHR-to-AI-inference-engine interoperability gaps as the primary barrier to platform utilization -- points to something the Department needs to take seriously before it designs any acceleration program. AI tools do not operate in isolation. They depend on structured, timely, accurate data feeds from EHR systems, lab systems, imaging systems, and increasingly from patient-generated data sources. When those feeds are incomplete, delayed, or formatted inconsistently, AI outputs degrade in ways that are not always visible to the clinician relying on them. A clinical decision support tool trained on clean, complete data from an academic medical center will not perform the same way when deployed against the fragmented, variable-quality data environments that characterize community hospitals and independent practices.⏎⏎The Department's existing interoperability authorities under the 21st Century Cures Act, including ONC's API requirements at 45 CFR 170.315(g)(10) and the information blocking provisions at 45 CFR 171, are the right foundation, but they were not designed with AI data dependencies in mind. Booz Allen recommends that ONC initiate a focused rulemaking or technical standards process to define minimum data quality and completeness standards for EHR data used as inputs to clinical AI tools. This is not a small undertaking, and we are not suggesting it can be done quickly. But it needs to happen before the Department creates incentives for AI adoption at scale, or the result will be widespread deployment of tools operating on data inputs that do not meet the quality thresholds those tools were validated against. That is a patient safety problem, and it is one that will not show up immediately in outcomes data because the failure modes are often silent.⏎⏎Booz Allen Hamilton Comments | HHS AI RFI 2025 | Page 7⏎⏎The TEFCA framework, while still maturing, offers one potential mechanism for establishing shared data quality expectations across participating networks. ONC should consider whether TEFCA participation requirements can be used to establish AI-readiness standards for data exchange, including minimum field completion rates, latency requirements for near-real-time AI inference use cases, and standardized approaches to handling data provenance and audit trails. Booz Allen has worked with several TEFCA Qualified Health Information Networks and the variation in data quality across those networks is substantial -- far more substantial than the current framework's governance requirements address. Without some floor on data quality, acceleration of AI adoption will produce adoption of unreliable AI, and the clinical and liability consequences of that will fall on patients and clinicians rather than on the vendors whose tools are performing below their validated specifications.⏎⏎Booz Allen Hamilton Comments | HHS AI RFI 2025 | Page 8⏎⏎HUMAN RESPONSIBILITY AT EVERY DECISION POINT⏎⏎Booz Allen wants to close on the accountability question because it is the one that the Department's RFI addresses least directly and that Booz Allen believes is most important. The question of who is responsible when an AI-assisted clinical decision goes wrong is not yet settled in federal regulation, in state licensing law, or in the clinical liability framework. That ambiguity is not a neutral condition. It creates an environment in which AI tools can be deployed in ways that diffuse clinical accountability without providing any mechanism for patients or regulators to identify where a decision was made and by whom.⏎⏎The Department should issue clear guidance -- and eventually pursue rulemaking -- establishing that the use of an AI tool in any clinical decision does not transfer, share, or reduce the accountability of the licensed clinician who makes that decision. This should be stated plainly and without the hedging language that tends to appear in federal AI guidance documents. The existing literature on automation bias (see Parasuraman & Manzey, "Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation," Human Factors, 2010) is clear that clinicians under time pressure will frequently defer to AI outputs without adequately evaluating them, particularly when the AI output is presented with high confidence scores. The regulatory framework should account for that behavioral reality, not assume it away by stating that humans remain "in the loop."⏎⏎Booz Allen Hamilton Comments | HHS AI RFI 2025 | Page 9⏎⏎Concretely, Booz Allen recommends:⏎⏎o Mandatory disclosure to patients when an AI tool has been used in their diagnosis or treatment recommendation, including what the tool recommended and whether the treating clinician agreed with or deviated from that recommendation. Patients have a right to know when an algorithm has influenced their care.⏎⏎o Prohibition on AI-only clinical decisions without human review in any setting receiving federal reimbursement. This should be a bright-line rule, not a default that can be contracted around.⏎⏎o Requirements that AI tool vendors maintain explainability documentation sufficient for a treating clinician to understand, in plain terms, why the tool produced a given output for a given patient. Black-box outputs in clinical settings are not acceptable when the stakes include patient safety. The FDA's discussion of transparency in its 2023 draft guidance on predetermined change control plans (88 Fed. Reg. 40436) gestures toward this but does not go far enough for high-stakes clinical applications.⏎⏎o Clear audit trail requirements for any AI-assisted clinical decision, including the data inputs the tool relied on, the version of the model in use at the time, and the clinician's documented response to the AI output. These audit trails should be retained in the patient's medical record and accessible for quality review and regulatory inspection.⏎⏎Booz Allen Hamilton Comments | HHS AI RFI 2025 | Page 10⏎⏎The Department should also be attentive to workforce implications that the RFI does not fully address. Clinical AI tools are frequently marketed as efficiency solutions, and there is pressure in some health system environments to use AI adoption as a rationale for reducing clinical staffing. Booz Allen is concerned that reimbursement models that reward AI utilization without requiring minimum human review standards could accelerate that dynamic. The appropriate use of AI in clinical care is to support clinician judgment, not to substitute for clinical staffing. HHS should make that principle explicit in any policy guidance it issues on clinical AI, and CMS should consider whether staffing standard requirements under the Medicare Conditions of Participation need to be updated to address AI-related substitution risks.⏎⏎One more thing worth flagging, and this is admittedly a somewhat different point from the above: the Department's RFI focuses on clinical care settings, but many of the AI tools being deployed in health systems operate across clinical and administrative functions simultaneously. A tool that schedules appointments, flags care gaps, and generates prior authorization requests may touch clinical decisions even if it is classified administratively. The regulatory framework should account for the actual function of AI tools, not just their nominal classification, or vendors will have strong incentives to classify tools in whatever category carries the lightest regulatory burden. ONC's existing approach to CDS classification under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) has already encountered this problem, and the AI context will make it significantly more acute.⏎⏎Booz Allen Hamilton Comments | HHS AI RFI 2025 | Page 11⏎⏎Booz Allen appreciates the opportunity to provide these comments and is available to discuss any of the issues raised here in greater detail. SYNTH-0025♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Charles Lee♔Society for Women's Health Research♔♔♔♔♔Society for Women's Health Research⏎Comments Submitted to HHS Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎RE: Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Federal Docket Submission — [Docket ID pending confirmation]⏎⏎⏎SWHR Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 1⏎⏎⏎EQUITY AUDITING AS A PRECONDITION, NOT AN AFTERTHOUGHT⏎⏎The Society for Women's Health Research (SWHR) submits these comments in response to HHS's request for input on regulatory and reimbursement actions to accelerate AI adoption in clinical care settings. SWHR recognizes the genuine potential of AI-assisted clinical decision support to improve diagnostic accuracy and reduce administrative burden. That said, the RFI as drafted contains a structural omission that, if left unaddressed, will systematically worsen health outcomes for the populations our organization exists to serve. The document solicits input on acceleration mechanisms — reimbursement pathways, R&D incentives, regulatory flexibility — without establishing any mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing or post-deployment bias surveillance requirements as threshold conditions for HHS endorsement or federal reimbursement. This is not a minor gap. It is the organizing problem around which every other policy recommendation in this comment is framed.⏎⏎The published evidence on algorithmic bias in clinical settings is now sufficiently developed that continued inaction constitutes a policy choice, not a knowledge deficit. Obermeyer et al. (2019) documented that a widely deployed commercial algorithm used to manage population health systematically underestimated illness severity in Black patients by using healthcare cost as a proxy for health need — a design choice that encoded historical access disparities directly into the model's outputs, reducing the proportion of Black patients identified for high-risk care management programs by more than half. Sjoding et al. (2020) demonstrated that pulse oximeters — a device so normalized in clinical settings that its bias was invisible to practitioners for decades — produced occult hypoxemia readings in Black patients at nearly three times the rate observed in white patients, a failure that almost certainly contributed to preventable deterioration during COVID-19 hospitalization surges. These are not edge cases. Gianfrancesco et al. (2018) identified multiple categories of structural bias in EHR-derived training data, including differential documentation rates, socioeconomic confounding, and missing data patterns that disproportionately affect Medicaid populations and patients receiving care in safety-net institutions. Seyyed-Kalantari et al. (2021) found that AI algorithms applied to chest radiographs in under-served populations systematically underdiagnosed pathology relative to performance benchmarks derived from academic medical center datasets. Adamson and Smith (2018) raised parallel concerns about dermatology AI trained predominantly on lighter skin tones, with predictable implications for diagnostic accuracy in patients of color. Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones (2020) documented how race-correction adjustments embedded in legacy clinical algorithms — including kidney function estimators and spirometry reference equations — carry discriminatory assumptions forward into AI systems that incorporate those outputs as input features. Char, Shah, and Magnus (2018) articulated the ethical architecture of this problem clearly: AI systems do not generate bias independently; they inherit and scale the biases present in the data and institutional structures from which they were trained.⏎⏎⏎SWHR Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎⏎THE COMPOUNDING PROBLEM OF AUTOMATION BIAS IN COMMUNITY SETTINGS⏎⏎What makes the acceleration framing in this RFI particularly concerning is the combination of two effects that, taken together, produce harm that is worse than either produces alone. First, Cabitza, Rasoini, and Gensini (2017) documented the phenomenon of automation bias in clinical settings — the well-characterized tendency of clinicians to defer to algorithmic outputs even when those outputs conflict with clinical observation, particularly when the AI system presents its recommendations with high apparent confidence. Sendak et al. (2020) observed in a qualitative study of deep learning deployment at Duke University Health System that clinicians frequently described AI outputs as authoritative in ways that suppressed independent diagnostic reasoning. Second — and this is the part the RFI does not adequately grapple with — model validation studies are overwhelmingly conducted in large, well-resourced academic medical centers. Wong et al. (2021) conducted external validation of a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model and found that performance degraded substantially when the model was applied outside the institution where it was developed, with concerning false-alert patterns that consumed nursing time without improving outcomes. The Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology's 2023 Algorithmic Bias Issue Brief explicitly flagged the gap between validation-site performance and real-world performance in community hospitals and rural facilities as a priority concern. What this means in practice: clinicians in under-resourced settings, where marginalized patients disproportionately receive care, are most likely to encounter AI systems performing below their published benchmarks, and are simultaneously most subject to automation bias effects that suppress the clinical skepticism that might otherwise catch those errors. Price, Gerke, and Cohen (2019) noted that liability frameworks for AI-assisted decision-making remain unsettled, which further complicates the institutional incentives for error reporting in these settings.⏎⏎SWHR therefore requests that HHS condition any federal reimbursement or regulatory endorsement of clinical AI systems on the following minimum requirements:⏎⏎1. Mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing, with stratified performance reporting disaggregated by race, ethnicity, sex, socioeconomic status, and geographic setting (rural/urban/safety-net), conducted by an independent third party rather than the deploying institution or vendor.⏎⏎2. Ongoing post-deployment bias surveillance protocols, with defined reporting thresholds and a federal repository for aggregated findings, modeled on the adverse event reporting infrastructure that governs medical devices under 21 CFR Part 803.⏎⏎3. Requirement that validation datasets for any HHS-reimbursed AI tool include a statistically adequate representation of Medicaid populations and patients from federally qualified health centers, not only from academic medical center cohorts.⏎⏎HHS has the regulatory authority and the evidentiary basis to act on these requirements now. The question of whether AI can accelerate care delivery has a clear answer. The question of whether HHS will establish the accountability architecture before deployment scales is the one this RFI should be answering, and the current draft does not.⏎⏎SWHR notes that the reimbursement coding inconsistencies documented in the 2024 Texas Medical Association survey — 38 distinct denial scenarios across four health systems — likely fall disproportionately on practices serving lower-income and rural patients, which further compounds♔♔2026-01-16T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-16T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔3♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI systems in healthcare inherit and amplify racial, socioeconomic, and institutional biases from training data, and their apparent authority makes those biases harder to detect and correct than human error.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔supportive♔Idaho♔policy director♔44♔A 2024 Texas Medical Association survey of 5,200 active physician members found that 61% reported using at least one AI-assisted diagnostic or administrative tool in their practice, yet 74% of those users identified inconsistent payer reimbursement policies as the primary barrier to deeper integration. SYNTH-0026♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Nancy Nelson♔Duke Clinical Research Institute♔♔♔♔♔RE: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket Submitted by: Nancy Nelson, Postdoctoral Fellow, Duke Clinical Research Institute⏎Date of Submission: March 2025⏎⏎⏎THE FRAMING PROBLEM⏎⏎The 2024 CHIME survey of 610 health system CIOs and senior IT executives deserves to be taken seriously. The finding that 67% of respondents identified the absence of clear HHS guidance on AI validation and post-deployment monitoring as the single greatest barrier to scaling clinical AI tools is a meaningful data point, and the documented average delay of 14 months in procurement decisions is a genuine institutional burden. These are not trivial concerns. Health systems serving high-proportion Medicare and Medicaid populations face real resource constraints, and the CHIME AI Task Force policy brief's documentation of interoperability failures around model cards and FHIR-based performance metadata reflects genuine technical friction (CHIME AI Task Force, 2024).⏎⏎But the inference HHS appears to draw from this evidence — that regulatory uncertainty is a problem to be dissolved rather than, in part, a democratic signal to be respected — is the precise point this comment contests. The RFI's stated goal of reducing "uncertainty that impedes AI innovation" reframes the deliberative function of regulatory scrutiny as an obstacle. That reframing is not neutral. It is a political choice about which values governance should serve, and it is a choice that HHS does not have the unilateral democratic mandate to make on behalf of the public.⏎⏎The remainder of this comment develops two arguments. First, that the embedding of AI systems in clinical infrastructure constitutes a form of institutional lock-in that forecloses future democratic choices in ways that require explicit democratic authorization before any acceleration posture is adopted. Second, that the opacity of proprietary clinical AI systems makes meaningful democratic oversight structurally impossible under current frameworks, concentrating consequential decision-making power in corporate entities with no accountability to local communities or patients. This comment does not address clinical safety or algorithmic bias in depth — those dimensions are addressed in other submissions — but focuses strictly on questions of governance, reversibility, and democratic legitimacy.⏎⏎⏎THE LOCK-IN PROBLEM IS NOT METAPHORICAL⏎⏎When health economists write about lock-in dynamics in healthcare markets, they typically mean contractual dependencies or switching costs (Dafny & Lee, 2016). Those mechanisms are real, but the lock-in problem with clinical AI is considerably more severe, and the mechanisms are worth naming with some precision.⏎⏎The first mechanism is the atrophy of institutional knowledge. When clinical workflows are reorganized around AI-generated outputs — whether risk stratification scores, triage recommendations, or documentation assistance — the tacit expertise that previously resided in clinical staff begins to erode. This is not speculative; it is a well-documented feature of automation dependency in complex sociotechnical systems. Coiera (2019) described this dynamic as "the last mile" problem: the practical knowledge required to function independently of an AI system degrades as clinicians habituate to deferring to it. Within a period of years, not decades, the institutional capacity to reverse a deployment decision atrophies even when documented harms accumulate. The decision to adopt, in other words, is not symmetrical with the decision to unadopt.⏎⏎The second mechanism is staffing reorganization. Health systems that deploy AI-assisted clinical decision support tools do not simply add a tool to an existing workflow; they restructure labor around that tool's outputs. Roles are redefined, supervision models shift, and in some cases, staffing ratios are recalibrated on the assumption that AI augmentation reduces the need for certain categories of human judgment (Topol, 2019; Shortliffe & Sepúlveda, 2018). Once those staffing changes are institutionalized — embedded in job descriptions, budgets, and collective bargaining agreements — the human redundancy required to safely disengage from the AI system may no longer exist.⏎⏎The third mechanism is contractual dependency. Proprietary AI systems for clinical use are typically licensed under multi-year enterprise agreements with significant switching costs and, in many cases, data-sharing provisions that make the health system's own patient data partially inaccessible or operationally entangled with the vendor's model improvement pipeline. The practical freedom to exit an AI deployment is therefore constrained not only by internal knowledge atrophy and staffing reorganization but by the legal architecture of the contracts governing the deployment.⏎⏎Taken together, these mechanisms mean that the decision to deploy a proprietary clinical AI system at scale is not a reversible experiment. It is, in a meaningful sense, a permanent structural commitment — or at minimum, one that becomes practically irreversible within a window far shorter than the democratic and regulatory learning cycles that would ordinarily govern major changes to medical practice. HHS's accelerationist framing, which treats deployment as the goal and oversight as friction, is not merely premature. It is structurally anti-democratic, because it forecloses future democratic choices before the public has had a meaningful opportunity to make them.⏎⏎⏎DEMOCRATIC OPTION VALUE AND THE PRECAUTIONARY DEMOCRATIC PRINCIPLE⏎⏎Democratic theory has long recognized that the foreclosure of future choices is itself a political act requiring authorization. The concept of option value — borrowed from financial theory but applied to democratic choice by theorists including Sheila Jasanoff — holds that preserving the capacity to make different choices in the future has intrinsic value, and that actions which irreversibly foreclose options impose a cost on democratic self-governance that cannot be recovered through subsequent deliberation (Jasanoff, 2016). This is not an argument against technological change. It is an argument that the pace and architecture of technological embedding in public institutions must be subject to democratic authorization, not merely administrative discretion.⏎⏎HHS is a federal agency operating under delegated statutory authority. That authority does not include a mandate to determine, on behalf of the American public, that medicine should be reorganized around proprietary AI infrastructure before adequate democratic deliberation has occurred. The RFI itself, while a welcome gesture toward public input, is not a substitute for that deliberation. Soliciting comments from industry stakeholders and researchers through a federal docket is a far cry from the kind of structured, inclusive, and adequately resourced democratic deliberation that a decision of this magnitude warrants. The population that would bear the consequences of accelerated AI deployment in clinical care — patients in rural communities, elderly Medicare beneficiaries, Medicaid-enrolled populations with limited ability to exit to alternative care settings — is not meaningfully represented in a CHIME survey of 610 health system CIOs.⏎⏎What this comment proposes is the adoption of something that might be called a precautionary democratic principle for clinical AI governance: the recognition that where a technology's deployment involves irreversible institutional change, where the mechanisms of that irreversibility operate faster than democratic learning cycles, and where the affected populations lack meaningful exit options, the burden of justification rests with those who would accelerate deployment, not those who would require additional deliberation. This principle is not novel. Versions of it appear in Mazzucato and Entsminger's (2021) analysis of public-option models in digital health governance, in Pasquale's (2015) account of accountability deficits in algorithmic systems, and in Jasanoff's broader work on the ethics of technological governance. What is novel is its application to a federal agency's explicit framing of regulatory oversight as an obstacle to innovation.⏎⏎⏎THE OPACITY PROBLEM AND DEMOCRATIC ACCOUNTABILITY⏎⏎A second structural concern warrants attention, though this comment treats it more briefly. The opacity of proprietary clinical AI systems is not merely a technical limitation amenable to better documentation requirements. It is a condition that makes democratic oversight structurally impossible under current frameworks.⏎⏎Pasquale (2015) argued that algorithmic systems whose internal logic cannot be audited concentrate decision-making power in ways that are qualitatively different from other forms of institutional power, because the opacity is not incidental but is actively maintained as a condition of competitive advantage. Clinical AI systems deployed under proprietary licensing arrangements are, in general, not auditable by the regulators who would nominally oversee them, the clinicians who deploy them, or the patients whose care they affect. Selbst and Barocas (2018) have written carefully about why the intuitive appeal of explainability requirements does not resolve this problem — explanation and auditability are not the same thing, and the former can be provided in ways that satisfy regulatory form while preserving substantive opacity. The Doshi-Velez et al. (2017) working paper on accountability of AI under law reached similar conclusions about the gap between legal requirements for explanation and genuine accountability.⏎⏎The consequence for democratic governance is not merely that individual patients cannot understand the systems affecting their care. It is that the institutions nominally responsible for democratic oversight — HHS, ONC, state health departments — lack the technical access to evaluate whether deployed systems are performing as represented, let alone whether the aggregate effects of widespread deployment are consistent with democratically established values. Obermeyer et al. (2019) documented this problem empirically in the context of a widely deployed population health algorithm, demonstrating that systematic racial bias had persisted undetected for years in a commercially deployed system. The detection required independent academic research, not regulatory oversight. That is a governance failure, not a technical one, and it illustrates why the opacity problem is inseparable from the democratic accountability problem.⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS REGARDING THE RFI'S REIMBURSEMENT QUESTIONS⏎⏎This comment focuses primarily on the RFI's questions regarding the regulatory and governance actions HHS might take to accelerate adoption, but one additional concern regarding reimbursement policy warrants direct statement.⏎⏎The RFI solicits input on reimbursement mechanisms that could reduce financial barriers to AI adoption. The concern here is straightforward:⏎⏎1. Reimbursement incentives are among the most powerful instruments available to HHS for shaping health system behavior. They operate at scale, they are difficult to retract once institutionalized, and they function as structural subsidies that accelerate deployment independent of whether adequate oversight frameworks exist.⏎⏎2. The deployment of reimbursement incentives for clinical AI tools before post-deployment monitoring standards, model card requirements, and audit mechanisms are in place would accelerate precisely the lock-in dynamics described above, while simultaneously reducing the financial incentive for health systems to invest in the institutional knowledge and staffing redundancy required to safely reverse those deployments.⏎⏎3. The populations most affected by premature deployment — Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries, rural patients, patients in safety-net institutions — are also the populations least likely to have exit options if deployed systems perform poorly.⏎⏎The CHIME survey documents that procurement delays are real and that legal uncertainty imposes costs. But the appropriate response to that uncertainty is not to reduce it by providing regulatory clarity in advance of adequate deliberation. It is to acknowledge that the uncertainty reflects the genuine unresolved state of democratic and scientific consensus about how clinical AI should be governed.⏎⏎⏎RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎This comment makes two recommendations, both of which are intentionally modest relative to the scope of the issues raised.⏎⏎First, HHS should commission an independent democratic deliberation process — structured along the lines of a citizens' assembly or deliberative mini-public, with adequate representation of patient populations, frontline clinicians, and community health advocates — before adopting any acceleration posture with respect to clinical AI. This is not a recommendation against eventual adoption. It is a recommendation that the decision about what pace and architecture of adoption is consistent with democratic values should be made through a process that is itself democratically legitimate. The RFI process does not meet that standard.⏎⏎Second, HHS should impose an interim moratorium on the development and deployment of reimbursement incentives designed to accelerate clinical AI adoption until post-deployment monitoring standards, model transparency requirements, and independent audit mechanisms are in place. The CHIME AI Task Force (2024) documented that interoperability constraints around model cards and performance metadata are already compounding procurement delays at institutions serving high-proportion Medicare and Medicaid populations. That documentation is an argument for addressing the interoperability infrastructure problem first — not for deploying reimbursement incentives that would accelerate adoption before the infrastructure exists to monitor what is being adopted.⏎⏎Neither of these recommendations is anti-technology. The research literature on clinical AI includes compelling evidence that well-governed deployment of AI tools can improve diagnostic accuracy and reduce clinician burden in specific, well-characterized contexts (Keane & Topol, 2018). The argument here is not that those benefits are illusory. It is that the governance architecture required to realize them equitably and reversibly does not yet exist, and that HHS's current framing — which treats the absence of that architecture as a reason to move faster, not a reason to build it first — has the causal logic inverted.⏎⏎The 14-month procurement delay documented in the CHIME survey is a genuine cost. But it is worth asking who bears that cost relative to the cost of accelerated lock-in in systems that cannot be audited, cannot be reversed without atrophying institutional knowledge, and whose performance in the specific populations served by safety-net institutions remains largely⏎⏎Duke Clinical Research Institute | HHS AI RFI Submission | March 2025♔♔2026-02-02T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-02T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔7♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Once AI systems are embedded in healthcare infrastructure, they become practically irreversible and resistant to democratic oversight, creating a permanent transfer of power from clinicians, patients, and regulators to technology vendors.♔academic_organization♔high♔supportive♔New Hampshire♔postdoctoral fellow♔38♔A 2024 CHIME survey of 610 health system CIOs and senior IT executives found that 67% identified the absence of clear HHS guidance on AI validation and post-deployment monitoring as the single greatest barrier to scaling clinical AI tools beyond pilot programs.
