SYNTH-0029♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Jessica Rivera♔Premier Inc.♔♔♔♔♔Premier Inc. Comments on HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information⏎Docket: HHS-2024-AI-RFI | 89 FR 22456⏎Submitted by: Jessica Rivera, Senior Vice President, Policy and Regulatory Affairs⏎Premier Inc., Charlotte, North Carolina⏎Date: April 2024⏎⏎Premier Inc. Comments | HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 1⏎⏎INTRODUCTION AND ORGANIZATIONAL GROUNDING⏎⏎Premier Inc. is a healthcare improvement company serving approximately 4,400 U.S. hospitals and health systems and more than 225,000 other provider organizations. Our organization's benchmarking and analytics infrastructure processes data from a substantial share of the U.S. healthcare market, and our policy engagement on health information technology spans more than a decade of active participation in ONC rulemaking, CMS payment reform, and interoperability standards development. We submit these comments in response to the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy and ONC's Health Sector AI Request for Information (89 FR 22456) with genuine respect for the Department's intent, but also with significant concern about the structural assumptions embedded in the RFI's framing.⏎⏎Our concern is not with the goal of accelerating beneficial AI adoption in clinical settings. Our concern is with the sequence and conditions under which acceleration is being proposed. The RFI as published is organized primarily around removing friction — regulatory, reimbursement-related, and administrative — from the AI deployment pathway. That framing assumes that friction is the primary obstacle to good outcomes. Our organization's benchmarking work, conducted across more than 1,200 healthcare facilities in collaboration with interoperability platform vendors, tells a different story. According to a 2024 InterSystems Corporation benchmarking report drawing on over 800 million patient record transactions annually, the leading cause of AI deployment stalls was not regulatory ambiguity or reimbursement uncertainty — it was data normalization failures, cited in 67% of deployment interruptions (InterSystems Corporation, 2024). That same study found that facilities with structured AI-readiness frameworks reduced integration timelines by 34% compared to facilities using ad hoc approaches. The implication is that the bottleneck is internal to health systems and is largely a data infrastructure problem, not a regulatory problem. HHS's acceleration agenda, as framed, does not address this. What it does address is clearing the path for vendor deployment — which is a different problem entirely, and one that benefits a different set of interests.⏎⏎Premier Inc. Comments | HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 2⏎⏎THE POLITICAL ECONOMY OF HEALTHCARE AI: WHAT THE RFI DOES NOT ASK⏎⏎The RFI solicits comment on regulatory actions, reimbursement modernization, and research-and-development investments HHS can make to accelerate AI adoption. What it does not ask — and what we think is the more consequential policy question — is who captures the value when AI is deployed at scale in clinical settings, and whether the market structure currently governing healthcare AI is capable of producing the outcomes HHS says it wants. We think HHS should be asking those questions before it commits to an acceleration agenda, and we are genuinely puzzled that they are absent from the RFI entirely.⏎⏎The healthcare AI market is structurally concentrated in ways that create serious alignment problems. A small number of large EHR vendors control the data environments through which most clinical AI tools must be deployed. Epic Systems alone serves approximately 38% of U.S. hospital beds. When AI tools require EHR integration to function — which most clinical decision support applications do — the EHR vendor effectively controls access to the deployment channel. Gans and Stern (2023) describe this dynamic as "platform envelopment," a process through which incumbent technology platforms extend their control into adjacent markets by leveraging their existing data and integration relationships (Gans & Stern, 2023, p. 104). In healthcare AI, platform envelopment means that the vendors best positioned to benefit from HHS's acceleration agenda are not necessarily the vendors with the best clinical products — they are the vendors with the deepest EHR integration relationships. That is a market structure problem, and reducing regulatory friction without addressing it will accelerate the wrong things.⏎⏎Dafny and Lee (2022) have documented the broader consequences of healthcare market concentration, including reduced quality, higher prices, and diminished responsiveness to patient and payer preferences (Dafny & Lee, 2022, p. 1331). The dynamics they describe in hospital and insurer markets are replicating themselves in health IT. The Federal Trade Commission's 2023 staff report on generative AI and the healthcare sector noted that incumbent EHR vendors and large technology companies have structural advantages in clinical AI markets that are likely to produce anti-competitive outcomes absent deliberate regulatory intervention (Federal Trade Commission, 2023, pp. 14–17). The FTC's analysis was produced independently of this RFI process, which makes its absence from the RFI's framing more notable, not less.⏎⏎Premier Inc. Comments | HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 3⏎⏎VENDOR LOCK-IN AND THE LIMITS OF INTEROPERABILITY MANDATES⏎⏎The RFI references interoperability as a mechanism for promoting AI adoption, and Premier Inc. strongly supports interoperability as a policy goal. But interoperability mandates, as currently structured, do not resolve the vendor lock-in problem in clinical AI — they may actually make it worse by creating a veneer of openness that legitimizes proprietary ecosystems without meaningfully constraining them. Adler-Milstein and Pfeifer (2023) examined the practical effects of ONC's interoperability rules on EHR market competition and found that while FHIR-based APIs expanded data portability in limited technical respects, they did not reduce switching costs or competitive dependency on incumbent vendors (Adler-Milstein & Pfeifer, 2023, p. 815). The study concluded that interoperability mandates, absent structural requirements around data portability, contract terms, and API pricing, function primarily as compliance exercises rather than as market-opening interventions.⏎⏎This matters enormously for clinical AI because the integration dependencies that create lock-in are not primarily at the data access layer — they are at the workflow layer. When a health system deploys an AI-assisted clinical decision support tool that is embedded in its EHR's native interface, the switching cost is not just the cost of moving data. It is the cost of retraining clinical staff, rebuilding workflow integrations, renegotiating contracts, and absorbing the productivity loss during transition. These costs are prohibitive for most health systems, and they insulate underperforming products from competitive pressure in ways that have no analog in markets with lower switching costs. A clinical AI product that produces suboptimal recommendations but is deeply embedded in a health system's EHR workflow will persist not because it is performing well, but because the cost of replacing it is too high. HHS's acceleration agenda, by encouraging rapid deployment before adequate performance standards exist, will accelerate the accumulation of these integration dependencies — and the lock-in they create will outlast whatever regulatory framework HHS eventually puts in place to govern AI performance.⏎⏎Our organization has observed this dynamic directly in our network. Health systems that deployed early-generation sepsis prediction tools from major EHR vendors in 2019 and 2020 are still operating those tools despite mounting evidence that their performance in diverse patient populations is substantially below what was claimed at deployment. The GAO examined this problem in its 2023 report on AI in health care, noting that the lack of post-market performance monitoring requirements for clinical AI tools means that underperforming products remain in use long after their limitations become apparent (Government Accountability Office, 2023, pp. 28–31). Accelerating deployment without post-market surveillance requirements does not solve this problem; it scales it.⏎⏎Premier Inc. Comments | HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 4⏎⏎THE REIMBURSEMENT QUESTION AND WHO ACTUALLY BENEFITS⏎⏎The RFI asks specifically about reimbursement modernization as a mechanism for accelerating AI adoption. We want to engage with this question carefully, because we think the framing of reimbursement reform in the AI context obscures a significant value transfer that HHS has not adequately analyzed.⏎⏎The standard argument for AI reimbursement reform goes roughly as follows: health systems will not invest in AI deployment if they cannot recover the costs through reimbursement, therefore CMS should develop payment mechanisms that recognize AI-assisted clinical services. This argument has surface plausibility, but it conflates the interests of health systems with the interests of AI vendors in ways that are not analytically justified. When a health system deploys a clinical AI tool, the primary financial beneficiary of reimbursement is typically not the health system — it is the vendor, through licensing fees and implementation contracts that are paid regardless of whether the tool improves outcomes. A health system that receives a new AI-assisted billing code from CMS does not pocket that revenue; it uses it, in part, to fund the licensing costs of the AI product that justified the billing code. The net financial effect on health systems is ambiguous at best. The net financial effect on vendors is straightforwardly positive. This is not a hypothetical concern. The National Academy for State Health Policy's 2024 issue brief on public-private partnerships in health AI documented multiple instances in which reimbursement structures for AI-assisted services were designed in ways that primarily benefited vendor licensing models rather than health system economics or patient outcomes (National Academy for State Health Policy, 2024, pp. 8–11).⏎⏎The political economy of this dynamic is worth examining directly. Litan and Singer (2022) analyzed the influence of health IT vendors on ONC rulemaking processes and found systematic evidence that vendor interests shaped both the framing of regulatory problems and the design of proposed solutions, in ways consistent with Stigler's (1971) foundational account of regulatory capture — the process by which regulated industries come to control the regulatory bodies nominally overseeing them (Litan & Singer, 2022, pp. 18–22; Stigler, 1971, p. 5). We are not alleging that HHS has been captured in any crude sense. But the structure of this RFI — its focus on removing regulatory friction, its emphasis on public-private partnerships, its framing of reimbursement reform as a tool for accelerating vendor-developed products — is more consistent with a vendor-drafted policy agenda than with an independent assessment of what the healthcare system needs. Kesselheim, Avorn, and Sarpatwari (2023) made a related observation about federal health technology policy more broadly, documenting how commercial interests shape the framing of policy problems in ways that systematically favor proprietary solutions over public-interest alternatives (Kesselheim et al., 2023, p. 1565). The RFI's silence on market concentration, vendor lock-in, and the economics of public-private data partnerships is not a neutral omission.⏎⏎Premier Inc. Comments | HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 5⏎⏎THE PUBLIC DATA PROBLEM⏎⏎There is a specific issue within the public-private partnership question that deserves direct attention, and that the RFI's framing largely avoids. A substantial share of the training data underlying commercial clinical AI products was generated in federally funded healthcare settings, processed through federally subsidized EHR systems (the HITECH Act allocated approximately $36 billion in EHR adoption incentives), and validated against federally maintained claims databases and registries. When commercial vendors develop AI products using this data under Cooperative Research and Development Agreements or similar partnership structures, the public's contribution to the product's development is not reflected in the ownership or licensing terms. Health systems — including the public and nonprofit institutions that generated the underlying data — then pay licensing fees to access products that were built, in material part, from their own patients' records.⏎⏎The National Academy for State Health Policy's analysis identified this as a structural inequity in the current public-private AI partnership model, recommending that any federally facilitated AI development agreements include provisions for public ownership stakes, royalty arrangements, or preferential licensing terms for public and nonprofit health systems (National Academy for State Health Policy, 2024, p. 13). Our organization endorses this recommendation strongly. The RFI's discussion of public-private partnerships does not engage with this question at all, which is a significant gap. If HHS proceeds to expand public-private AI partnerships without addressing the ownership and licensing economics, it will be using public resources to subsidize the development of proprietary products that public institutions will then be required to license back at market rates. That is not an acceleration agenda for the health system — it is a subsidy program for technology vendors.⏎⏎Premier Inc. Comments | HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 6⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE SURVEY DATA AND WHAT IT ACTUALLY SHOWS⏎⏎Our organization's 2024 Global Summit survey of 94 health system administrators found that regulatory ambiguity around AI model validation and reimbursement pathways was ranked among the top three barriers to scaling AI-assisted clinical decision support tools. We want to be precise about what this finding does and does not show, because we think it is being read selectively in industry commentary on this RFI.⏎⏎The finding shows that health system administrators perceive regulatory ambiguity as a significant barrier. It does not show that regulatory ambiguity is the primary cause of poor AI adoption outcomes. Perception surveys of administrators will reliably identify regulatory friction as a top concern because regulatory compliance is a salient cost that administrators directly manage — it appears in their budgets, generates legal risk, and requires dedicated staff time. The structural market problems we have described in this comment — concentration, lock-in, misaligned vendor incentives, data ownership inequities — are less salient to individual administrators because they operate at a market level rather than an institutional level. An administrator who is paying too much for a locked-in AI product may perceive that problem as a contracting issue or a budget constraint rather than as a market structure failure. The fact that regulatory friction is more visible than market structure failure does not mean it is more consequential. HHS should be cautious about designing policy primarily in response to administrator perception surveys, particularly when those surveys were conducted at vendor-sponsored industry events where the framing of questions may itself reflect vendor priorities.⏎⏎Premier Inc. Comments | HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 7⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS REGARDING THE RFI'S REGULATORY QUESTIONS⏎⏎The RFI asks, among other things, what regulatory actions HHS can take to reduce barriers to AI adoption in clinical settings. We want to address this question directly, though our answer is probably not what the RFI's drafters anticipated.⏎⏎The regulatory actions most likely to produce good outcomes are not deregulatory. They are structural. The absence of mandatory pre-market performance benchmarking requirements for clinical AI tools — particularly tools that influence diagnostic and treatment decisions — means that vendors can make efficacy claims that are not independently verified before deployment. The GAO documented this gap in its 2023 report and recommended that HHS develop a clearer regulatory framework for AI tools that fall outside FDA's current oversight jurisdiction, noting that a significant share of clinical AI applications are structured as quality improvement tools or clinical decision support software in ways that place them outside existing regulatory pathways (Government Accountability Office, 2023, pp. 19–22). We agree with the GAO's analysis. The appropriate regulatory response is to close this gap, not to widen it in the name of acceleration.⏎⏎We are also concerned about the RFI's framing of AI governance as primarily a question of standards development and voluntary frameworks. Voluntary frameworks have a poor track record in health IT markets. The ONC's information blocking rules, which were implemented as mandatory requirements rather than voluntary guidance, produced measurably better compliance outcomes than predecessor voluntary interoperability initiatives precisely because they carried enforcement consequences. If HHS wants AI governance to produce meaningful behavioral change among vendors, it will need enforcement mechanisms, not just frameworks. The political economy literature on health IT regulation suggests that vendors will participate constructively in voluntary framework development processes while simultaneously structuring their commercial practices to minimize the operational impact of whatever framework emerges (Litan & Singer, 2022, p. 24). This is not cynicism about individual vendors — it is a predictable institutional response to regulatory environments that lack enforcement teeth.⏎⏎Premier Inc. Comments | HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 8⏎⏎There is also the question of what "acceleration" means in practice for health systems of different sizes and resource levels. The RFI's framing implicitly assumes that faster deployment is better deployment, and that the health systems currently not deploying AI are failing to capture value they should be capturing. Our organization works with health systems across the full size and resource spectrum, and our experience is that the health systems moving most cautiously on AI deployment are often doing so for well-founded reasons — inadequate data infrastructure, insufficient technical staff to evaluate vendor claims, prior negative experiences with health IT deployments that did not deliver promised benefits, and legitimate concern about clinical liability in the absence of clear performance standards. Treating these as barriers to overcome rather than as rational responses to an immature market is a policy framing error that will produce predictable harms. The InterSystems benchmarking data we cited earlier makes this concrete: facilities with structured AI-readiness frameworks significantly outperformed facilities that deployed rapidly without adequate preparation (InterSystems Corporation, 2024). Acceleration without readiness infrastructure is not a shortcut — it is a different pathway to a worse outcome.⏎⏎Premier Inc. Comments | HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 9⏎⏎PRECONDITIONS FOR ANY RESPONSIBLE ACCELERATION AGENDA⏎⏎Our organization wants to be constructive in this comment, and we recognize that there are genuine policy actions HHS can take to improve AI adoption outcomes. But we want to be clear that we do not think acceleration itself is the right policy goal. The right goal is good outcomes — for patients, for health systems, and for the public that funds a substantial share of U.S. healthcare. Acceleration may or may not serve that goal depending on the conditions under which it occurs. The following are what we consider preconditions for any responsible acceleration agenda:⏎⏎1. Mandatory market concentration review. HHS, in coordination with the FTC and DOJ Antitrust Division, should conduct a formal market structure analysis of the clinical AI sector before committing to an acceleration agenda. This analysis should examine EHR vendor control over AI deployment channels, the competitive dynamics of clinical decision support markets, and the extent to which current market concentration is likely to produce anti-competitive outcomes under accelerated deployment conditions. The FTC's 2023 staff report on generative AI and healthcare provides a starting framework (Federal Trade Commission, 2023), but it has not been translated into specific regulatory action in the health AI context.⏎⏎2. Interoperability standards that address workflow portability, not just data portability. ONC's existing interoperability rules address data access at the API layer. They do not address the workflow integration dependencies that create the most durable forms of vendor lock-in in clinical AI. HHS should direct ONC to develop interoperability standards that specifically address AI model portability — including requirements for standardized model input and output formats, prohibition on proprietary workflow integration requirements that create artificial switching costs, and transparency requirements for AI model performance data that enable health systems to make genuine comparative assessments of competing products. Adler-Milstein and Pfeifer's analysis of the limits of current interoperability mandates should inform this work (Adler-Milstein & Pfeifer, 2023).⏎⏎3. Public ownership conditions on federally facilitated AI development. Any AI development activity conducted under CRADA agreements, cooperative agreements, or other federal partnership structures should include provisions requiring that the resulting products be made available to public and nonprofit health systems on preferential licensing terms, or that the federal government retain a royalty interest in products commercialized from federally facilitated research. The NASHP's 2024 issue brief provides specific drafting recommendations for these provisions (National Academy for State Health Policy, 2024).⏎⏎4. Independent cost-benefit analysis of vendor licensing economics. HHS should commission an independent economic analysis of the net financial effects of AI deployment on health system budgets, with specific attention to vendor licensing costs, implementation contract structures, and the distribution of financial benefits between health systems and vendors. This analysis should be completed and made public before HHS commits to reimbursement reforms that would effectively subsidize AI deployment at scale.⏎⏎5. Mandatory post-market performance surveillance. Any acceleration agenda should be conditioned on the establishment of mandatory post-market performance monitoring requirements for clinical AI tools, with public reporting of performance data stratified by patient population, care setting, and time since deployment. The GAO recommended movement in this direction in its 2023 report (Government Accountability Office, 2023), and HHS has not yet acted on that recommendation.⏎⏎6. Regulatory ambiguity resolution that does not favor incumbents. Where HHS does act to reduce regulatory ambiguity, it should do so in ways that do not preferentially benefit incumbent EHR vendors. Specifically, AI validation and certification pathways should be designed to accommodate products from vendors without existing EHR market presence, and should not use EHR integration as a proxy for clinical validation.⏎⏎Premier Inc. Comments | HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 10⏎⏎CONCLUSION IS NOT THE RIGHT WORD FOR WHAT FOLLOWS⏎⏎We want to close by being direct about something that the formal structure of a regulatory comment makes it easy to obscure. The RFI as published reads, to our organization's policy staff, as a document that has already decided on its answer and is soliciting comments to validate it. The framing of regulatory friction as the primary barrier, the emphasis on public-private partnerships without any discussion of ownership economics, the focus on reimbursement modernization without any analysis of who captures the resulting value — these are not neutral analytical choices. They are choices that consistently favor a particular set of interests, and those interests are not primarily the interests of patients or health systems.⏎⏎We are not suggesting bad faith on the part of HHS or ONC staff. The dynamics Litan and Singer (2022) describe, and that Stigler (1971) theorized more generally, do not require bad faith — they require only that the regulatory process be more accessible to well-resourced parties with concentrated interests than to diffuse stakeholders with harder-to-quantify concerns. Health systems have resources and can participate in this process, which is why Premier Inc. is submitting these comments. But the structural interests of the clinical AI vendor community are more concentrated, more legible in policy terms, and more consistently represented in the policy development process than the interests of the patients who will actually be affected by the tools being deployed. Kesselheim and colleagues' documentation of how commercial interests shape federal health technology policy framing is relevant here not as an accusation but as a description of a structural tendency that requires active correction (Kesselheim et al., 2023, p. 1567).⏎⏎The healthcare AI market is at an early enough stage that deliberate policy choices can still shape its structure in ways that serve the public interest. Once the integration dependencies described in this comment are fully established — once major health systems have deployed AI tools from incumbent EHR vendors and accumulated the switching costs that make displacement prohibitive — the window for structural intervention will have closed. Dafny and Lee's analysis of healthcare market concentration dynamics suggests that once concentration reaches a certain threshold, the policy tools available to address it become significantly less effective (Dafny & Lee, 2022, p. 1333). The analogy to hospital market consolidation is instructive: federal policy has spent the better part of two decades trying to address the consequences of hospital consolidation that occurred in the 1990s and 2000s, with limited success, because the structural conditions that enabled consolidation were not addressed at the time.⏎⏎HHS has an opportunity here that it will not have again in five years. The question is whether the Department is willing to use that opportunity to address the structural economics of the healthcare AI market, or whether it will use it to accelerate deployment under conditions that will entrench the current market structure and the misaligned incentives it produces. Our organization's position is that the latter course is not an acceleration agenda — it is a foreclosure of the conditions under which genuinely beneficial AI adoption could occur.⏎⏎We appreciate the Department's willingness to receive public comment on these questions, and we are available to discuss any aspect of this submission with HHS and ONC staff.⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Jessica Rivera⏎Senior Vice President, Policy and Regulatory Affairs⏎Premier Inc.⏎Charlotte, North Carolina⏎⏎jessica.rivera@premierinc.com⏎www.premierinc.com/policy⏎⏎Premier Inc. SYNTH-0030♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Kenneth King♔Patient Advocate Foundation♔♔♔♔♔Patient Advocate Foundation | HHS AI RFI Docket | Page 1⏎⏎─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────⏎⏎COMMENT OF PATIENT ADVOCATE FOUNDATION IN RESPONSE TO⏎HHS HEALTH SECTOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE REQUEST FOR INFORMATION:⏎ACCELERATING AI ADOPTION IN CLINICAL CARE⏎⏎Submitted by: Kenneth King, Campaign Director⏎Patient Advocate Foundation⏎421 Butler Farm Road, Hampton, VA 23666⏎kking@patientadvocate.org⏎⏎Docket Reference: HHS-ONC-2024-AI-RFI⏎⏎─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────⏎⏎THE EMPIRICAL RECORD HAS ALREADY SPOKEN⏎⏎The framing of this RFI — that the central policy challenge is accelerating AI adoption — reflects a sequencing error that Patient Advocate Foundation finds professionally alarming. The peer-reviewed literature documenting algorithmic harm to marginalized patients is not sparse, not preliminary, and not confined to edge cases. It is dense, replicable, and growing. Sjoding and colleagues demonstrated in 2020 that pulse oximeters, a device so foundational that its AI-adjacent risk was largely unconsidered, produced clinically significant overestimates of oxygen saturation in Black patients at rates sufficient to delay treatment for occult hypoxemia (Sjoding et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 383(25), 2477–2478). That finding did not emerge from a theoretical model. It emerged from retrospective analysis of real patients who received inadequate care. Obermeyer and colleagues identified that a widely deployed commercial risk-scoring algorithm systematically assigned lower risk scores to Black patients than to White patients with equivalent disease burden, effectively rationing access to care management programs along racial lines (Obermeyer et al., Science, 366(6464), 447–453, 2019). The mechanism was not malice; it was the use of prior healthcare expenditure as a proxy for health need, a proxy that encodes the documented reality that Black patients historically receive less care per unit of illness. Wong and colleagues externally validated Epic's widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model and found substantial degradation in predictive performance across hospital settings, with sensitivity and positive predictive value falling sharply outside the academic medical centers where the model was originally trained (Wong et al., JAMA Internal Medicine, 181(8), 1065–1070, 2021). Adamson and Smith documented that dermatology diagnostic AI tools trained predominantly on images of lighter-skinned patients produced materially inferior diagnostic accuracy for patients with darker skin tones (Adamson & Smith, JAMA Dermatology, 154(11), 1247–1248, 2018). Seyyed-Kalantari and colleagues found that AI algorithms applied to chest radiographs in under-served populations produced systematic underdiagnosis bias, with patients from lower-income and minority backgrounds receiving less accurate diagnostic outputs from the same models deployed in better-resourced settings (Seyyed-Kalantari et al., Nature Medicine, 27(12), 2176–2182, 2021). Patient Advocate Foundation does not characterize these findings as a warning about what AI might do. These are descriptions of what AI has already done, in deployed clinical environments, to real patients whose conditions were misclassified and whose care was accordingly compromised.⏎⏎Patient Advocate Foundation | HHS AI RFI Docket | Page 2⏎⏎─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────⏎⏎THE VALIDATION-GENERALIZABILITY GAP AND THE SAFETY-NET PROBLEM⏎⏎What concerns this organization most — and what the RFI conspicuously omits any serious treatment of — is the structural relationship between where AI tools are validated and where they will actually be deployed at scale. Academic medical centers with large, well-curated, richly annotated datasets are the environments in which most commercial clinical AI products are developed and internally validated. Community hospitals, rural critical access facilities, and safety-net institutions serving predominantly Medicaid and uninsured populations are the environments in which those same tools will be broadly deployed once reimbursement pathways are established and regulatory endorsement is granted. These two environments are not interchangeable. Gianfrancesco and colleagues identified that electronic health record data used to train machine learning algorithms contains systematic biases arising from differential documentation practices, differential access to care, and differential coding intensity across patient populations, all of which degrade model generalizability in precisely the settings where marginalized patients receive care (Gianfrancesco et al., JAMA Internal Medicine, 178(11), 1544–1547, 2018). Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones documented that race-correction practices embedded in clinical algorithms have historically compounded rather than corrected for structural health disparities, producing outputs calibrated to patterns of unequal treatment rather than underlying biological reality (Vyas et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 383(9), 874–882, 2020). Wiens and colleagues articulated the responsible deployment framework that the field has largely failed to operationalize: that deployment decisions must be preceded by rigorous external validation in the target population, not the training population (Wiens et al., Nature Medicine, 25(9), 1337–1340, 2019). The GAO reached substantively similar conclusions in its 2023 report on AI in health care, noting that existing federal oversight mechanisms are poorly positioned to detect performance degradation across demographic subgroups after deployment (GAO-23-105491, 2023). The National Academy for State Health Policy and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation similarly documented in 2023 that state-level AI governance frameworks are fragmented and inadequate, with no jurisdiction having implemented comprehensive equity-centered pre-deployment requirements (NASPH & RWJF, Algorithmic Bias in Health Care, 2023).⏎⏎There is also a mechanism problem that the RFI does not address. Automation bias — the documented tendency of clinicians to defer to algorithmic outputs even when those outputs conflict with their own clinical judgment — means that AI errors are in several respects harder to catch than equivalent human errors. Char, Shah, and Magnus identified this as among the most consequential ethical challenges in clinical AI implementation, precisely because it transforms tool error into systemic practice error without any clear attribution point (Char et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 378(11), 981–983, 2018). Pierson and colleagues further documented that algorithmic approaches to pain management in under-served populations can perpetuate treatment disparities embedded in historical prescribing patterns, even when the stated goal of the tool is equity improvement (Pierson et al., Nature Medicine, 27(1), 136–140, 2021). The literature is not ambiguous on these points.⏎⏎─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────⏎⏎SPECIFIC POLICY DEMANDS⏎⏎Patient Advocate Foundation respectfully but firmly requests that HHS condition any regulatory endorsement, reimbursement pathway development, or federal facilitation of clinical AI deployment on the following requirements, which reflect the minimum threshold of responsible governance given the evidence record above:⏎⏎1. Mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing: Any AI tool seeking Medicare or Medicaid reimbursement coverage or inclusion in any HHS-endorsed clinical decision support framework must demonstrate pre-deployment performance parity across race, ethnicity, sex, age, insurance status, and primary language subgroups, tested in population cohorts representative of the intended deployment environment, not the development environment.⏎⏎2. Mandatory post-deployment bias surveillance: Covered entities deploying reimbursed AI tools must implement ongoing monitoring of algorithmic outputs stratified by demographic subgroup, with defined thresholds for performance divergence that trigger mandatory review and, where warranted, suspension of deployment pending revalidation.⏎⏎3. Transparent external validation requirements: HHS should require that external validation studies be conducted in community and safety-net settings prior to broad deployment approval, not retrospectively. The Wong et al. findings regarding Epic's sepsis model are a direct illustration of why post-hoc external validation is insufficient as a safety mechanism.⏎⏎4. Equity audit methodology standardization: HHS should convene a technical standards process to define minimum acceptable methodologies for subgroup equity auditing, because the absence of standardized methodology currently allows vendors to conduct and report equity analyses in ways that obscure rather than reveal disparate performance.⏎⏎Patient Advocate Foundation | HHS AI RFI Docket | Page 3⏎⏎─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────⏎⏎HHS has the regulatory authority and the administrative infrastructure to require these safeguards as conditions of reimbursement and coverage determination. The omission of any mandatory equity framework from this RFI is not a neutral policy choice. It is a decision to proceed with deployment acceleration while the evidence of disparate harm accumulates. Patient Advocate Foundation's direct program work with patients navigating coverage denials and care gaps has consistently shown that the populations most likely to be harmed by biased AI tools are the same populations least equipped to identify the source of the harm, contest an algorithmic determination, or access alternative care pathways. The 34-percentage-point variation in AI-assisted imaging reimbursement denial rates across Medicare Administrative Contractor jurisdictions documented in RBMA's 2024 member survey data is one illustration of how uneven the current landscape already is before mandatory equity requirements are in place.⏎⏎HHS should not finalize any regulatory or reimbursement framework that facilitates broader clinical AI deployment without first establishing the mandatory pre-deployment and post-deployment equity requirements described above. SYNTH-0031♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Joshua Clark♔♔♔♔♔♔To the Office of the Deputy Secretary, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services:⏎⏎MY EXPERIENCE AT UNM HEALTH, AND WHAT IT MEANS FOR THIS RULEMAKING⏎⏎Eleven days. That is how long I waited, in November of last year, after my cardiologist at UNM Health flagged what the automated triage system had labeled an "anomaly" on my echocardiogram. I am sixty-two years old. I understand, in a way that perhaps not every patient does, how workflow systems operate — I have scheduled things, routed things, and tracked bottlenecks for a living for the better part of three decades. What I watched happen to my own case was not a technical failure in any narrow sense. The algorithm flagged the finding. The algorithm queued it for secondary review. The algorithm, presumably, moved on. What the algorithm did not do, and what no human being in that chain felt obligated to do in its place, was pick up a telephone and tell a sixty-two-year-old man in Albuquerque that he might be waiting a while, and why. The finding turned out to be a calibration artifact. Not a medical finding at all. The eleven days of quiet catastrophizing I did in my apartment were caused entirely by a system that had been designed to route responsibility away from any identifiable person. I want the Department to sit with that for a moment before it proceeds.⏎⏎WHAT "ACCELERATION" LOOKS LIKE FROM THE PATIENT SIDE OF THE TRANSACTION⏎⏎The RFI uses the phrase "enhance productivity" in describing the goals of AI adoption in clinical settings, and I want to be direct: that framing concerns me in ways that go beyond my personal experience. Francis Peabody wrote in 1927, in JAMA, that "the secret of the care of the patient is in caring for the patient" as a person rather than a case (JAMA 88(12): 877-882). That observation has not aged out of relevance. What Peabody understood, and what this Department's framing seems not to, is that medicine is a relational practice at its core — that diagnosis depends on interpreting ambiguity, fear, body language, and context that no pattern-matching system can access. Abraham Verghese has written and spoken at length about the irreducible diagnostic value of the physical and relational clinical encounter, and Danielle Zulman and her colleagues at Stanford documented in 2020 that measurable clinical outcomes improve when physicians are genuinely present with their patients, not merely proximate to a screen displaying algorithmic outputs (JAMA 323(1): 70-81). These are not sentimental observations. They are empirical ones.⏎⏎What worries me about acceleration, specifically, is what happens to clinical judgment when it is exercised less frequently. Goddard and colleagues published a systematic review in 2012 documenting that clinician reliance on automated recommendations degrades independent reasoning over time — what the literature calls automation bias (JAMIA 19(1): 121-127). Obermeyer and Emanuel made a related point in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2016: the structural risk with algorithmic systems in clinical settings is not that they will be wrong in obvious ways, but that their confidence will displace the clinical judgment that might have caught what they missed (NEJM 375: 1216-1219). Even Eric Topol, who is as enthusiastic an advocate for AI in medicine as anyone writing today, acknowledged in his 2019 Nature Medicine piece that the human clinical relationship is irreplaceable and that AI should be deployed in ways that give physicians more time with patients, not less (Nature Medicine 25: 44-56). The Department is not proposing to follow that logic. It is proposing to accelerate a process without first establishing what guardrails ensure the relational substrate of care is not eroded in the process.⏎⏎I want to be specific about what I am asking, because I recognize that a comment like this can easily be dismissed as technophobia, and I want to be clear that it is not. I am not opposed to AI in clinical care. I am opposed to AI deployment that:⏎⏎1. Removes identifiable human accountability from time-sensitive patient communications, as happened in my case at UNM Health.⏎2. Redefines clinical quality in terms of throughput and triage efficiency rather than relational outcomes, which the empathy literature suggests are not separable from clinical outcomes — Hojat and colleagues demonstrated in 2011 that physician empathy produced measurable improvements in diabetic patient outcomes independent of the technical quality of the intervention (Academic Medicine 86(3): 359-364).⏎3. Proceeds without mandatory disclosure to patients that an AI system, rather than a clinician, has made a triage or prioritization decision affecting their care.⏎⏎The Department is asking what regulatory actions it can take to accelerate adoption. I am asking it to first answer a question it has not yet posed to itself: what does a patient owe an algorithm, and what does an algorithm owe a patient? Because right now, in my experience, the answer to the second question is nothing. The algorithm flagged, queued, and moved on, and the hospital system treated that as a complete transaction. It was not. There was a man on the other end of it who spent eleven days not sleeping well, not eating well, and not telling his family what he was afraid of because he did not want to frighten them over something that might be nothing. It was nothing. But I did not know that for eleven days because the system had no mechanism for a human being to look at the queue and notice that a follow-up communication had not been sent.⏎⏎I would ask the Department not to issue reimbursement incentives for AI-assisted triage systems until minimum standards for patient notification and accountable human review are established. That is a specific, implementable demand, and I believe it is the right place to start.⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Joshua Clark⏎Albuquerque, New Mexico♔♔2026-01-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔3♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Medicine is fundamentally a human relationship built on judgment, context, and trust, and AI threatens to reduce patients to data points and clinicians to machine overseers.♔individual♔high♔angry♔New Mexico♔administrative assistant♔62♔When my cardiologist at UNM Health flagged an "anomaly" on my echocardiogram and the follow-up was routed through some new automated triage system, I sat in genuine cardiac limbo for eleven days waiting for a human to review what turned out to be a calibration artifact — not a medical finding at all. Royal Lane⏎Irving, TX 75063⏎⏎Susan Martinez, JD, MPH⏎Director of Health Policy⏎ACEP Washington Office⏎2121 K Street NW, Suite 325⏎Washington, DC 20037⏎⏎June 28, 2024⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue SW⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎Attention: Health Sector AI Request for Information Docket⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care, 89 Fed. Reg. 47210 (May 31, 2024)⏎⏎---⏎⏎ACEP COMMENTS | HHS AI RFI | DOCKET HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 1⏎⏎THE GOVERNANCE DEFICIT PRECEDING DEPLOYMENT⏎⏎The American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP) submits these comments in response to the Department's request for information on regulatory, reimbursement, and research-and-development actions to accelerate artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings. ACEP represents more than 40,000 emergency physicians practicing across every care setting in which AI deployment is now actively occurring, often ahead of any coherent governance structure to support it. The Department has framed this RFI principally around acceleration. ACEP urges the Department to reconsider that framing entirely, because the more consequential policy question is not how quickly these tools can be deployed, but whether the institutional conditions necessary for meaningful democratic accountability can be established before irreversible structural dependencies foreclose that possibility.⏎⏎The empirical starting point for these comments is not ACEP's own membership data, though that data is extensive and troubling in its own right. The Association of periOperative Registered Nurses published findings in October 2024, presented at the AORN Global Surgical Conference in Chicago, drawn from a survey of more than 2,200 perioperative nurses across 47 states. Sixty-eight percent of respondents reported direct exposure to at least one AI-assisted surgical or anesthesia monitoring tool within their facility in the prior twelve months. Only 19 percent indicated they had received any structured training on interpreting AI-generated alerts or integrating AI outputs into intraoperative decision-making (AORN, 2024 Member Survey on AI Exposure and Training Readiness in Perioperative Settings, October 2024). These numbers are not primarily a workforce training problem, though they are that too. They represent something more structurally significant: the systematic decoupling of deployment velocity from governance readiness. Tools are being embedded into clinical workflows before the institutions deploying them have developed the accountability mechanisms, the interpretive frameworks, or the staff competencies to exercise meaningful oversight of those tools. ACEP sees the same pattern in emergency departments across the country, where AI-assisted triage, sepsis prediction, and diagnostic imaging tools are increasingly present without corresponding clinical governance protocols.⏎⏎ACEP COMMENTS | HHS AI RFI | DOCKET HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 2⏎⏎THE IRREVERSIBILITY PROBLEM AND PATH DEPENDENCE⏎⏎This governance deficit would be recoverable if the technologies in question were reversible. They are not. Paul Pierson's foundational work on increasing returns and path dependence (Pierson, "Increasing Returns, Path Dependence, and the Study of Politics," American Political Science Review, 94(2), 2000) provides the conceptual architecture for understanding why this matters so acutely in health sector AI. Once an AI-assisted clinical decision support system is embedded into an electronic health record workflow, once reimbursement codes are structured around its outputs, once clinical staff have been retrained to rely on its alerts rather than developing independent interpretive competencies, the institutional cost of reversing that dependency becomes prohibitive. Leemore Dafny and Thomas Lee have documented precisely this dynamic in the context of health platform economics more broadly, showing that structural barriers to market exit and regulatory reversal in health information technology create conditions under which initial deployment decisions effectively determine long-term institutional trajectories (Dafny & Lee, "Health Care Platform Lock-In: Structural Barriers to Market Exit and Regulatory Reversal," New England Journal of Medicine, 388(14), 2023). The HHS RFI, by treating acceleration as the primary policy objective, risks producing exactly the kind of premature lock-in that forecloses future regulatory correction.⏎⏎ACEP does not contend that AI has no role in emergency medicine. The Department and ACEP's own membership have documented genuine clinical benefits in specific, well-validated applications. Eric Topol's work has been instructive on the potential for AI to restore physician attention to patient interaction by reducing cognitive load in documentation and pattern recognition (Topol, Deep Medicine: How Artificial Intelligence Can Make Healthcare Human Again, Basic Books, 2019). The GAO's 2023 report on AI in health care similarly acknowledged a range of applications with demonstrated clinical utility (GAO, Artificial Intelligence in Health Care: Benefits and Challenges of Technologies to Augment Patient Care, GAO-23-105980, 2023). ACEP's concern is not categorical opposition. The concern is that the Department is being asked by commercial interests and by internal constituencies within HHS to treat deployment velocity as a proxy for progress, when the actual measure of progress should be whether governance structures are keeping pace with deployment.⏎⏎ACEP COMMENTS | HHS AI RFI | DOCKET HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 3⏎⏎THE DEMOCRATIC LEGITIMACY QUESTION⏎⏎The RFI does not adequately engage with what ACEP regards as the foundational question: who decided that AI-mediated clinical decision-making was an appropriate direction for American health care, and through what legitimate democratic process was that decision made? This is not a rhetorical question. The European Parliament's Committee on Civil Liberties, Justice and Home Affairs grappled with precisely this issue in its 2023 analysis of algorithmic decision-making, concluding that health sector AI governance has proceeded in most jurisdictions without the kind of deliberative public mandate that decisions of this magnitude ordinarily require (European Parliament, "Democratic Accountability in Algorithmic Decision-Making: Lessons for Health Sector AI Governance," PE 740.248, 2023). Frank Pasquale has made the complementary argument that the displacement of human clinical expertise by algorithmic systems is not a neutral technical decision but a political one, carrying distributional consequences that should be subject to democratic deliberation rather than administrative acceleration (Pasquale, New Laws of Robotics: Defending Human Expertise in the Age of AI, Harvard University Press, 2020). HHS, by soliciting comment on how to accelerate adoption rather than on whether and under what conditions adoption should proceed, has already made an implicit policy choice that belongs properly to a deliberative public process.⏎⏎The structural impossibility of meaningful oversight of proprietary black-box systems compounds this democratic legitimacy problem considerably. Andrew Selbst and Solon Barocas have demonstrated that the demand for explainability in algorithmic systems frequently produces what they term "the intuitive appeal of explainable machines" — the appearance of transparency without the substance of it, in which explanations generated for regulatory compliance do not actually allow external reviewers to identify the mechanisms driving algorithmic outputs (Selbst & Barocas, "The Intuitive Appeal of Explainable Machines," Fordham Law Review, 87(3), 2018). Brent Mittelstadt, Chris Russell, and Sandra Wachter extended this analysis in the context of AI fairness and accountability frameworks, showing that post-hoc explanation methods systematically fail to expose the training data characteristics and optimization objectives that most consequentially shape model behavior (Mittelstadt, Russell & Wachter, "Explaining Explanations in AI," FAccT Proceedings, 2019). Emergency medicine is a particularly high-stakes domain for this problem. When a sepsis prediction model generates an alert at 2:47 a.m. in a crowded emergency department, the attending physician cannot interrogate the model's reasoning in any meaningful sense. The physician can accept or override the alert. But without access to the model's architecture, training data provenance, and validation methodology, neither the physician nor ACEP nor HHS can meaningfully assess whether the alert reflects genuine clinical signal or reflects a pattern artifact in the training data that happens to correlate with outcomes in the training population but does not generalize to the patient in front of the physician.⏎⏎ACEP COMMENTS | HHS AI RFI | DOCKET HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 4⏎⏎o  The Department should commission a structured public deliberation process, with representation from patients, clinicians, health equity advocates, and technology critics, before finalizing any deployment-facilitation policy.⏎⏎o  HHS should condition any reimbursement or regulatory accommodation for AI-assisted clinical decision support on mandatory disclosure of model architecture, training data characteristics, and ongoing performance monitoring data to a publicly accessible federal registry.⏎⏎o  The RFI's framing should be reoriented away from acceleration and toward precautionary governance, with explicit acknowledgment that irreversibility of institutional AI dependencies constitutes a distinct regulatory risk category warranting its own analytical framework.⏎⏎o  HHS should require, as a condition of any federal health care program payment for AI-assisted clinical services, that vendors demonstrate the ability of facility clinical staff to meaningfully interpret and override AI outputs — not merely acknowledge them.⏎⏎o  The Department should establish an independent technical review body, insulated from vendor influence, to conduct prospective evaluation of AI tools prior to their deployment in federally reimbursed clinical settings.⏎⏎ACEP COMMENTS | HHS AI RFI | DOCKET HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 5⏎⏎THE UNINTENDED CONSEQUENCES PROBLEM IN EMERGENCY SETTINGS⏎⏎Enrico Coiera, Joan Ash, and Marc Berg documented in 2022 the now well-established pattern by which health information technology generates unintended consequences that are structurally predictable but systematically underweighted in pre-deployment analysis (Coiera, Ash & Berg, "The Unintended Consequences of Health Information Technology Revisited," Yearbook of Medical Informatics, 31(1), 2022). Emergency departments are the clinical environment in which these unintended consequences are most likely to manifest acutely and most difficult to reverse once embedded. The cognitive architecture of emergency medicine — high patient volume, compressed decision cycles, frequent interruption, limited longitudinal patient data — creates conditions in which AI alert fatigue, automation bias, and deskilling effects are not hypothetical risks but predictable operational outcomes. ACEP's policy team has received reports from member physicians at facilities in New York, Texas, and Ohio describing AI-generated sepsis alerts with positive predictive values well below what was represented at the time of vendor contracting, creating alert loads that physicians are managing by developing heuristics for systematic override that themselves introduce new error patterns. These are not edge cases. They are the foreseeable consequence of deploying tools whose performance in controlled validation settings does not transfer reliably to the operational conditions of high-volume emergency departments.⏎⏎Ziad Obermeyer and Eric Topol have documented the mechanisms by which AI systems trained on historically biased clinical data reproduce and in some cases amplify existing health care disparities (Obermeyer & Topol, "Artificial Intelligence, Bias, and Patient Safety," JAMA, 325(24), 2021). Emergency departments serve disproportionately uninsured, underinsured, and socially marginalized patient populations — precisely the populations most likely to be underrepresented in the training data of commercially developed AI tools and most likely to experience adverse outcomes from model performance degradation in their demographic subgroups. ACEP is particularly concerned that the RFI's emphasis on accelerating adoption does not adequately account for the distributional consequences of deploying tools whose performance characteristics may diverge systematically across patient populations in ways that neither facilities nor regulators are currently equipped to detect. The AORN survey data cited earlier is relevant here too: if 81 percent of perioperative nurses have received no structured training on interpreting AI outputs, the assumption that clinical staff will function as a reliable check on algorithmically generated errors is not operationally supportable.⏎⏎ACEP COMMENTS | HHS AI RFI | DOCKET HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 6⏎⏎ACEP's specific concern about the reimbursement question posed in the RFI is that payment incentives attached to AI tool use will, if structured without corresponding performance accountability requirements, function as deployment subsidies rather than as quality incentives. The history of health IT reimbursement under the HITECH Act provides instructive precedent. Meaningful use incentives accelerated EHR adoption at a pace that outran clinical workflow integration capacity, producing well-documented physician burnout, documentation quality degradation, and patient safety events attributable to interface design failures that would have been correctable under a slower, more deliberate adoption trajectory. ACEP is not arguing against reimbursement accommodation for AI tools that demonstrate genuine clinical value in emergency settings. The organization is arguing that payment design must be conditioned on prospective performance validation, ongoing post-market surveillance with publicly reported results, and demonstrated vendor compliance with disclosure standards — not simply on tool deployment.⏎⏎The Department should also attend carefully to the vendor-to-facility disclosure problem identified in the AORN survey analysis. ACEP's policy team has reviewed vendor contracting practices at member facilities and identified a consistent pattern in which performance representations made during the procurement process are not accompanied by contractual commitments to ongoing performance monitoring or data sharing with facility clinical governance committees. This is not an incidental contracting problem. It is a structural feature of a market in which vendors bear no regulatory obligation to disclose post-deployment performance data and in which facilities lack the technical capacity to conduct independent performance assessment. Without federal disclosure requirements, the information asymmetry between vendors and deploying institutions will persist regardless of how many acceleration-oriented policy accommodations HHS provides.⏎⏎ACEP COMMENTS | HHS AI RFI | DOCKET HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 7⏎⏎CONCLUSION WITHHELD — SPECIFIC REQUEST TO THE DEPARTMENT⏎⏎ACEP respectfully requests that HHS reframe this initiative around democratic legitimacy and precautionary governance rather than around deployment velocity. The Department should commission a structured public deliberation process before any deployment-facilitation policy is finalized — one that is not organized by vendor consortia or by internal HHS constituencies with institutional interests in AI adoption, but by an independent body with genuine representation from the patient and clinician communities that will bear the consequences of these decisions. The path dependence risks documented in the health platform lock-in literature are not abstract. They describe a specific mechanism by which regulatory windows close. Once AI-mediated clinical decision-making is structurally embedded in federally reimbursed care delivery, the institutional cost of re-establishing human clinical primacy becomes a political obstacle that no subsequent administration is likely to overcome.⏎⏎ACEP's policy team is available to provide technical assistance on governance framework design, performance monitoring methodology, and emergency medicine-specific deployment standards. SYNTH-0035♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Stephanie Green♔American Psychological Association♔♔♔♔♔American Psychological Association — Comments Submitted to HHS Docket on AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎Stephanie Green, Community Organizing and Policy Division⏎American Psychological Association⏎750 First Street NE, Washington, DC 20002⏎⏎Submitted electronically via regulations.gov⏎⏎⏎PRELIMINARY STATEMENT⏎⏎⏎The democratic stakes of this rulemaking are not incidental to its technical substance — they are the substance. The American Psychological Association submits these comments not to oppose technological progress in healthcare, but to name what HHS appears unwilling to name: that the Department's framing of this RFI presupposes an answer to a question the public has not yet been asked. The RFI's stated goal of reducing "uncertainty that impedes AI innovation" — language drawn directly from the Federal Health IT Strategic Plan 2024–2030 (ONC, 2023) — positions democratic scrutiny itself as the impediment. We believe that framing is not a neutral policy choice. It is a governance posture, and it carries consequences that no subsequent regulatory correction will be able to fully reverse.⏎⏎We address here primarily the RFI's questions concerning the regulatory environment for clinical AI adoption, and the appropriate federal posture toward accelerating that adoption. We do not address every question posed, because real engagement with the democratic concerns at stake requires depth rather than breadth.⏎⏎⏎THE PROBLEM OF IRREVERSIBILITY⏎⏎⏎There is a concept in technology governance literature that has received insufficient attention in federal health policy: the idea that certain technological embeddings are, for practical purposes, permanent. Langdon Winner argued in 1980 that artifacts carry politics — that the choices embedded in a technological system are not neutral and do not remain available for renegotiation once the system has been institutionalized (Winner, 1980, "Do Artifacts Have Politics?" Daedalus, 109(1), 121–136). Sheila Jasanoff, writing more recently, extended this insight to argue that societies must exercise democratic judgment about technology before lock-in occurs, because after the fact, the governance options available to democratic institutions are structurally narrowed by the technical dependencies already in place (Jasanoff, 2016, The Ethics of Invention: Technology and the Human Future, W.W. Norton). Neither of these scholars was writing about healthcare AI specifically. But their frameworks apply with particular force here.⏎⏎When AI systems are embedded into clinical decision-support workflows, electronic health records, and diagnostic imaging pipelines, the institutional knowledge required to function without them atrophies. This is not a speculative concern. Dafny and Lee (2016, "The Good Merger," New England Journal of Medicine, 374(18), 1701–1703) documented analogous lock-in dynamics in the context of healthcare system consolidation: once institutional dependencies are established, the cost of reversal becomes prohibitive not merely financially but operationally, and the practical governance authority that regulators nominally retain becomes largely theoretical. The same dynamic applies to AI dependency. Friedman, Wong, and Blumenthal (2010, "Achieving a Nationwide Learning Health System," Science Translational Medicine, 2(57), 57cm29) observed that health IT infrastructure, once embedded at scale, shapes all subsequent clinical and regulatory practice in ways that resist fundamental reconfiguration. The point is not that AI in clinical settings will necessarily produce bad outcomes. The point is that once the infrastructure is in place and the human capacity to function without it has degraded, no future HHS secretary, no future Congress, and no future regulatory proceeding can meaningfully restore the prior state. The decision to accelerate is, therefore, not a reversible policy experiment. It is a permanent transfer of clinical governance into a technological regime whose terms are set by private vendors, and HHS is proposing to execute that transfer without a democratic mandate to do so.⏎⏎⏎APA Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎⏎THE BLACK BOX PROBLEM AND DEMOCRATIC OVERSIGHT⏎⏎⏎The second dimension of our concern is structural rather than merely procedural. Even if one were to accept that the acceleration agenda is democratically legitimate — which we do not — the AI systems being deployed into clinical settings are, by design, inaccessible to the oversight mechanisms that democratic governance relies upon to identify and correct harmful policy. Frank Pasquale documented this dynamic comprehensively in The Black Box Society (2015, Harvard University Press): proprietary algorithmic systems are structured to resist external scrutiny not as a side effect of their complexity but as a condition of their commercial viability. The competitive advantage embedded in a clinical AI system is precisely the logic that cannot be examined. Regulators cannot audit what vendors will not disclose. Clinicians cannot interrogate what they cannot see. Patients cannot contest decisions whose basis is legally protected as trade secret.⏎⏎This is not a hypothetical problem. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan demonstrated in 2019 that a widely deployed algorithm used to manage the health of millions of patients contained systematic racial bias that was invisible to the clinicians and administrators relying upon it, because the internal logic of the system was structurally inaccessible to them (Obermeyer et al., 2019, "Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations," Science, 366(6464), 447–453). The bias was discovered not through routine oversight but through independent academic research — a mechanism that cannot be institutionalized as a substitute for regulatory accountability. Virginia Eubanks has shown that when algorithmic systems become infrastructure in domains like public benefits and child welfare, the democratic accountability mechanisms that normally operate to correct harmful policy are rendered inoperative not because oversight is impossible in principle, but because the systems are designed and deployed in ways that make accountability practically unreachable (Eubanks, 2018, Automating Inequality, St. Martin's Press). Healthcare AI is following the same trajectory.⏎⏎The Texas Medical Association's Health Information Technology Committee documented in its 2024 policy review that among approximately 4,200 practicing physicians surveyed, 58% had encountered at least one AI-assisted diagnostic or clinical decision-support tool in their practice setting within the prior 12 months, yet only 23% had received any formal guidance from payers or federal agencies on reimbursement eligibility for AI-augmented services (TMA Health Information Technology Committee, 2024, Policy Review: Physician Perspectives on AI-Augmented Clinical Decision Support). The three barriers physicians identified most consistently were liability ambiguity when AI outputs inform clinical decisions, inconsistent payer coverage determinations, and the absence of standardized validation requirements for AI tools entering the market. These findings were gathered across six regional town halls that spanned both urban academic medical centers and rural critical-access hospitals throughout Texas. What this data tells us is not simply that deployment is outpacing regulation — though it is — but that deployment is outpacing the deliberative infrastructure required for democratic accountability. Clinicians are encountering systems whose governance terms they do not understand, whose internal logic they cannot access, and whose liability implications remain unresolved. That is not a temporary implementation gap that acceleration will eventually close. It is a structural condition that acceleration deepens.⏎⏎⏎APA Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎⏎THE DEMOCRATIC PREEMPTION ARGUMENT⏎⏎⏎We want to be precise about what we mean when we say that HHS's acceleration agenda constitutes democratic preemption. We are not arguing that AI in healthcare is inherently illegitimate, or that the Department lacks authority to act in this space. We are arguing something more specific: that the decision about whether medicine should be organized around AI-augmented decision-making at scale is a decision that belongs to the public, and that HHS is making it unilaterally by treating acceleration as the default posture before the public has had any meaningful opportunity to deliberate on the question.⏎⏎Ronald Dworkin argued that certain domains of human dignity warrant protection from efficiency-based displacement as a matter of democratic principle — that a society's right to insist on human primacy in some domains is not a preference to be weighed against competing interests but a structural feature of democratic self-governance (Dworkin, 1977, Taking Rights Seriously, Harvard University Press). Medicine is one of those domains. So is criminal justice. So is education. The reason is not that efficiency is irrelevant in these domains — it plainly is relevant — but that the relationship between a patient and a clinician, or between a student and a teacher, or between a defendant and a court, carries a form of human accountability that algorithmic mediation structurally cannot replicate, and that the public has a legitimate interest in preserving even at efficiency cost. Eric Topol's influential work on AI in healthcare (Deep Medicine, 2019, Basic Books) has been widely cited in support of deployment optimism, and we do not dismiss it entirely. But Topol's framework understates the lock-in risk: the scenario in which AI frees clinicians to be more human by handling routine cognitive tasks assumes that the governance conditions for maintaining human primacy remain intact after deployment. Coiera's more cautionary analysis of the gap between AI deployment and sustainable clinical integration is instructive here — he has documented the way in which systems that appear to augment clinical judgment in controlled settings can gradually displace the judgment they were meant to support once they become infrastructure (Coiera, 2019, "The Last Mile: Where Artificial Intelligence Meets Reality," Journal of Medical Internet Research, 21(11), e16323). The augmentation narrative and the displacement outcome are not mutually exclusive; they can coexist within the same deployment trajectory, with augmentation characterizing the early phase and displacement characterizing the mature phase after institutional knowledge has atrophied.⏎⏎The RFI, by framing its central purpose as the acceleration of adoption, has already answered the question of whether medicine should move in this direction. It has done so not through legislation, not through notice-and-comment rulemaking on the fundamental governance question, and not through any process that would give the public a genuine opportunity to say that some clinical domains should remain stubbornly human. The Department has instead embedded the acceleration presumption in the architecture of the inquiry itself, so that every response to the RFI — including this one — is structurally positioned as commentary on how to accelerate rather than on whether to accelerate. We want to name that framing explicitly, because it is doing significant governance work that the Department has not acknowledged.⏎⏎⏎APA Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 4⏎⏎⏎WHAT A DEMOCRATICALLY LEGITIMATE PROCESS WOULD REQUIRE⏎⏎⏎The American Psychological Association is not in a position to enumerate every procedural requirement for a democratically legitimate federal approach to clinical AI. But we can identify several features that any such approach would need to include, based on the arguments above:⏎⏎1. A prior and separate deliberative process on the fundamental question of whether and to what extent AI-mediated decision-making should be embedded in core clinical functions, conducted with genuine public participation and not presupposing acceleration as the answer.⏎⏎2. Mandatory transparency requirements for any AI system used in clinical decision support, including disclosure of training data provenance, validation methodology, and known performance limitations, as a condition of market entry — not as a post-hoc aspiration.⏎⏎3. A statutory or regulatory moratorium on deployment in defined high-stakes clinical contexts — including inpatient psychiatric care, pediatric diagnosis, and end-of-life decision support — pending completion of the deliberative process described above.⏎⏎4. Federal investment in the research infrastructure needed to evaluate AI systems in community-based and rural clinical settings, where the TMA data suggests deployment is already occurring without adequate governance support, and where the populations served have historically had the least access to recourse when algorithmic systems produce harmful outcomes.⏎⏎5. An explicit acknowledgment by HHS that the acceleration posture reflected in the current RFI is itself a governance choice with irreversible consequences, and that the Department will not treat democratic scrutiny as an obstacle to innovation but as a precondition of legitimate policy.⏎⏎We recognize that some of these recommendations would require legislative action beyond the Department's current authority. We raise them nonetheless, because the appropriate response to a governance gap is not to proceed as though the gap does not exist.⏎⏎⏎APA Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 5⏎⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE REIMBURSEMENT QUESTION⏎⏎⏎The RFI also solicits comment on reimbursement structures for AI-augmented clinical services. The APA has concerns about this dimension of the inquiry as well, though we address it only briefly here. The TMA survey finding that only 23% of physicians who had encountered clinical AI tools had received guidance on reimbursement eligibility (TMA HIT Committee, 2024) is not simply an implementation problem to be solved by clarifying CMS billing codes. It reflects a deeper governance failure: reimbursement policy is being asked to do the work of democratic legitimation, as if resolving the payer coverage question would also resolve the question of whether the deployment is appropriate. It will not. Reimbursement frameworks that create financial incentives for AI-augmented services before the deliberative process we describe above has occurred will accelerate the lock-in dynamic by introducing economic dependencies that further narrow the governance options available to future policymakers. The sequencing matters enormously, and the current RFI has the sequence inverted.⏎⏎We are also concerned that the framing of reimbursement questions in the RFI focuses almost entirely on reducing barriers to adoption rather than on the governance conditions that would need to be in place for adoption to be democratically accountable. This is consistent with the broader acceleration posture we have critiqued, but it is worth noting specifically in the reimbursement context because the economic infrastructure being built now will be extremely difficult to dismantle if the deliberative process eventually produces a different answer about the appropriate scope of clinical AI.⏎⏎⏎CONCLUSION AND DIRECT REQUEST⏎⏎⏎The American Psychological Association urges HHS to reframe this RFI — and any subsequent rulemaking it generates — around democratic legitimacy and precautionary governance rather than acceleration. The Department should acknowledge explicitly that the decision to embed AI at scale in clinical care is a permanent governance choice, not a reversible policy experiment, and that executing that choice without a democratic mandate is not a technical matter but a matter of constitutional and ethical accountability. The current framing treats the public's right to deliberate as friction to be reduced. We are asking HHS to treat it as the condition that makes any of this legitimate in the first place.⏎⏎Specifically, we request that HHS issue a supplemental request for comment focused exclusively on the question of democratic process — asking what deliberative mechanisms the public believes should precede large-scale clinical AI deployment, rather than asking only how to accelerate the deployment that the Department has already decided to pursue. That supplemental process should be designed in consultation with community organizations, patient advocacy groups, and the clinical professional associations that represent the practitioners who will be most directly affected, and it should be conducted on a timeline that allows genuine public participation rather than one calibrated to the pace of vendor deployment.⏎⏎The TMA data from 2024 documents 4,200 physicians already navigating AI tools without adequate governance infrastructure. That number will be larger by the time any rulemaking generated by this RFI takes effect. The window for democratic deliberation on the fundamental question is narrowing, and it is narrowing because of choices HHS is making right now about how to frame the inquiry.⏎⏎We would welcome the opportunity to discuss these concerns further with staff from ASTP/ONC or the Office of the Deputy Secretary. Contact information for the APA's policy division is available at⏎⏎www.apa.org/policy/health-it-contact♔♔2026-02-04T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-04T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔8♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Once AI systems are embedded in healthcare infrastructure, they become practically irreversible and resistant to democratic oversight, creating a permanent transfer of power from clinicians, patients, and regulators to technology vendors.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔frustrated♔Vermont♔community organizer♔48♔A 2024 TMA Physician Survey of 4,200 practicing physicians across Texas found that 58% had encountered at least one AI-assisted diagnostic or clinical decision-support tool in their practice setting within the prior 12 months, yet only 23% reported receiving any formal guidance from payers or federal agencies on reimbursement eligibility for AI-augmented services.
