SYNTH-0036♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Margaret Wilson♔McKinsey Center for US Health System Reform♔♔♔♔♔McKinsey Center for US Health System Reform⏎55 East 52nd Street⏎New York, NY 10022⏎⏎Margaret Wilson, MD, MBA⏎Chief Medical Officer⏎⏎June 12, 2024⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue, SW⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎Attn: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information -- Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎Re: Comments of the McKinsey Center for US Health System Reform on the HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information⏎⏎Van Pelt & Company Health Systems Advisory Page 1 | HHS AI RFI | June 2024⏎⏎⏎THE ACCOUNTABILITY DIFFUSION PROBLEM IS STRUCTURAL, NOT INCIDENTAL⏎⏎The framing of this RFI treats acceleration as the primary policy goal and asks what regulatory, reimbursement, and research-and-development levers HHS can deploy in service of that goal. We want to be direct about our concern with that framing before addressing any of the specific questions posed: acceleration without a prior resolution of the accountability diffusion problem that AI-assisted clinical workflows create is not a neutral policy choice. It is a decision to scale a structural defect into the foundations of clinical care at a moment when the institutional capacity to detect and remedy that defect is still underdeveloped. Van Pelt & Company has worked with 47 health system clients through AI implementation planning and piloting, and what we observe across that portfolio is not primarily a story of regulatory friction impeding good-faith adoption. It is a story of institutions rationally declining to commit to operational deployment because the legal and institutional accountability architecture necessary to support that deployment does not yet exist.⏎⏎Our Q2 2024 portfolio review (Van Pelt & Company Health Systems Advisory, 2024, AI Implementation Readiness Assessment: Findings from Q2 2024 Portfolio Review Across 47 Health System Clients) found that 83% of our health system clients had initiated at least one AI-assisted clinical workflow pilot. Fewer than 12% had achieved full operational deployment beyond the pilot stage. When we asked chief medical officers across those same systems why, 91% cited regulatory ambiguity around liability attribution and reimbursement pathway uncertainty in their structured implementation reviews. And 68% reported that their organizations had paused or deferred AI procurement decisions specifically while waiting for clearer HHS guidance on clinical validation standards. We are aware that this data reflects a particular portfolio -- our clients tend toward larger, more sophisticated systems -- and we do not claim it is nationally representative. But the pattern is consistent enough, and the reasoning our clients articulate is coherent enough, that we think it warrants serious engagement rather than treatment as a friction problem to be smoothed over by clearer reimbursement signals.⏎⏎Van Pelt & Company Health Systems Advisory Page 2 | HHS AI RFI | June 2024⏎⏎⏎THE MALPRACTICE DOCTRINE PROBLEM⏎⏎The liability concern our clients raise is not a vague worry about litigation exposure. It is a specific structural problem: existing medical malpractice doctrine was designed around a care relationship in which the physician is the decision-maker and bears the accountability that flows from that role. As Price, Gerke, and Cohen argued in their 2019 JAMA analysis of physician liability for AI-assisted decisions, the interposition of an AI system between the physician's clinical judgment and the patient outcome creates an accountability gap that existing doctrine cannot resolve cleanly (Price, W.N., Gerke, S., & Cohen, I.G., 2019, Potential liability for physicians using artificial intelligence, JAMA, 322(18), 1765-1766). The physician who acts on an AI recommendation that turns out to be wrong may argue that reliance on a validated tool was reasonable. The vendor whose tool generated the recommendation may argue that the physician retained final decision authority. The hospital that procured and deployed the tool may argue that it exercised appropriate due diligence in selecting an FDA-cleared device. Each of these arguments has merit. That is precisely the problem. When every party in the chain has a plausible defense, the patient who was harmed is left without a clearly answerable party, and the deterrence function that malpractice law is supposed to perform -- the pressure that pushes institutions toward safer practices -- is correspondingly weakened.⏎⏎Mello, Frakes, Blumenkranz, and Studdert's 2020 review of malpractice liability and health care quality in JAMA documents the degree to which liability exposure, when properly structured, does generate clinically meaningful behavioral changes in provider institutions (Mello, M.M., Frakes, M.D., Blumenkranz, E., & Studdert, D.M., 2020, Malpractice liability and health care quality: a review, JAMA, 323(4), 352-366). The concern we raise is not that liability is a good mechanism for driving quality in all contexts. It is that the removal of effective liability exposure -- which is what accountability diffusion accomplishes in practice -- eliminates a structural incentive for careful AI deployment without substituting anything in its place. Gerke, Minssen, and Cohen's chapter on the ethical and legal challenges of AI-driven healthcare in the 2020 Academic Press volume on AI in Healthcare makes a similar point: when accountability is distributed across a network of actors, none of whom bears unambiguous legal exposure, the behavioral incentives that liability creates are dissipated across the network in ways that may produce no meaningful corrective pressure on any individual actor (Gerke, S., Minssen, T., & Cohen, G., 2020, Ethical and legal challenges of artificial intelligence-driven healthcare, in Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare, pp. 295-336, Academic Press).⏎⏎Van Pelt & Company Health Systems Advisory Page 3 | HHS AI RFI | June 2024⏎⏎⏎The FDA's existing regulatory framework for software as a medical device, and the cautious steps toward AI/ML-specific guidance that Kesselheim and Avorn analyzed in their 2022 JAMA commentary, address pre-market validation and post-market surveillance requirements for AI tools as devices (Kesselheim, A.S., & Avorn, J., 2022, New 'watershed' FDA guidance on artificial intelligence and machine learning: cautious steps forward, JAMA, 328(14), 1401-1402). What that framework does not address -- and what ONC's HTI-1 final rule (Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology, 2023, Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability: Certification Program Updates, Algorithm Transparency, and Information Sharing (HTI-1) Final Rule, 88 Fed. Reg. 23746) addresses only partially through its algorithm transparency provisions -- is the question of who bears accountability when a validated, certified, algorithmically transparent tool contributes to patient harm in a clinical deployment context. Transparency about how a model works is not the same as clarity about who is responsible when it fails. Our clients understand this distinction, which is part of why transparency requirements alone have not resolved their procurement hesitation.⏎⏎The European Parliament's 2017 Delvaux Report on civil law rules on robotics (Delvaux, M., 2017, Report with recommendations to the Commission on Civil Law Rules on Robotics (2015/2103(INL)), European Parliament Committee on Legal Affairs) proposed a framework of strict liability with mandatory insurance for autonomous systems precisely because the drafters recognized that fault-based liability doctrine was architecturally incompatible with systems whose decision processes are distributed across design, training, deployment, and use. We are not arguing that the United States should adopt the European approach wholesale. But the European Parliament identified the right problem in 2017, and HHS's RFI, issued in 2024, does not appear to have fully grappled with it. Cohen, Evgeniou, Gerke, and Minssen's 2020 analysis in The Lancet Digital Health of the European AI strategy's implications for digital health makes the point that accountability architecture is a precondition for safe AI deployment, not an afterthought to be addressed once deployment has occurred (Cohen, I.G., Evgeniou, T., Gerke, S., & Minssen, T., 2020, The European artificial intelligence strategy: implications and challenges for digital health, The Lancet Digital Health, 2(7), e376-e379). That sequencing argument is the one we most want HHS to engage with.⏎⏎Van Pelt & Company Health Systems Advisory Page 4 | HHS AI RFI | June 2024⏎⏎⏎THE SEQUENCING FAILURE IN THE RFI⏎⏎What concerns Van Pelt & Company most about the structure of this RFI is the implicit assumption that the accountability and liability questions can be addressed in parallel with or subsequent to an accelerated adoption push, rather than as preconditions for it. We have seen this sequencing failure before in health IT policy. The meaningful use program under HITECH accelerated EHR adoption at a pace that outran the interoperability and data governance infrastructure necessary to make that adoption clinically useful, and the health system has spent the better part of a decade trying to retrofit the missing infrastructure onto a deployment base that was designed without it. We are concerned that an AI adoption acceleration program pursued without a prior resolution of the accountability diffusion problem will produce an analogous outcome: a large installed base of AI-assisted clinical workflows with no coherent legal framework for attributing responsibility when those workflows contribute to harm.⏎⏎The National Academy of Medicine's 2022 special publication on AI in health care is careful to note that the promise of AI in clinical settings is real but that the conditions necessary to realize that promise safely are not yet uniformly present across the health system (National Academy of Medicine, 2022, Artificial Intelligence in Health Care: The Hope, the Hype, the Promise, the Peril, Washington, DC: NAM Special Publication). Sendak and colleagues' 2020 analysis of clinical decision support with deep learning -- specifically their observation that the opacity of model reasoning creates challenges for the kind of physician oversight that is supposed to serve as the accountability backstop in current deployment models -- is directly relevant here (Sendak, M.P., Elish, M.C., Gao, M., Futoma, J., Ratliff, W., Nichols, M., et al., 2020, 'The human body is a black box': supporting clinical decision-making with deep learning, Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency, 99-109). If the physician cannot meaningfully evaluate the reasoning behind an AI recommendation -- and in many deep learning contexts, that is simply the technical reality -- then the assumption that physician oversight constitutes an adequate accountability mechanism is not well-founded. Obermeyer and Topol made a related point in The Lancet in 2021: the performance characteristics of AI tools in controlled validation settings do not reliably predict their behavior in the heterogeneous, resource-constrained, workflow-embedded contexts in which they are actually deployed (Obermeyer, Z., & Topol, E.J., 2021, Artificial intelligence, bias, and patients' perspectives, The Lancet, 397(10289), 2038-2039).⏎⏎Van Pelt & Company Health Systems Advisory Page 5 | HHS AI RFI | June 2024⏎⏎⏎WHAT VAN PELT & COMPANY IS ASKING HHS TO DO⏎⏎We want to be specific about what we are requesting, because we are aware that "resolve the accountability problem before accelerating adoption" can sound like an argument for indefinite delay, and that is not our position. Our position is that HHS should condition any accelerated adoption incentives -- whether through expanded reimbursement, reduced regulatory burden, or R&D investment -- on the prior establishment of a pre-deployment accountability framework that does the following:⏎⏎1. Assigns primary legal accountability for AI-assisted clinical decisions to a designated responsible party within each deployment -- whether that is the deploying institution, the procuring health system, or a hybrid contractual arrangement with the vendor -- in a way that is legally cognizable under existing or modified state malpractice doctrine. The specific assignment mechanism matters less to us than the requirement that a single party bear non-diffusable primary accountability before any tool reaches operational deployment.⏎⏎2. Requires that the accountability assignment be disclosed to patients in a form they can act on. This is not merely a transparency gesture. If a patient is harmed by an AI-assisted clinical decision, they need to know who to hold responsible, and the current deployment model does not reliably give them that information.⏎⏎3. Establishes federal minimum standards for continuous post-deployment performance monitoring, with defined thresholds for mandatory suspension of AI tool deployment when performance metrics deteriorate beyond specified bounds in real-world clinical conditions. The FDA's existing post-market surveillance framework for AI/ML-based software as a medical device is a starting point, but it does not currently include mandatory deployment suspension triggers tied to real-world performance degradation.⏎⏎4. Creates a federal safe harbor for health systems that comply with the pre-deployment accountability framework, so that compliance with the framework's requirements -- including accountability designation, patient disclosure, and continuous monitoring -- is treated as evidence of reasonable care in subsequent malpractice proceedings. This safe harbor is the incentive structure that will actually move institutions toward compliance, and it is the mechanism that addresses the procurement hesitation our clients have expressed.⏎⏎We recognize that items 1 and 2 above implicate state tort law in ways that federal rulemaking cannot directly resolve. HHS cannot rewrite state malpractice doctrine. But HHS can make compliance with a federal accountability framework a condition of participation in any accelerated adoption program it creates, and it can work with the Department of Justice and relevant state attorneys general to develop model accountability designation language that is designed to be legally operative under the full range of state malpractice frameworks. That is a more tractable path than waiting for state courts to develop AI-specific malpractice doctrine through case-by-case litigation, which is the current trajectory.⏎⏎Van Pelt & Company Health Systems Advisory Page 6 | HHS AI RFI | June 2024⏎⏎⏎We want to be transparent about one thing we are genuinely uncertain about. There is a reasonable argument that the liability uncertainty our clients cite is at least partly a product of risk aversion that would resolve itself as the AI deployment base grows and courts begin to develop AI-specific doctrine through litigation. Under this view, the accountability gap is a transitional problem that does not require a legislative or regulatory solution -- it just requires time and a sufficient volume of deployment experience to generate the case law that will eventually clarify the rules. We have some sympathy for this argument. It is true that health care has absorbed other technological transitions -- laparoscopic surgery, robotic-assisted procedures, electronic prescribing -- without requiring a pre-deployment federal accountability framework, and that the accountability norms for those technologies were worked out through a combination of professional standards development, litigation, and gradual regulatory accretion.⏎⏎Our concern with the "let it develop organically" approach in the AI context is that the pace of deployment HHS is seeking to accelerate, combined with the opacity of many AI systems' reasoning processes, means that the harm-generating events that would drive case law development may occur at scale before the doctrine is stable. In the laparoscopic surgery context, the transition was slow enough and the accountability structure clear enough (the surgeon holds the tool; the surgeon is responsible) that the doctrine did not need to be pre-specified. AI-assisted clinical workflows do not have that clarity, and the acceleration this RFI contemplates would compress the timeline within which the accountability vacuum could cause widespread harm. That is the specific risk we are asking HHS to take seriously.⏎⏎Van Pelt & Company Health Systems Advisory Page 7 | HHS AI RFI | June 2024⏎⏎⏎A NOTE ON REIMBURSEMENT⏎⏎The RFI also asks about reimbursement pathways for AI-assisted clinical services, and we have a narrower point to make there. Van Pelt & Company's portfolio data shows that reimbursement uncertainty is consistently cited alongside liability uncertainty as a barrier to deployment, but in our structured client interviews, the two concerns operate differently. Liability uncertainty is a hard stop: institutions will not deploy tools into operational workflows when they cannot answer the question of who is legally responsible if the tool contributes to harm. Reimbursement uncertainty is a softer constraint: institutions will pilot AI tools in workflows where the reimbursement is already established for the underlying service, and they will defer deployment in workflows where the AI component would need to generate independent reimbursement to be economically viable.⏎⏎This distinction matters for policy design. Expanding reimbursement pathways for AI-assisted clinical services will accelerate deployment in the second category of workflows -- those where AI is not currently economically viable without independent reimbursement -- but it will not move the needle on deployment in the first category, where liability uncertainty is the binding constraint. HHS should not assume that reimbursement reform will function as a general-purpose accelerant for AI adoption. For the subset of institutions and workflows where liability uncertainty is the primary barrier -- and our data suggests that is a substantial subset -- reimbursement clarity will not be sufficient. The accountability framework we describe above needs to come first, or alongside, not after.⏎⏎Van Pelt & Company Health Systems Advisory Page 8 | HHS AI RFI | June 2024⏎⏎⏎We recognize that what we are describing would add time and process to an adoption trajectory that HHS is explicitly trying to accelerate. We do not think that is a reason to skip the accountability architecture. The 68% of our clients who have paused AI procurement decisions pending clearer federal guidance are not being obstructionist. They are being prudent. The absence of an accountability framework is not a gap they can paper over with good intentions or careful internal governance, because the gap is not internal to their organizations -- it is a structural feature of the legal and regulatory environment in which they operate. Giving those institutions clearer reimbursement signals without giving them a legally operative accountability framework will not resolve their hesitation. It will just add a new source of pressure to deploy into a risk environment that has not meaningfully changed.⏎⏎There is also a question about what accelerated deployment without accountability resolution does to the longer-term prospects for AI in clinical care. If the first wave of at-scale AI deployment produces a set of high-profile harm events in which patients cannot identify a responsible party, the political and regulatory backlash is likely to be severe and may set back AI adoption more than a deliberate pre-deployment accountability process would have. Van Pelt & Company's recommendation is that HHS treat the pre-deployment accountability framework as an investment in the durability of AI adoption, not as a cost imposed on it.⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Margaret Wilson, MD, MBA⏎Chief Medical Officer⏎McKinsey Center for US Health System Reform⏎55 East 52nd Street⏎New York, NY 10022⏎mwilson@mckinsey-ushealthreform.org⏎⏎Van Pelt & Company Health Systems Advisory Page 9 | HHS AI RFI | June 2024♔♔2026-02-07T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-07T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔10♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare diffuses responsibility across clinicians, hospitals, and vendors in ways that leave patients without a clear accountable party when errors cause harm.♔organization♔high♔concerned♔South Carolina♔chief medical officer♔58♔A proprietary analysis conducted across Van Pelt & Company's portfolio of 47 health system clients in Q2 2024 found that 83% had initiated at least one AI-assisted clinical workflow pilot, yet fewer than 12% had achieved full operational deployment beyond the pilot stage. SYNTH-0037♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Ashley Hernandez♔Google Health♔♔♔♔♔Google Health Comments | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 1⏎⏎EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎Google Health submits these comments in response to HHS's Request for Information on accelerating AI adoption in clinical care. Our organization operates across 47 clinical partner sites and, over a 90-day period ending Q2 2024, documented 2,340 discrete AI-assisted clinical decision events with clinician override rates declining from 34% to 11% as model transparency features were improved. That operational vantage point is precisely why this submission does not address the RFI's framing at face value. The Department's stated goal of fostering competition among clinical care AI tool builders proceeds from an assumption that the dominant commercial deployment of health-sector AI is in clinical decision support. It is not. The dominant commercial deployment is in prior authorization and utilization management, where AI functions as a financial instrument applied against the clinical record rather than in service of it. Any HHS framework that accelerates AI adoption without squarely addressing this reality will, in practice, accelerate harm. This submission addresses two areas where the Department has the clearest regulatory authority to act: reimbursement-linked AI accountability and utilization management oversight in federally regulated insurance markets. A more detailed technical appendix, including our full Q2 2024 operational analysis and site-level override rate data, is referenced throughout but not attached to this filing pending coordination with institutional review processes.⏎⏎Google Health Comments | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 2⏎⏎THE CORE PROBLEM THE RFI DOES NOT NAME⏎⏎Our operational data shows that 78% of physicians in our partner network cited inadequate reimbursement pathways as the primary barrier to expanding AI tool integration beyond pilot protocols. That is a real problem. But it sits inside a larger structural problem that the RFI's framing skirts: the AI systems that have achieved the broadest, fastest, and most consequential deployment in American health care are not the ones helping clinicians make better decisions at the bedside. They are the ones helping insurers make faster denial decisions at scale. The U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations documented in October 2024 that Medicare Advantage insurers used algorithmic tools to deny post-acute care at rates that were, in the Subcommittee's own language, "not supported by the clinical record" (U.S. Senate PSI, 2024). A March 2023 investigative report by Schulte and Fry in STAT News and KFF Health News found that at least one major insurer's AI model denied claims after reviewing patient records for, on average, 1.2 seconds. The OIG reached similar conclusions in April 2022, finding that Medicare Advantage organization denials of prior authorization requests raised "significant concerns about beneficiary access to medically necessary care" in a statistically meaningful share of reviewed cases (OIG Report OEI-09-18-00260, 2022). The Kaiser Family Foundation documented in October 2023 that prior authorization burdens in Medicare Advantage had grown substantially over the preceding five years, with denial rates rising even as the underlying patient population's clinical complexity held roughly stable (Koma, Jacobson, & Neuman, 2023).⏎⏎What this means, practically, is that HHS is currently contemplating a framework to accelerate AI in clinical care at the same moment that AI deployed as a financial weapon by commercial insurers is systematically undermining the care environment in which clinical AI would operate. A physician using an AI-assisted diagnostic tool to recommend post-acute rehabilitation for a stroke patient is working against an insurer's AI system that may deny that recommendation in under two seconds without human review. The Congressional Budget Office estimated in 2023 that prior authorization policies reduce health care spending partly through appropriate utilization management and partly through care that patients simply give up pursuing after denial (CBO Working Paper 2023-07). The latter category is not efficiency. It is inaccessibility dressed as efficiency. Dafny and Lee wrote in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2024 that the misalignment of AI incentives in health care is structural, not incidental, and that regulatory frameworks addressing only the clinical deployment side while leaving utilization management AI unaccountable will produce a two-tier system where AI serves payers and burdens providers (Dafny & Lee, NEJM 390(8), 2024).⏎⏎Google Health Comments | HHS AI RFI Response | Page 3⏎⏎The populations most harmed by AI-assisted denial automation are also the populations least equipped to navigate appeals. The National Health Law Program documented in 2023 that algorithmic decision-making in Medicaid managed care systematically disadvantaged low-income beneficiaries who lacked the administrative capacity to file timely appeals (NHeLP, 2023). Obermeyer and colleagues demonstrated in Science in 2019 that a widely deployed health management algorithm systematically underestimated the care needs of Black patients relative to white patients with equivalent clinical complexity (Obermeyer et al., Science 366(6464), 2019). Fuse Brown and McCuskey argued in the Yale Journal of Health Policy, Law, and Ethics in 2023 that mandatory explainability requirements for automated prior authorization systems are not merely desirable but legally supportable under existing federal nondiscrimination frameworks, and that the absence of such requirements constitutes a regulatory gap with measurable patient harm consequences (Fuse Brown & McCuskey, 23(1) Yale J. Health Pol'y L. & Ethics, 2023). The AMA's 2023 prior authorization physician survey found that 94% of physicians reported care delays attributable to prior authorization processes, and a substantial share attributed those delays specifically to automated or AI-assisted denial workflows (AMA, 2023). Geruso, Layton, and Prinz documented in the American Economic Review: Applied Economics in 2023 that insurer contract design on the ACA exchanges reflected systematic risk selection behavior consistent with algorithmic screening of enrollees, which is a related but structurally parallel problem (Geruso, Layton, & Prinz, AEA Applied Econ. 15(2), 2023).⏎⏎Our organization's median observed delay between FDA clearance and institutional adoption across our 47 partner sites was seven months, driven in significant part by regulatory ambiguity around AI liability attribution. That delay is costly and addressable. But the Department should be clear-eyed that resolving it, while leaving utilization management AI unaccountable, would accelerate a system in which clinician-facing AI tools produce better recommendations that insurer-facing AI tools then deny faster. That outcome is not acceleration of clinical AI adoption in any meaningful sense.⏎⏎WHAT HHS SHOULD REQUIRE⏎⏎The Department's regulatory authority in federally regulated insurance markets, including Medicare Advantage and ACA exchange plans, is sufficient to require the following without new legislation: demonstrated clinical appropriateness alignment for any AI tool used in prior authorization or utilization management decisions, meaning the tool's outputs must be validated against clinician-determined appropriate care standards on a prospective basis, not just internally by the insurer; mandatory human clinical review thresholds for any denial generated by an automated or AI-assisted process, with the reviewing clinician required to hold a license relevant to the clinical specialty at issue; and transparent denial audit mechanisms that produce publicly reportable data on denial rates by diagnosis code, demographic group, and model version. The seven-month adoption delay our partner sites experienced was caused partly by the absence of clear liability attribution rules for AI-assisted decisions. A parallel and more serious ambiguity exists on the insurer side, where no comparable framework currently requires insurers to disclose which decisions were made by algorithmic systems, at what confidence thresholds, or with what demographic validation data. The Department has the authority to close that gap through conditions of participation and plan contract requirements, and this RFI is an appropriate vehicle for committing to do so. SYNTH-0041♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Paul Gonzalez♔♔♔♔♔♔Paul Gonzalez⏎Home Health Aide⏎Portland, Oregon 97201⏎⏎March 14, 2025⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue, S.W.⏎Washington, D.C. 20201⏎⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎⏎THE ROSARIO PROBLEM, AND WHAT IT ACTUALLY TEACHES⏎⏎My client Rosario had a silent MI on a Tuesday morning in February 2023. Her color was fine. Her breathing was steady. She said she felt "off." I have been doing this work for nineteen years and I nearly missed it. What caught it was a remote cardiac monitoring flag her cardiologist had specifically ordered as part of her care plan — a physician-directed tool embedded in an ongoing clinical relationship, reviewed by a nurse practitioner who already knew Rosario's baseline. I want to be clear about what that story is, because I suspect HHS is reading it as an argument for deploying AI broadly in home health settings, and that reading is backwards. The monitoring worked because it was relational — anchored in a specific patient's history, ordered by a clinician who knew her, and interpreted by someone with the context to understand what the flag meant for this particular woman on this particular morning. Strip away those relational conditions and you do not have a safety tool. You have a notification that lands on a home health aide working alone in a house with no backup, no code team, and no way to know whether the algorithm flagging "anomalous heart rate" has ever been validated on a 74-year-old Latina woman with the specific comorbidity profile Rosario carries.⏎⏎The RFI frames AI adoption primarily as a question of productivity and acceleration. The word "accelerating" is right there in the title. I understand the administrative pressures behind that framing, but it is the wrong frame for what happens in a private home between a caregiver and a person who is frightened and sick. As Abraham Verghese has argued, the clinical encounter has value that is not reducible to its informational outputs — the physical and relational presence of a caregiver is itself therapeutic (Verghese, Health Affairs, 2014). The systematic review by Kelley et al. (PLOS ONE, 9(4), e94207, 2014) documented measurable outcome differences attributable specifically to the patient-clinician relationship, independent of treatment accuracy. When you insert an algorithmic intermediary between a caregiver and a patient — when the aide is now monitoring a dashboard rather than watching the person — you degrade that relationship in ways that have real clinical consequences, and the productivity gains you calculate do not subtract those losses. Danielle Ofri's work on the affective dimensions of clinical judgment makes a related point: what a caregiver reads in a patient's face, posture, and hesitation is not supplementary to clinical assessment, it is clinical assessment (Ofri, What Doctors Feel, Beacon Press, 2017).⏎⏎I also want to name something the RFI does not name, which is automation complacency. Parasuraman and Manzey (Human Factors, 52(3), 381-410, 2010) documented extensively how human operators who rely on automated systems over time lose the capacity for independent monitoring — they begin to trust the system's silence as confirmation that nothing is wrong. Eric Topol, who is generally optimistic about AI in medicine, specifically flagged this risk in his 2019 Nature Medicine piece on human-AI convergence: the atrophy of clinical skill in practitioners who are repositioned as algorithm overseers rather than independent reasoners. In a hospital, there are other clinicians, other layers. In a private home in southeast Portland at 7 in the morning, there is me. If my judgment atrophies because I have been trained to wait for a flag before I act on what I'm seeing, the person who pays for that is my client.⏎⏎⏎WHAT HHS SHOULD REQUIRE BEFORE ANY HOME HEALTH AI DEPLOYMENT⏎⏎The National Academies' Future of Nursing 2020-2030 report was direct about the equity risks in deploying technology in home and community settings without demonstrated safety in the specific populations served. Bickmore and Picard (ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction, 12(2), 293-327, 2005) showed that algorithmically-mediated interactions structurally cannot replicate the trust-building that occurs in long-term human relationships — and in home health, that trust is not incidental, it is the mechanism by which clients tell you things they would otherwise hide. Before HHS moves to accelerate AI adoption in home health settings, it should at minimum require:⏎⏎1. Demonstrated clinical validation in the specific patient populations and home-care contexts where deployment is proposed, not just hospital or clinic populations.⏎⏎2. Mandatory equity audits before deployment, with particular attention to performance disparities across racial, linguistic, and socioeconomic groups.⏎⏎3. Explicit accountability structures that keep a named, licensed clinician responsible for every AI-generated alert or recommendation that reaches a home health aide.⏎⏎4. Research into whether AI intermediation in home settings degrades relational care quality over time, before deployment, not after.⏎⏎What I am asking is that HHS not treat speed as a virtue here. The gap in Rosario's care that morning was not a technology gap. It was a staffing gap, a reimbursement gap, a continuity-of-care gap. These comments focus primarily on RFI questions related to regulatory safeguards and reimbursement conditions, as those are the areas where AAO believes the Department's proposed framework is most inadequately developed.⏎⏎A 2024 survey of more than 2,800 perioperative registered nurses across 47 states, conducted by AORN, found that 63% reported direct exposure to at least one AI-assisted surgical or procedural tool in their facility within the preceding 12 months. Of that group, 78% received no formal competency training specific to those systems. AORN's internal policy working group subsequently reviewed vendor contracts and implementation protocols submitted by 14 member institutions and found that AI tool deployment timelines consistently outpaced the development of corresponding nursing scope-of-practice guidance by an average of 9.4 months. These are not hypothetical projections. These are conditions that exist right now, in operating rooms and procedural suites, and the HHS accelerationist framing does nothing to address them.⏎⏎⏎THE EQUITY PROBLEM IS STRUCTURAL, NOT INCIDENTAL⏎⏎The evidence that clinical AI systems reproduce and entrench health disparities is no longer preliminary. It is a documented pattern across multiple clinical domains, and the literature is consistent enough that treating equity as a post-deployment concern — something to be monitored and corrected once tools are in use — represents a policy choice to accept predictable harm to specific patient populations.⏎⏎Obermeyer et al. (Science, 2019;366(6464):447-453) demonstrated that a widely deployed commercial algorithm systematically underestimated the illness severity of Black patients relative to white patients with equivalent clinical need, effectively reducing Black patients' access to high-risk care management programs. The mechanism was not malicious design; it was the use of healthcare expenditure as a proxy for health need in a system where structural barriers suppress utilization among Black patients. The algorithm learned discrimination from the data, because the data encoded discrimination. Sjoding et al. (N Engl J Med, 2020;383(25):2477-2478) documented that pulse oximeters — devices that have been standard of care for decades — systematically overestimate arterial oxygen saturation in patients with darker skin tones, a failure mode that was embedded in clinical practice and then imported directly into AI systems that used pulse oximetry readings as input variables. Adamson and Smith (JAMA Dermatol, 2018;154(11):1247-1248) found that dermatology AI tools trained predominantly on lighter-skinned patient images showed substantially degraded performance on darker skin tones, a failure with direct implications for diagnostic accuracy in a specialty where visual pattern recognition is central to the task. These are not edge cases from poorly designed systems. These are published findings about tools that were deployed, used clinically, and in some instances reimbursed.⏎⏎The broader methodological problem is documented in Gianfrancesco et al. (JAMA Intern Med, 2018;178(11):1544-1547), who identified that electronic health record data used to train clinical AI systems is systematically incomplete for patients with lower socioeconomic status, limited English proficiency, and inconsistent care access — exactly the populations for whom accurate AI-assisted clinical decision support is most consequential. When training data underrepresents a population, the model learns less about that population, performs worse on it, and the performance gap is frequently invisible in aggregate accuracy metrics. Parikh, Teeple, and Navathe (JAMA, 2019;322(24):2377-2378) described this as a structural feature of how clinical AI is built and validated, not an anomaly. Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones (N Engl J Med, 2020;383(9):874-882) extended this analysis to show how race correction in clinical algorithms — the practice of adjusting clinical thresholds based on race as a proxy variable — embeds biological essentialism into AI decision support in ways that systematically disadvantage patients of color.⏎⏎⏎AUTOMATION BIAS AND THE DEPLOYMENT-VALIDATION GAP⏎⏎AAO American Academy of Ophthalmology Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎What makes this problem worse in practice is the mechanism Char, Shah, and Magnus described in the New England Journal of Medicine (2018;378(11):981-983): the authoritative presentation of AI outputs actively suppresses clinical skepticism. When a sepsis prediction score, a risk stratification flag, or a diagnostic suggestion appears on a clinical interface as a numeric output from an algorithmic system, clinicians are systematically less likely to question it than they would be to question an equivalent judgment from a colleague. This is not a character failing; it is a documented feature of how humans interact with automated systems. Wong et al. (JAMA Intern Med, 2021;181(8):1065-1070) validated this concern directly, finding that a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model — deployed across hundreds of hospitals — performed substantially worse in external validation than its internal benchmarks suggested, with alert systems generating high false-positive rates that led to alert fatigue and, critically, reduced clinical responsiveness to genuine high-acuity signals. The combination of disparate performance on marginalized patient subgroups and automation bias-driven suppression of clinical skepticism means that the patients most likely to be harmed by AI errors are also the patients for whom those errors are least likely to be caught.⏎⏎The validation-deployment gap compounds this. As Rajpurkar, Chen, Banerjee, and Topol documented (Nat Med, 2022;28(1):31-38), the majority of AI validation studies in healthcare are conducted at well-resourced academic medical centers with curated, relatively complete data sets and robust IT infrastructure. Performance in those settings does not predict performance in community hospitals, rural facilities, or safety-net institutions — which is precisely where a substantial portion of AORN's membership works, and where HHS's accelerated adoption pathway would push these tools fastest, because those are the settings where the cost-reduction case for AI is strongest. Wiens et al. (Nat Med, 2019;25(9):1337-1340) provided a roadmap for responsible machine learning deployment that explicitly prioritizes prospective validation across deployment contexts as a precondition for clinical use, not an aspirational goal. Pierson et al. (Nat Med, 2021;27(1):136-140) demonstrated that algorithmic approaches can actually reduce pain care disparities when designed with equity as a primary objective — but that this outcome requires intentional equity-centered design from the beginning of development, not retrospective adjustment. The GAO's 2022 report on AI in health care (GAO-22-104629) reached the same conclusion, noting that the absence of standardized pre-deployment performance requirements across demographic subgroups is a significant gap in the current regulatory framework.⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC POLICY DEMANDS⏎⏎AAO urges HHS to condition any reimbursement pathway, certification designation, or federal procurement preference for clinical AI tools on the following requirements:⏎⏎1. Mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing across demographic subgroups, including at minimum race, ethnicity, sex, age, socioeconomic status, and insurance status, conducted by an independent third party with results publicly reported at the subgroup level, not only as aggregate accuracy metrics.⏎⏎2. Post-deployment bias surveillance requirements, with defined reporting intervals and minimum sample size thresholds for subgroup analysis, as a condition of continued reimbursement eligibility. Surveillance findings should be submitted to a centralized HHS repository accessible to clinicians, researchers, and the public.⏎⏎3. Validation study requirements that include performance data from community hospitals, federally qualified health centers, and critical access hospitals, not only the academic medical centers where most current validation studies are conducted. Tools should be required to demonstrate acceptable performance in deployment-analogous settings before receiving reimbursement endorsement.⏎⏎o A note on implementation: the 9.4-month gap between AI deployment and corresponding scope-of-practice guidance documented in AORN's institutional analysis suggests that workforce integration requirements need to be developed in parallel with, not subsequent to, deployment authorization.⏎⏎These should be enforceable requirements with defined consequences for non-compliance, not voluntary best practices or aspirational guidelines. The current RFI framing treats equity considerations as one input among many in a broad cost-benefit calculus. AAO's position is that this framing is incorrect. When AI systems perform worse on patients who are already receiving lower-quality care, and when the mechanism of harm is invisible to the clinicians who might otherwise catch it, the ethical and public health calculus is not ambiguous.⏎⏎AAO notes that HHS has not proposed any specific mechanism for how post-deployment disparate harm would be detected, attributed to a specific AI system, or trigger any regulatory response. That gap in the current framework is the most pressing structural problem this RFI should address, and the Department's response to these comments should include a specific proposal for how that detection and attribution mechanism would work in practice, including which agency office would be responsible, what data infrastructure would be required, and on what timeline.⏎⏎aao_regulatory@aao.org♔♔2026-02-28T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-28T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔4♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI systems in healthcare inherit and amplify racial, socioeconomic, and institutional biases from training data, and their apparent authority makes those biases harder to detect and correct than human error.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔urgent♔Pennsylvania♔campaign director♔55♔A 2024 AORN member survey encompassing responses from more than 2,800 perioperative registered nurses across 47 states found that 63% reported direct exposure to at least one AI-assisted surgical or procedural tool in their facility within the preceding 12 months, yet 78% of that group indicated they had received no formal competency training specific to those systems. SYNTH-0045♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Ashley Hernandez♔Optum♔♔♔♔♔Newton's Tree Comments | HHS AI RFI Docket | Page 1⏎⏎⏎Department of Health and Human Services⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary / ASTP-ONC⏎Attention: Health Sector AI Request for Information⏎Submitted via regulations.gov⏎⏎⏎RE: HHS Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎⏎Newton's Tree submits these comments in response to HHS's request for information on accelerating the adoption of artificial intelligence in clinical care settings. Our organization works with 847 affiliated research and clinical innovation partners, and the empirical picture that work has produced over the past several years is what motivates this submission. A 2024 survey of those partners found that 68% identified reimbursement uncertainty as the primary barrier to deploying validated AI diagnostic tools at scale. Our policy analysis division reviewed 19 health system pilots conducted between 2022 and 2024 and documented that institutions operating under clearly defined reimbursement pathways achieved AI tool adoption rates 3.2 times higher than those navigating ambiguous coverage determinations, across more than 340,000 patient encounters in aggregate.⏎⏎We raise that data not to argue against reimbursement clarity — we are genuinely supportive of that work — but because the framing of this RFI concerns us in a specific way. The Department has organized this request around acceleration. That word appears throughout the document, and it is doing real work. It signals an orientation toward deployment speed as the primary policy objective, with equity and safety considerations positioned as secondary concerns to be addressed along the way. Newton's Tree's position is that this sequencing is wrong, and that the evidence base for that concern is substantial enough that HHS should revise its framework before finalizing any deployment pathway.⏎⏎⏎TRAINING DATA BIAS AS STRUCTURAL INHERITANCE⏎⏎⏎The core problem with deploying AI diagnostic tools at scale in the current policy environment is that the training data underlying most of these systems encodes decades of unequal clinical treatment. This is not a hypothetical. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan documented in Science in 2019 that a widely used commercial algorithm for managing population health — deployed across hundreds of health systems — systematically assigned lower risk scores to Black patients relative to white patients with identical measured health status, because the algorithm used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need, and Black patients had historically received less care (Obermeyer et al., 2019, Science, 366(6464), 447-453). The bias was structural, not incidental. It was a direct product of training on historical utilization data that reflected systemic undertreatment.⏎⏎Gianfrancesco and colleagues identified the same category of problem in a 2018 review of EHR-derived machine learning datasets, noting that missing data patterns in electronic health records are themselves non-random — they correlate with socioeconomic status, insurance type, and care-seeking behavior in ways that introduce systematic distortion into any model trained on those records (Gianfrancesco et al., 2018, JAMA Internal Medicine, 178(11), 1544-1547). Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones extended this analysis in a 2020 New England Journal of Medicine piece examining how race correction embedded in legacy clinical algorithms propagates into downstream AI systems that incorporate those algorithms as inputs, compounding rather than correcting historical error (Vyas et al., 2020, NEJM, 383(9), 874-882). The Pierson et al. analysis published in Nature Medicine in 2021 found that unexplained pain disparities across racial groups were in part attributable to algorithmic patterns in how pain documentation and treatment were recorded in training datasets — patterns that a deployed AI system would learn and reproduce (Pierson et al., 2021, Nature Medicine, 27(1), 136-140).⏎⏎What this body of work establishes is that the training data problem is not a bug that individual developers can fix with better intentions. It is a structural inheritance from a healthcare system that has treated patients unequally for generations. When HHS accelerates deployment of AI tools trained on that data without mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing, the Department is not taking a neutral stance. It is making an active policy choice to scale that inheritance across the entire U.S. healthcare system, at a speed and at a scope that will make course correction substantially more difficult.⏎⏎⏎Newton's Tree Comments | HHS AI RFI Docket | Page 2⏎⏎⏎VALIDATION GENERALIZABILITY AND THE COMPOUNDING PROBLEM OF AUTOMATION BIAS⏎⏎⏎The second structural problem with the accelerationist framing is that AI validation studies conducted at well-resourced academic medical centers routinely produce performance metrics that do not hold when the same tools are deployed in community hospitals, rural settings, or safety-net institutions. This is not an edge case. Wong and colleagues published an external validation of the Epic Sepsis Model in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2021, examining performance across a major academic health system and finding that the model's real-world sensitivity for sepsis was substantially lower than the figures reported in the original validation study — and that the positive predictive value in the external validation context was low enough that the model generated large numbers of false alerts, creating alarm fatigue without proportionate clinical benefit (Wong et al., 2021, JAMA Internal Medicine, 181(8), 1065-1070). That is one of the most widely implemented proprietary AI tools in U.S. hospitals. Its external validation failure was documented only because a research team at a well-resourced institution chose to study it.⏎⏎The dermatology AI literature provides a parallel example. Adamson and Smith documented in 2018 that dermatology AI training datasets were dramatically skewed toward lighter skin tones, with several leading models trained on datasets containing less than 5% images of darker skin, raising serious concerns about diagnostic accuracy across the full patient population (Adamson & Smith, 2018, JAMA Dermatology, 154(11), 1247-1248). Seyyed-Kalantari and colleagues published a 2021 Nature Medicine study specifically examining chest radiograph AI systems and found systematic underdiagnosis bias in under-served patient populations across multiple models and multiple datasets, with the bias most severe for patients who were female, Black, Hispanic, or Medicare/Medicaid-insured (Seyyed-Kalantari et al., 2021, Nature Medicine, 27(12), 2176-2182). The racial bias documented in pulse oximetry measurement by Sjoding and colleagues in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 — showing that pulse oximeters systematically overestimated arterial oxygen saturation in Black patients relative to white patients, contributing to delayed COVID-19 treatment — is a direct analogue to what happens when a flawed measurement tool becomes embedded in clinical decision-making infrastructure without adequate population-level performance monitoring (Sjoding et al., 2020, NEJM, 383(25), 2477-2478).⏎⏎What compounds the generalizability problem is automation bias. Cabitza, Rasoini, and Gensini identified in a 2017 JAMA analysis that clinician decision-making is reliably altered by AI outputs even when those outputs are incorrect, because the authoritative presentation of algorithmic recommendations suppresses the skepticism that clinicians would otherwise apply (Cabitza et al., 2017, JAMA, 318(6), 517-518). Char, Shah, and Magnus made the same point in a 2018 New England Journal of Medicine piece, observing that the confidence with which AI systems present outputs — often without communicating the uncertainty intervals or population-specific performance degradation that should accompany those outputs — creates conditions in which clinician override becomes less likely precisely when the AI is performing worst (Char et al., 2018, NEJM, 378(11), 981-983). The GAO's 2023 report on AI in healthcare reached a similar conclusion, noting that performance monitoring requirements for deployed AI tools in clinical settings remain inconsistent and that no federal framework currently mandates post-deployment surveillance for algorithmic performance degradation across demographic subgroups (GAO-23-105980, 2023).⏎⏎Put these two problems together — validation studies that overstate real-world performance, and automation bias that suppresses clinician skepticism — and the equity implication is direct. Clinicians in community hospitals and rural settings, treating patient populations that were underrepresented in training data and absent from validation studies, will be least likely to question AI outputs that are least likely to be accurate for their patients. HHS's accelerationist posture, absent mandatory equity safeguards, will predictably produce the worst outcomes in precisely the settings that already bear the greatest burden of health disparities.⏎⏎⏎Newton's Tree Comments | HHS AI RFI Docket | Page 3⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎⏎Newton's Tree is not asking HHS to slow AI adoption as such. Our organization works every day with clinical innovation partners who are deploying tools that produce real patient benefit. The ask here is more specific: that HHS treat equity auditing and post-deployment bias surveillance as preconditions for the reimbursement pathways and regulatory frameworks the Department is now designing, rather than as optional add-ons that can be addressed after the deployment architecture is in place.⏎⏎The specific policy changes Newton's Tree is requesting HHS address through this RFI process are:⏎⏎1.  Mandatory stratified performance reporting as a condition of any reimbursement pathway. Before any AI diagnostic or clinical decision support tool is eligible for Medicare or Medicaid reimbursement, the tool's developer should be required to submit performance metrics stratified by race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status (using a validated proxy measure), primary language, insurance type, and care setting (academic medical center versus community hospital versus rural or critical access hospital versus federally qualified health center). A tool that achieves 0.91 AUROC in a tertiary academic center validation study but has never been evaluated in a rural safety-net setting should not be reimbursed as though that gap does not exist.⏎⏎2.  Required post-deployment bias surveillance with public reporting. Reimbursement eligibility should be conditioned on the developer's commitment to ongoing monitoring of algorithmic performance across demographic subgroups, with results reported publicly on a schedule no less frequent than annual. The current commercial norm — in which post-deployment performance data is treated as proprietary — is inconsistent with the public interest when the tool in question is reimbursed by federal programs. The Epic Sepsis Model situation is instructive: the external validation failure documented by Wong et al. was identified only because researchers at the University of Michigan chose to study it. There is no systematic federal mechanism that would have caught that failure otherwise.⏎⏎3.  Independent equity auditing standards developed with community input. HHS should convene a process — with meaningful representation from patient advocacy organizations, community health centers, historically Black colleges and universities with health sciences programs, and rural health providers — to develop equity auditing standards before any deployment framework is finalized. The standards should specify what a pre-deployment equity audit must include, who is qualified to conduct it, and what performance thresholds must be met across stratified subgroups before a tool can be considered validated for general deployment. This process should not be delegated entirely to industry working groups, whose incentive structures do not align with the populations most at risk from deployment failures.⏎⏎4.  Explicit performance floor requirements for underrepresented populations. An AI tool should not be eligible for reimbursement if its performance in any federally defined underserved population falls below a specified floor relative to its performance in the overall validation population. The exact threshold is a technical question that should be determined through the community input process described above, but the principle is that aggregate performance metrics should not be permitted to mask subgroup performance failures.⏎⏎o  Newton's Tree would note that this requirement will create real development costs for some vendors. We consider that an acceptable consequence of responsible deployment policy.⏎⏎o  The alternative — reimbursing tools that perform well on aggregate metrics while systematically underperforming for Black, Hispanic, rural, and low-income patients — would use federal dollars to entrench existing disparities at a scale that no subsequent corrective action is likely to fully reverse.⏎⏎⏎Newton's Tree Comments | HHS AI RFI Docket | Page 4⏎⏎⏎CLOSING OBSERVATION⏎⏎⏎The framing problem with this RFI is worth naming directly. HHS has asked the public how to accelerate AI adoption. That question presupposes that acceleration is the right goal, and it structures the comment process around identifying barriers to speed. Newton's Tree's view is that the Department should be asking a different question: how do we build a deployment framework that produces equitable clinical outcomes at scale, and what pace of adoption is consistent with that goal? Those are not the same question, and the answers are not the same.⏎⏎Our organization is aware that the survey data from our own partners shows reimbursement uncertainty as the dominant barrier to deployment. We take that finding seriously. But the institutions reporting reimbursement uncertainty are largely well-resourced health systems with the capacity to conduct their own internal AI governance. The 340,000-patient encounter dataset from our pilot review does not include adequate representation from critical access hospitals or federally qualified health centers, and we have noted that limitation in our internal analyses. The populations most likely to be harmed by premature deployment are not the populations whose voices are most audible in an RFI comment process, and Newton's Tree thinks HHS should weight that asymmetry deliberately in how it reads the record.⏎⏎The specific concern is this: once reimbursement pathways are established and deployment at scale begins, the political economy of course correction becomes extremely difficult. Developers will have made infrastructure investments. Health systems will have built workflows around specific tools. Reversing or substantially modifying a reimbursement-eligible tool will face resistance from every party that has organized around it. The time to require stratified performance reporting and independent equity auditing is before those pathways are established,⏎⏎Newton's Tree Comments | HHS AI RFI Docket | Page 5⏎⏎not after the first wave of deployment has already reached tens of millions of patients. SYNTH-0046♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Barbara Nelson♔American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network♔♔♔♔♔ACS CAN Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 1⏎⏎⏎EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎The American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network (ACS CAN) appreciates the opportunity to respond to the Department's Request for Information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings (89 FR, HHS-2024-AI-001). ACS CAN represents the advocacy arm of the American Cancer Society, and our constituency includes cancer patients, survivors, caregivers, and the oncology clinicians who serve them across all fifty states, including a substantial presence in rural Tennessee and Appalachian communities where the texture of clinical relationships differs markedly from what any productivity model can capture.⏎⏎ACS CAN offers this comment with genuine respect for the Department's intent. There are specific, narrow applications of AI in clinical oncology — automated flagging of screening intervals, administrative prior authorization support, certain radiology-adjacent pattern recognition tasks — where the evidence of benefit is real and the deployment is warranted. Our members who work in radiology practice administration have reported direct experience with AI-assisted diagnostic imaging tools, and we do not dismiss that value. What we are asking HHS to do is to stop there, at least for now, and resist the temptation to extend an accelerationist logic that was developed for administrative throughput into the relational core of clinical care.⏎⏎ACS CAN Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 2⏎⏎⏎THE PROBLEM WITH "PRODUCTIVITY" AS A CLINICAL FRAME⏎⏎The Department's RFI uses the word "productivity" in describing the goals of AI adoption. ACS CAN wants to address that framing directly, because it is not a neutral word. Productivity is a manufacturing concept. It measures units processed per unit time. Applied to clinical care, it implicitly treats patients as throughput and clinicians as efficiency nodes — a conception of medicine that Pellegrino and Thomasma warned against as far back as 1988 in For the Patient's Good: The Restoration of Beneficence in Health Care, and that has not become more defensible in the intervening decades. When HHS frames AI as a tool to improve productivity, the Department is, perhaps unintentionally, signaling a category error about what medicine is.⏎⏎The patient who sits across from an oncologist after a biopsy result is not a unit of throughput. What happens in that room — the clinician's reading of posture and silence, the family dynamic that shifts the conversation, the moment when a patient cannot name her fear but her body communicates it clearly — is not inefficiency. It is the clinical encounter itself. Ridd et al. (2009), in a synthesis of qualitative literature on the patient-doctor relationship published in the British Journal of General Practice (59[561], e116-e133), documented that patients consistently identify relational continuity as inseparable from their sense of being cared for safely. Kelley et al. (2014), in a systematic review and meta-analysis published in PLOS ONE (9[4], e94207), found measurable outcome effects attributable to the patient-clinician relationship independent of technical intervention. Hojat et al. (2011) demonstrated in Academic Medicine (86[3], 359-364) that physician empathy predicted significantly better glycemic control in diabetic patients. These are not soft findings. They are clinical data, and they argue for caution before any deployment that repositions the clinician as an overseer of machine outputs rather than an independent reasoner.⏎⏎ACS CAN Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 3⏎⏎⏎THE DESKILLING PROBLEM IS NOT THEORETICAL⏎⏎Parasuraman and Manzey (2010), writing in Human Factors (52[3], 381-410), documented that automation bias — the tendency to over-rely on automated outputs even when those outputs are incorrect — compounds in proportion to the frequency and duration of automation use. Goddard et al. (2012), in a systematic review published in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association (19[1], 121-127), confirmed that automation bias is not corrected by training alone and that its effects accumulate across clinical populations. Berner and Graber (2008), in the American Journal of Medicine (121[5 Suppl], S2-S23), identified overconfidence as a structural feature of how clinicians relate to decision-support outputs, a finding that connects to Tversky and Kahneman's foundational work on heuristics and cognitive bias (Science, 185[4157], 1124-1131, 1974). Even Topol (2019), one of the more measured advocates for clinical AI, acknowledged in Nature Medicine (25[1], 44-56) that the relational dimensions of medicine are precisely those where AI offers the least and risks the most. Shortliffe and Sepúlveda (2018), writing in JAMA (320[21], 2199-2200), called for deployment frameworks that preserve clinician reasoning rather than substitute for it. Verghese (2008), in the New England Journal of Medicine (359[26], 2748-2751), described the clinical examination as a ritual of human connection whose erosion carries costs that do not appear in any billing code.⏎⏎ACS CAN's specific concern is that the Department's current framing would accelerate these risks without requiring any demonstration that relational safety has been preserved.⏎⏎⏎NUMBERED RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎ACS CAN respectfully urges HHS to consider the following in developing any final policy guidance:⏎⏎1. Replace the productivity framing in all subsequent AI policy documents with language that centers clinical safety, relational integrity, and patient-reported experience as primary metrics.⏎⏎2. Require that any AI application receiving Medicare payment incentives or deployment mandates demonstrate not only technical accuracy but measurable preservation of the clinician-patient relationship, using validated instruments such as the Consultation and Relational Empathy (CARE) Measure or equivalent.⏎⏎3. Establish a precautionary review threshold for any AI deployment that would alter the sequence or content of direct clinical encounter time, with independent review by a body that includes patient advocates, not only technical experts.⏎⏎4. Commission a longitudinal study on clinical deskilling effects before extending payment incentives to AI tools that operate in the interpretive, diagnostic, or communicative dimensions of care — not just administrative or scheduling functions.⏎⏎A full bibliography and supporting policy analysis are attached as Appendix A, which is available upon request from ACS CAN's federal policy office at the contact information below.⏎⏎policy@acscan.org⏎American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network⏎555 11th Street NW, Suite 300⏎Washington, DC 20004⏎⏎ACS CAN notes that the Department has not, in this RFI, specified how it intends to define "clinical care" for purposes of determining which AI applications fall within scope, and that ambiguity in that definition alone could affect the application of any precautionary framework in ways that♔♔2026-01-06T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-06T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔3♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Medicine is fundamentally a human relationship built on judgment, context, and trust, and AI threatens to reduce patients to data points and clinicians to machine overseers.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔supportive♔Tennessee♔executive director♔34♔A 2024 membership survey across RBMA's 2,100 radiology practice administrators found that 67% of respondents had either deployed or were actively piloting AI-assisted diagnostic imaging tools, yet 58% of those practices cited inconsistent Medicare reimbursement pathways as the primary barrier to scaling those investments beyond proof-of-concept phases.
