SYNTH-0047♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔William Gonzalez♔Patient Privacy Rights Foundation♔♔♔♔♔Patient Privacy Rights Foundation⏎Comments Submitted to the HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information⏎Docket: HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL-RFI⏎Submitted by: William Gonzalez, Policy Director⏎⏎wwww.patientprivacyrights.org | comments@patientprivacyrights.org⏎⏎Patient Privacy Rights Foundation | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 1⏎⏎⏎THE FRAMING PROBLEM THIS RFI DOES NOT ACKNOWLEDGE⏎⏎The Patient Privacy Rights Foundation appreciates the Department's interest in understanding how regulatory and reimbursement structures shape AI adoption in clinical settings. Regulatory clarity does matter. Uncertainty about liability frameworks and validation standards has real costs, and our organization does not dispute that. But the framing of this RFI — organized almost entirely around "accelerating" AI adoption as though speed is the governing policy value — treats a contested premise as settled ground, and that is a problem we cannot let pass without direct comment. The RFI's language about "fostering competition among clinical care AI tool builders" appears, for instance, in a document that contains no corresponding language about the deployment of AI in insurance denial processing, prior authorization adjudication, or coverage determination. This is not a minor omission. It is, we would argue, the central analytical failure of this solicitation. HHS cannot coherently develop policy to accelerate AI in clinical care while remaining silent on the parallel and already-deployed use of AI as a financial weapon against the patients that clinical care is meant to serve.⏎⏎The Department has in its own possession the evidence it needs to understand why this silence is indefensible. The HHS Office of Inspector General documented in April 2022 that some Medicare Advantage organizations were denying prior authorization requests in patterns that raised serious concerns about beneficiary access to medically necessary care (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General, OEI-09-18-00260, April 2022). That report preceded by roughly eighteen months the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations' far more detailed examination, which found that major insurers had deployed AI tools to systematically override physician judgments at scale, with denial rates that could not be explained by clinical criteria alone (U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, S. Prt. 118-22, October 2023). The Senate report named specific insurers and specific algorithms. It documented internal communications. And yet this RFI, published by the same Department whose Inspector General raised those flags two years earlier, does not once grapple with the denial-automation context. We find that genuinely difficult to explain.⏎⏎Patient Privacy Rights Foundation | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎⏎WHAT THE EVIDENCE ACTUALLY SHOWS ABOUT AI IN INSURANCE DENIAL PROCESSING⏎⏎The Kaiser Family Foundation's March 2024 issue brief on Medicare Advantage prior authorization denial rates documented that beneficiaries who appeal AI-assisted denials face a structurally disadvantaged process: denial rates at the initial stage run substantially higher than in traditional Medicare, and the appeals burden is designed — whether intentionally or not — to be prohibitive for elderly, disabled, and low-income patients who lack the administrative capacity to navigate multi-stage review (Koma, W., Cubanski, J., & Neuman, T., Kaiser Family Foundation Issue Brief, March 2024). The low reversal rate on appeal is frequently cited as evidence that initial denials are correct. Our organization reads it differently. A low reversal rate in a system where fewer than a statistically meaningful fraction of denied beneficiaries ever complete the full appeals process tells us almost nothing about accuracy. It tells us about attrition. The Center for Medicare Advocacy documented in January 2024 that systematic patterns of automated denial correlate strongly with beneficiary characteristics that have nothing to do with clinical necessity — age, dual-eligibility status, geographic region — and recommended specific regulatory remedies that HHS has not yet acted upon (Center for Medicare Advocacy, Policy Report, January 2024). The Congressional Budget Office's April 2024 working paper on prior authorization trends in Medicare Advantage further confirmed that the financial incentives structuring insurer behavior in this space create systematic pressure toward denial optimization rather than clinical accuracy (Congressional Budget Office, CBO Working Paper 2024-03, April 2024).⏎⏎This matters for the RFI's questions about reimbursement because the same reimbursement architecture that this solicitation asks how to reform is currently being gamed, in documented ways, by AI tools that HHS has not regulated. The American Medical Association's 2023 prior authorization survey found that 94 percent of physicians reported that prior authorization burdens had delayed necessary patient care, and a substantial proportion reported that AI-assisted denial processes were specifically responsible for clinically unjustifiable outcomes (American Medical Association, AMA Policy Research Perspectives, 2023). Siddhartha Mukherjee's February 2024 ProPublica investigation documented specific cases in which algorithmic denial systems flagged and denied treatments that the patient's own physician had ordered, with no meaningful human clinical review interposed before the denial became operative (Mukherjee, S., ProPublica Health Investigations Series, February 2024). The question this RFI should be asking — and is not — is whether HHS will require that a qualified human clinician review and affirm any AI-generated prior authorization denial before it becomes final. The existing framework under 42 C.F.R. § 422.566–422.574 governs organization determinations and appeals in Medicare Advantage but does not specify the clinical review requirements that must precede an AI-assisted initial denial. That gap is not technical. It is a policy choice, and it is currently costing patients access to care.⏎⏎Patient Privacy Rights Foundation | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎⏎THE EQUITY DIMENSION THAT THIS SOLICITATION UNDERWEIGHTS⏎⏎Our organization wants to be precise about the demographic stakes here, because the RFI's framing of AI adoption as broadly beneficial to patients glosses over a body of research that complicates that story substantially. Obermeyer and colleagues documented in Science in 2019 that a widely-deployed commercial algorithm used to manage population health systematically underestimated the care needs of Black patients, producing racially disparate outputs from facially neutral inputs (Obermeyer, Z., Powers, B., Vogeli, C., & Mullainathan, S., Science 366(6464): 447–453, 2019). That finding was published more than five years ago. The regulatory response — at HHS, at CMS, at ONC — has been incomplete at best. The National Health Law Program's September 2023 policy brief catalogued the enforcement gaps that persist across federal agencies with jurisdiction over algorithmic discrimination in health insurance, and concluded that existing legal frameworks are insufficient to address the specific mechanisms through which AI systems produce disparate outcomes in coverage and care decisions (National Health Law Program, NHeLP Policy Brief No. 47, September 2023). Geruso and Layton's analysis of upcoding behavior in Medicare Advantage risk adjustment is also relevant here, because it documents the broader pattern of financial optimization behavior among Medicare Advantage insurers that provides the organizational context within which AI denial tools operate — these are not isolated technical errors, they are rational responses to incentive structures (Geruso, M. & Layton, T., Journal of Political Economy 128(3): 984–1026, 2020).⏎⏎The RFI asks how HHS can support clinical AI adoption in ways that are equitable. Our answer is that equity in clinical AI adoption is not achievable while AI-assisted denial systems operate without algorithmic transparency requirements, without mandatory equity audits, and without the kind of human clinical review backstop that basic medical ethics would seem to require. We recognize there is a tension here: the same regulatory clarity that would help responsible clinical AI developers bring validated tools to market would also, if poorly designed, entrench incumbent insurer AI systems that are currently operating in a low-oversight environment. HHS should be aware that the institutions most prepared to comply quickly with new AI governance frameworks are not necessarily the institutions whose AI use most urgently requires oversight.⏎⏎Patient Privacy Rights Foundation | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 4⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC REGULATORY ACTIONS WE ARE REQUESTING⏎⏎The Patient Privacy Rights Foundation is requesting that HHS take three specific actions in response to this RFI, and we want to be direct about why we believe they are necessary. First, HHS should issue guidance under 42 C.F.R. § 422 that explicitly requires a qualified human clinician to review and affirm any AI-generated prior authorization denial before that denial becomes final and communicated to the beneficiary. The current regulatory framework does not require this, and the consequences of that gap are documented above. Second, HHS should impose algorithmic transparency requirements on Medicare Advantage organizations that deploy AI in coverage determination processes — requirements that include disclosure of the algorithm's training data sources, validation methodology, and documented accuracy rates stratified by race, age, disability status, and dual-eligibility classification. This is not an unreasonable ask. It is the minimum informational basis for any meaningful oversight. Third, HHS should institute a moratorium on new AI denial system deployments by Medicare Advantage organizations pending completion of demonstrated equity and accuracy audits conducted by independent third parties, with results submitted to CMS for review.⏎⏎We are aware that some stakeholders will characterize these requests as obstacles to innovation. The precedent established by Schulte and Fry's documentation of electronic health record implementation failures is instructive here: when a technology with significant patient safety implications is deployed at scale without adequate governance infrastructure, the resulting harms are real, they fall disproportionately on vulnerable populations, and they take years to remediate (Schulte, F. & Fry, E., Kaiser Health News & Fortune, March 2019). Our organization is not opposed to AI in health care. We are opposed to the deployment of AI systems in high-stakes coverage determination contexts without the governance frameworks that the documented harms clearly warrant. The RFI's timeline for comment closes in a matter of weeks, and we note that the Department has not, to our knowledge, scheduled any public hearings specifically focused on the insurance denial AI context — a gap in the engagement process that we would ask HHS to reconsider before finalizing any policy⏎⏎Patient Privacy Rights Foundation | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 5⏎⏎responses to this solicitation.⏎⏎REFERENCES⏎⏎Center for Medicare Advocacy. SYNTH-0048♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Mark Lewis♔♔♔♔♔♔Mark Lewis⏎Vienna, Virginia 22182⏎⏎Submitted to: HHS Office of the Deputy Secretary / ASTP-ONC⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎⏎I. THE COORDINATION PROBLEM THAT ALREADY EXISTS⏎⏎When my mother was discharged from Inova Fairfax Hospital following her second stroke in October 2022, I spent the better part of three weeks attempting to reconcile care instructions that had been issued by five different specialists who, as far as I could tell, had never compared notes in any systematic way. The pulmonologist's dosing schedule for her corticosteroid taper conflicted with the neurologist's anticoagulation guidance. The physical therapy intake form assumed a degree of upper-body mobility she had not had since the first stroke. I kept a color-coded binder — an actual three-ring binder, with printed tabs — because the discharge packet was not coherent enough to function as a single document. I had the flexibility to do that. I work from home, I have a graduate degree, and I can read clinical notes without having to look up every third term. Most family caregivers I encountered in that neurology waiting room did not have those advantages.⏎⏎I am raising this not as a complaint about the clinicians involved, many of whom were excellent. The problem was structural. Responsibility for my mother's coordinated care was distributed across multiple institutional actors in a way that made it genuinely unclear who was accountable for the overall picture. The HHS Office of the National Coordinator acknowledged this kind of coordination failure in its 2020 Strategy on Reducing Regulatory and Administrative Burden Relating to the Use of Health IT and EHRs, which identified fragmented clinical information flows as a persistent source of patient safety risk. The strategy proposed workflow improvements. It did not resolve the underlying question of who is legally and institutionally responsible when fragmentation causes harm.⏎⏎That unresolved question is the one this RFI should be answering before it proposes to accelerate anything.⏎⏎⏎II. WHAT "ACCELERATION" MEANS IN THIS CONTEXT⏎⏎The RFI's framing is worth examining directly. HHS is asking what regulatory, reimbursement, and research-and-development actions the Department can take to accelerate AI adoption in clinical care. The word "accelerate" does real work in that sentence. It presupposes that the primary obstacle to beneficial AI adoption is regulatory friction, and that removing or reducing that friction is the appropriate policy response. I want to be careful here, because I do not think that framing is entirely wrong. There are AI applications in radiology and pathology that appear to improve diagnostic accuracy, and the GAO documented several of these in its 2020 report on AI in health care (GAO-21-7SP), acknowledging both the potential benefits and the significant governance challenges that remained unresolved at that time.⏎⏎But the acceleration framing has a structural problem that this comment is specifically about. When a clinical decision is made by a physician, the legal framework for accountability is reasonably well-established. Negligence doctrine, respondeat superior, hospital credentialing requirements, state medical board oversight: these are imperfect instruments, but they assign liability to identifiable human actors and institutions. When an AI system participates in that decision, the chain of proximate cause becomes harder to trace. Tobia et al., writing in the Journal of Law and the Biosciences in 2021, document this in detail, arguing that AI intermediation in clinical decision-making strains existing negligence doctrine in ways that current tort law is not equipped to resolve. The question of whether the physician, the hospital, or the AI vendor bears liability for a harmful AI-assisted recommendation is genuinely unresolved in most jurisdictions. Accelerating adoption before that question is answered is a policy choice with foreseeable consequences.⏎⏎⏎III. THE LIABILITY VACUUM⏎⏎What concerns me is not that AI tools are being developed or even deployed. It is that they are being deployed into a liability structure that was not designed to accommodate them, and HHS appears to be proposing to move faster rather than slower in that environment.⏎⏎Frank Pasquale described this dynamic with precision in The Black Box Society (Harvard University Press, 2015): algorithmic intermediaries create institutional insulation from accountability because the complexity of their outputs makes it difficult to assign responsibility for specific outcomes to specific actors. In a clinical context, that insulation has direct consequences for patients. If an AI-assisted triage recommendation leads to a delayed diagnosis, the patient's family will face the following sequence of questions when they try to understand what happened:⏎⏎1. Did the physician override the AI recommendation, and if so, was that override documented?⏎2. If the physician followed the AI recommendation, did the recommendation reflect a defect in the underlying model, a data input error, or a known limitation that was not communicated at the point of care?⏎3. Was the AI system FDA-cleared for this specific clinical application, and if so, does FDA clearance constitute any form of warranty against the harm that occurred?⏎4. Is the hospital liable for deploying the system, the vendor liable for developing it, or the physician liable for relying on it without sufficient independent verification?⏎⏎These are not hypothetical questions. They are the questions that a family caregiver would have to answer to pursue any accountability claim, and the current regulatory environment provides no clear path through them. Char, Shah, and Magnus identified this ethical challenge in their 2018 New England Journal of Medicine piece on implementing machine learning in health care, noting that opacity in AI decision-making creates specific problems for informed consent and for post-hoc attribution of clinical responsibility. Price and Cohen, writing in Nature Medicine in 2019, made a related point about accountability gaps in algorithmic clinical tools, observing that existing privacy and liability frameworks were not designed with AI intermediation in mind and that the gap between existing law and current deployment practice was already wide.⏎⏎The gap has not closed. The RFI does not propose to close it. It proposes to accelerate adoption into it.⏎⏎⏎IV. THE SPECIFIC PROBLEM WITH AI LAYERED ONTO COORDINATION FAILURES⏎⏎I want to return briefly to the coordination problem I described in Section I, because I think the interaction between existing fragmentation and AI intermediation is underappreciated in the RFI's framing.⏎⏎My mother's care was already fragmented across five specialists when she was discharged. The discharge documentation was already inconsistent. The cognitive load of reconciling those inconsistencies fell on me, a family member with no clinical training and no formal role in the care team. Now consider what would have happened if an AI-assisted care coordination tool had been layered onto that environment. The optimistic scenario is that the AI would have flagged the dosing conflict between the pulmonologist and the neurologist and surfaced it for resolution. That is a genuine potential benefit, and I do not dismiss it.⏎⏎The less optimistic scenario is that the AI would have generated a synthesized care plan that appeared coherent but reflected one specialist's inputs more heavily than another's, without any documentation of that weighting. Or that the AI's recommendation would have been logged in the EHR in a way that subsequent clinicians treated as authoritative, without any clear record of which human had reviewed and approved it. Obermeyer and Emanuel made the foundational observation in their 2016 New England Journal of Medicine piece on big data and clinical medicine that opacity in algorithmic decision-making specifically complicates the attribution of clinical outcomes. When something goes wrong in an AI-assisted care pathway, the question of which human made which decision, and on what informational basis, becomes genuinely difficult to reconstruct.⏎⏎That difficulty is not a technical problem to be solved by better logging. It is a structural accountability problem that requires a regulatory solution prior to broad deployment.⏎⏎⏎V. WHAT HHS SHOULD REQUIRE BEFORE PERMITTING AI IN CLINICAL DECISION PATHWAYS⏎⏎I am not asking HHS to halt AI development in health care. I am asking HHS to condition deployment acceleration on demonstrated accountability infrastructure. Specifically, before any AI system is permitted to participate in a clinical decision pathway, meaning any pathway in which an AI output could influence a treatment, diagnosis, or care coordination decision, HHS should require the following:⏎⏎1. Clear legal assignment of liability. The deploying institution (hospital, health system, or clinical practice) must formally accept liability for AI-assisted decisions made within its care environment, subject to separate indemnification arrangements with vendors. Patients should not be required to identify the AI vendor to pursue a negligence claim.⏎⏎2. Mandatory human override documentation. Every instance in which a clinician follows or overrides an AI recommendation must be documented in the EHR in a standardized, machine-readable format. This documentation must identify the specific clinician who reviewed the AI output, the specific recommendation that was reviewed, and the clinical rationale for the decision. This is not administratively impossible. It is a design requirement that vendors can be required to build.⏎⏎3. Patient notification at the point of care. Patients and family caregivers must be informed, in plain language, when an AI system has participated in a clinical recommendation. This is a basic informed consent requirement. The fact that it is not currently standard practice is a significant gap.⏎⏎4. Pre-deployment accountability review. HHS should require that any AI system used in a clinical decision pathway have a documented accountability framework reviewed by an independent body before deployment, addressing the liability questions in item 1 above and the override documentation requirements in item 2.⏎⏎I recognize that some of these requirements would slow certain deployments. That is acceptable. The alternative is a healthcare system in which AI-assisted decisions are made at scale with no clear mechanism for patients or families to understand who is responsible when something goes wrong.⏎⏎⏎VI. A DIRECT RESPONSE TO THE RFI'S ACCELERATION FRAMING⏎⏎The RFI asks what actions HHS can take to accelerate AI adoption. I want to be direct: the answer is not to remove accountability requirements that have not yet been established. The current absence of a clear liability framework for AI-assisted clinical decisions is not a regulatory burden. It is a gap that leaves patients without recourse. Filling that gap before accelerating adoption is not an obstacle to innovation. It is a precondition for deploying innovation responsibly.⏎⏎I have some sympathy for the argument that overly prescriptive regulation could discourage beneficial AI applications. I genuinely do. But the accountability requirements I have described above are not prescriptive in the sense of dictating technical architecture. They are outcome requirements: document who decided what, assign liability to a named institution, tell the patient when AI is involved. These are not technically burdensome. They are the minimum infrastructure for a healthcare system in which AI participates in clinical decisions affecting real people.⏎⏎What I experienced at Inova Fairfax was a coordination system that had already diffused accountability to the point where no single clinician could give me a coherent account of my mother's overall care plan. I am not willing to accept a regulatory framework that layers AI intermediation onto that diffusion and calls it progress. The families sitting in that neurology waiting room, many of them less prepared than I was to navigate clinical documentation, deserve a system in which someone is clearly and legally answerable for what happens to their family member. That is not a sentimental ask. It is a basic structural requirement that the current RFI does not address, and that HHS should address before it proceeds with any acceleration agenda.⏎⏎The specific mechanism I would ask HHS to commit to is a formal rulemaking process, with public comment, on AI liability assignment in clinical settings, prior to any reimbursement incentive or regulatory relief measure designed to accelerate AI adoption. The sequencing matters. Reimbursement incentives will drive deployment. Deployment at scale before accountability frameworks exist will produce harms that are difficult to attribute and therefore difficult to remediate. The GAO flagged this sequencing risk in GAO-21-7SP and recommended that HHS address governance frameworks alongside adoption promotion. That recommendation has not been implemented in any systematic way, and this RFI does not appear to be moving toward implementing it.⏎⏎I would also ask that HHS consider, in any future rulemaking on this topic, the specific situation of family caregivers who function as de facto care coordinators without any formal clinical role and without any legal standing to compel accountability from the institutions managing their family member's care. That population is large, it is disproportionately composed of people with limited institutional access, and the accountability gaps I have described above fall hardest on them.♔♔2026-01-05T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-05T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔6♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare diffuses responsibility across clinicians, hospitals, and vendors in ways that leave patients without a clear accountable party when errors cause harm.♔individual♔high♔supportive♔Virginia♔caregiver♔39♔When my mother was discharged from Inova Fairfax after her second stroke, I spent three weeks reconciling contradictory care instructions across five different specialists — a pulmonologist's dosing note conflicting with her neurologist's, a physical therapy schedule that assumed she had mobility she no longer had. SYNTH-0049♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Linda Taylor♔Epic Research♔♔♔♔♔Epic Research Community Advocacy Division⏎Comments Submitted to HHS Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎Re: Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket No. HHS–2024–AI–RFI–001⏎⏎⏎I. ORGANIZATIONAL PERSPECTIVE AND SCOPE OF THESE COMMENTS⏎⏎Epic Research submits these comments on behalf of the communities we serve across Nevada and the broader intermountain West, populations that have historically experienced unequal access to quality clinical care and that stand to bear disproportionate costs if the federal government accelerates AI adoption without mandatory equity safeguards. We do not oppose AI in healthcare. We do oppose the framing embedded in this RFI, which treats acceleration as the presumptive good and asks only how fast to move, rather than who gets harmed when the movement is premature. That distinction matters enormously to the patients in Clark County's safety-net clinics and the rural communities along Nevada's Highway 93 corridor who have no academic medical center nearby and no margin for algorithmic error.⏎⏎These comments address two of the RFI's core question areas: what regulatory actions HHS should take to ensure safe and equitable AI deployment, and what reimbursement conditions should attach to federally endorsed AI tools. We do not address the full scope of the RFI because the equity dimensions of those two questions alone demand serious treatment, and because we believe HHS has not adequately accounted for the documented evidence of algorithmic harm that already exists in the peer-reviewed literature.⏎⏎⏎II. THE EVIDENCE BASE FOR ALGORITHMIC BIAS IS NOT HYPOTHETICAL⏎⏎Epic Research Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎The framing of AI bias as a future risk to be monitored is empirically untenable. The harms are documented, specific, and patterned. Sjoding, M. W., Dickson, R. P., Iwashyna, T. J., Gay, S. E., and Valley, T. S. published findings in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 demonstrating that pulse oximeters — devices already deeply embedded in clinical workflows — systematically overestimated oxygen saturation in Black patients, masking hypoxemia and delaying intervention (NEJM, 383(25), 2477–2478). This is not a new AI algorithm failing at the prototype stage. This is a deployed technology, in use across thousands of hospitals, producing racially differentiated errors that clinicians largely did not catch because the device's authoritative numerical output discouraged scrutiny.⏎⏎The same pattern appears across AI domains. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan demonstrated in Science in 2019 that a widely used commercial algorithm for health population management systematically assigned lower risk scores to Black patients than to white patients with equivalent illness burden, effectively rationing care management resources away from those who needed them most (Science, 366(6464), 447–453). The mechanism was not explicit racial coding — it was the use of healthcare cost as a proxy for health need, a substitution that encoded decades of differential access into the model's training signal. Adamson and Smith documented in JAMA Dermatology in 2018 that dermatology AI trained predominantly on lighter-skinned image datasets underperformed substantially on images of darker skin tones, with implications for melanoma detection in populations already underserved by dermatology specialists (JAMA Dermatology, 154(11), 1247–1248). And Wong and colleagues published external validation data in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2021 showing that Epic's own proprietary sepsis prediction model — the Sepsis Prediction and Optimization of Therapy tool — generated high false-positive rates that consumed nursing time without improving mortality outcomes, with performance degrading in community hospital settings relative to the academic centers where the model was trained (JAMA Internal Medicine, 181(8), 1065–1070).⏎⏎These are not edge cases. They are a pattern. Gianfrancesco, Tamang, Yazdany, and Schmajuk identified in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2018 that EHR-based machine learning models systematically inherit the selection biases embedded in clinical documentation, including differential coding practices, unequal rates of diagnostic workup, and patterns of underdocumentation in underserved populations (JAMA Internal Medicine, 178(11), 1544–1547). Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones argued in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 that race-adjusted clinical algorithms — including the estimated glomerular filtration rate calculator and the vaginal birth after cesarean risk calculator — have encoded racial essentialism into clinical decision support in ways that produce systematically worse care for Black patients, and that this problem is structural rather than incidental (NEJM, 383(9), 874–882). The point is not that every AI system is biased. The point is that the conditions that produce bias are endemic to how these systems are built and where they are trained, and that HHS's RFI does not adequately reckon with that structural reality.⏎⏎⏎III. THE VALIDATION-DEPLOYMENT GAP AND THE AUTOMATION BIAS PROBLEM⏎⏎Epic Research Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎One mechanism by which algorithmic errors evade detection deserves specific attention because it has direct policy implications. Cabitza, Rasoini, and Gensini identified in JAMA in 2017 the problem of automation bias in clinical settings: when a decision support system produces an output, clinicians are systematically less likely to question it than they would be to question their own reasoning or a colleague's verbal recommendation (JAMA, 318(6), 517–518). The numerical or probabilistic authority of AI outputs — a risk score, a flagged finding, a prioritized worklist item — creates cognitive conditions in which errors are harder to catch than equivalent human errors, not easier. This is not a failure of individual clinicians. It is a predictable consequence of how humans process authoritative-seeming information.⏎⏎The automation bias problem is compounded by what we might call the validation-deployment gap. Wiens and colleagues laid out in Nature Medicine in 2019 a framework for responsible ML deployment that specifically identified external validation — testing a model in the real-world settings where it will actually be used, not just in the academic environment where it was trained — as a necessary precondition for safe deployment (Nature Medicine, 25(9), 1337–1340). The problem is that most FDA-cleared AI algorithms have been validated primarily at large academic medical centers with relatively affluent, well-documented patient populations and robust IT infrastructure. When those tools are deployed at a critical-access hospital in Elko, Nevada, or a federally qualified health center in North Las Vegas, the patient population is different, the data quality is different, the documentation patterns are different, and the clinical workflow context is different. Seyyed-Kalantari and colleagues demonstrated this empirically in Nature Medicine in 2021, showing that AI algorithms applied to chest radiographs produced systematically higher underdiagnosis rates in underserved patient populations, with the performance gap correlating with socioeconomic and demographic factors (Nature Medicine, 27(12), 2176–2182). The communities that are already medically underserved are also the communities where AI tools are most likely to underperform. Acceleration without site-specific validation requirements means that the tools will be deployed fastest in the settings where they are least likely to work correctly and where patients have the fewest alternative sources of care.⏎⏎⏎IV. WHAT HHS MUST REQUIRE: PRE-DEPLOYMENT EQUITY AUDITING AND POST-DEPLOYMENT SURVEILLANCE⏎⏎Epic Research Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 4⏎⏎Given the documented evidence above, Epic Research urges HHS to condition any federal reimbursement pathway, endorsement mechanism, or procurement preference for AI clinical tools on the following requirements. These are not aspirational standards. They are the minimum necessary conditions for responsible deployment.⏎⏎o Pre-deployment equity auditing: Before any AI clinical decision support tool receives Medicare or Medicaid reimbursement or is included in any HHS-endorsed technology list, the developer must submit performance data stratified by race, ethnicity, sex, age, insurance status, and socioeconomic proxy variables. This stratification must be conducted on a validation dataset that includes meaningful representation from the care settings where the tool will be deployed, not only from the academic centers where it was developed. Char, Shah, and Magnus argued in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2018 that the ethical deployment of ML in healthcare requires explicit attention to how training data encodes historical inequities, and that this attention must be built into pre-deployment review rather than retrofitted after harm occurs (NEJM, 378(11), 981–983). HHS should operationalize that principle through concrete pre-market requirements, not voluntary guidance.⏎⏎o Post-deployment bias surveillance: Reimbursement should be conditioned on ongoing monitoring. Developers and deploying institutions should be required to report performance metrics stratified by the demographic variables listed above on at least an annual basis, with a mechanism for rapid reporting when performance anomalies are detected. The National Academy for State Health Policy documented in its 2023 policy brief on algorithmic bias in Medicaid managed care that most states currently have no systematic mechanism for detecting when an AI tool is producing racially differentiated outputs in practice, and that the absence of such mechanisms means disparate harm can persist for years before it is identified (NASHP, 2023). HHS has the authority and the responsibility to establish federal standards that fill this gap.⏎⏎o Site-specific validation requirements for high-risk settings: Deployment at critical-access hospitals, federally qualified health centers, and rural health clinics should require additional validation evidence demonstrating acceptable performance in those specific care environments, given the documented degradation of model performance across institutional contexts.⏎⏎o Transparent reporting of training data demographics: The ONC's 2023 issue brief on algorithmic transparency and equity in health IT identified the absence of standardized training data demographic disclosures as a significant gap in current regulatory frameworks (ONC Issue Brief, 2023). HHS should require that any federally endorsed AI tool disclose the demographic composition of its training dataset in standardized, machine-readable format as a condition of endorsement or reimbursement.⏎⏎⏎V. THE STRUCTURAL PROBLEM THAT CANNOT BE ENGINEERED AWAY⏎⏎Epic Research Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 5⏎⏎We want to be direct about something the RFI's framing tends to obscure. The bias in these systems is not a bug that better engineering will eventually eliminate. It is a structural consequence of training on historical data that reflects decades of discriminatory treatment, differential access, and unequal documentation. When a sepsis prediction model learns from EHR data generated in a system where Black patients were undertreated, undertested, and underdocumented relative to their white counterparts, the model learns those patterns. It operationalizes them. It reproduces them at scale and at speed, and it does so with an air of scientific authority that makes the reproduction harder to see than the original human discrimination was.⏎⏎Vyas and colleagues made this point with particular clarity regarding race correction in clinical algorithms — the adjustments built into tools like the eGFR calculator effectively encoded a false biological essentialism that produced systematically worse nephrology referral rates for Black patients, not because any individual clinician intended harm, but because the algorithm was trusted and the structural bias was invisible (NEJM, 383(9), 874–882). The same logic applies to any AI system trained on healthcare data generated in a structurally unequal system. Acceleration amplifies that problem. More deployments, more settings, more clinical decisions influenced by biased outputs, faster.⏎⏎Epic Research Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 6⏎⏎We are not asking HHS to stop AI development. We are asking HHS to stop treating equity safeguards as optional features that can be added after the deployment ecosystem is established. That sequencing has failed in every prior context where it has been tried. The communities we represent in Nevada — including the approximately 340,000 residents of Clark County who rely on safety-net and Medicaid-funded care — do not have the luxury of waiting for a second generation of better-validated tools after the first generation has already distorted their clinical care.⏎⏎The ONC's own 2023 issue brief acknowledged that current regulatory frameworks contain significant gaps in equity oversight for health IT, and that existing transparency and non-discrimination provisions do not reach the specific mechanisms by which AI tools produce disparate outputs (ONC Issue Brief, 2023). HHS should treat that acknowledgment not as background context but as an action item. The RFI asks what the Department can do to accelerate AI adoption. Epic Research's answer is that the Department should first do what is necessary to make adoption safe — and that the documented evidence of algorithmic bias in pulse oximetry, sepsis prediction, chest radiograph analysis, dermatology screening, and population health management makes clear that "safe" has not yet been defined in terms that protect the patients most at risk.⏎⏎The absence of mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing and post-deployment bias surveillance is not a regulatory gap that exists because it is technically difficult to fill. It exists because the policy process has not yet treated it as a prerequisite rather than an aspiration. SYNTH-0050♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Thomas Jackson♔IBM Watson Health Alumni Network♔♔♔♔♔IBM Watson Health Alumni Network | HHS AI RFI Comments | Docket HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 1⏎⏎Thomas Jackson, Senior Healthcare Administrator⏎IBM Watson Health Alumni Network⏎Billings, Montana 59101⏎⏎Submitted via regulations.gov⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎IBM Watson Health Alumni Network | HHS AI RFI Comments | Docket HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 2⏎⏎I. PRELIMINARY STATEMENT⏎⏎Our network includes healthcare administrators, clinical informatics professionals, and health system leaders who have spent the better part of two decades deploying, evaluating, and in many cases decommissioning AI systems across institutional settings. We do not approach this RFI as skeptics of technology. A 2024 internal deployment analysis across 47 health system partners integrating AI-assisted radiology tools found that AI-assisted reads reduced average radiologist turnaround time by 38% while maintaining a false-negative rate below 0.3% across more than 2.1 million chest imaging studies. We cite that figure not to endorse the Department's direction, but to establish that we have operational standing to say what we are about to say, and that our objections do not come from ignorance of what these systems can do.⏎⏎What concerns us is not the capability of clinical AI. What concerns us is the framing of this RFI itself, and the policy logic that framing encodes. HHS asks how it can "reduce uncertainty that impedes AI innovation" in clinical settings. Read that phrase carefully. It treats public oversight as an obstacle to be cleared rather than a legitimate democratic interest to be served. That framing is not neutral. It is a policy commitment disguised as an administrative question, and our network believes the Department should be held accountable for it.⏎⏎II. ON THE QUESTION OF IRREVERSIBILITY AND DEMOCRATIC FORECLOSURE⏎⏎The RFI does not ask whether clinical AI adoption should be accelerated. It asks how. That is not a small distinction. When a federal agency structures a public comment process around the assumption that a particular policy direction is already decided, and then solicits input only on implementation mechanics, it engages in what we would describe as democratic preemption. The public's right to decide whether medicine should remain organized primarily around human judgment, human accountability, and human institutions is foreclosed before the first comment is filed.⏎⏎This matters because AI embedding in clinical and administrative workflows is not reversible in any practical sense. Coiera, Ash, and Berg documented in their 2016 review in the Yearbook of Medical Informatics how health information technology, once embedded, reshapes institutional knowledge, staffing models, and clinical culture in ways that persist long after the original systems are replaced or fail (Coiera, Ash, & Berg, 2016). The same dynamic applies with considerably more force to AI systems, which do not merely automate tasks but reorganize the cognitive and institutional architecture around those tasks. Once a radiology department restructures its staffing model around AI-assisted reads, once an emergency department builds its triage workflow around algorithmic risk scores, once a health system's procurement and documentation processes are rebuilt around vendor-supplied decision support, the institutional knowledge required to operate without those systems begins to atrophy. Within five to seven years, reversal is not a policy option. It is a crisis scenario.⏎⏎HHS's acceleration agenda, if successful, will produce exactly that condition across hundreds of health systems simultaneously. The 84% of participating institutions in our partner network who cited reimbursement uncertainty as a barrier to broader AI adoption were not describing a problem that HHS should solve by eliminating that uncertainty in favor of adoption. They were describing a normal and appropriate feature of a healthcare system that has not yet decided, at a democratic level, how much of its clinical judgment it wishes to cede to vendor systems. Removing that uncertainty by creating reimbursement pathways and standardized deployment frameworks does not resolve the underlying question. It simply answers it without asking.⏎⏎IBM Watson Health Alumni Network | HHS AI RFI Comments | Docket HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 3⏎⏎III. ON THE STRUCTURAL OPACITY OF PROPRIETARY CLINICAL AI⏎⏎There is a second dimension to this problem that the RFI's framing actively obscures. Proprietary AI systems deployed in clinical settings are not transparent to regulators, clinicians, or patients in any operationally meaningful sense. Frank Pasquale's analysis in The Black Box Society (2015) established the basic governance problem: algorithmic systems that control consequential decisions are, by design and by commercial incentive, structurally resistant to external scrutiny. In clinical AI, that problem is compounded by the technical complexity of model architecture, the proprietary nature of training data, and the gap between published performance metrics and real-world deployment behavior.⏎⏎Selbst and Barocas argued in their 2018 Fordham Law Review analysis that the "intuitive appeal of explainable machines" obscures the degree to which post-hoc explanations of algorithmic outputs do not actually expose the causal structure of model decisions (Selbst & Barocas, 2018). Doshi-Velez and Kim made a related point in their 2017 work on interpretable machine learning: that interpretability is not a binary property but a contested and context-dependent one, and that regulatory frameworks which treat it as a checkable box will systematically underestimate model opacity in real deployment environments (Doshi-Velez & Kim, 2017). Mittelstadt, Russell, and Wachter extended this argument to the governance context, finding that current explanation frameworks for AI systems fail to support the kind of contrastive, socially grounded accountability that democratic oversight requires (Mittelstadt, Russell, & Wachter, 2019).⏎⏎What this means practically is that HHS cannot create meaningful oversight of systems it cannot inspect, and it cannot inspect systems whose vendors have no legal obligation to disclose model architecture, training data composition, or performance degradation over time. The absence of standardized HHS guidance on clinical AI validation requirements, which our network's procurement analysis found extended average vendor-to-deployment cycles by 14 months compared to institutions operating under clearer international regulatory frameworks, is not simply an efficiency problem. It is a symptom of the fact that no one, including HHS, currently has the tools to evaluate what these systems are actually doing at scale. Shortliffe and Sepúlveda noted in their 2018 JAMA commentary that clinical decision support systems require ongoing validation in deployment contexts that differ materially from validation environments, and that the gap between trial performance and clinical performance is a structural feature of the field, not an anomaly (Shortliffe & Sepúlveda, 2018).⏎⏎The Department's response to this governance gap, as encoded in this RFI, is to accelerate deployment anyway. We find that difficult to justify on any administrative law theory we are aware of.⏎⏎IBM Watson Health Alumni Network | HHS AI RFI Comments | Docket HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 4⏎⏎IV. ON THE DISTRIBUTION OF HARMS AND THE QUESTION OF WHOSE MEDICINE THIS IS⏎⏎The governance problem is not evenly distributed. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan demonstrated in their 2019 Science paper that a widely deployed commercial algorithm used to manage population health systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients, not because of explicit racial coding but because the algorithm used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need, embedding the structural inequities of healthcare access directly into its outputs (Obermeyer et al., 2019). Virginia Eubanks documented in Automating Inequality (2018) how algorithmic systems deployed in public benefit contexts consistently concentrate their error costs on populations with the least institutional power to contest or correct those errors. The National Academy of Medicine's 2022 special publication on AI in health care identified health equity as one of the central unresolved challenges in clinical AI deployment, noting that performance disparities across demographic groups are common in published models and frequently invisible in aggregate performance metrics (National Academy of Medicine, 2022).⏎⏎Our specific concern regarding this RFI is as follows:⏎⏎o The populations most likely to bear the error costs of accelerated AI deployment are rural, low-income, and minority communities whose clinical needs are underrepresented in training data and whose institutions have the least capacity to monitor model performance post-deployment.⏎⏎o The populations most likely to benefit from efficiency gains are large urban health systems with the administrative infrastructure to capture and operationalize those gains.⏎⏎o HHS's reimbursement and regulatory acceleration agenda, if implemented as framed, will widen that gap rather than narrow it, because it removes barriers to deployment without conditioning deployment on equity performance.⏎⏎o The 47 health system partners in our network's analysis were not representative of rural critical access hospitals, Federally Qualified Health Centers, or Indian Health Service facilities. Extrapolating from their performance data to a policy framework for the health sector broadly is a methodological error we want to name explicitly.⏎⏎The concentration of AI decision-making authority in distant vendor systems is, at its core, a question about who governs medicine. Topol observed in his 2019 Nature Medicine analysis that the integration of AI into clinical care raises fundamental questions about the physician-patient relationship and the distribution of clinical authority (Topol, 2019). Hoffman and Podgurski argued in their 2013 American Journal of Law and Medicine analysis that the use of large biomedical datasets in clinical decision-making raises governance questions that cannot be resolved through purely technical frameworks (Hoffman & Podgurski, 2013). These are not questions that an RFI process can resolve, and they are not questions that HHS has the democratic mandate to resolve unilaterally by building a reimbursement and regulatory architecture that makes one answer to them effectively permanent.⏎⏎IBM Watson Health Alumni Network | HHS AI RFI Comments | Docket HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 5⏎⏎V. SPECIFIC REQUESTS TO THE DEPARTMENT⏎⏎Our network does not oppose federal engagement with clinical AI governance. We oppose the specific framing of this RFI, which treats acceleration as the goal and oversight as an obstacle. If HHS proceeds with rulemaking or policy guidance in this area, we request that the Department address the following before establishing any reimbursement pathways or deployment frameworks:⏎⏎1. Publish a formal analysis of which clinical workflow categories, once restructured around AI systems, would require crisis-level institutional response to reverse, and disclose what mitigation obligations the Department believes it has in those cases.⏎⏎2. Require as a condition of any reimbursement coverage determination for clinical AI that vendors disclose training data demographic composition, model architecture at a level sufficient for independent audit, and documented performance variance across patient subgroups.⏎⏎3. Commission an independent assessment of whether the current FDA Software as a Medical Device framework, combined with existing ONC certification requirements, actually provides the oversight infrastructure that HHS's acceleration agenda assumes is in place. Our network's operational experience suggests it does not.⏎⏎4. Conduct a separate RFI process specifically directed at frontline clinicians, rural health system administrators, and community health organizations, whose perspectives on AI governance are systematically absent from the comment record that large health systems and technology vendors dominate.⏎⏎The procurement timeline analysis we cited earlier, the 14-month gap between vendor contract and deployment in institutions operating without clear regulatory frameworks, is real and worth addressing. But the solution to that problem is not to remove oversight. The solution is to build oversight frameworks that are actually capable of doing what oversight is supposed to do, which is give the public confidence that consequential decisions about their care are being made by systems that someone with authority and accountability has actually examined.⏎⏎We are not aware of any current federal framework that meets that standard for clinical AI, and we do not believe that⏎⏎IBM Watson Health Alumni Network | HHS AI RFI Comments | Docket HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 6⏎⏎accelerating deployment through reimbursement incentives while that gap remains unaddressed is a defensible position for the Department to take. Our network will be monitoring subsequent guidance closely and reserves the right to submit supplemental comments if draft regulatory text is published.⏎⏎Thomas Jackson⏎Senior Healthcare Administrator, IBM Watson Health Alumni Network⏎tjackson@ibmwatsonhealthalumni.net⏎Billings, MT 59101♔♔2026-01-06T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-06T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔6♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Once AI systems are embedded in healthcare infrastructure, they become practically irreversible and resistant to democratic oversight, creating a permanent transfer of power from clinicians, patients, and regulators to technology vendors.♔organization♔high♔angry♔Montana♔healthcare administrator♔60♔A 2024 internal deployment analysis across 47 health system partners integrating Harrison.ai's radiology AI tools found that AI-assisted reads reduced average radiologist turnaround time by 38% while maintaining a false-negative rate below 0.3% across more than 2.1 million chest imaging studies. SYNTH-0051♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Melissa Scott♔American Society of Human Genetics♔♔♔♔♔AMERICAN SOCIETY OF HUMAN GENETICS⏎Comments in Response to HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI-001⏎Submitted by Melissa Scott, Executive Director⏎American Society of Human Genetics⏎⏎EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎The American Society of Human Genetics (ASHG) submits these comments with significant concern that the framing of HHS's request for information conflates two categorically different uses of artificial intelligence in health care: AI deployed to support clinical decision-making for patients, and AI deployed to automate coverage denials for the financial benefit of insurers. Our member organizations — 847 clearinghouses and health information exchanges processing in excess of 4.2 billion claims transactions annually — occupy a unique vantage point on this distinction. They sit, structurally, at the intersection of clinical data flows and administrative coverage determinations, and what our Q3 2024 policy working group documented in that position is not a story of AI accelerating care. It is a story of AI being deployed at industrial scale to obstruct it. HHS must be clear-eyed about what it is accelerating before issuing guidance that treats all health sector AI as presumptively beneficial.⏎⏎These comments address two of the RFI's core questions: first, what regulatory actions HHS should take to govern AI use in coverage determination workflows, and second, what accountability mechanisms are necessary before any further federal support for AI deployment in prior authorization and claims adjudication. We do not address clinical AI bias, workforce impacts, or vendor market dynamics, which merit separate comment processes. Our concern here is narrower and more urgent: the use of AI as a financial weapon against patients seeking medically necessary care.⏎⏎The scale of what is already happening in the field is not speculative. The Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations documented in October 2023, in its report "Denial, Delay, Deny: How Medicare Advantage Insurers Use AI to Override Physician Judgments" (S. Prt. 118-22), that major Medicare Advantage organizations were using AI-driven prior authorization tools to generate denials at rates that bore no relationship to clinical inappropriateness determinations. The Subcommittee found that one large insurer's AI system was denying post-acute care claims at a rate that exceeded 90 percent in certain categories, with individual claim reviews lasting as little as 1.2 seconds — a duration that cannot, by any reasonable standard, constitute clinical review. This is not an edge case or a malfunction. It is the system operating as designed. The HHS Office of Inspector General reached a parallel conclusion in April 2022, finding in OIG Report OEI-09-18-00260 that Medicare Advantage organizations were denying prior authorization requests that met Medicare coverage criteria, and that beneficiaries and providers who appealed those denials succeeded at rates exceeding 75 percent when they managed to complete the appeals process at all.⏎⏎That last clause — "when they managed to complete the appeals process at all" — is where the consumer protection crisis lives, and it is a crisis that HHS's framing of AI adoption as a competitive clinical opportunity does not acknowledge. The appeals architecture established under 42 C.F.R. §§ 422.566 through 422.574 was designed for a pre-algorithmic era in which individual denials were individually reviewed, and individual patients or their providers could contest individual determinations through a process that, while burdensome, was at least responsive to the specific facts of a specific case. What AI-driven denial automation has done to that architecture is to invert its logic entirely. When an algorithm processes tens of thousands of prior authorization requests per day and denies a statistically predictable percentage of them based on pattern-matching against cost-containment thresholds rather than clinical criteria, the appeals process does not scale with the denial volume. Patients — elderly, disabled, or low-income patients in particular — are left holding individual appeals rights against an industrial denial apparatus. The Kaiser Family Foundation documented in its March 2023 issue brief on prior authorization in Medicare Advantage that fewer than one percent of denied beneficiaries filed formal appeals, not because the denials were appropriate, but because the process is structurally designed to be abandoned. ProPublica and The Capitol Forum's investigative reporting on UnitedHealth's AI denial practices, published in November 2023, documented specific cases in which physician-ordered care was overridden by algorithmic determinations, patients were discharged from post-acute facilities prematurely, and the human cost of those decisions — including documented patient deterioration — was absorbed entirely by patients and their families, not by the insurer whose algorithm generated the denial.⏎⏎ASHG's recommendations are organized below, followed by a reference to the supporting data appendix that our policy working group has compiled from member transaction records.⏎⏎RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎1. HHS should impose a moratorium on the use of AI or algorithmic tools as the primary or determinative basis for prior authorization denials in Medicare Advantage, Medicaid managed care, and federally facilitated marketplace plans pending the establishment of federal minimum safety standards for such tools. This moratorium is not a permanent prohibition on AI in coverage determination; it is a recognition that the current deployment environment lacks the safeguards that any other high-stakes automated decision system would require before federal agencies endorsed its expansion. The American Medical Association's 2023 prior authorization physician survey found that 94 percent of physicians reported that prior authorization delays caused patients to abandon recommended treatment, and 33 percent reported that prior authorization had contributed to a serious adverse event for a patient in their care. These are not tolerable baseline conditions for a regulatory acceleration agenda.⏎⏎2. HHS should require, as a condition of Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care contract participation, that any AI or algorithmic tool used in prior authorization or claims adjudication meet a mandatory human review threshold: specifically, that no denial of a prior authorization request for post-acute care, durable medical equipment, behavioral health services, or specialty pharmaceuticals may be issued without documented attestation of individualized clinical review by a licensed clinician with relevant specialty training. The 1.2-second review times documented by the Senate Permanent Subcommittee are not compliant with this standard. They cannot be made compliant through software modifications. They represent a structural choice by insurers to substitute algorithmic cost-containment for clinical judgment, and that choice must have regulatory consequences.⏎⏎3. HHS should establish algorithmic transparency requirements applicable to any AI tool used in coverage determination, including mandatory public disclosure of: (a) the training data sources and time periods used to develop the model; (b) the outcome metrics the model is optimized to predict; (c) denial rate benchmarks by care category, patient demographic, and geography; and (d) the frequency and methodology of model validation and updating. The National Academy for State Health Policy's January 2024 tracker of state laws challenging insurer use of AI in prior authorization identified at least fourteen states that had enacted or were actively advancing legislation in this area — a regulatory patchwork that is itself a market dysfunction, and one that federal transparency standards could rationalize. The absence of federal disclosure requirements has created the precise compliance uncertainty that our member survey documented, with 78 percent of clearinghouses and health information exchanges reporting interoperability and governance barriers tied to inconsistent AI governance frameworks across jurisdictions.⏎⏎4. HHS should direct CMS to revise the Medicare Advantage prior authorization and utilization management reporting requirements to capture AI-specific metrics, including the percentage of prior authorization decisions in which AI tools generated the initial determination, the override rate when human reviewers revisit AI-generated denials, and the correlation between AI denial rates and subsequent appeal outcomes. The CMS Office of the Actuary's 2023 Annual Report to Congress on Medicare Advantage Prior Authorization and Utilization Management documented aggregate denial rates but did not disaggregate AI-generated denials from human-initiated denials — a gap that makes it impossible to assess the scale of the problem at the federal level even as investigative reporting and state-level data paint an increasingly detailed picture of it.⏎⏎5. HHS should clarify, in binding guidance rather than sub-regulatory communication, that the use of AI tools optimized for cost-containment outcomes as a proxy for medical necessity determinations is not consistent with the coverage criteria established under Medicare and Medicaid statute. The current regulatory environment has created what amounts to a plausible deniability structure: insurers deploy AI tools that generate denials at scale, disclaim that the AI is making the "final" determination, and point to nominal human sign-off processes that the Senate Subcommittee found in practice to involve no substantive clinical review. Ledford's February 2024 analysis in Health Affairs Forefront documented that this nominal-review architecture is now standard across major commercial and Medicare Advantage insurers, and that the human reviewer's role in most systems is functionally ministerial — approving or transmitting AI-generated outputs rather than independently evaluating clinical appropriateness. Binding guidance that defines what constitutes a legally sufficient medical necessity determination in the AI-assisted context is not optional; it is the predicate for any enforcement action under existing statute.⏎⏎The RFI's framing of AI adoption as primarily a question of how to accelerate deployment is, in our assessment, the wrong starting question for a department whose statutory mandate includes protecting beneficiary access to medically necessary care. The more appropriate question is: what conditions must be met before the federal government endorses and incentivizes expanded use of AI in coverage determination workflows that have already demonstrated the capacity to harm patients at scale? Acceleration without accountability is not a health policy; it is a liability transfer — from insurers who profit from algorithmic denials to patients who cannot navigate the appeals process those denials trigger.⏎⏎ASHG acknowledges that there are genuine and promising applications of AI in clinical care settings, including in genetic medicine and diagnostics, that merit federal support. The organization does not oppose AI in health care categorically. What the organization does oppose, with specificity and with data, is the current trajectory in which the most widely deployed and financially consequential AI in the health sector is denial automation, and in which HHS's regulatory attention is directed toward removing friction for AI adoption rather than establishing the safety floor below which that adoption cannot go. Obermeyer and colleagues' 2019 analysis in Science (366(6464), 447–453) demonstrated that health care algorithms trained on cost-based proxies systematically underestimate the care needs of Black patients relative to white patients with equivalent clinical burden — a finding that should have produced mandatory bias auditing requirements for any AI tool used in coverage determination. It did not. The lesson of that failure is not that the federal government moves too slowly on AI governance; it is that the federal government has not yet established that AI governance in coverage determination is a priority at all.⏎⏎Our member organizations processed 4.2 billion claims transactions in the most recent annual reporting period. They see, in aggregate, what individual patients and providers cannot see in isolation: the systematic patterns in which AI-driven denial tools operate, the demographic distributions of denial rates, the geographic concentrations of appeal filings, and the downstream effects on care utilization when algorithmic denials go unchallenged. The data our policy working group compiled for the appendix referenced below — Appendix A: Member Survey Data on AI-Assisted Claims Adjudication and Denial Patterns, Q3 2024, available upon request from ASHG's policy office — documents denial rate variance by insurer and care category that is not explicable by clinical appropriateness differences across those categories. The variance is explicable by cost-containment optimization, which is what the AI tools at issue are actually built to do.⏎⏎The 61 percent of our member organizations that reported deferring or scaling back AI investments pending clearer federal signals are not waiting for permission to innovate. They are waiting for evidence that the federal government has thought carefully about what AI in this context actually does to patients, and whether any of the regulatory infrastructure that governs coverage determination has been updated to account for it. That evidence has not yet been produced. Schulte and Fry documented in their 2019 Kaiser Health News and Fortune investigation of electronic health record failures that the pattern of deploying complex administrative technology without adequate governance frameworks, then managing the consequences reactively, has already cost the health system enormously in both financial and human terms. The AI denial automation context is not identical to the EHR adoption failure, but the structural dynamic — accelerated deployment, deferred accountability, distributed harm — is recognizable.⏎⏎ASHG urges HHS to restructure the questions this RFI is asking. Before the Department solicits input on how to accelerate AI adoption, it should solicit input on what accountability conditions are necessary before acceleration is appropriate. The moratorium, human review threshold, transparency disclosure, CMS reporting revision, and binding guidance recommendations above represent ASHG's assessment of the minimum conditions that must be in place. They are not a complete framework; a complete framework would require notice-and-comment rulemaking that this RFI cannot substitute for. But they are the predicate without which any acceleration agenda is, in our assessment, premature.⏎⏎Melissa Scott⏎Executive Director⏎American Society of Human Genetics⏎policy@ashg.org⏎⏎ASHG Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 7⏎⏎Appendix A: Member Survey Data on AI-Assisted Claims Adjudication and Denial Patterns, Q3 2024 — not attached to this submission; available upon request from the ASHG policy office. SYNTH-0054♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Emily King♔♔♔♔♔♔Emily King Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 1⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue, S.W.⏎Washington, D.C. 20201⏎⏎Re: Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎My mother was admitted to St. Cloud Hospital in January 2023 with an ambiguous cardiac presentation. My mother was in active distress during that entire window. I run a health-tech consulting firm that works with independent clinics across greater Minnesota, and I watch that same fragmented, delay-prone workflow repeat itself in nearly every rural practice I advise, where staffing is too thin and the margin for that kind of inefficiency is essentially zero. So I want to be clear that I am not writing this comment as someone skeptical of AI in medicine. The efficiency case is real and I have seen it up close.⏎⏎What concerns me, and why I am submitting this comment, is that the RFI's framing treats the deployment of AI in clinical care as primarily a regulatory clearance problem. The question HHS is asking is roughly: what barriers can we remove to accelerate adoption? I think that question is incomplete in a way that matters. The barriers that deserve the most scrutiny are not the ones slowing deployment down — they are the ones that, if removed prematurely, would allow deployment to proceed without adequate attention to what medicine actually is.⏎⏎Emily King Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎ON THE RELATIONAL DIMENSION OF CLINICAL CARE⏎⏎The research on this is not ambiguous. Kelley and colleagues conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials published in PLOS ONE in 2014 (Kelley JM, Kraft-Todd G, Schapira L, et al., PLOS ONE, 9(4):e94207) and found that the patient-clinician relationship itself, independent of treatment modality, produced measurable effects on health outcomes. Not satisfaction scores. Outcomes. Abraham Verghese, Nigam Shah, and Robert Harrington made a related argument in JAMA in 2018 (Verghese A, Shah NH, Harrington RA, JAMA, 319(1):19-20) that the physician's embodied presence and attentiveness are not incidental features of care that technology can substitute around — they are constitutive of what care is. I keep coming back to that framing because it is not sentimental. It is a claim about the mechanism by which clinical encounters produce benefit.⏎⏎Eric Topol's 2019 piece in Nature Medicine (Topol EJ, Nature Medicine, 25:44-56) is frequently cited in AI policy discussions as support for ambitious AI deployment, and Topol does make a strong case for AI-assisted diagnostics. What gets omitted in those citations, though, is that Topol himself argues the goal should be liberating physician time for deeper patient engagement, not replacing that engagement with automated interaction. The National Academy of Medicine's 2019 special publication on AI in health care made a similar point — that the "hope" and the "hype" need to be disaggregated carefully, and that deployment decisions require attention to relational and contextual factors that current AI validation frameworks largely do not capture (NAM, Artificial Intelligence in Health Care: The Hope, the Hype, the Promise, the Peril, Washington DC, 2019).⏎⏎There is also a deskilling concern I want to name, not because it is the central argument here, but because it is relevant to the reimbursement question the RFI raises. Timothy Hoff's research on primary care physicians adapting to work innovations (Hoff T, Health Care Management Review, 2011, 36(4):338-348) documented how reliance on structured decision-support tools can gradually erode the diagnostic reasoning capacities that make physicians effective in the first place — particularly in ambiguous presentations, which is precisely the category where AI tools are most likely to be wrong or underspecified. If HHS accelerates reimbursement for AI-assisted workflows without building in requirements that clinicians maintain independent assessment capacity, we may produce a generation of providers who are competent when the algorithm is right and dangerously underprepared when it is not.⏎⏎Emily King Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS REGARDING THE RFI'S REIMBURSEMENT PROPOSALS⏎⏎The RFI asks broadly about reimbursement mechanisms that could accelerate AI adoption. I want to address this narrowly, because I think the reimbursement question is where the structural risk is highest.⏎⏎Current CMS reimbursement structures do not adequately distinguish between AI tools that augment physician judgment and AI tools that are designed to replace discrete clinical decisions. The ONC certification program, as structured under the 21st Century Cures Act final rule (85 Fed. Reg. 25642, May 1, 2020), establishes interoperability and information-blocking standards but does not impose requirements about how AI-generated outputs must be presented to clinicians or what human review must occur before those outputs affect a care decision. That gap is significant.⏎⏎Before HHS expands reimbursement eligibility for AI-assisted clinical decision tools, I would ask the Department to require the following, at minimum:⏎⏎1. Demonstrated relational safety standards — meaning that any AI tool seeking reimbursement eligibility must show, through pre-deployment testing in actual clinical environments, that its use does not measurably reduce the time or quality of direct patient-clinician interaction. This is not the same as showing the tool is diagnostically accurate. Accuracy and relational safety are separate properties.⏎⏎2. Human accountability checkpoints that are structural, not advisory. The current approach in most EHR-integrated tools is to display an AI recommendation with an option for the clinician to override. That framing places the burden of proof on the human to justify departure from the algorithm, which is exactly backwards from a safety standpoint. Reimbursement eligibility should require that the tool's interface structure places affirmative confirmation of physician judgment at the decision point, not passive acceptance of an AI output.⏎⏎3. Post-deployment monitoring requirements with defined thresholds for suspension. Right now there is no standardized mechanism by which a clinic in Sauk Centre or Willmar, Minnesota can report that an AI tool is producing a pattern of clinically concerning recommendations and have that report trigger a regulatory response on a defined timeline. That infrastructure needs to exist before we expand deployment, not after.⏎⏎I want to be honest that I am not entirely sure how to operationalize the first of those requirements — measuring relational quality in a way that is both valid and not so burdensome that it becomes another documentation tax on already-stretched rural practices is genuinely hard. Bickmore and colleagues did some interesting work on how virtual agent interactions can be structured to preserve relational elements for low-health-literacy patients (Bickmore TW, Pfeifer LM, Jack BW, CHI Conference Proceedings, 2009), but that work was in a very different context and I would not want to overextend it. The point is that the measurement problem is solvable, and HHS should invest in solving it as a precondition to expanded reimbursement eligibility, not as a research priority that runs in parallel with deployment.⏎⏎The forty minutes my mother's physician spent manually reconciling medication records is a real problem. I am not arguing for the status quo. What I am arguing is that the answer to that problem cannot be to remove the conditions under which a physician remains genuinely responsible for the decision she is making. The reimbursement framework HHS builds here will shape clinical culture for a long time, and the incentive structures it creates will determine whether AI tools get deployed in ways that extend physician judgment or gradually substitute for it.⏎⏎One logistical note: the RFI's comment portal timed out twice during submission, and I was unable to attach the supplementary clinic survey data I had prepared.
