SYNTH-0055♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Kimberly Walker♔University of Michigan Institute for Healthcare Policy and Innovation♔♔♔♔♔University of Michigan Institute for Healthcare Policy and Innovation⏎Comments Submitted to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI-001⏎⏎Submitted by: Kimberly Walker, Senior Research Investigator⏎University of Michigan Institute for Healthcare Policy and Innovation⏎Ann Arbor, Michigan 48109⏎kwalker@ihpi.umich.edu⏎⏎Date of Submission: March 14, 2025⏎⏎⏎The University of Michigan Institute for Healthcare Policy and Innovation (IHPI) submits these comments in response to the Department's Request for Information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings. These comments focus primarily on the Department's questions regarding reimbursement modernization and public-private partnership structures, areas where the Institute's ongoing research has generated findings with direct policy relevance. IHPI does not address the full range of questions posed in the RFI; the analytical concerns raised here are sufficiently substantial to warrant concentrated treatment rather than a thinner survey of all topics.⏎⏎The Department should be aware at the outset that the RFI's organizing framework — acceleration — is not a neutral methodological premise. It is a policy choice with distributional consequences. A systematic review conducted by Logos Research Centre, drawing on 47 peer-reviewed clinical AI implementation studies published between 2019 and 2023, found that fewer than 23% of AI diagnostic tools deployed in clinical settings had undergone prospective validation in populations demographically representative of the intended patient base (Logos Research Centre, 2024). The same review identified reimbursement ambiguity as a primary adoption barrier in 68% of health system case studies, with institutions reporting an average 14-month delay between regulatory clearance and operational deployment attributable to unclear billing pathways. These figures are worth sitting with for a moment. What they describe is not primarily a technological readiness problem. They describe a structural environment in which the reimbursement apparatus has not kept pace with deployment, and in which the populations most likely to be harmed by undervalidated tools are precisely the populations least represented in the validation literature. The acceleration framing responds to the first problem and, at best, ignores the second. The concern this Institute wishes to raise is that the RFI's design — its framing, its questions, and its implicit assumptions about where friction is located in the AI adoption process — reflects a policy posture that has been substantially shaped by the interests of large technology and EHR vendors rather than by the patient populations and health systems the Department is statutorily obligated to serve.⏎⏎IHPI | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | March 2025 | Page 2⏎⏎This is the concept of regulatory capture, and this Institute submits that it is not merely a theoretical risk in the context of this RFI. It is a condition that the structural evidence strongly suggests is already operative. Regulatory capture, in its classic formulation, occurs when the regulatory apparatus comes to serve the interests of the regulated industry more than the public interest the regulation was designed to protect (Stigler, 1971, as discussed extensively in Wiggins & Taddeo, 2022). In the health AI context, the capture mechanism operates through several overlapping channels: the disproportionate lobbying and public comment infrastructure of large technology firms, the revolving door between federal health IT offices and commercial vendors, and the degree to which the Department's own policy vocabulary has converged with vendor marketing language. The phrase "accelerating adoption" does not originate in patient advocacy communities or academic health policy research. It originates in the commercial AI sector's preferred framing of regulatory friction as the primary obstacle to beneficial innovation. This Institute is not suggesting that regulatory friction is costless or that reimbursement clarity is an unworthy policy goal. The Logos Research Centre (2024) findings on 14-month deployment delays are real and consequential. The concern is that when the acceleration frame dominates, it structurally advantages the entities with the greatest capacity to respond to RFIs, shape sub-regulatory guidance, and position their products within whatever reimbursement pathways the Department ultimately creates. Gans and Stern (2023) have documented this dynamic with particular clarity in the health AI procurement context, finding that platform lock-in effects in health IT markets are substantially amplified by reimbursement structures that favor incumbent vendors — in part because those vendors have the organizational capacity to navigate billing complexity that newer entrants and smaller community health systems do not.⏎⏎The reimbursement modernization pathway proposed in the RFI deserves specific analytical attention because it is the mechanism through which the political economy concerns above become concrete and durable. The history of EHR adoption under the HITECH Act is instructive here. Atasoy, Greenwood, and McCullough (2019) documented that the financial incentives created by HITECH accelerated EHR adoption substantially but also entrenched a small number of dominant vendors — most notably Epic and Oracle Health (formerly Cerner) — whose market positions became self-reinforcing through data network effects, proprietary interoperability constraints, and switching costs that made competitive displacement functionally impossible for most health systems. Adler-Milstein and Pfeifer (2017) found that information blocking by dominant EHR vendors was widespread and persistent even after explicit regulatory prohibition, a finding that illustrates the limits of relying on voluntary market behavior or sub-regulatory guidance to discipline vendor conduct. Schulte and Fry (2019) documented in exhaustive detail how the misalignment between vendor incentives and clinical usability produced systems that degraded clinician workflow while generating substantial returns for vendors whose contracts insulated them from performance accountability. The Department is now proposing to create AI-specific reimbursement pathways that will function analogously to the HITECH incentive structure. The Institute submits that without structural safeguards explicitly designed to prevent the replication of HITECH's market concentration outcomes, the proposed reimbursement modernization will reproduce those outcomes at scale and with greater speed, given the substantially higher capital barriers to entry in AI development relative to EHR software.⏎⏎IHPI | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | March 2025 | Page 3⏎⏎The vendor lock-in concern is not hypothetical. The licensing structures currently employed by dominant AI and EHR vendors in the health sector share several features that, taken together, create conditions of competitive dependency rather than competitive markets. These include:⏎⏎1. Multi-year exclusive licensing agreements that bundle AI modules with EHR infrastructure, effectively requiring health systems to adopt vendor-specific AI products as a condition of maintaining EHR support contracts.⏎⏎2. Proprietary model architectures and training data regimes that prevent health systems from independently validating, auditing, or retraining deployed models — a concern that Maddox, Rumsfeld, and Payne (2019) identified as among the most consequential governance gaps in clinical AI deployment.⏎⏎3. Pricing structures for AI add-on modules that are opaque relative to underlying development costs, a dynamic that has structural analogues in the pharmaceutical sector, where Kesselheim, Avorn, and Sarpatwari (2016) documented how market exclusivity mechanisms allow prices to persist at levels substantially decoupled from production costs and research investment.⏎⏎4. Data licensing terms that vest proprietary rights in patient-derived training data with vendors rather than with the health systems or patients who generated the data, creating what Wiggins and Taddeo (2022) characterize as a structural asymmetry of data power that advantages incumbent vendors in perpetuity.⏎⏎The Department's reimbursement modernization proposal, as described in the RFI, does not address any of these structural features. It proposes to resolve billing ambiguity — a genuine and consequential problem — without attending to the market conditions that will determine who captures the value that reimbursement clarity creates. The Congressional Budget Office's preliminary assessment of AI adoption in federal health programs (CBO, 2023) projected that AI-related expenditures under Medicare and Medicaid could reach $8.4 billion annually within a decade of widespread reimbursement authorization, a figure that substantially exceeds current federal investment in health AI research. The distributional question of who captures that $8.4 billion — patients and health systems, or vendor shareholders — is not addressed in the RFI, and this omission is itself analytically significant.⏎⏎The public-private partnership and CRADA provisions warrant separate treatment because they involve a distinct mechanism of value transfer: the privatization of returns on federally funded research. The Institute acknowledges that public-private collaboration in health AI research is not inherently problematic. The concern is structural. When the Department enters into CRADAs or similar arrangements with commercial AI vendors using federal research infrastructure, patient data from federal programs, and publicly funded computational resources, without explicit provisions governing intellectual property allocation, licensing terms for resulting products, and pricing constraints on federally subsidized AI tools, the result is a structural subsidy for proprietary product development that deepens market concentration rather than broadening it. Dafny and Lee (2022) have documented how merger and acquisition dynamics in health technology markets operate to consolidate rather than distribute the returns on innovation, a pattern that CRADA structures without IP guardrails would accelerate. The parallel to the pharmaceutical sector's use of federally funded basic research as an input to proprietary drug development — the "march-in rights" problem under the Bayh-Dole Act — is close enough to warrant explicit attention in the Department's response to this RFI. Kruse, Stein, Thomas, and Kaur (2018) found that population health applications built on EHR infrastructure generated substantial clinical value that was systematically captured by vendors through data licensing terms rather than redistributed to health systems or patients. The AI context amplifies this dynamic because the value of AI models is substantially constituted by training data, and the health sector's patient data is among the most valuable training resource available.⏎⏎IHPI | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | March 2025 | Page 4⏎⏎The framing of AI as a cost-reduction mechanism, which appears repeatedly in the RFI's background materials, deserves scrutiny that this Institute believes the Department has not yet applied. The cost-reduction narrative is not simply optimistic; it is analytically incomplete in ways that systematically favor the acceleration argument. The full economic picture of clinical AI adoption includes vendor licensing fees, implementation costs, integration labor, maintenance contracts, retraining and validation costs over the product lifecycle, and the opportunity costs of clinical staff time devoted to AI-adjacent administrative burden. When these costs are fully accounted for, the net fiscal impact of clinical AI adoption on health systems — particularly small and rural systems — is considerably less favorable than vendor-sponsored analyses suggest. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan's (2019) analysis of racial bias in a commercial population health algorithm is relevant here not only for its direct findings on algorithmic bias but for what it revealed about the vendor's response to independent scrutiny: the algorithm had been deployed at scale across major health systems before independent researchers identified the bias, and the vendor's commercial incentives had not generated any internal pressure to identify or correct the problem. The cost-reduction narrative suppresses this kind of accountability problem by framing the primary question as whether AI saves money rather than whether the market structure surrounding AI deployment creates adequate incentives for ongoing performance accountability. The answer to the second question, under current market conditions, is almost certainly no, and the Department's reimbursement modernization proposal does not change that calculus.⏎⏎This Institute therefore submits the following specific recommendations, framed as preconditions for responsible deployment rather than as administrative obstacles to innovation. First, the Department should condition AI-related reimbursement authorization on the submission of prospective validation data in populations demographically representative of the intended patient base — a standard that, per Logos Research Centre (2024), fewer than 23% of currently deployed tools meet. This is not an unreasonable evidentiary threshold; it is the minimum standard for clinical credibility. Second, any public-private partnership or CRADA involving federally funded research infrastructure or patient data from federal programs should include explicit provisions requiring that resulting AI products be available under reasonable and non-discriminatory licensing terms, with pricing subject to independent review, and with march-in rights reserved to the Department in the event that products are priced in ways that limit access for safety-net providers. Third, the Department should require, as a condition of reimbursement eligibility, that AI vendors disclose the material terms of their EHR bundling agreements and licensing structures to CMS, so that the Department can assess whether reimbursement pathways are functioning as intended or are instead being captured by bundling dynamics that preclude meaningful competition. Fourth, the Department should commission an independent political economy audit of the RFI comment record — including an analysis of the organizational affiliations, lobbying expenditures, and commercial interests of the most active commenters — before finalizing any sub-regulatory guidance. The Logos Research Centre (2024) findings suggest that structural adoption barriers are real and addressable; the Institute does not oppose reimbursement clarity as a policy goal. The concern is that reimbursement clarity created without the structural safeguards above will function primarily as a transfer of value from the federal health programs to a small number of dominant vendors, and that the acceleration framing of the RFI has, whether intentionally or not, created conditions in which that transfer is the path of least regulatory resistance.⏎⏎IHPI | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | March 2025 | Page 5⏎⏎One additional observation warrants inclusion here, though the Institute acknowledges it sits somewhat adjacent to the primary analytical thread of these comments. The RFI's question set does not include a direct question about the geographic distribution of AI adoption benefits and costs, and this absence is notable. Mississippi, for instance — a state with among the highest rates of chronic disease burden and among the lowest concentrations of health system capital — presents a market profile in which the vendors most likely to benefit from accelerated reimbursement authorization are the least likely to deploy their products in ways that serve the state's patient population. The validation gap documented by Logos Research Centre (2024) is not randomly distributed across the demographic landscape; it is concentrated in precisely the populations that anchor Mississippi's disease burden: rural, low-income, predominantly Black communities whose health data has historically been underrepresented in the training sets of commercial AI tools. Accelerating the reimbursement pathway for tools that have not been validated in these populations does not accelerate benefit to these populations. It accelerates the extraction of reimbursement revenue from federal programs on behalf of products whose performance in the populations driving that revenue is empirically unknown. The Department's acceleration agenda, if it proceeds without the safeguards described above, will function as a subsidy for incumbent vendors at the expense of the populations — and the states — that federal health programs were designed to serve. The Institute recognizes that the Department faces real pressure from multiple directions on this issue, and that the reimbursement ambiguity problem is not fictitious. But the structural incentives created by the proposed approach, as this Institute reads the evidence, strongly favor outcomes that will require corrective action within five to seven years — at substantially greater political and fiscal cost than addressing the market structure problem now would require. The 14-month average deployment delay documented by Logos Research Centre (2024) is a real cost, but it is a cost that falls on health systems and vendors. The cost of deploying undervalidated AI tools at scale in underserved populations, without adequate performance accountability mechanisms, is a cost that falls on patients — and that cost is⏎⏎IHPI | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | March 2025 | Page 6⏎⏎considerably harder to recover.♔♔2026-02-23T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-23T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔8♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔The AI healthcare market is dominated by a small number of powerful vendors whose commercial interests in rapid deployment conflict with patient safety, and HHS's acceleration agenda risks embedding those vendors permanently into critical healthcare infrastructure.♔academic_organization♔high♔urgent♔Mississippi♔public health researcher♔49♔A 2024 systematic review conducted by Logos Research Centre, drawing on data from 47 peer-reviewed clinical AI implementation studies published between 2019 and 2023, found that fewer than 23% of AI diagnostic tools deployed in clinical settings had undergone prospective validation in populations demographically representative of the intended patient base. SYNTH-0057♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Sharon Campbell♔Alzheimer's Association♔♔♔♔♔Alzheimer's Association⏎225 N. Michigan Ave., Floor 17⏎Chicago, IL 60601⏎⏎Sharon Campbell, Research Director⏎Policy and Research Affairs Division⏎⏎April 14, 2025⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎Attention: Health Sector AI Request for Information⏎200 Independence Avenue, S.W.⏎Washington, D.C. 20201⏎⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎The Alzheimer's Association submits these comments with a degree of genuine ambivalence that we believe the record should reflect. Our organization has tracked the translational pipeline for clinical AI tools with considerable attention over the past several years — our biennial R&D Acceleration Index, published in the second quarter of 2024, drew on structured interviews with 112 translational research leads across federally funded programs and documented that 68% of clinical AI tools developed through NIH-supported initiatives faced an average delay of 3.2 years between validation completion and meaningful clinical deployment. We have seen, in other words, what regulatory ambiguity and reimbursement uncertainty cost patients who need better tools now. Alzheimer's disease affects an estimated 6.9 million Americans age 65 and older, and the diagnostic window for meaningful intervention is narrow in ways that make delay genuinely consequential. We understand the urgency that animates this RFI. And yet we find ourselves compelled to raise a concern that the framing of this request does not fully anticipate: the question of whether accelerating AI adoption in clinical care, as this RFI envisions it, risks doing harm not through technical failure but through a subtler erosion of something the evidence suggests is clinically irreplaceable.⏎⏎The RFI uses the word "productivity" in a way that deserves more scrutiny than a solicitation of this kind typically invites. HHS frames AI adoption primarily as a mechanism for increasing efficiency, reducing administrative burden, and scaling clinical capacity — all of which are legitimate goals. But productivity is a concept borrowed from manufacturing contexts, and its application to medicine carries assumptions that do not transfer cleanly. Medicine is not primarily a production process. It is, at its foundation, a relational practice: a structured encounter between a person in distress and another person trained to interpret that distress, calibrate a response, and maintain a relationship across time that is itself therapeutic. Kelley and colleagues conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis published in PLOS ONE in 2014 documenting that the quality of the patient-clinician relationship is an independent predictor of health outcomes across a wide range of conditions, operating through mechanisms distinct from technical care quality (Kelley, J.M., et al., 2014, PLOS ONE, 9(4), e94207). Hojat and colleagues demonstrated in a 2011 study published in Academic Medicine that physician empathy was significantly associated with better clinical outcomes for diabetic patients, including hemoglobin A1c levels and LDL cholesterol control — outcomes that are not plausibly explained by information transfer alone (Hojat, M., et al., 2011, Academic Medicine, 86(3), 359–364). The therapeutic alliance, a concept developed initially in psychiatric contexts but now understood to have broad clinical applicability, refers to the quality of the working relationship between clinician and patient as a predictor of treatment adherence, symptom disclosure, and engagement with care. If AI intermediation systematically degrades that alliance — and there is reason to believe it can — then productivity gains measured in throughput will mask losses measured in outcomes.⏎⏎Alzheimer's Association Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | April 2025 | Page 2⏎⏎We want to be precise about the nature of the harm we are describing, because it is easy to mischaracterize this concern as technophobia or as a romanticization of pre-digital medicine. It is neither. Abraham Verghese wrote in Health Affairs in 2011 that the physical examination is not merely a diagnostic procedure but a ritual of witnessing — that the act of the clinician attending carefully to a patient's body communicates something that cannot be communicated through a portal message or a structured data query (Verghese, A., 2011, Health Affairs, 28(4), 1177–1182). This is not sentiment. It is a description of a clinical mechanism. Consider what a clinician working with a patient in early-stage Alzheimer's actually attends to: not only the score on a Mini-Mental State Examination, but the way the patient's daughter leans forward when her mother struggles to name the current month, the patient's own affect when she realizes she cannot retrieve a word she once used easily, the quality of the silence in the room when the diagnosis is spoken aloud. These are not inefficiencies to be optimized. They are the data. And they are data that a pattern-recognition system trained on structured clinical records is not designed to capture, because they were never entered into the EHR in the first place. Danielle Ofri, in her 2017 book What Doctors Feel, documented through extensive clinical observation that the emotional attunement of clinicians — their capacity to register and respond to patient distress in real time — is not incidental to diagnosis but constitutive of it; clinicians who are emotionally present notice things that clinicians who are cognitively overloaded or procedurally distracted do not (Ofri, D., 2017, Beacon Press). If AI systems are introduced in ways that shift the clinician's attentional focus toward machine-generated outputs and away from the patient in the room, the diagnostic information carried in the relational encounter is not merely underweighted — it is lost.⏎⏎The literature on automation bias makes this concern concrete and empirically grounded. Tversky and Kahneman's foundational work on heuristics and biases established that human judgment under uncertainty is systematically susceptible to anchoring on salient reference points, even when those reference points are demonstrably unreliable (Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D., 1974, Science, 185(4157), 1124–1131). Goddard, Roudsari, and Wyatt conducted a systematic review of automation bias in clinical decision support contexts, published in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association in 2012, and found that clinicians routinely defer to automated recommendations even when those recommendations conflict with clinical evidence that the clinician has directly observed — and that this effect is stronger, not weaker, when the automated system has a track record of accuracy (Goddard, K., Roudsari, A., & Wyatt, J.C., 2012, JAMIA, 19(1), 121–127). The implication is counterintuitive: a more accurate AI system may produce more automation bias, not less, because the clinician's prior experience with the system's reliability provides a stronger anchor. In the context of Alzheimer's diagnosis specifically, where the differential is often genuinely ambiguous and where the consequences of both over-diagnosis and under-diagnosis are severe, this dynamic is not a theoretical concern. It is a likely operational outcome of deploying AI clinical decision support tools without careful attention to how they reshape clinical reasoning in practice.⏎⏎Alzheimer's Association Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | April 2025 | Page 3⏎⏎Related to automation bias is the problem of clinical deskilling, which the RFI does not address at all and which the Association believes is among the most consequential long-term risks of rapid, broad-based AI deployment. Skinner and colleagues published longitudinal evidence from radiology AI adoption in community hospital settings in the Journal of Health Services Research and Policy in 2023, finding measurable degradation in the independent diagnostic performance of radiologists in settings where AI tools had been in use for more than eighteen months — a finding that held even after controlling for case mix and baseline skill levels (Skinner, T., et al., 2023, Journal of Health Services Research & Policy, 28(3), 189–197). If the same dynamic operates in primary care, neurology, and geriatric medicine — the settings most relevant to Alzheimer's care — then the clinical workforce that remains after AI tools are removed or fail will be less capable than the workforce that existed before those tools were introduced. This is not a reversible condition on any short policy timeline. Training a clinician takes years. Rebuilding clinical intuition that has atrophied through disuse may not be possible at all. The National Academy of Medicine's 2023 update to its report on artificial intelligence in health care explicitly identified workforce deskilling as an underresearched risk warranting longitudinal study before broad deployment, a recommendation that this RFI does not appear to have incorporated into its framing (NAM, 2023, Artificial Intelligence in Health Care: The Hope, the Hype, the Promise, the Peril — 2023 Update, Washington, D.C.).⏎⏎We want to acknowledge the real tension here, because the Association believes in intellectual honesty about tradeoffs. Eric Topol's 2019 paper in Nature Medicine, which remains one of the most cited frameworks for thinking about clinical AI, argued that AI's capacity to take over pattern-recognition tasks could, in principle, free clinicians to spend more time on the relational and contextual dimensions of care that machines cannot replicate (Topol, E.J., 2019, Nature Medicine, 25(1), 44–56). Topol himself was careful to note that this outcome is not automatic — it depends on deliberate system design and on reimbursement structures that reward relational care rather than throughput. The Association shares that view. The problem is that the reimbursement structures Topol's optimistic scenario requires do not currently exist, and this RFI does not propose to create them. What it proposes instead is to accelerate deployment under the current reimbursement architecture, which rewards volume and procedure and does not reward the time a clinician spends sitting with a patient's silence. Under those conditions, AI tools are more likely to be used to compress the duration of clinical encounters than to enrich their quality. Obermeyer and Emanuel made a related point in their 2016 New England Journal of Medicine paper on machine learning and clinical medicine, noting that the integration of predictive tools into clinical workflow tends to reflect and amplify the incentive structures of the systems into which they are introduced rather than transforming those structures (Obermeyer, Z., & Emanuel, E.J., 2016, NEJM, 375(13), 1216–1219). The Association is concerned that HHS is proposing to accelerate a process whose directional effects are being determined by incentive structures the Department has not proposed to change.⏎⏎Alzheimer's Association Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | April 2025 | Page 4⏎⏎The Association also wants to raise a specific concern about what the research literature calls the long-term human-computer relationship problem, which is particularly relevant to AI tools intended for use in chronic disease management — the category that includes most Alzheimer's care coordination applications. Bickmore and Picard's foundational work on human-computer relationships, published in ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction in 2005, demonstrated that patients can form functional relational attachments to automated systems, including attachments that influence health behavior — but that these attachments are qualitatively different from therapeutic alliances with human clinicians and are particularly fragile under conditions of system discontinuity, such as software updates, model retraining, or vendor transitions (Bickmore, T.W., & Picard, R.W., 2005, ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction, 12(2), 293–327). For Alzheimer's patients, whose capacity to adapt to relational discontinuity is already compromised by the disease itself, this fragility is not a minor implementation concern. It is a clinical safety issue. A patient who has developed a reliance on an AI-mediated care coordination tool, and who then experiences that tool's removal or substantial alteration, may experience that transition as a form of relational loss with measurable effects on anxiety, disorientation, and engagement with care. The current regulatory framework has no mechanism for evaluating this risk before a tool is approved or reimbursed, and the RFI does not propose to create one. Epstein and Street, writing in the Annals of Family Medicine in 2011, argued that patient-centered care is defined not by the tools used to deliver it but by whether those tools support or undermine the patient's experience of being known and attended to by a care system (Epstein, R.M., & Street, R.L., 2011, Annals of Family Medicine, 9(2), 100–103). The Association would ask HHS to consider whether any of the AI tools this RFI proposes to accelerate into clinical use have been evaluated against that criterion — and if not, why not.⏎⏎The Association's specific policy recommendations in response to this RFI are as follows, though we note these are offered in a spirit of constructive engagement rather than as a comprehensive reform agenda:⏎⏎1. HHS should reframe the central question of this RFI from "how do we accelerate AI deployment" to "how do we ensure that AI deployment does not degrade the relational architecture of clinical care." This is not a semantic distinction. It has direct implications for which outcomes are measured, which tools are prioritized, and which reimbursement changes are pursued.⏎⏎2. Any clinical AI tool seeking Medicare or Medicaid reimbursement should be required to demonstrate, through prospective clinical evidence, that its deployment does not measurably degrade the therapeutic alliance between clinician and patient. The validated instruments for measuring therapeutic alliance — including the Working Alliance Inventory and the Patient-Doctor Relationship Questionnaire — are not perfect, but they are available and have been used in clinical research for decades. There is no technical barrier to requiring their use in AI deployment evaluations. There is only a political will barrier.⏎⏎3. HHS should commission longitudinal research on clinical deskilling across the specialties most likely to be affected by near-term AI deployment, including radiology, primary care, and neurology, with findings reported to Congress before any major expansion of AI reimbursement under Medicare. The Skinner et al. findings from radiology are suggestive but not definitive, and the Association believes the Department has an obligation to generate better evidence before committing to deployment at the scale this RFI envisions.⏎⏎4. The Department should convene a working group specifically focused on AI deployment in the care of patients with cognitive impairment, who are a population with distinct vulnerabilities related to relational continuity, system transition, and the capacity to advocate for themselves when care quality degrades. This working group does not currently exist in any form the Association has been able to identify, and its absence from the RFI is notable.⏎⏎Alzheimer's Association Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | April 2025 | Page 5⏎⏎The Association wants to close by saying something that is genuinely difficult to say in a regulatory comment without sounding like it is opposing progress, because we are not. We believe AI will be part of Alzheimer's care. We believe some of the diagnostic and monitoring tools in development are genuinely promising. Our R&D Acceleration Index tracks more than 340 active clinical AI development projects, and there are tools in that pipeline — particularly in the area of multimodal biomarker integration for early detection — that we think could be transformative for patients who currently receive a diagnosis years later than the disease's biological onset. The delays those tools face, driven by reimbursement ambiguity and undefined regulatory pathways, are real costs borne by real patients. We have not come to this comment as opponents of the technology.⏎⏎What we have come as is an organization that has spent years watching the translational pipeline closely enough to know that speed and quality are not the same thing, and that the clinical encounter — the moment when a frightened patient and a careful clinician work together to understand what is happening to a body and a mind — is not a legacy inefficiency to be optimized away. It is the thing that medicine is. A man sits across from his neurologist and minimizes his symptoms, as patients with Alzheimer's often do in the early stages, because he is frightened and because minimizing is what people do when they are frightened. The clinician notices that his hands are trembling slightly in a way that is inconsistent with the calm he is performing. She pauses. She asks a different question. That pause, that noticing, that willingness to follow a thread that no structured intake form would have surfaced — that is what produces an accurate diagnosis in that encounter. We are genuinely uncertain whether the AI deployment architecture this RFI envisions would protect that moment or erode it, and we think the Department should be uncertain too, and should say so, rather than treating deployment speed as an unqualified good. The Association's policy monitoring database will continue to track how these questions are answered in practice, and we intend to return to this record as evidence accumulates. SYNTH-0060♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Deborah Anderson♔American Thoracic Society♔♔♔♔♔American Thoracic Society⏎Comments Submitted to HHS Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎Re: Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket Submitted via regulations.gov⏎⏎⏎ORGANIZATIONAL CONTEXT AND THE EQUITY PROBLEM HHS HAS NOT ADDRESSED⏎⏎The American Thoracic Society represents clinicians, researchers, and public health professionals working across pulmonary medicine, critical care, and sleep medicine, with significant organizational presence in community health settings across rural and underserved regions of the United States. Our network includes clinical implementation sites in North Dakota and six adjacent states where safety-net institutions serve populations with limited access to specialist care. This comment addresses a specific and serious gap in the RFI as structured: HHS has articulated a detailed framework for accelerating AI adoption but has said almost nothing about how the Department will prevent AI systems from replicating and amplifying the health disparities that already define the communities most likely to depend on the care settings where these tools will first be deployed at scale.⏎⏎That is not a peripheral concern. It is the central public health question this RFI raises, even if unintentionally.⏎⏎The literature on algorithmic bias in clinical AI is no longer speculative. It is a documented, replicated body of findings. Obermeyer and colleagues, writing in Science in 2019, demonstrated that a widely used commercial algorithm for identifying high-risk patients systematically underestimated illness severity in Black patients relative to white patients with equivalent clinical need, because the algorithm used healthcare cost as a proxy for health status — and historical spending patterns encoded decades of differential access (Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S. Science. 2019;366(6464):447-453). Sjoding and colleagues published findings in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 showing that pulse oximeters — a technology so routine it is almost invisible — produced clinically significant measurement errors in patients with darker skin pigmentation at rates that went undetected for years precisely because the discrepancy was consistent and therefore looked like signal rather than noise (Sjoding MW et al. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(25):2477-2478). Adamson and Smith documented in JAMA Dermatology that machine learning diagnostic tools in dermatology were trained almost entirely on images of lighter-skinned patients, producing accuracy gaps that track almost perfectly with the populations least represented in academic medical center datasets (Adamson AS, Smith A. JAMA Dermatol. 2018;154(11):1247-1248).⏎⏎These are not edge cases. They are the pattern. And the RFI HHS has published proposes to accelerate the spread of AI tools built on the same kinds of training data, validated in the same kinds of academic institutions, without any mandatory requirement that developers demonstrate performance equity across demographic subgroups before deployment in community health settings.⏎⏎⏎ATS Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎WHY ACCELERATION WITHOUT EQUITY INFRASTRUCTURE IS A DOCUMENTED RISK, NOT A THEORETICAL ONE⏎⏎Wong and colleagues published an external validation of a widely implemented sepsis prediction algorithm in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2021 and found that the tool's performance degraded substantially outside the academic medical center environment where it was trained, with the model generating high false-positive rates that consumed clinical resources without improving patient outcomes (Wong A, Otles E, Donnelly JP, et al. JAMA Intern Med. 2021;181(8):1065-1070). Seyyed-Kalantari and colleagues documented in Nature Medicine that AI algorithms applied to chest radiographs showed systematic underdiagnosis bias in underserved patient populations, meaning the patients who most needed accurate diagnosis were the ones the models were least likely to identify correctly (Seyyed-Kalantari L et al. Nat Med. 2021;27(12):2176-2182). These are precisely the populations served by the community health centers in our network.⏎⏎There is a mechanism that makes this worse than equivalent human error, and HHS should understand it clearly. Gianfrancesco and colleagues, writing in JAMA Internal Medicine, documented that electronic health record data used to train clinical AI encodes not just clinical patterns but access patterns — who got which tests, who received follow-up, whose symptoms were taken seriously — and that these structural biases are invisible in the output because the algorithm presents them as objective findings rather than as products of a discriminatory history (Gianfrancesco MA et al. JAMA Intern Med. 2018;178(11):1544-1547). Sendak and colleagues have described the way that clinical AI tools acquire an authoritative quality in practice that suppresses the normal skepticism clinicians apply to imperfect information — the tool produces a number or a risk score, and the clinician's cognitive default is to treat it as more reliable than their own uncertain judgment (Sendak MP et al. Proc ACM Conf Fairness Accountability Transparency. 2020:99-109). The combination of embedded historical bias and automation-driven deference means that AI tools can produce disparate harm at scale before anyone notices the pattern, because the harm looks like clinical reality rather than algorithmic error.⏎⏎Wiens and colleagues articulated a responsible deployment framework in Nature Medicine that called explicitly for ongoing post-deployment monitoring as a non-negotiable component of clinical AI implementation — not as a best practice but as a structural requirement (Wiens J et al. Nat Med. 2019;25(9):1337-1340). Char, Shah, and Magnus similarly argued in the New England Journal of Medicine that machine learning implementation in health care requires prospective ethical analysis, not retrospective correction (Char DS, Shah NH, Magnus D. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(11):981-983). The National Academy for State Health Policy's 2023 policy brief on algorithmic accountability in state Medicaid programs identified the absence of standardized demographic performance reporting as the single most consistent gap across existing state-level oversight frameworks (NASHP Policy Brief. 2023). HHS is positioned to close that gap nationally. The RFI, as written, does not indicate any intention to do so.⏎⏎⏎ATS Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Page 2 [continued]⏎⏎SPECIFIC REQUESTS FOR HHS ACTION⏎⏎Our organization asks HHS to address the following before establishing any reimbursement pathway or regulatory accommodation that would accelerate AI adoption in clinical settings:⏎⏎1. Mandatory pre-deployment equity impact assessments. Any AI tool seeking CMS reimbursement or ONC certification should be required to demonstrate performance equivalence across racial, ethnic, socioeconomic, and geographic subgroups, tested in care settings representative of the deployment environment — not solely in the academic medical centers where most current validation studies are conducted. Vyas and colleagues have documented extensively how race-corrective adjustments embedded in clinical algorithms perpetuate rather than correct disparity, and any equity assessment framework must account for that dynamic (Vyas DA, Eisenstein LG, Jones DS. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(9):874-882).⏎⏎2. Post-deployment bias surveillance with public reporting requirements. Facilities deploying AI tools in clinical care should be required to collect and report demographic-stratified outcome data at regular intervals, with results made publicly available in a standardized format. Pierson and colleagues demonstrated in Nature Medicine that algorithmic analysis of pain treatment patterns revealed unexplained disparities in underserved populations that would not have been visible without systematic disaggregation of outcome data (Pierson E et al. Nat Med. 2021;27(1):136-141). That kind of analysis should not be optional.⏎⏎3. Conditioning reimbursement on demonstrated equity performance. Any CMS billing pathway created for AI-assisted diagnostics or clinical decision support should include a performance equity condition — meaning that tools showing statistically significant outcome disparities across demographic subgroups would lose reimbursement eligibility until the disparity is corrected. This is not an unusual regulatory instrument; CMS applies performance conditions in other quality programs, and there is no principled reason AI tools should be exempt.⏎⏎Our network's deployment data, collected across 14 months of community health center implementation sites, shows that facilities in rural and low-income settings are already struggling to evaluate the equity implications of the AI tools being offered to them. Vendors do not routinely provide subgroup performance data disaggregated by race or income. Facilities do not have the analytic infrastructure to generate it independently. And there is no regulatory requirement that either party close that gap. One site coordinator in Bismarck, North Dakota told us in a structured interview that the vendor's validation documentation referenced performance in a single academic health system in the mid-Atlantic region and contained no data at all on patient populations resembling the ones the tool would actually be used to treat.⏎⏎That is the gap HHS has the authority to close, and this RFI is the appropriate vehicle for doing so. Our organization is prepared to provide additional data from our clinical network to support HHS in developing a workable equity assessment framework, and we ask that the Department issue a specific supplemental request for comment on mandatory equity auditing standards before finalizing any accelerated adoption pathway. The technical capacity to do this well exists; what is missing is the regulatory requirement that it be done at all. The communities we serve cannot afford to wait for post-deployment correction cycles that begin only after patients have been harmed.⏎⏎For questions regarding this comment, contact:⏎American Thoracic Society, Health Policy Division⏎atspolicy@thoracic.org⏎25 Broadway, New York, NY 10004♔♔2026-02-17T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-17T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔4♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI systems in healthcare inherit and amplify racial, socioeconomic, and institutional biases from training data, and their apparent authority makes those biases harder to detect and correct than human error.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔supportive♔North Dakota♔community organizer♔52♔A 2024 survey conducted across our network of 847 clinical implementation sites found that 68% of frontline providers identified reimbursement uncertainty as the primary barrier to sustained AI tool adoption, outpacing technical integration challenges (41%) and workforce training gaps (33%). SYNTH-0061♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Thomas Sanchez♔National Physicians Alliance♔♔♔♔♔NATIONAL PHYSICIANS ALLIANCE⏎Comments in Response to HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI⏎Submitted by: Thomas Sanchez, Director of Government Affairs⏎National Physicians Alliance | Washington, D.C.⏎⏎National Physicians Alliance Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 1⏎⏎EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎The National Physicians Alliance (NPA) represents over 1,200 member institutions spanning academic medical centers, community hospitals, and integrated health systems. A 2024 survey of our membership found that 68% have deployed at least one AI-enabled clinical decision support (CDSS) tool, yet fewer than 22% have established formal governance frameworks to evaluate ongoing algorithmic performance or address model drift. A concurrent NPA policy analysis reviewing 47 peer-reviewed implementation studies published between 2021 and 2024 identified reimbursement uncertainty as the single most frequently cited barrier to scaling validated AI tools from pilot programs into standard care pathways. These findings inform the NPA's core concern with this RFI: HHS is preparing to accelerate AI adoption in healthcare without adequately reckoning with the fact that the most profitable and rapidly expanding deployed application of AI in this sector is not clinical decision support — it is denial automation.⏎⏎The phrase "AI in healthcare" is a contested term. It encompasses both CDSS tools designed to improve diagnostic accuracy (Rajpurkar P, Chen E, Banerjee O, Topol EJ, "AI in health and medicine," Nature Medicine, 2022;28(1):31-38) and automated prior authorization denial engines deployed by major insurers to maximize claim rejection volume with minimal physician review. These are not equivalent applications. One is designed to help clinicians serve patients. The other is designed to protect insurer margins. Any HHS acceleration framework that treats them as categorically similar will, in practice, turbocharge the latter at the expense of the former.⏎⏎National Physicians Alliance Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎THE ASYMMETRY THE RFI DECLINES TO NAME⏎⏎The NPA's most significant concern with HHS's framing in this RFI is the Department's apparent decision to treat AI reimbursement policy as a mechanism to "foster competition among clinical care AI tool builders" without addressing the asymmetry of incentives already shaping the market. Clinical AI tools face uncertain reimbursement pathways, high governance burdens, and the full weight of FDA regulatory scrutiny where applicable. AI denial engines deployed by insurers face none of those barriers. They are already generating substantial returns. The UnitedHealth Group subsidiary NaviHealth deployed an AI model that, according to reporting by Mukherjee and Ross in STAT News (November 2023), denied post-acute care claims for elderly Medicare Advantage patients at rates dramatically exceeding what independent physician review would have supported — in some documented cases, within seconds of submission, with no meaningful human clinical judgment applied. The U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations reached similar conclusions in its November 2024 report, "Denial, Delay, Disappear: How Medicare Advantage Insurers Use Algorithms to Deny Care," which found systematic use of algorithmic tools to deny care in ways that the Subcommittee concluded were inconsistent with clinical evidence and beneficiary medical needs.⏎⏎The Office of Inspector General documented related patterns in April 2022 (OIG Report OEI-09-18-00260), finding that some Medicare Advantage organizations denied prior authorization requests that met Medicare coverage rules. The American Medical Association's 2023 Prior Authorization Physician Survey found that 94% of physicians reported that prior authorization delays patient care, and 33% reported that a patient experienced a serious adverse event as a direct result of a prior authorization denial. The Kaiser Family Foundation's March 2023 issue brief by Koma, Cubanski, and Neuman documented that prior authorization use in Medicare Advantage is pervasive and that appeal rates remain low — not because denials are appropriate, but because elderly and low-income patients lack the administrative capacity to navigate multi-step appeals processes. The CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule (CMS-0057-F, Federal Register, January 2024) took meaningful steps toward transparency, but it does not establish enforceable clinical appropriateness standards for algorithmically generated denials, and it does not require insurers to disclose the demographic disaggregation of denial rates.⏎⏎This is the policy vacuum into which HHS is now proposing to inject an acceleration framework. The NPA does not believe that is a sound sequencing of regulatory priorities.⏎⏎National Physicians Alliance Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎HEALTH EQUITY IS NOT A SECONDARY CONSIDERATION⏎⏎The NPA addresses specifically the RFI's questions regarding health equity implications of AI adoption, because the documented evidence is alarming and the RFI's treatment of it is insufficient. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan demonstrated in Science (2019;366(6464):447-453) that a widely deployed commercial algorithm used to manage population health systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients, resulting in less care being allocated to a sicker population. The mechanism was not explicit racial coding — it was the use of healthcare cost as a proxy for health need, a variable that encodes historical inequities directly into algorithmic outputs. The National Partnership for Women and Families documented in its January 2024 policy brief on algorithmic discrimination in health insurance that similar proxy-variable problems appear in denial-optimization models, where factors correlated with race, disability status, and socioeconomic position produce disparate denial rates that insurers are not currently required to report or remediate.⏎⏎The research on automation bias compounds this concern. Goddard, Roudsari, and Wyatt's systematic review in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association (2012;19(1):121-127) documented that clinicians and reviewers consistently over-rely on algorithmic recommendations even when those recommendations are incorrect — a finding with direct implications for the "human review" provisions that insurers claim justify their AI denial workflows. When a physician reviewer is presented with an AI-generated denial recommendation and given 90 seconds to adjudicate a complex post-acute care case, that review is not meaningfully independent. Schulman and Richman made a related point in JAMA (2023;329(12):983-984), arguing that prior authorization in chronic disease management functions less as a clinical safeguard than as an administrative barrier specifically calibrated to reduce utilization by patients who cannot sustain a prolonged appeals process.⏎⏎National Physicians Alliance Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 4⏎⏎NUMBERED RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎The NPA respectfully submits the following specific recommendations for HHS consideration:⏎⏎1. HHS must condition any AI reimbursement incentive, adoption subsidy, or regulatory accommodation on demonstrated compliance with clinical appropriateness standards validated by independent clinical bodies — not by the deploying insurer.⏎⏎2. HHS must establish mandatory human review thresholds for AI-generated prior authorization decisions, with minimum time standards that are clinically meaningful rather than perfunctory. A 90-second review of a complex skilled nursing facility admission does not constitute independent physician judgment.⏎⏎3. HHS must require transparent denial rate reporting disaggregated by patient age, race, disability status, and income level, submitted to CMS on a quarterly basis and made publicly available. The absence of this data is not accidental — it is a structural feature of a market in which opacity is profitable.⏎⏎4. HHS must explicitly exclude cost-containment-optimized denial AI from any "acceleration" framework. The RFI's language about fostering AI competition should apply to clinical tools designed to improve patient outcomes, and HHS should say so clearly in any subsequent guidance or rulemaking.⏎⏎5. Any insurer deploying an AI system that generates prior authorization decisions at scale must register that system with HHS, disclose its training data sources and outcome validation methodology, and submit to periodic independent auditing — a framework analogous to what CMS-0057-F begins to establish for interoperability but extended explicitly to algorithmic denial tools.⏎⏎The NPA acknowledges that the governance frameworks necessary to implement these recommendations do not yet exist in complete form, and the organization is prepared to work with HHS and ASTP/ONC to develop technically sound implementation standards. However, the sequencing matters enormously. Acceleration before accountability is not a neutral policy choice — it is a choice that will disproportionately harm the patients least equipped to absorb the consequences. Member institutions have told NPA directly, at the 2024 annual convening and in subsequent written correspondence, that they are watching clinical AI investment stall while insurer AI investment in denial automation scales without regulatory friction.⏎⏎A full bibliography of cited works and the NPA's 2024 membership survey methodology are provided in Appendix A, which is available upon request from the NPA Office of Government Affairs.⏎⏎thomas.sanchez@nationalphysiciansalliance.org⏎[Appendix A — transmitted separately per docket submission instructions; confirmation of receipt requested]♔♔2026-01-20T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-20T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔4♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI-powered insurance decision-making automates prior authorization denials and coverage restrictions in ways that are opaque, unappealable, and systematically biased against vulnerable patients.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔supportive♔New York♔director of government affairs♔30♔A 2024 survey of our 1,200 member institutions—spanning academic medical centers, community hospitals, and integrated health systems—found that 68% have deployed at least one AI-enabled clinical decision support tool, yet fewer than 22% have established formal governance frameworks to evaluate ongoing algorithmic performance or address model drift.
