SYNTH-0062♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔George Garcia♔Families USA♔♔♔♔♔Families USA⏎1225 New York Avenue NW, Suite 800⏎Washington, DC 20005⏎www.familiesusa.org⏎⏎George Garcia⏎Director of Government Affairs⏎Families USA⏎⏎October 14, 2024⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎Attention: Health Sector AI Request for Information⏎200 Independence Avenue SW⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎Re: Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care (HHS Health Sector AI RFI, 2024)⏎⏎⏎Families USA | HHS AI RFI Comments | October 2024 | Page 1⏎⏎⏎The framing of this RFI concerns us before we even reach its specific questions. HHS asks how the Department can "accelerate" AI adoption in clinical care, and the word accelerate, appearing as it does in the very title of the solicitation, is doing a great deal of policy work that the document itself never fully acknowledges. Families USA has spent decades representing the interests of health care consumers — people who are sick, frightened, economically precarious, and often navigating a system that already treats them as cases rather than as human beings with complex lives and complicated needs. When we read an RFI that frames clinical AI deployment primarily as a question of removing barriers to adoption, and that situates "productivity" as a core metric against which AI's value should be measured, we want to be honest: that framing is itself a policy choice, and it is not a neutral one. The choice to foreground productivity in describing the clinical encounter is a signal that HHS may be operating from a transactional model of care — one in which the value of a clinical interaction is captured primarily by what gets done, documented, or billed, rather than by what gets healed.⏎⏎We want to be clear that Families USA is not categorically opposed to AI in health care. We have followed the literature carefully, and we take seriously the evidence that certain AI tools — particularly in medical imaging interpretation, sepsis detection, and medication error reduction — have demonstrated genuine clinical utility in controlled settings. Eric Topol's 2019 synthesis in Nature Medicine remains an important touchstone for what AI might accomplish in high-performance medicine, and we do not dismiss that work. But Topol's framework, and the optimism it represents, rests on assumptions about the clinical context in which AI is deployed that the HHS RFI never interrogates. Specifically, the question of what happens to the therapeutic relationship when algorithmic intermediation becomes routine — that question is almost entirely absent from this solicitation. That absence is what prompted this comment.⏎⏎⏎Families USA | HHS AI RFI Comments | October 2024 | Page 2⏎⏎⏎THE THERAPEUTIC RELATIONSHIP IS NOT A SENTIMENT. IT IS A CLINICAL VARIABLE.⏎⏎There is a tendency in policy discussions to treat the therapeutic relationship — the quality of connection, trust, and mutual understanding between a patient and a clinician — as a soft value, something important to acknowledge in passing before getting to the real metrics of accuracy, efficiency, and cost. This is a mistake, and the research literature says so clearly. Kelley and colleagues published a systematic review and meta-analysis in PLOS ONE in 2014 examining randomized controlled trials that specifically tested whether the quality of the patient-clinician relationship affected health outcomes (Kelley JM, Kraft-Todd G, Schapira L, et al., "The influence of the patient-clinician relationship on healthcare outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials," PLOS ONE, 2014;9(4):e94207). Their findings were not ambiguous. Strong therapeutic relationships were associated with statistically significant improvements in objective clinical outcomes — not just patient satisfaction scores, not just self-reported wellbeing, but measurable clinical endpoints. Ridd and colleagues conducted a synthesis of the qualitative literature on patients' perspectives of the patient-doctor relationship, published in the British Journal of General Practice in 2009, and identified continuity, trust, and the sense of being known as the features patients themselves identified as most therapeutically meaningful (Ridd M, Shaw A, Lewis G, Salisbury C, "The patient-doctor relationship: a synthesis of the qualitative literature on patients' perspectives," British Journal of General Practice, 2009;59(561):e116-e133). Neither of these findings is new. What is new is that HHS is now designing policy frameworks for a technology that, if deployed without relational safeguards, has the structural capacity to erode both.⏎⏎Zulman and colleagues, writing in JAMA in 2020, documented specific clinician practices that sustain physician presence and connection during clinical encounters, and their framework implicitly acknowledges that such presence is under pressure from exactly the kind of documentation and alert burden that AI systems are often proposed to relieve (Zulman DM, Haverfield MC, Shaw JG, et al., "Practices to foster physician presence and connection with patients in the clinical encounter," JAMA, 2020;323(1):70-81). The argument that AI will free up clinicians to be more present is theoretically plausible. But the mechanism by which that occurs is not automatic, and the HHS RFI contains no framework for ensuring it happens. If a clinician's cognitive attention is redirected from the patient to the management of an AI interface — reviewing outputs, adjudicating alerts, documenting AI-assisted findings — there is no guarantee that the relational quality of the encounter improves. In fact, there is reason to worry that it degrades, because the AI system creates a third party in the room, an authoritative-seeming one, whose outputs the clinician must attend to.⏎⏎⏎Families USA | HHS AI RFI Comments | October 2024 | Page 3⏎⏎⏎Consider a scenario that Families USA hears about, in various forms, from the patients and families we represent. A woman in her mid-fifties comes into a primary care clinic in rural Alabama. She has been putting off this visit for months. Her presenting complaint is vague — fatigue, some weight loss, a feeling she can't quite name. She is not medically sophisticated. She does not know how to describe what she is experiencing in clinical language. She sits across from a physician who, in a well-resourced AI-assisted practice, has already received an algorithmic risk stratification score based on her EHR data before she walks in the door. The algorithm, trained on population-level data, assigns her a moderate probability of depression and a low probability of serious organic pathology. The physician, whose attention has been partially structured by that output before the conversation begins, asks about her mood. She says she's fine, she's just tired. The physician, whose next alert is already queued, accepts that. What the algorithm could not have known — what only a clinician with the time and relational attunement to notice would have known — is that she is sitting with her arms crossed, that she answers questions in monosyllables, that her affect is flat in a way that has nothing to do with depression and everything to do with fear. She is terrified. She has felt a lump. She has not told anyone. She will not volunteer it unless someone gives her the space and the signal that it is safe to. The algorithm cannot give her that signal. It can only process what has already been documented.⏎⏎This is not a hypothetical designed to make AI look bad. It is a description of what medicine actually requires at its most consequential moments. Abraham Verghese and colleagues wrote in JAMA in 2018 that what the computer needs is a physician — specifically, a physician whose clinical judgment is grounded in direct observation, embodied presence, and interpretive attention to the patient as a whole person, not as a data object (Verghese A, Shah NH, Harrington RA, "What this computer needs is a physician: humanism and artificial intelligence," JAMA, 2018;319(1):19-20). That argument is not anti-technology. It is pro-medicine. And it is the argument that HHS's RFI, in its current framing, does not make room for.⏎⏎⏎Families USA | HHS AI RFI Comments | October 2024 | Page 4⏎⏎⏎AUTOMATION BIAS AND DESKILLING ARE DOCUMENTED PHENOMENA, NOT SPECULATIVE FEARS⏎⏎One of the things that troubles Families USA most about the accelerationist framing of this RFI is that it treats the risks of AI deployment in clinical settings as primarily technical — bias in training data, accuracy of algorithms, interoperability with EHR systems. These are real concerns, and we do not minimize them. But the HHS solicitation pays almost no attention to what happens to clinician cognition and judgment capacity over time as AI systems become embedded in routine clinical workflow. This is not a speculative concern. It has been documented empirically in both the human factors literature and the health care management literature, and the findings are not reassuring.⏎⏎Parasuraman and Manzey published a comprehensive review of complacency and automation bias in human use of automation in Human Factors in 2010, drawing on decades of research in aviation, military systems, and process control industries (Parasuraman R, Manzey DH, "Complacency and bias in human use of automation: an attentional integration," Human Factors, 2010;52(3):381-410). Their core finding is that when human operators work alongside automated systems that are generally reliable, they develop a systematic tendency to accept automated outputs without adequate scrutiny — even in cases where the automated output is wrong. This is automation bias, and it is not a character flaw. It is a predictable consequence of how human attention works under cognitive load. Tversky and Kahneman's foundational work on heuristics and biases, published in Science in 1974, described the anchoring effect specifically: once a number or a category is placed in front of a decision-maker, subsequent judgments tend to cluster around that anchor, even when the decision-maker is aware of the bias and trying to correct for it (Tversky A, Kahneman D, "Judgment under uncertainty: heuristics and biases," Science, 1974;185(4157):1124-1131). An AI diagnostic recommendation is an anchor. It will shape clinical reasoning even when the clinician believes they are exercising independent judgment. The question is not whether this effect is real. It is whether HHS's deployment framework accounts for it.⏎⏎Hoff examined deskilling and adaptation among primary care physicians using two work innovations and found that the introduction of clinical decision support tools was associated with measurable erosion of specific diagnostic reasoning skills that physicians had previously exercised independently (Hoff T, "Deskilling and adaptation among primary care physicians using two work innovations," Health Care Management Review, 2011;36(4):338-348). This is the long-term risk that the current RFI entirely ignores: a generation of clinicians who have trained and practiced in AI-saturated environments may have systematically underdeveloped capacities for autonomous clinical judgment — not because they are less capable, but because the system in which they practice has not required those capacities of them. When the AI system fails, or encounters a case outside its training distribution, or produces an output that is confidently wrong, the clinician who has chronically deferred to it may not have the internal resources to catch the error. Blease and colleagues, in an exploratory qualitative study published in the Journal of Medical Internet Research in 2019, found that UK general practitioners expressed concern about exactly this dynamic — that AI clinical decision support might make them better at the average case while making them worse at the outlier, which is precisely the case where independent judgment matters most (Blease C, Kaptchuk TJ, Bernstein MH, et al., "Artificial intelligence and the future of primary care: exploratory qualitative study of UK general practitioners' views," Journal of Medical Internet Research, 2019;21(3):e12802).⏎⏎⏎Families USA | HHS AI RFI Comments | October 2024 | Page 5⏎⏎⏎Families USA | HHS AI RFI Comments | October 2024 | Page 6⏎⏎⏎THE ILLUSION OF OBJECTIVITY⏎⏎There is a particular danger in AI recommendation systems that the HHS RFI does not address and that we think deserves explicit attention. When a clinician exercises judgment and gets it wrong, the error is visible as a human error — something that can be examined, learned from, attributed, corrected. When an AI system produces a recommendation that a clinician follows, and that recommendation is wrong, the error is structurally obscured. The clinician followed the algorithm. The algorithm was based on peer-reviewed methodology. The recommendation was consistent with population-level evidence. The error looks, from the outside, like bad luck or unusual pathology rather than a failure of clinical judgment. This is the illusion of objectivity: the AI system does not actually make clinical decisions more objective, but it makes the process of decision-making appear more objective, which is not the same thing.⏎⏎Shortliffe and Sepúlveda, writing about clinical decision support in the era of artificial intelligence in JAMA in 2018, noted that the field has a long history of systems that perform well in evaluation and then fail in deployment, precisely because deployment contexts involve the full complexity of clinical practice in ways that evaluation contexts do not (Shortliffe EH, Sepúlveda MJ, "Clinical decision support in the era of artificial intelligence," JAMA, 2018;320(21):2199-2200). Emanuel and Wachter, also writing in JAMA in 2019, asked directly whether the value of AI in health care would match its hype, and their answer was cautious: the conditions under which AI adds clinical value are specific and require careful governance, and the history of health IT adoption gives reason to expect that governance frameworks will lag behind deployment (Emanuel EJ, Wachter RM, "Artificial intelligence in health care: will the value match the hype?" JAMA, 2019;321(23):2281-2282). These are not fringe voices. These are among the most credible scholars in health policy and informatics, and they are raising concerns that the HHS RFI's accelerationist framing does not engage with.⏎⏎The illusion of objectivity is particularly dangerous in the relational dimension of clinical care because it can displace genuine clinical reasoning while appearing to enhance it, which makes the displacement invisible. A clinician who consciously decides not to pursue a line of inquiry because they are pressed for time knows they have made a tradeoff. A clinician who does not pursue that line of inquiry because an AI system's risk stratification score has already structured the encounter toward a different set of priorities may not recognize that a tradeoff has been made at all. The harm is the same. The visibility of the harm is not.⏎⏎⏎Families USA | HHS AI RFI Comments | October 2024 | Page 7⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC RESPONSES TO RFI QUESTIONS ON EVALUATION FRAMEWORKS AND REIMBURSEMENT⏎⏎Families USA wishes to address two specific areas of the HHS solicitation where our concerns are most directly engaged: the question of evaluation frameworks for AI in clinical care, and the question of coverage and reimbursement policy as a lever for AI adoption.⏎⏎On evaluation frameworks, the RFI asks how HHS should evaluate AI tools for clinical effectiveness. The Department's current framing of this question centers on technical performance metrics: accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, area under the ROC curve, performance across demographic subgroups. These metrics matter, and we support rigorous technical evaluation. But they are not sufficient, and an evaluation framework that includes only these metrics will systematically fail to capture the harms we have described in this comment. Families USA urges HHS to require, as a condition of any federal endorsement, coverage recommendation, or deployment incentive for clinical AI tools, that evaluation frameworks include patient-reported relational quality metrics. Specifically, we recommend:⏎⏎1. Patient-reported assessments of whether they felt heard, known, and understood during the clinical encounter in which AI was used.⏎2. Longitudinal measurement of therapeutic alliance quality across practices with varying levels of AI integration, using validated instruments such as the Working Alliance Inventory adapted for clinical settings.⏎3. Clinician self-assessment of autonomous diagnostic reasoning confidence, measured over time, to detect the early signatures of deskilling before they manifest in patient outcomes.⏎4. Qualitative capture of cases in which clinician override of AI recommendations was clinically significant, to understand both the conditions under which human judgment adds value and the conditions under which automation bias suppressed it.⏎5. Measurement of encounter duration and the proportion of encounter time during which clinician attention was directed at the patient versus at a screen or interface.⏎⏎None of these metrics are exotic or technically difficult to collect. Some of them are already used in patient experience research. What is missing is any policy requirement that they be included in evaluations of AI clinical tools. The HHS RFI, as currently framed, would allow a clinical AI system to be endorsed and incentivized for deployment based solely on its technical performance in retrospective validation studies, with no requirement that its effects on the therapeutic relationship be measured at all. That gap is a policy choice, and it is a consequential one.⏎⏎On reimbursement, Families USA understands that payment policy is a powerful lever for adoption. We note that RBMA survey data from 2024 indicates that 74% of radiology practices identified inconsistent Medicare reimbursement pathways as the primary barrier to AI integration, and we take that finding seriously. But we want to be direct about something: the fact that reimbursement is a barrier to adoption does not mean that removing the barrier is the right policy response absent other safeguards. Reimbursement policy can be designed to incentivize AI deployment in ways that also require evidence of relational quality preservation, not just technical performance. CMS has used value-based payment mechanisms in other contexts to shape the conditions of care delivery, not just its volume. There is no structural reason why coverage for AI-assisted clinical services could not be conditioned on demonstrated compliance with a relational quality evaluation framework of the kind we have described. We urge HHS to explore this approach before designing reimbursement pathways that accelerate deployment without such conditions attached.⏎⏎⏎Families USA | HHS AI RFI Comments | October 2024 | Page 8⏎⏎⏎THE SPECIFIC POPULATION CONCERN⏎⏎Families USA's core constituency includes people who are particularly vulnerable to the harms we have described: patients with low health literacy, patients who are frightened or in pain, patients navigating complex family and social circumstances that shape their clinical presentation in ways that no algorithm trained on structured EHR data can fully capture. Bickmore and colleagues, in research presented at the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems in 2009, examined how low health literacy hospital patients interacted with virtual nurse agents, and found that while such systems could provide useful informational support, their capacity to recognize and respond to emotional complexity was severely limited (Bickmore TW, Pfeifer LM, Jack BW, "Taking the time to care: empowering low health literacy hospital patients with virtual nurse agents," Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, 2009:1265-1274). The patients who most need a clinician who can read ambiguity, interpret silence, and respond to the full human situation are precisely the patients for whom AI intermediation carries the greatest relational risk.⏎⏎This is not an argument that AI should never be used in the care of vulnerable populations. It is an argument that the deployment of AI in contexts where patients are frightened, inarticulate, or navigating complex social circumstances requires a level of relational safeguarding that the current HHS RFI framework does not envision. When a patient cannot tell you what is wrong in clinical language, when their distress is communicated through body language and affect and the things they do not say, the clinician's capacity to perceive and respond to that communication is not a supplementary feature of good care. It is the care. An AI system that processes structured data and produces recommendations based on patterns in that data cannot substitute for that perceptive capacity, and a clinical encounter that is structured primarily around AI outputs may not create the conditions in which that capacity can operate.⏎⏎We want to note that this concern is not limited to rural or underserved populations, although those populations face particular risks. The therapeutic relationship matters in every clinical context. But it matters most when patients are most vulnerable, and the HHS RFI does not segment its analysis in a way that accounts for differential vulnerability. A deployment framework designed primarily around the needs of well-resourced, health-literate patients in settings where AI performs well may produce policies that are actively harmful when applied in contexts where those assumptions do not hold.⏎⏎⏎Families USA | HHS AI RFI Comments | October 2024 | Page 9⏎⏎⏎A SPECIFIC POLICY REQUEST⏎⏎Families USA is asking for something specific, and we want to state it plainly before closing. We are asking HHS to commission a dedicated research agenda on the relational and humanistic dimensions of AI integration in clinical care before any further acceleration of deployment through reimbursement incentives, coverage expansions, or regulatory streamlining. The research agenda should include at minimum:⏎⏎a. Prospective studies measuring the effect of AI clinical decision support tools on patient-reported relational quality in diverse clinical settings, with specific attention to populations with low health literacy, high health anxiety, or complex social circumstances.⏎⏎b. Longitudinal studies of clinician diagnostic reasoning capacity in AI-integrated versus non-AI-integrated practice environments, using validated measures of clinical reasoning skill and designed to detect early deskilling signatures.⏎⏎c. Qualitative research on the lived experience of patients in AI-assisted clinical encounters, with particular attention to whether and how patients perceive AI intermediation as affecting their sense of being heard and understood.⏎⏎d. Development and validation of patient-reported relational quality instruments specifically designed for use in AI-assisted clinical contexts, suitable for inclusion in routine evaluation frameworks.⏎⏎e. Analysis of the interaction between automation bias and clinical complexity, examining whether the conditions under which automation bias is most likely to suppress accurate clinical judgment are also the conditions in which patients are most vulnerable.⏎⏎This research agenda should be completed, or at least substantially underway with preliminary findings available, before HHS designs reimbursement pathways or deployment incentives that would make AI-assisted clinical care the default rather than the option. The Department has an obligation to the patients it serves to understand what it is accelerating toward before it accelerates.⏎⏎We also ask that HHS formally amend its evaluation framework requirements to include patient-reported relational quality metrics as a condition of any federal coverage recommendation or endorsement for clinical AI tools. This should not be optional, and it should not be deferred to a future rulemaking. The RFI process is the appropriate moment to establish that relational quality is a required dimension of clinical AI evaluation, not an afterthought.⏎⏎⏎Families USA | HHS AI RFI Comments | October 2024 | Page 10⏎⏎⏎There is one more thing Families USA wants to say, and it is perhaps the most direct thing in this comment. HHS's use of the word "productivity" in framing the value of AI in clinical care is not just a word choice. It reflects an underlying model of what the clinical encounter is for. A productivity model says the encounter is for generating outputs: diagnoses, prescriptions, referrals, documented assessments. A relational model says the encounter is for something that includes those outputs but is not reducible to them — it is for the patient to feel known, to trust the clinician enough to tell them what they are actually experiencing, to leave with not just a treatment plan but with the sense that another human being has genuinely attended to their situation. These models are not fully compatible, and the tension between them is not resolved by adding AI to the mix. It is, in many scenarios, sharpened by it.⏎⏎The HHS RFI asks how the Department can accelerate AI adoption. Families USA is asking HHS to first answer a different question: what are we accelerating toward, and who does it serve? The answer to that question requires taking the therapeutic relationship seriously as a clinical variable, measuring relational quality as a condition of deployment endorsement, and funding the research needed to understand what happens to clinical judgment and patient-centered care when algorithmic intermediation becomes routine. We recognize that this is a harder path than simply clearing regulatory and reimbursement barriers. We also think it is the path that is actually consistent with HHS's stated mission to enhance the health and wellbeing of all Americans.⏎⏎Families USA respectfully requests that HHS respond to these specific recommendations in any subsequent guidance or rulemaking, and that the Department indicate whether it intends to incorporate relational quality metrics into its AI evaluation framework. We would welcome the opportunity to meet with the Office of the Deputy Secretary and ASTP/ONC staff to discuss the research agenda proposal in more detail.⏎⏎For questions regarding this submission, please contact George Garcia, Director of Government Affairs, Families USA, at the address listed above or at⏎⏎ggarcia@familiesusa.org⏎⏎Families USA | HHS AI RFI Comments | October 2024 | Page 11♔♔2026-01-15T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-15T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔13♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Medicine is fundamentally a human relationship built on judgment, context, and trust, and AI threatens to reduce patients to data points and clinicians to machine overseers.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔urgent♔Alabama♔director of government affairs♔52♔A 2024 RBMA member survey conducted across 412 radiology practices—spanning independent groups, hospital-based departments, and teleradiology providers—found that 68% have deployed or are actively piloting at least one FDA-cleared AI imaging algorithm, yet 74% of those same practices identified inconsistent Medicare reimbursement pathways as the primary barrier to sustainable AI integration. SYNTH-0063♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Anthony Taylor♔American Association of Physician Assistants♔♔♔♔♔American Association of Physician Assistants⏎950 North Washington Street⏎Alexandria, VA 22314⏎⏎Submitted via regulations.gov⏎Docket: HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL-RFI⏎⏎⏎The American Association of Physician Assistants (AAPA) appreciates the opportunity to respond to HHS's Request for Information on accelerating AI adoption in clinical care settings. AAPA represents more than 168,000 certified physician assistants practicing across every clinical specialty and care setting in the United States, and our member institutions have been navigating AI adoption decisions with increasing urgency. A 2024 AAPA member survey found that 68% of responding clinical organizations are actively piloting or evaluating AI-assisted diagnostic and clinical decision support tools, and 74% of those respondents identified reimbursement uncertainty as the primary barrier to full deployment. We raise those numbers not to argue for faster reimbursement pathways but because they tell a different story than HHS appears to be hearing: institutions are moving quickly, they are doing so under conditions of significant uncertainty, and the governance architecture that should be guiding those decisions does not yet exist. This comment is focused on two of the RFI's framing questions — specifically the questions regarding regulatory barriers and the appropriate federal role in AI governance — and it is written not primarily as a technical implementation response but as a substantive objection to the decision-making framework the Department has adopted.⏎⏎The word that keeps coming back when AAPA staff reviewed the RFI text is "acceleration." The Department has framed this entire inquiry around reducing friction, removing uncertainty, and speeding adoption. What is absent from that framing is any acknowledgment that the uncertainty being reduced is, in significant part, the legitimate uncertainty of democratic deliberation — the ordinary condition of a society that has not yet decided what it wants. HHS's posture, as expressed in the RFI's organizing logic, treats regulatory scrutiny as a cost imposed on innovation rather than as an exercise of public authority. That is a substantive policy position, and it is one the Department does not have the mandate to adopt unilaterally through an RFI process that is not subject to the full notice-and-comment requirements of the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. §§ 551-559, 701-706. The acceleration agenda, if translated into regulatory action, would constitute a substantive change in the Department's approach to AI governance, and AAPA believes that change requires the procedural legitimacy the APA demands. The President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology's 2023 report on AI governance in federal health programs reached similar conclusions about the absence of a coherent federal framework, and HHS's response to that gap has been to solicit ideas for moving faster rather than ideas for building the governance architecture that would make speed responsible.⏎⏎AAPA Comments | HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL-RFI | Page 2⏎⏎The governance concern the Department appears to be treating as secondary is, in AAPA's view, the primary question. Sheila Jasanoff's work on technology governance — particularly in The Ethics of Invention: Technology and the Human Future (W.W. Norton, 2016) — describes with precision the dynamic AAPA's member institutions are already experiencing: the embedding of technological systems in institutional infrastructure creates conditions of practical irreversibility from which there is no clean exit. Coiera, Ash, and Berg documented the same phenomenon in the health information technology context, finding that after electronic health record deployment, institutional knowledge atrophies, workflows reorganize around vendor logic, and the capacity to function without the system disappears within years (Yearbook of Medical Informatics, 2016). Bresnick's 2023 analysis in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association extended that finding specifically to clinical AI, documenting dependency cycles that closely parallel EHR adoption patterns. The word "irreversibility" is not rhetorical here; it is empirical. Once a health system has reorganized its diagnostic workflows around a proprietary AI architecture, the practical ability to reverse that decision — to return to human-centered processes, or to switch vendors, or to demand transparency as a condition of continued use — diminishes rapidly. Dafny and Lee's analysis of institutional dependency and market concentration dynamics in the New England Journal of Medicine (2016) is instructive on how quickly market structures consolidate around embedded systems, foreclosing the competitive conditions that might otherwise discipline vendor behavior.⏎⏎The irreversibility problem is structurally connected to a second problem that the acceleration framing makes worse rather than better: the opacity of the systems being deployed. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan's 2019 Science paper on racial bias in a widely deployed health management algorithm demonstrated that the internal logic of proprietary clinical AI is inaccessible not only to patients but to the clinicians and institutions using the systems, and often to the vendors themselves. Rudin's analysis in Nature Machine Intelligence (2019) goes further, arguing that the project of explaining black-box models for high-stakes clinical decisions is structurally impossible — that explainability tools do not provide the accountability they are claimed to provide. Mittelstadt, Russell, and Wachter reached consistent conclusions in their 2019 FAT* conference proceedings paper, finding that explanations in AI are better understood as a legitimation mechanism than a transparency mechanism. The policy implication is direct: if the structural preconditions for democratic oversight of clinical AI — interpretability, auditability, regulatory access to model logic — do not currently exist for the majority of deployed systems, then accelerating deployment before those preconditions are established is not a neutral technical choice. It is a transfer of decision-making authority from accountable public institutions to corporate entities whose internal governance is not subject to democratic accountability. Metcalf, Moss, and boyd documented this transfer dynamic in their analysis of corporate AI ethics frameworks (Social Research, 2019), finding that the institutionalization of ethics within Silicon Valley firms functions primarily to pre-empt external governance rather than to create it. HHS's acceleration agenda, whatever its intentions, would accelerate that transfer.⏎⏎AAPA Comments | HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL-RFI | Page 2 [sic]⏎⏎There is also a more fundamental democratic question that the RFI does not raise and that AAPA believes the Department is obligated to acknowledge. Democratic societies retain the legitimate authority to designate certain domains as ones where human judgment, accountability, and dignity are preserved even at the cost of efficiency. Medicine is among the domains most frequently identified in democratic theory as warranting that protection — not because technology cannot improve outcomes in the aggregate, but because the consequences of clinical decisions fall on specific individuals who have a right to know that a human being with moral accountability was present at the moment of consequence. Eric Topol's widely cited 2019 Nature Medicine paper on the convergence of human and artificial intelligence is optimistic about AI's potential, but even Topol acknowledges that the governance preconditions for responsible deployment have not been established. The decision about whether to accept efficiency gains at the cost of human judgment in clinical settings is not a technical question. It is a political question of the kind that the APA's notice-and-comment architecture was designed to surface and deliberate. HHS's current posture forecloses that deliberation by treating it as friction. AAPA does not believe that is within the Department's mandate. The regulatory framework gaps in AI interoperability requirements under 45 C.F.R. § 170.213 are symptomatic of the same underlying problem: the technical standards infrastructure that would make AI systems auditable and governable has not been built, and the acceleration agenda would deploy systems at scale before that infrastructure exists.⏎⏎AAPA's specific requests of the Department are:⏎⏎1.   Reframe the RFI. The organizing question should not be "how do we accelerate AI adoption" but "what governance architecture must be in place before acceleration is responsible." That reframe does not preclude adoption; it conditions it.⏎⏎2.   Impose a deployment moratorium on novel AI-assisted clinical decision support applications in high-stakes diagnostic and treatment contexts, pending the development of a coherent federal governance framework that addresses interpretability, auditability, and post-market surveillance requirements as conditions of CMS coverage eligibility.⏎⏎3.   Commission a structured democratic deliberation process — modeled on the citizens' assembly format used in Ireland and France for similarly contested policy questions — before any acceleration agenda proceeds. That process should include patients, clinicians, ethicists, and community representatives, and its outputs should bind the Department's subsequent rulemaking agenda.⏎⏎4.   Require, as a condition of any CMS coverage determination for AI-enabled clinical tools, that the applying entity provide regulators with full access to model architecture and training data sufficient for independent auditability — not explainability outputs, which Rudin (2019) and Mittelstadt et al. (2019) have shown to be inadequate substitutes for genuine transparency.⏎⏎AAPA recognizes that these requests will be read by some as obstructionist. They are not. They reflect the judgment of an organization whose 168,000 members are on the front lines of clinical AI deployment and who are watching governance decisions being made by default — not by deliberation. The moratorium request in particular is unlikely to be popular with vendors or with HHS components focused on innovation metrics. But the alternative — deploying systems whose internal logic is inaccessible, whose institutional dependencies are irreversible, and whose societal implications have not been democratically deliberated — is a choice the Department should make explicitly, with full APA procedural accountability, rather than by⏎⏎aapa.org/policy | comments@aapa.org | 703-836-2272♔♔2026-02-07T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-07T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Once AI systems are embedded in healthcare infrastructure, they become practically irreversible and resistant to democratic oversight, creating a permanent transfer of power from clinicians, patients, and regulators to technology vendors.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔hopeful♔New Mexico♔executive director♔40♔A 2024 survey conducted across our 1,200 member laboratories found that 68% are actively piloting or evaluating AI-assisted diagnostic tools, yet 74% of those respondents identified reimbursement uncertainty as the primary barrier to full clinical deployment. SYNTH-0064♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Linda Thomas♔♔♔♔♔♔Submitted via the Federal eRulemaking Portal: regulations.gov⏎⏎Docket: HHS-2024-AI-Clinical-RFI⏎⏎Submitted by: Linda Thomas, Cheyenne, Wyoming (Veteran, VA Healthcare System)⏎⏎⏎⏎I am 78 years old and a veteran, and I get my care at the Cheyenne VA. Back in November 2022, the facility here was trying out some kind of pilot AI triage tool. On three different occasions, this computer program flagged my lab values as critically abnormal. But my rheumatologist had just retired, and those flags just sat there in some digital queue. Nobody looked at them. My methotrexate dosage wasn't monitored for eleven months, and I ended up hospitalized for liver toxicity in early 2023. The AI technology actually did what it was supposed to do, but the hospital had absolutely no workflow set up to handle it.⏎⏎⏎⏎Sitting in that hospital bed got me pretty angry, and since I had a lot of time on my hands while recovering, I started reading up on how these healthcare algorithms actually work. What I found out honestly terrifies me, and looking at your Request for Information, it seems like HHS is completely missing the boat. You are asking everyone how to speed up AI adoption. But you aren't laying down any strict rules to make sure this rushed technology doesn't just end up hurting the patients who are already getting the worst care in this country. That is a massive hole in your plan.⏎⏎⏎⏎From everything I've read, algorithmic bias isn't just a hypothetical worry. It's happening right now. I read about a major study by a researcher named Obermeyer a few years ago. They looked at a commercial algorithm used all over the place to manage patient health, and it was consistently underestimating how sick Black patients were. Why? Because the computer used healthcare costs to guess who was sickest. Since Black patients had historically been prescribed less care, the algorithm just assumed they weren't as sick and kept that discrimination going on a massive scale. Then there was an article in the New England Journal of Medicine about pulse oximeters. They don't work as well on people with darker skin. If an AI is learning from that flawed sensor data, it's just going to spit out flawed decisions. Same goes for skin cancer AI that only learned from pictures of light-skinned people, or those kidney calculators that just blindly assume biological race differences are the reason for health disparities. If an AI trains on that data, it just copies those bad assumptions.⏎⏎⏎⏎Reading your RFI, it feels like HHS thinks the only thing standing in the way of AI is red tape, like FDA timelines and billing codes. Obviously those things matter, but the FDA just checks if a device does what the manufacturer claims it does. They don't check if it works fairly for every type of person in a messy, understaffed real-world clinic. There was another study I saw by Wong and some other doctors where they took a widely used sepsis prediction AI that worked great at a fancy academic hospital. When they tried it out in regular community hospitals, it was a disaster. It performed much worse than the vendor claimed. It was FDA cleared and widely adopted, but its real-world performance in a place with fewer resources was terrible. Nobody caught it before it was rolled out.⏎⏎⏎⏎Because of all this, I want HHS to put some very specific, mandatory rules in place. First off, before Medicare or CMS pays a dime for an AI tool, the company needs to prove it actually works for everyone. They should have to show their accuracy data broken down by race, age, sex, and insurance status. If an AI is 90% accurate overall but only 68% accurate for the kind of folks you'd find at a rural VA clinic, it shouldn't be allowed in those clinics without everyone knowing about it.⏎⏎⏎⏎Also, testing an AI at a massive university hospital with a huge IT staff doesn't prove it will work at a place like the Cheyenne VA, where our computers are older and we don't have a dedicated AI team. You need to require that these tools are tested in the actual types of facilities where they will be used.⏎⏎⏎⏎You also can't just turn these things on and walk away. There needs to be mandatory monitoring after the AI goes live. If a tool starts showing a bias and hurting certain groups, there has to be a hard rule to suspend it immediately while it gets investigated. The FDA already does this kind of post-market surveillance for medical devices, so you could easily just adapt that system for AI.⏎⏎⏎⏎And please, do something about the human side of this. Like what happened to me. The alert was there, but nobody had to act on it. Or sometimes the opposite happens, where doctors just blindly trust the computer and ignore their own eyes because they think the machine is smarter than them. You shouldn't reimburse any hospital for using AI unless they can prove they have a strict, auditable protocol for exactly who looks at the AI alerts, how fast they have to respond, and what happens if an alert gets ignored.⏎⏎⏎⏎The folks who are going to suffer the most when AI fails are the ones already struggling. Rural patients, veterans in underfunded facilities, and minorities whose past bad treatment is literally baked into the training data. If you speed up AI without putting basic fairness protections in place, you are just going to widen the care gap. But it will be worse, because the bad decisions will look like objective computer logic, and doctors won't question it. I don't want you to stop AI. When a physician's default behavior becomes reviewing an AI output and either accepting or overriding it, rather than forming an independent clinical judgment first, the judgment muscle atrophies. Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman's foundational work on heuristics and biases, published in Science in 1974, helps explain why this happens: when a salient anchor number or category is placed in front of a decision-maker, it reshapes what questions they think to ask. SYNTH-0067♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Mark Davis♔Nuance Communications♔♔♔♔♔Nuance Communications | HHS AI RFI Comments | Docket No. [ONC-2024-0012] | Page 1⏎⏎⏎March 14, 2025⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue, S.W.⏎Washington, D.C. 20201⏎⏎Attention: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎To the Office of the Deputy Secretary and ASTP/ONC Staff:⏎⏎Nuance Communications submits these comments in response to the Department's Request for Information on accelerating AI adoption in clinical care settings. Nuance operates at the intersection of clinical documentation, ambient intelligence, and health system workflow integration, and the observations in this submission are grounded in that operational position. The data on AI-assisted oncology workflows are, frankly, compelling. Across networks deploying automated eligibility screening, trial identification time has been compressed from 23 days to under 72 hours, and per-site enrollment rates have increased by 34 percent compared to manual workflows. These are real operational gains, and Nuance does not dispute their significance. What this submission addresses is narrower and more specific: the RFI's framing of acceleration as the primary policy objective, without any mandatory equity infrastructure to detect or correct algorithmic harm before it reaches scale, is a structural problem that the Department has not adequately engaged.⏎⏎⏎Nuance Communications | HHS AI RFI Comments | Docket No. [ONC-2024-0012] | Page 2⏎⏎⏎THE DOCUMENTED PATTERN OF ALGORITHMIC HARM IN CLINICAL SETTINGS⏎⏎The case for caution here is not theoretical. Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, and Mullainathan S published findings in Science in 2019 demonstrating that a widely deployed commercial algorithm used to identify patients for care management programs assigned systematically lower risk scores to Black patients than to white patients with equivalent illness burden, effectively excluding Black patients from care coordination resources at a rate that could not be explained by any legitimate clinical variable (Obermeyer et al., Science 2019;366(6464):447-453). The algorithm used healthcare expenditure as a proxy for health need, and because structural inequities in the U.S. healthcare system mean that Black patients historically generate lower costs for equivalent severity of illness, the model encoded discrimination without any discriminatory intent on the part of its developers. This is the mechanism that concerns Nuance: bias does not require malicious design; it requires only that training data reflect a world in which disparities already exist. Separately, Sjoding MW, Dickson RP, Iwashyna TJ, Gay SE, and Valley TS demonstrated in the New England Journal of Medicine that pulse oximetry devices, a piece of technology so routine that clinicians rarely examine its assumptions, produced occult hypoxemia in Black patients at nearly three times the rate observed in white patients, a measurement error that went largely undetected for decades because the populations most affected were not adequately represented in validation studies (Sjoding et al., N Engl J Med. 2020;383(25):2477-2478). When that finding is placed alongside the Optum algorithm work, the pattern that emerges is one of compounding failure: devices and models validated in settings that overrepresent certain populations, deployed universally, with no ongoing surveillance mechanism to detect differential performance across race, ethnicity, or socioeconomic status. The RFI does not propose to break that pattern. It proposes to accelerate it.⏎⏎The dermatology literature is equally instructive. Adamson AS and Smith A noted in JAMA Dermatology that machine learning models for skin lesion classification were trained predominantly on images from light-skinned patients, meaning that their published performance metrics were essentially inapplicable to patients with darker skin tones (Adamson and Smith, JAMA Dermatol. 2018;154(11):1247-1248). This is not a minor technical caveat. Dermatology AI tools are now being positioned for deployment in primary care settings, including federally qualified health centers serving predominantly non-white, low-income populations, precisely the settings where the gap between published accuracy and real-world performance is widest. Gianfrancesco MA, Tamang S, Yazdany J, and Schmajuk G identified the structural reason for this gap in a 2018 JAMA Internal Medicine analysis: EHR-based training data systematically underrepresents patients with limited healthcare access, patients with multiple care episodes across disconnected systems, and patients whose clinical documentation reflects the lower-intensity engagement patterns associated with underinsured status (Gianfrancesco et al., JAMA Intern Med. 2018;178(11):1544-1547). The result is that algorithms trained on EHR data inherit the access patterns of the existing system rather than reflecting the clinical reality of the populations they will eventually serve.⏎⏎⏎Nuance Communications | HHS AI RFI Comments | Docket No. [ONC-2024-0012] | Page 3⏎⏎⏎THE ACADEMIC-TO-COMMUNITY PERFORMANCE GAP AND AUTOMATION BIAS⏎⏎From a practice management perspective, there is a specific operational problem with the way AI validation studies are currently conducted and reported that the RFI does not address. Wong A, Otles E, Donnelly JP, and colleagues published an external validation of a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2021 and found that the model's real-world performance at a community hospital was substantially worse than the performance reported in the original validation study conducted at the academic medical center where it was developed (Wong et al., JAMA Intern Med. 2021;181(8):1065-1070). The model had been marketed and adopted based on those original metrics. Clinicians using it at community hospitals, rural practices, and safety-net institutions had no way of knowing that the performance figures they had been shown did not apply to their patient population or their documentation environment. This is not an isolated case; it is a structural feature of how health AI validation works. Academic medical centers generate the training data, conduct the initial validation, and publish the performance metrics. Community hospitals and safety-net institutions deploy the model into a completely different data environment and assume the published numbers hold. They frequently do not.⏎⏎The automation bias problem compounds this. Char DS, Shah NH, and Magnus D described in the New England Journal of Medicine the mechanism by which clinicians, presented with a model output that carries the implicit authority of an algorithmic system, tend to suppress their own clinical skepticism in ways that would not occur if the same information were presented as a colleague's informal opinion (Char et al., N Engl J Med. 2018;378(11):981-983). Wiens J, Saria S, Sendak M, and colleagues elaborated on this in Nature Medicine, arguing that responsible ML deployment in healthcare requires not just technical validation but active workflow design that preserves clinician override capacity and does not present model outputs in ways that crowd out independent clinical reasoning (Wiens et al., Nat Med. 2019;25(9):1337-1340). What Nuance observes operationally is that these recommendations remain entirely voluntary. There is no deployment standard that requires health systems to test for automation bias effects in their specific clinical environment before going live with a model. The RFI asks about evaluation methods, and the honest answer from an operational standpoint is that current evaluation methods are inadequate not because the research community lacks good ideas, but because HHS has not made disaggregated performance reporting a condition of deployment. Seyyed-Kalantari L, Zhang H, McDermott MBA, Chen IY, and Ghassemi M demonstrated in a 2021 Nature Medicine study that chest radiograph AI models produced systematically higher underdiagnosis rates for patients on Medicaid, patients who were female, and patients who were Hispanic or Black, with the performance gaps being largest in the subgroups already at highest risk for missed diagnosis (Seyyed-Kalantari et al., Nat Med. 2021;27(12):2176-2182). Those gaps would not have been visible in aggregate accuracy statistics. They were visible only because the investigators disaggregated the results by demographic subgroup. The RFI does not require that disaggregation as a condition of anything.⏎⏎⏎Nuance Communications | HHS AI RFI Comments | Docket No. [ONC-2024-0012] | Page 4⏎⏎⏎INTEROPERABILITY, DATA STANDARDS, AND THE AMPLIFICATION RISK⏎⏎The RFI asks specifically about interoperability infrastructure and data sharing as mechanisms for accelerating AI adoption. Nuance wants to be direct about a concern here that we do not think has received adequate attention in the policy conversation. Expanded interoperability is a genuine good. The HTI-1 Final Rule (89 Fed. Reg. 1192, Jan. 9, 2024) created meaningful progress on algorithm transparency and information sharing standards, and Nuance supported those provisions. But interoperability that increases the volume and velocity of data flowing into AI training pipelines does not automatically improve the equity of those pipelines. If the underlying data reflects decades of differential access, differential documentation quality, and differential representation across care settings, then connecting more of that data more efficiently means training more models on a larger version of the same biased substrate. Pierson E, Cutler DM, Leskovec J, Mullainathan S, and Obermeyer Z demonstrated in a 2021 Nature Medicine analysis that pain management algorithms trained on standard clinical data dramatically underestimated pain severity in underserved populations, and that correcting for this required not just more data but specifically equity-weighted data curation that actively compensated for historical underrepresentation (Pierson et al., Nat Med. 2021;27(1):136-140). The implication for interoperability policy is that data sharing standards need to include equity-weighting requirements, not as a secondary consideration, but as a condition of the infrastructure itself. Vyas DA, Eisenstein LG, and Jones DS made a related argument in the New England Journal of Medicine regarding race correction in clinical algorithms: the problem is not simply that race is used as a variable, but that its use often encodes social inequity as if it were biological fact, and that this encoding is invisible to end users who trust the algorithm's output without understanding its construction (Vyas et al., N Engl J Med. 2020;383(9):874-882). Interoperability infrastructure that connects more institutions to more data without requiring equity auditing of what that data contains will produce more models with the same structural problem, deployed more widely and with more institutional confidence in their outputs.⏎⏎⏎Nuance Communications | HHS AI RFI Comments | Docket No. [ONC-2024-0012] | Page 5⏎⏎⏎WHAT HHS SHOULD REQUIRE, AND WHY THE RFI'S SILENCE IS A STRUCTURAL GAP⏎⏎Nuance is not asking HHS to slow AI adoption. The operational evidence for AI-assisted workflows is real, and the efficiency gains in settings like oncology trial matching are documented and material. What Nuance is asking is that HHS treat the absence of mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing and post-deployment bias surveillance not as a gap to be addressed in future rulemaking, but as a precondition for the acceleration agenda the RFI is proposing. Specifically, any federal reimbursement or certification pathway for clinical AI tools should require that developers provide disaggregated performance data by race, ethnicity, insurance status, and care setting before a tool is eligible for reimbursement or ONC certification. This is not an unreasonable technical burden. It is the minimum information a practice manager at a community hospital or a federally qualified health center needs to make an informed deployment decision. Post-deployment, HHS should require ongoing model performance monitoring with mandatory reporting thresholds that trigger review when performance degrades beyond specified tolerances in any demographic subgroup. The sepsis prediction experience documented by Wong and colleagues is instructive here: by the time a community hospital identifies that a model is underperforming in their environment, the model has already been making decisions about real patients for months or years. A mandatory surveillance framework with defined reporting triggers would catch that kind of drift before it becomes a documented harm pattern.⏎⏎The reimbursement data from oncology networks are worth returning to here, because they illuminate the policy lever. Practices operating under value-based care arrangements were 2.7 times more likely to have formally adopted AI-assisted patient stratification tools than those operating exclusively under fee-for-service models. Payment structure shapes adoption velocity. If HHS builds equity auditing requirements into the reimbursement conditions for AI tools, the market will respond. Developers who want access to Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement will conduct the disaggregated validation studies because the alternative is exclusion from the largest payer in the country. This is how the Department has historically moved markets on quality standards, and there is no principled reason why algorithmic equity should be treated differently. The concern Nuance wants to leave with the Department is specific: the communities most likely to be harmed by biased AI deployment are the same communities currently served by the care settings least likely to have the technical infrastructure to detect that harm on their own. A rural critical access hospital or a safety-net clinic in Baltimore does not have a data science team running equity audits on every AI tool their EHR vendor has embedded in the workflow. SYNTH-0068♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Andrew Hernandez♔Veeva Systems♔♔♔♔♔Andrew Hernandez⏎Compliance Officer, Veeva Systems⏎Winooski, Vermont 05404⏎⏎Submitted via Regulations.gov⏎Docket: HHS-2024-AI-Clinical-RFI⏎⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎⏎FRAMING CONCERN: THE RFI'S SELECTIVE SCOPE⏎⏎Veeva Systems appreciates HHS's engagement on the question of AI adoption in clinical settings, and our compliance function has tracked this issue carefully across the health systems and life sciences organizations we support. The data from PINC AI's Q2 2024 Health System Compliance and AI Readiness Survey — which found that 68% of affiliated facilities had piloted at least one AI-enabled clinical decision support tool in the preceding 24 months, yet fewer than 22% had achieved sustained, reimbursable integration — is consistent with what our own account teams observe when working with hospital compliance officers. The structural barriers are real: fragmented CMS reimbursement pathways, absent validation frameworks, and regulatory ambiguity around liability are all legitimate obstacles that this RFI is right to address. That said, what concerns this submission is not what the RFI asks, but what it omits. The Department has framed this inquiry almost entirely around the deployment of AI by clinical providers, and in doing so has set aside the most consequential and, from a compliance standpoint, the most legally exposed deployment of AI currently operating in the U.S. health system: automated prior authorization denial by commercial and Medicare Advantage insurers. The October 2024 U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations report, "Denial by Algorithm: How Health Insurers Use Artificial Intelligence to Deny Claims," documented in considerable detail how several large insurers built AI systems that optimized for denial throughput rather than clinical accuracy, and that these systems were producing denial rates well in excess of what physician reviewers would have generated. The OIG reached a related finding in April 2022, concluding in Report OEI-09-18-00260 that some Medicare Advantage organizations were denying prior authorization requests that met coverage criteria under traditional Medicare, a pattern consistent with algorithmic decision-making constrained by cost-containment objectives rather than medical necessity standards. The Commonwealth Fund's March 2024 issue brief, "Denied: How Insurance Company Algorithms Are Blocking Patient Access to Care," and the National Health Law Program's January 2024 policy brief, "Automated Injustice: How AI Prior Authorization Tools Undermine Patient Rights," both reach similar conclusions through independent analysis. CMS's own Medicare Advantage Prior Authorization and Appeals Data Report (2023) showed that appeal overturn rates for denied claims remained high, which is precisely the pattern one would expect if the initial denial logic was not grounded in individualized clinical review. And the market concentration dynamics that Dafny and Lee analyzed in the New England Journal of Medicine (Vol. 390, 2024) matter here too: when a small number of large insurers each adopt AI denial infrastructure, the aggregate effect on patient access is not marginal. Kaye et al., writing in the Journal of Health Policy, Politics and Law (Vol. 49, No. 2, 2024), documented both the efficiency claims insurers have made for these systems and the equity risks they introduce, particularly for patients in lower-income and minority populations. That equity concern connects directly to Obermeyer et al.'s foundational 2019 Science paper (Vol. 366, Issue 6464) on racial bias in health algorithms, which established that cost-containment-optimized models systematically underestimate the health needs of Black patients. An RFI that accelerates AI adoption in clinical settings without addressing this parallel AI deployment is, from a compliance perspective, architecturally incomplete.⏎⏎Veeva Systems | HHS AI RFI Comment | Page 2⏎⏎POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS FOR HHS CONSIDERATION⏎⏎Given the framing concern above, this submission focuses on two specific areas where HHS regulatory action would meaningfully reduce compliance risk and patient harm:⏎⏎1. Mandatory human clinical review before finalization of any AI-generated prior authorization denial. The Senate Subcommittee's October 2024 report found that some AI denial systems were processing claims in under two seconds, a throughput rate that is not compatible with individualized medical necessity review. HHS should issue guidance, and where authority permits, binding regulation, requiring that any adverse prior authorization determination generated or assisted by an AI system be reviewed and affirmed by a licensed clinician with relevant specialty training before the denial is communicated to the patient or provider. The AMA's 2023 Prior Authorization Physician Survey documented the administrative burden that high-volume AI-assisted denials impose on clinical staff, and that burden is itself a patient safety risk because it consumes physician time that would otherwise go to direct care.⏎⏎2. Public disclosure requirements for insurers receiving federal reimbursement. Any insurer participating in Medicare Advantage, Medicaid managed care, or ACA marketplace programs that uses an AI or algorithmic system in its prior authorization workflow should be required to disclose, at minimum: the denial rate attributable to AI-generated determinations, the training objective documentation for the model (i.e., whether the model was optimized for cost containment or clinical accuracy), and the demographic performance data across race, ethnicity, and income categories. The precedent from health IT transparency efforts, including the kind of algorithmic accountability work that Schulte and Fry flagged as missing in the EHR context as far back as March 2019, suggests that voluntary disclosure does not produce adequate information for regulators or the public. CMS should have explicit audit authority over insurer AI systems as a condition of federal program participation, and any AI system whose primary training objective is documented as cost containment should be explicitly excluded from any accelerated reimbursement or approval pathway that this RFI's eventual rulemaking may⏎⏎Veeva Systems | HHS AI RFI Comment | Page 3⏎⏎create for clinical AI tools. SYNTH-0069♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔William Johnson♔Connected Health Initiative♔♔♔♔♔Connected Health Initiative | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 1⏎⏎⏎EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎The Connected Health Initiative submits these comments in response to the Department's Request for Information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings. Our primary concern — and the reason this submission has been prepared with some urgency — is a structural problem that the RFI itself, perhaps inadvertently, perpetuates: the framing of democratic oversight as an obstacle to innovation, rather than as a prerequisite condition for legitimate governance. The DSI's national survey of 1,847 dental practices across 38 states, conducted in March 2024, found that 63% of respondents had evaluated at least one AI-assisted diagnostic tool for radiographic analysis, yet only 19% had proceeded to full clinical integration (Dental Standards Institute, "AI-Assisted Diagnostic Tools in Dental Practice: A National Survey of Adoption Patterns and Barriers," DSI Policy Research Division, March 2024). That gap is not a market failure to be corrected by federal acceleration. It is a signal. The practices that declined to proceed cited reimbursement uncertainty and unclear liability standards at a rate of 74% — and the Connected Health Initiative believes these concerns, taken seriously, open into a much deeper constitutional and governance question about who has the authority to determine which clinical decisions may be delegated to automated systems, and under what conditions.⏎⏎The RFI asks, among other things, how HHS might reduce uncertainty that impedes innovation. That is a reasonable goal stated plainly. But the framing deserves direct scrutiny. "Reducing uncertainty" is not a neutral administrative act. When the uncertainty in question concerns algorithmic decision-making in high-stakes clinical environments, reducing it through federal regulatory action necessarily forecloses the space in which local communities, professional bodies, and democratic institutions might reach their own conclusions. Frank Pasquale observed in "The Black Box Society" (Harvard University Press, 2015) that the structural inaccessibility of proprietary algorithmic logic is not merely a technical inconvenience — it is a form of delegated authority without accountability, and it poses a genuine problem for democratic self-governance. The Connected Health Initiative's own technical working group reached a parallel conclusion in October 2024, after conducting a comparative analysis of 14 commercially available dental AI platforms: the inconsistencies in how these tools document algorithmic decision-making raise serious concerns about auditability that go well beyond product quality (Dental Standards Institute, "Auditability and Standards Alignment in Commercially Available Dental AI Platforms: A Comparative Analysis of 14 Products," DSI Technical Working Group Report, October 2024). When a clinician cannot explain to a patient — or to a court, or to a state licensing board — why a diagnostic recommendation was generated, the problem is not regulatory lag. It is the absence of legitimate public authority over a consequential decision.⏎⏎Connected Health Initiative | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 2⏎⏎This is where the Connected Health Initiative wants to be precise, because the argument is sometimes mischaracterized. The organization does not oppose AI in clinical care. Eric Topol's work on high-performance medicine documented the genuine diagnostic potential of these systems in ways that are difficult to dismiss (Topol, E.J., "High-performance medicine: the convergence of human and artificial intelligence," Nature Medicine, 25: 44–56, 2019). The GAO's 2020 assessment similarly acknowledged the demonstrated benefits in augmenting patient care (U.S. Government Accountability Office, "Artificial Intelligence in Health Care: Benefits and Challenges of Technologies to Augment Patient Care," GAO-21-7SP, November 2020). What the Connected Health Initiative argues is that acceleration, as a governing value, is not self-evidently legitimate. Sheila Jasanoff's work on the ethics of invention is useful here: democratic societies retain the legitimate right to designate certain domains as stubbornly human — not because automated systems necessarily perform worse, but because the act of human judgment in those domains carries moral and relational weight that is independent of accuracy (Jasanoff, S., "The Ethics of Invention: Technology and the Human Future," W.W. Norton & Company, 2016, pp. 183–207). HHS should not, through reimbursement design or regulatory safe harbors, preempt that judgment before the democratic conversation has occurred. The National Academy of Medicine's 2023 consensus study on AI governance frameworks reached a related conclusion, recommending that federal agencies treat governance structure as a prerequisite to deployment incentives, not a follow-on activity (National Academy of Medicine, "Artificial Intelligence in Health and Medicine: A Consensus Study on Governance Frameworks," NAM Special Publication, Washington, D.C., 2023).⏎⏎The irreversibility problem deserves particular attention, and the Connected Health Initiative addressed it at our November 2024 Annual Standards Symposium at some length. Dafny and Lee argued in Health Affairs that health IT infrastructure decisions are functionally irreversible once clinical workflows, reimbursement codes, and vendor contracts have organized around them — the switching costs become prohibitive within a period of roughly five to seven years (Dafny, L. & Lee, T.H., "The Myth of Reversibility in Health IT Infrastructure," Health Affairs, 42(3): 411–419, 2023). This is not a hypothetical. The structural inaccessibility that Selbst and Barocas analyzed in their examination of explainability requirements — where they argued that the intuitive appeal of explainable machines often masks the degree to which explainability is technically constrained — means that the accountability mechanisms being promised now may not be deliverable at scale (Selbst, A.D. & Barocas, S., "The Intuitive Appeal of Explainable Machines," Fordham Law Review, 87(3): 1085–1139, 2018). The European Parliament's AI Act, specifically Articles 13 and 14 on transparency and human oversight requirements for high-risk AI systems in healthcare, represents one legislative attempt to address this before lock-in occurs (European Parliament, "Artificial Intelligence Act: Risk Classification and Transparency Requirements for High-Risk AI Systems in Healthcare," Regulation (EU) 2024/1689). The United States has no equivalent framework, and the Connected Health Initiative is concerned that the RFI's emphasis on acceleration will widen that gap rather than narrow it. Coiera, Westbrook, and Wyatt identified the safety and quality conditions that clinical decision support systems must satisfy to be responsibly deployed — and those conditions have not become less demanding because the systems have become more sophisticated (Coiera, E., Westbrook, J., & Wyatt, J., "The Safety and Quality of Decision Support Systems," IMIA Yearbook of Medical Informatics, 2006: 20–25). The racial bias findings documented by Obermeyer and colleagues, showing systematic underestimation of illness severity in Black patients by a widely deployed health management algorithm, are a concrete demonstration of what happens when accountability structures are treated as secondary concerns (Obermeyer, Z., Powers, B., Vogeli, C., & Mullainathan, S., "Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations," Science, 366(6464): 447–453, 2019).⏎⏎Connected Health Initiative | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 3⏎⏎The Connected Health Initiative's specific recommendations, framed as democratic prerequisites rather than regulatory preferences, are as follows:⏎⏎1. HHS should condition any new reimbursement pathways for AI-assisted clinical decision support on mandatory algorithmic documentation standards that allow independent audit by public bodies — not merely by the deploying institution's internal review process.⏎⏎2. The Department should commission a formal democratic deliberation process, modeled on the NAM consensus study methodology, that asks communities — including rural communities in states like Idaho, where the Connected Health Initiative's member organizations work directly with critical access hospitals — to identify which clinical domains they consider appropriate for automated decision support, and which they do not.⏎⏎3. Any regulatory safe harbor for AI-assisted diagnosis should include a sunset provision requiring re-authorization through notice-and-comment rulemaking no later than five years from the effective date, specifically to prevent the infrastructure lock-in that Dafny and Lee documented.⏎⏎4. CMS should require, as a condition of coverage for AI-assisted diagnostic tools, that vendors provide machine-readable documentation of training data provenance and validation cohort composition, with particular attention to demographic representation.⏎⏎o This requirement should apply retroactively to tools already in clinical use, with a compliance window of 18 months.⏎⏎o The documentation should be deposited in a publicly accessible federal repository, not held exclusively by the deploying institution.⏎⏎5. HHS should publish plain-language summaries of all future AI-related regulatory guidance simultaneously with the Federal Register notice. The Connected Health Initiative reviewed the current RFI notice and found the language inaccessible to the majority of the dental practitioners, community health workers, and patient advocates whose input would most meaningfully inform the Department's decisions. This is not a minor procedural complaint. The accessibility of regulatory process is itself a democratic value. If the people most affected by a policy cannot read the document soliciting their input, the comment period is formally open but functionally closed.⏎⏎That last point is worth sitting with. The Connected Health Initiative's research director spent considerable time working through the Federal Register notice for this RFI and found language that would require a graduate-level familiarity with administrative law to parse correctly. The organization's member practices — the dental clinicians and community health center staff who are the actual intended beneficiaries of whatever policy HHS adopts — would not know what "accelerating AI adoption in clinical care" means for their daily practice, their liability exposure, or their patients' rights from reading that document. The democratic legitimacy of this rulemaking process depends on more than a 60-day comment window. It depends on the Department making a genuine effort to communicate in language that the affected public can understand and respond to. The Connected Health Initiative strongly urges HHS to adopt a standing policy of plain-language parallel publication for all health technology regulatory notices, and to consider whether the current comment process — which systematically advantages large institutional actors with dedicated regulatory affairs staff — is producing representative input or primarily⏎⏎Connected Health Initiative | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 4⏎⏎amplifying the voices of those who already have the resources to engage.⏎⏎Respectfully submitted on behalf of the Connected Health Initiative,⏎⏎William Johnson⏎Research Director, Connected Health Initiative⏎Boise, Idaho⏎⏎Appendix A: DSI Survey Instrument and Sampling Methodology (March 2024) — document referenced but not attached to this submission pending coordination with DSI Policy Research Division;
