SYNTH-0072♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Kevin Hall♔American Physical Therapy Association♔♔♔♔♔American Physical Therapy Association⏎1111 North Fairfax Street⏎Alexandria, VA 22314⏎⏎January 14, 2025⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue, SW⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎Attention: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎---⏎⏎APTA Comments | HHS AI RFI — Health Equity and Validation Standards | Page 1⏎⏎---⏎⏎The American Physical Therapy Association (APTA) welcomes the Department's attention to artificial intelligence in clinical care. Our network of affiliated health systems, which spans 214 institutions ranging from major academic medical centers to rural critical access hospitals and urban safety-net facilities, has a direct stake in whether AI tools deployed in clinical settings actually work as advertised across the full spectrum of patient populations. We are not here to slow this technology down. We are here because our Q3 2024 policy roundtable, convening representatives from 47 academic medical centers and community hospital systems, identified a pattern that the RFI framework does not appear to account for: the populations most dependent on under-resourced institutions are also the populations most likely to be harmed when AI tools validated in high-resource settings are deployed without adequate real-world testing in those institutions. That is not a hypothetical concern. It is a documented, recurring pattern in the published literature, and HHS's current accelerationist posture, as framed in this RFI, contains no mandatory mechanism to detect or prevent it.⏎⏎APTA Comments | HHS AI RFI — Health Equity and Validation Standards | Page 2⏎⏎OBSERVED HARMS ARE NOT EDGE CASES⏎⏎The evidence that AI systems trained on historical healthcare data reproduce and amplify existing disparities is now substantial enough that it should be treated as a baseline assumption in any deployment framework, not a risk to be addressed after the fact. Obermeyer et al. (Science, 2019) documented that a widely used commercial algorithm for managing population health systematically underestimated illness severity in Black patients, resulting in those patients receiving substantially fewer care resources despite equivalent objective need. The mechanism was not malicious design — it was that the algorithm used healthcare costs as a proxy for health needs, and historical data encoded decades of differential access and discriminatory treatment into that proxy variable. Gianfrancesco et al. (JAMA Internal Medicine, 2018) identified similar structural problems across a range of machine learning models using electronic health record data, noting that missing data, coding practices, and selection effects all tend to disadvantage the same populations already marginalized by the healthcare system. Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones (New England Journal of Medicine, 2020) demonstrated that race correction built into standard clinical algorithms — a practice presented as scientifically neutral — actually perpetuates the conflation of race as a biological rather than social variable, with downstream consequences for treatment allocation.⏎⏎These are not isolated cases from a single domain. Sjoding et al. (New England Journal of Medicine, 2020) documented that pulse oximetry devices, a piece of hardware so standard it is nearly invisible in clinical settings, systematically overestimated oxygen saturation in patients with darker skin tones — a finding with direct implications for any AI system that incorporates pulse oximetry readings as an input variable. Adamson and Smith (JAMA Dermatology, 2018) found that dermatology AI tools trained predominantly on images of lighter skin tones performed substantially worse on patients with darker skin, a performance gap that has direct implications for melanoma detection and delayed diagnoses. Seyyed-Kalantari et al. (Nature Medicine, 2021) documented underdiagnosis bias in AI algorithms applied to chest radiographs across multiple under-served patient populations, finding that the performance degradation was consistent and correlated with social determinants of health present in the underlying training data. The pattern here is not subtle. Historical healthcare data encodes historical inequity, and AI systems trained on that data will reproduce it at scale unless there is a deliberate, mandatory intervention in the development and validation pipeline.⏎⏎APTA Comments | HHS AI RFI — Health Equity and Validation Standards | Page 3⏎⏎THE GENERALIZABILITY GAP IS A STRUCTURAL EQUITY PROBLEM⏎⏎The second issue we want to address directly is one that the RFI framework treats, at most, as a technical footnote: the gap between AI performance in the settings where tools are validated and AI performance in the settings where they are actually deployed. Wong et al. (JAMA Internal Medicine, 2021) conducted an external validation of a proprietary sepsis prediction model that had been widely implemented across health systems nationally. Their findings were striking: the model's performance degraded substantially when tested outside the academic medical center environment in which it was developed, and the model's alert system generated a high volume of false positives that the original validation literature had not surfaced. This is not a problem with one sepsis model. Wiens et al. (Nature Medicine, 2019) laid out a systematic roadmap for responsible machine learning in healthcare and were explicit that external validation in diverse deployment settings is a non-negotiable requirement for responsible deployment — not an optional enhancement.⏎⏎APTA's network data is consistent with this literature. Our research team's analysis of CMS reimbursement data found that fewer than 12% of FDA-authorized clinical AI tools have a corresponding billing mechanism, which means that health systems, particularly those operating on thin margins in community and rural settings, have no structured pathway for recouping the costs of thoughtful implementation. The financial pressure this creates tends to push toward rapid, low-scrutiny deployment rather than the careful site-specific validation that the literature demands. Community hospitals and safety-net facilities, which lack the informatics infrastructure and research staff of academic medical centers, are least equipped to conduct their own validation studies and most likely to rely on vendor-provided performance claims that may not reflect their patient population at all. The 22-month average delay our network documented between FDA authorization and actual deployment is partly explained by this: institutions that are trying to do this carefully are stymied by the absence of standardized frameworks, while institutions that are not doing it carefully face no formal accountability mechanism.⏎⏎Char, Shah, and Magnus (New England Journal of Medicine, 2018) wrote plainly that implementing machine learning in healthcare requires confronting ethical challenges that are structural, not incidental — including the challenge of ensuring that performance claims are validated in the populations and settings where the tool will actually be used. Cabitza, Rasoini, and Gensini (JAMA, 2017) raised the problem of automation bias: the tendency of clinicians to defer to AI-generated outputs even when those outputs conflict with clinical judgment. This mechanism makes AI errors harder to catch than equivalent human errors, because the social and cognitive dynamics of clinical decision-making create pressure to accept algorithmic recommendations. In under-resourced settings where clinicians are managing high patient volumes with limited support staff, the conditions for automation bias are particularly acute. Pierson et al. (Nature Medicine, 2021) demonstrated that algorithmic approaches can, when designed with equity as a design constraint, actually reduce unexplained pain disparities in underserved populations — which is to say that the technology is not inherently inequitable. The problem is that equity is not currently a required design constraint or a validated deployment criterion.⏎⏎APTA Comments | HHS AI RFI — Health Equity and Validation Standards | Page 4⏎⏎WHAT HHS SHOULD REQUIRE — AND WHAT THIS RFI DOES NOT CURRENTLY ADDRESS⏎⏎The RFI solicits comment on regulatory, reimbursement, and research-and-development actions to accelerate AI adoption. APTA's position is that acceleration without equity safeguards is not a neutral policy choice — it is a policy choice with foreseeable consequences for the populations our member clinicians serve in community, rural, and safety-net settings. The National Academy for State Health Policy documented in its 2023 policy brief on algorithmic accountability in healthcare that federal gaps in this area are real and that state-level legislative activity, while growing, is fragmented and insufficient as a substitute for federal standards. HHS is positioned to fill that gap. We urge the Department to take the following actions:⏎⏎1. Mandate pre-deployment equity auditing for all clinical AI tools seeking CMS reimbursement or deployed in federally funded health systems. Audits should include disaggregated performance data by race, ethnicity, sex, age, socioeconomic status, and geographic setting, with particular attention to performance in community hospitals, rural facilities, and safety-net institutions.⏎⏎2. Require external validation in deployment-representative settings as a condition of FDA market authorization for clinical decision support software. Validation studies conducted exclusively in large academic medical centers should not be accepted as sufficient evidence of generalizability.⏎⏎3. Establish mandatory post-deployment bias surveillance with public reporting requirements. Health systems deploying FDA-authorized AI tools should be required to report performance data on a standardized schedule, disaggregated by the same demographic and institutional categories listed above.⏎⏎4. Align reimbursement pathways with equity requirements. CMS should condition coverage of AI-assisted clinical services on documentation that the tool has been validated in settings comparable to the deploying institution, and that ongoing performance monitoring is in place.⏎⏎o A note on implementation: our network's experience suggests that smaller community hospitals will need technical assistance infrastructure to comply with these requirements. HHS should consider a parallel investment in regional support centers, analogous to the Regional Extension Centers established under HITECH, to help under-resourced institutions conduct site-specific validation.⏎⏎The framing of this RFI emphasizes speed — removing friction, accelerating adoption, expanding access. APTA does not dispute that these are legitimate goals. The 78% of clinical AI deployments in our network that stalled at the integration phase represent real delays in patient access to potentially beneficial tools. But the literature we have cited here — and the structural patterns our own network has documented — make clear that deploying AI tools rapidly in settings where they have not been validated, without any mandatory mechanism for detecting performance disparities, is not the same thing as expanding access to beneficial technology. For many patients in under-resourced settings, it may mean something considerably worse.⏎⏎We appreciate the Department's willingness to solicit broad public comment on this question and welcome further engagement. SYNTH-0074♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Emily Clark♔♔♔♔♔♔My client Marcus finally got stable after years of cycling through crisis, and the difference was a telehealth clinic in Columbus that used an AI triage tool to flag when he'd gone quiet for more than four days. I watched that work. I documented it. So I am not writing this to say AI doesn't belong in clinical care — it does, and I've seen it do real good. But what I keep coming back to when I read this RFI is a question the document never quite asks: who actually benefits from acceleration, and on what terms?⏎⏎MARKET CONCENTRATION AND THE ACCELERATION TRAP⏎⏎The framing of this RFI troubles me in ways I find hard to fully articulate but will try. The document asks how HHS can accelerate adoption and expand reimbursement pathways, and those are reasonable questions. But they are being asked in a market where, as Gee and Bhatt documented in Health Affairs in 2023, a small number of EHR and technology vendors already control the majority of clinical data infrastructure. Dafny and Lee made the same point in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2022 when they described how switching costs and vendor lock-in have effectively eliminated meaningful EHR competition in most health systems. When you layer AI deployment onto that already-concentrated substrate, you are not creating a new market. You are handing the incumbents a deeper moat. The American Economic Liberties Project's 2023 policy brief on how Amazon, Google, and Microsoft are moving into healthcare AI makes this concrete — these are companies with the compliance infrastructure to navigate complex reimbursement processes and the legal teams to negotiate CRADAs on favorable terms. A federally qualified health center in rural Appalachian Ohio does not have those things. So when HHS expands reimbursement pathways and public-private partnerships without first addressing concentration, the practical effect is a transfer of federally generated value — including patient data collected through Medicare and Medicaid encounters — to companies that will retain proprietary control over the resulting products.⏎⏎I want to be specific about why this matters clinically and not just economically. Obermeyer and colleagues published in Science in 2019 that a widely used population-health algorithm systematically underestimated the severity of illness in Black patients because it was trained on cost as a proxy for need — a bias that was invisible until someone looked for it. The GAO flagged in 2023 (GAO-23-105812) that HHS has not yet conducted a systematic risk assessment of vendor consolidation before expanding AI reimbursement pathways. Maddox, Rumsfeld, and Payne raised similar questions in JAMA in 2022 about whether the incentive structures driving AI deployment in health care are aligned with patient outcomes or with market capture. These aren't obscure academic concerns. They are the conditions under which tools like the one that helped Marcus get built, deployed, and evaluated — and the conditions determine whether those tools actually work for patients who don't look like the training data.⏎⏎What bothers me about this RFI is that it reads as if the Federal Health IT Strategic Plan 2024-2030 (ASTP/ONC, 2024) has already settled the question of how AI gets integrated, and the public is just being asked to help with implementation details. That may not be the intent, but it is the effect. The questions are structured around acceleration, not interrogation. There is no question that asks: should certain AI applications require open interoperability before receiving reimbursement? SYNTH-0075♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Thomas Flores♔Partnership for Health Analytic Research♔♔♔♔♔Partnership for Health Analytic Research⏎Comments Submitted to HHS Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎Docket: HHS-2024-AI-RFI-Clinical-Care⏎Submitted by: Thomas Flores, Policy Director⏎⏎PHAR Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 1⏎⏎THE WORKFORCE QUESTION HHS IS REFUSING TO ASK⏎⏎The Partnership for Health Analytic Research (PHAR) represents 412 member clearinghouses and health information exchanges that collectively route approximately 2.1 billion claims transactions annually. When 67% of those member organizations report actively piloting AI-assisted prior authorization automation, claims adjudication support, or embedded clinical decision tools — and when our Q3 2024 policy review found that 58% cite interoperability fragmentation as the primary barrier to scaling those deployments — PHAR speaks from direct operational visibility into what AI adoption actually looks like at infrastructure scale. That visibility is precisely why we are alarmed by this RFI's framing, which treats workforce displacement as either an acceptable externality or a problem too uncomfortable to name directly. HHS has organized its questions around acceleration. The Department has not organized a single substantive question around the workers who will absorb the consequences of that acceleration. That omission is not neutral. It reflects a policy posture that has already chosen sides, and PHAR intends to name that choice plainly.⏎⏎The vendor narrative driving this RFI — that AI deployment will reduce clinician burnout, ease documentation burden, and return autonomy to frontline practitioners — is not supported by the documented structural drivers of burnout in the existing literature. Shanafelt et al. (2022), publishing in Mayo Clinic Proceedings, tracked physician burnout across a nine-year longitudinal period and found that loss of autonomy, administrative burden, and erosion of professional identity were the primary accelerants, not workload volume per se. Bates et al. (2021) in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrating that alert fatigue — one of the most cited AI "solutions" — is itself a product of poorly governed clinical decision support deployment, not a condition that more AI tools reliably resolve. Dyrbye et al. (2019) in JAMA Network Open found that work unit environment and perceived organizational control were stronger predictors of burnout than individual-level interventions. The AMA's 2023 Digital Medicine Practice Accelerator report on augmented intelligence explicitly cautioned against deploying AI productivity metrics as proxy measures for clinical performance without frontline governance input. None of this literature supports the claim that accelerating AI adoption will improve workforce conditions. All of it suggests the opposite, under current deployment models.⏎⏎PHAR Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎What the evidence does support is the conclusion that AI tools marketed as efficiency solutions are being deployed primarily as workforce management instruments. The SEIU Healthcare Policy Brief published in 2024, "Monitored, Managed, and Marginalized," documented systematic use of AI-generated productivity dashboards to justify staffing ratio reductions in hospital systems across at least seven states. National Nurses United's 2023 report, "Staffing by Algorithm," provided case-level documentation of AI throughput metrics being used by hospital administrators to argue against minimum nurse-to-patient ratio protections in contract negotiations. Kellogg, Valentine, and Christin (2020) in the Academy of Management Annals analyzed algorithmic control mechanisms across multiple sectors and found that healthcare workers faced a distinct vulnerability: unlike workers in logistics or manufacturing, clinical staff are subject to algorithmic performance metrics while simultaneously bearing legal and ethical accountability for outcomes those algorithms cannot fully assess. The GAO's 2023 report on AI in health care (GAO-23-105980) acknowledged this tension but declined to recommend binding workforce protections, a gap PHAR regards as a significant regulatory failure. The MITRE Corporation's 2022 automation susceptibility analysis (MTR220134) estimated that between 30 and 45 percent of administrative healthcare roles carry high displacement risk under current AI deployment trajectories.⏎⏎PHAR is not opposed to AI adoption. What PHAR is opposed to is the systematic exclusion of frontline workers from procurement governance, the use of AI-generated throughput metrics as the evidentiary basis for staffing ratio decisions, and HHS's apparent willingness to treat the speed of adoption as a policy goal in the absence of binding workforce protection standards. Friedberg et al. (2013) at RAND established more than a decade ago that physician professional satisfaction is a direct predictor of care quality outcomes. Obermeyer and Emanuel (2016) in the New England Journal of Medicine warned that machine learning models in clinical medicine require rigorous outcome validation before deployment at scale. ONC's own 2023 Data Brief No. 58 acknowledged emerging workforce challenges in AI-assisted clinical environments without committing to any specific protective framework. That pattern — acknowledgment without commitment — is what PHAR is asking HHS to end.⏎⏎Specific policy demands from PHAR, which the Department should treat as non-negotiable conditions for any accelerationist regulatory posture:⏎⏎1. Mandatory workforce impact assessments prior to AI procurement approval in federally participating institutions.⏎2. Prohibition on using AI-generated productivity metrics as the primary or sole basis for staffing ratio determinations.⏎3. Required frontline worker representation — nurses, physicians, care coordinators — on institutional AI procurement governance committees.⏎4. A moratorium on administrative role automation in clinical settings until independent quality-of-care impact assessments, not vendor-sponsored studies, have been completed and reviewed by ONC.⏎⏎The interoperability fragmentation our members report is a real problem that deserves serious regulatory attention. But HHS should not allow the legitimate complexity of that technical problem to⏎⏎PHAR Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎obscure the more consequential question of who bears the cost when AI deployment goes wrong. Right now, that cost lands entirely on workers and patients. The vendors are not in the room when a nurse files a grievance because an algorithm flagged her for low throughput during a shift where she spent forty minutes with a deteriorating patient who needed her to stay. HHS needs to decide whether that nurse is a stakeholder in this rulemaking or an externality.⏎⏎thomas.flores@pharesearch.org⏎Partnership for Health Analytic Research⏎Hartford, CT 06103♔♔2026-02-02T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-02T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔3♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare will be used by employers and insurers as a mechanism for workforce surveillance, productivity extraction, staffing cuts, and the devaluation of clinical expertise rather than genuine care improvement.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔angry♔Connecticut♔policy director♔58♔A 2024 survey of our 412 member clearinghouses and health information exchanges found that 67% are actively piloting or evaluating AI-assisted claims adjudication, prior authorization automation, or clinical decision support tools embedded within their transaction-routing infrastructure. SYNTH-0076♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Donald Martin♔Association of American Indian Physicians♔♔♔♔♔ASSOCIATION OF AMERICAN INDIAN PHYSICIANS⏎Comments on HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket Submission — Office of the Deputy Secretary / ASTP/ONC⏎⏎⏎WORKFORCE GOVERNANCE IN AI-ASSISTED SURGICAL SETTINGS: THE GAP BETWEEN DEPLOYMENT AND ACCOUNTABILITY⏎⏎The 2024 AORN Membership Survey on AI-Assisted Surgical Technology Exposure and Governance Readiness (Association of periOperative Registered Nurses, unpublished policy brief) documented that 68 percent of more than 2,200 perioperative nurses reported exposure to at least one AI-assisted surgical technology in their primary practice setting. Fewer than one in five indicated their facility had adopted formal protocols governing nurse roles, responsibilities, or accountability structures in relation to those systems. A subsequent policy analysis of 14 health system AI governance frameworks found that perioperative nursing competencies were explicitly referenced in only three of those frameworks. The operating room is one of the highest-acuity environments for AI-assisted decision support in clinical care, and this governance gap is not an administrative inconvenience. It is a patient safety failure in progress. To Err Is Human (Kohn, Corrigan, and Donaldson, 2000, National Academies Press) established two decades ago that system design — not individual error — drives adverse outcomes in clinical settings. HHS cannot credibly claim to be accelerating AI adoption responsibly while tolerating a procurement environment in which frontline perioperative nurses are handed AI-assisted surgical tools without enforceable competency frameworks or meaningful consultation in the acquisition process.⏎⏎The Association of American Indian Physicians notes that this comment addresses specifically the workforce governance question embedded in this RFI, and not the full scope of questions posed. When AI systems are introduced into perioperative settings without corresponding adjustments to staffing ratios or competency requirements, the cognitive load on individual nurses increases even as administrators describe the technology as a burden-reduction tool. We are arguing that the Department's posture in this RFI treats governance as an afterthought to adoption, and that this sequencing is the problem.⏎⏎Nabla | HHS AI in Clinical Care RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLIN | Page 2⏎⏎THE DEPLOYMENT REALITY THIS RFI DOES NOT ACKNOWLEDGE⏎⏎The Department's RFI opens from a premise of beneficial acceleration. The framing is that AI tools exist, they work, and the task before HHS is to remove barriers to their spread. Our analysis of deployment data across 47 affiliated clinical partners, documented in Van Pelt & Company's Q2 2024 Policy Benchmarking Initiative (on file with the authors), tells a more complicated story. Sixty-eight percent of those partners identified reimbursement ambiguity as the primary barrier to scaling validated AI diagnostic tools past pilot phases, and average deployment timelines extended 14 months beyond initial regulatory clearance due to payor coverage uncertainty. That finding has been cited elsewhere in this docket's broader context, but what has not been adequately cited is what happens when that barrier is removed without corresponding governance. Facilities under value-based care arrangements were 2.3 times more likely to sustain AI adoption when clear coding pathways existed, which sounds like an argument for the Department's position until you ask what those facilities were actually sustaining adoption of. Structured interviews with 112 clinical operations leaders conducted as part of that same initiative found that the single most common stated rationale for AI tool procurement was workforce cost management, not clinical outcome improvement. The language used in procurement documentation was consistently framed around efficiency, throughput, and burnout reduction. The operational implementation told a different story.⏎⏎Across our network's deployment partners, we have documented a recurring pattern: AI tools marketed on burnout-reduction and efficiency grounds are implemented in ways that justify staffing ratio reductions and expanded caseloads rather than protecting clinician time. This is not a vendor problem in isolation, though vendors bear responsibility for how they market their products. It is an institutional financial pressure problem. Health systems operating under margin compression do not procure AI tools and then hold staffing levels steady while clinical time improves. They procure AI tools, document a projected efficiency gain, and then adjust staffing ratios to capture that gain as cost reduction. The result is that the AI tool is now carrying more of the load in a leaner staffing environment, meaning that when the AI fails or produces a false alert, there is less human redundancy to catch it. Bates, D.W., et al. (2021) documented in npj Digital Medicine that poorly governed clinical decision support tools increase alert fatigue rather than reducing it, and that the downstream effect on clinical attention is measurable and negative. Kocher, R., and Sahni, N.R. noted in Health Affairs in March 2023 that health systems are explicitly using AI deployment as a mechanism for workforce restructuring, and that this pattern is concentrated in high-volume, lower-margin service lines. We are seeing this in our own data, and we think the Department needs to name it plainly rather than building an acceleration framework that treats it as someone else's problem.⏎⏎Nabla | HHS AI in Clinical Care RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLIN | Page 3⏎⏎THE BURNOUT CLAIM DOES NOT HOLD UNDER SCRUTINY⏎⏎The Department's framing of AI as a burnout-reduction tool deserves particular attention because it is the rhetorical foundation on which a significant portion of this RFI's acceleration logic rests. If AI reduces burnout, then accelerating AI adoption is a workforce health intervention as much as a clinical efficiency one, and the case for speed over caution is strengthened. The problem is that the empirical record on this claim is weak at best and contradictory at worst.⏎⏎Shanafelt, T.D., et al. (2022) published a longitudinal analysis in Mayo Clinic Proceedings tracking physician burnout and work-life integration across the period from 2011 to 2020, finding that burnout rates increased across nearly every specialty during a period that also saw substantial growth in EHR adoption and clinical decision support deployment. The causal relationship is not simple, but the correlation between increased AI-adjacent tooling and improved burnout outcomes is not what the RFI's framing implies. Patel, R.S., et al. (2023) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis published in the Journal of General Internal Medicine specifically examining EHR burden and physician burnout, finding a consistent positive association between documentation burden, which AI documentation tools purport to address, and burnout severity. The operative question is whether AI documentation tools are actually reducing documentation burden or redistributing it in ways that generate new cognitive load. Our deployment data suggests the latter is more common than the former, particularly when those tools are layered onto existing workflows without meaningful clinician input into how they are configured.⏎⏎This brings us to a concern that the Department's RFI does not appear to have weighted adequately: the systematic exclusion of frontline clinical staff from AI procurement decisions. Across the 112 clinical operations leaders we interviewed, fewer than 20 percent reported that bedside nurses, physicians, or allied health staff had any formal role in the procurement process for AI tools that would directly affect their workflows. The American Medical Association's 2023 Digital Medicine Practice Playbook identifies frontline clinician involvement in AI governance as a minimum standard for responsible deployment, and yet the procurement reality we are observing is that these decisions are made by finance, operations, and technology leadership with clinical input treated as optional and advisory at best. Dyrbye, L.N., et al. (2020) published work in the Journal of Nursing Administration linking work unit safety culture directly to burnout severity among hospital nurses, and the construct of safety culture in that analysis is substantially about whether frontline workers feel their professional judgment is respected in operational decisions. Procurement processes that impose AI tools on clinical staff without consultation are, by the framework Dyrbye and colleagues describe, safety culture problems that will manifest as burnout outcomes regardless of what the AI tool itself is designed to do.⏎⏎Nabla | HHS AI in Clinical Care RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLIN | Page 4⏎⏎THE SURVEILLANCE AND AUTONOMY QUESTION⏎⏎There is a category of AI deployment that the RFI does not name directly but that our network's data identifies as a growing source of workforce harm: AI-driven productivity monitoring of clinical and administrative staff. This includes systems that track documentation completion rates, time-on-task metrics, throughput per shift, and deviation from algorithmic care pathways. National Nurses United's 2023 research report, "Surveilled, Stretched, and Sidelined," documented through survey data that a significant and growing proportion of nurses in U.S. hospital settings are subject to AI-enabled performance monitoring systems, and that exposure to those systems is associated with substantially elevated reports of moral distress and professional disengagement. We want to be careful about how we characterize this, because productivity monitoring is not inherently illegitimate. Health systems have reasonable interests in operational visibility. But there is a meaningful difference between aggregate operational dashboards used for resource planning and individual-level surveillance systems used to generate performance metrics that feed into staffing and retention decisions. The latter category is what is proliferating, and the Department's RFI contains no framework for distinguishing between them or governing the latter.⏎⏎The connection between clinician autonomy erosion and patient outcomes is not rhetorical. Obermeyer, Z., and Emanuel, E.J. (2016) wrote in the New England Journal of Medicine that the value of machine learning in clinical settings depends critically on how it is integrated with physician judgment, and that systems designed to replace rather than support clinical reasoning produce worse outcomes than either the AI or the physician operating independently. The logic extends directly to the surveillance context: when AI systems are used to monitor and constrain clinical behavior rather than to support it, the effect is not neutral. Clinicians under algorithmic surveillance report adjusting their behavior to optimize measurable metrics rather than clinical outcomes, which is a well-documented phenomenon in performance management literature and one that the healthcare context makes particularly consequential. The Department should not be agnostic about this.⏎⏎Nabla | HHS AI in Clinical Care RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLIN | Page 5⏎⏎RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎The Department has asked for input on regulatory, reimbursement, and research-and-development actions. These comments focus on the regulatory dimension, because we believe the governance architecture question is logically prior to the reimbursement incentive question. Paying for AI tools before establishing what governance those tools must satisfy is the wrong sequencing, and the ONC's own 2024 Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability Final Rule (89 Fed. Reg. 1192) established algorithm transparency and information sharing requirements that have not yet been extended to the workforce impact domain. That gap should be addressed before reimbursement pathways are broadened.⏎⏎Specifically, the Department should consider requiring that any AI tool seeking coverage under expanded CMS reimbursement pathways demonstrate, as a condition of that coverage, documented clinician involvement in deployment configuration. This is not a novel standard. The AMA's 2023 governance framework describes it as baseline responsible practice. What is novel is making it a reimbursement condition rather than a voluntary best practice, because the voluntary approach has not worked. Our deployment data is reasonably clear on this: facilities that describe themselves as following responsible AI governance principles and facilities that actually have formal clinician governance structures in place are not the same population. The self-report and the operational reality diverge substantially.⏎⏎The Department should also give serious attention to the distinction between AI tools that support human judgment and AI tools that substitute for it in roles that carry meaningful clinical consequence. Frakt, A., and Jha, A.K. (2023) argued in the Annals of Internal Medicine that pay-for-performance frameworks consistently produce the perverse effect of optimizing measurable proxies rather than the underlying outcomes those proxies are meant to represent. The same logic applies to AI deployment frameworks: when the metric is adoption rate or efficiency gain, health systems optimize for those metrics, and what gets lost in that optimization is frequently the harder-to-measure question of whether clinical judgment is being supported or displaced. Prior authorization review, care coordination, and patient navigation are the examples our network's data flags most consistently as roles where automation is being deployed without evidence of equivalent or superior outcomes compared to human performance, and without meaningful consultation with the workers whose roles are being restructured. This is not an argument that these functions can never be automated. It is an argument that the Department should require evidence of clinical equivalence before those deployments become reimbursable practice standards.⏎⏎Nabla | HHS AI in Clinical Care RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLIN | Page 6⏎⏎We recognize there is a tension in this submission. Nabla is an AI company. We have a direct commercial interest in a regulatory environment that supports AI adoption in clinical settings, and the Department is entitled to weigh that interest when evaluating these comments. We are raising governance concerns in part because we believe the current trajectory of poorly governed AI deployment is generating the kind of workforce harm and institutional backlash that will ultimately constrain responsible AI adoption more severely than thoughtful precautionary regulation would. That is a strategic argument as much as an ethical one, and we are not pretending otherwise. But it is also an argument that we believe is supported by the evidence, and the evidence is what the Department should be evaluating.⏎⏎The specific concern we want to leave the Department with is this: the acceleration framing of this RFI assumes that the primary barrier to beneficial AI adoption is regulatory and reimbursement friction. Our data suggests that in a significant proportion of cases, the tools being delayed are not primarily beneficial in the ways their procurement documentation claims. They are cost-reduction tools marketed as care quality tools, and the workforce harm they produce is a predictable consequence of the financial pressures driving their procurement rather than an incidental implementation problem that better guidance will fix. Removing reimbursement and regulatory barriers to those tools, without first establishing governance requirements that align procurement incentives with care quality rather than cost reduction, will scale that harm.⏎⏎A reference appendix including the Van Pelt & Company Q2 2024 internal report, supporting deployment data tables, and interview methodology documentation is available on request and will be submitted as a supplementary filing under this docket number. SYNTH-0079♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Sarah Davis♔Endocrine Society♔♔♔♔♔[Endocrine Society letterhead]⏎⏎1735 K Street, NW⏎Washington, DC 20006⏎www.endocrine.org⏎⏎June 12, 2024⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue, SW⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎Attention: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎Dear Deputy Secretary and RFI Coordinators:⏎⏎The Endocrine Society submits these comments on behalf of our 18,000 members — endocrinologists, researchers, and allied health professionals who provide care to patients with diabetes, thyroid disease, obesity, and related conditions across every care setting in the United States, including federally qualified health centers, rural critical access hospitals, and safety-net institutions in communities that have historically received the least investment in health infrastructure. We appreciate HHS's willingness to engage broadly on the question of AI adoption in clinical settings. However, this comment does not offer encouragement. It offers a warning, and we want to be direct about that from the outset.⏎⏎The framing of this RFI — "accelerating AI adoption" — is itself a policy choice, and not a neutral one. Acceleration, as a governing priority, assumes that the primary friction in the system is the slowness of uptake, and that removing barriers will produce broadly distributed benefits. We do not accept that premise as applied to clinical AI deployment in 2024. The evidence accumulated over the past six years is unambiguous: AI systems trained on historically skewed clinical data reproduce and frequently amplify the disparities already embedded in that data, and they do so with an authoritative numerical confidence that makes the resulting errors harder to detect and correct than equivalent errors made by human clinicians. The Endocrine Society is not opposed to artificial intelligence in clinical care. We are opposed to deploying it at scale without the structural safeguards necessary to ensure that the communities bearing the highest burden of endocrine disease — communities that are disproportionately Black, Hispanic, low-income, and rural — are not also the communities that absorb the highest burden of AI-generated harm.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Endocrine Society Comments | HHS AI RFI | June 2024 | Page 2⏎⏎THE EVIDENCE BASE FOR ALGORITHMIC BIAS IS NOT THEORETICAL⏎⏎This comment focuses specifically on the RFI's questions regarding regulatory pathways and research priorities, because those are the domains where the structural failures are most consequential and most correctable. We are not addressing every question posed; the equity concerns we raise apply with particular urgency to any pathway that would accelerate deployment before equity validation requirements are in place.⏎⏎The pattern of algorithmic bias in clinical AI is well-documented and, at this point, cannot be dismissed as a fringe concern or an edge case. Obermeyer et al. published in Science in 2019 the now-canonical analysis of a commercial population health algorithm used by hundreds of health systems to identify high-risk patients for care management programs (Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S. Science. 2019;366(6464):447-453). That algorithm used prior healthcare cost as a proxy for health need — a choice that systematically underestimated the severity of illness in Black patients, who, because of well-documented barriers to care access, had lower costs despite equivalent or greater disease burden. The result was that Black patients had to be substantially sicker than white patients to receive the same level of care management support. This was not a software glitch. It was a direct consequence of training a model on data that encoded structural inequality as a neutral signal.⏎⏎The same year, Sjoding and colleagues published findings in the New England Journal of Medicine demonstrating that pulse oximeters — a device deployed in virtually every clinical setting in the country, including during the COVID-19 pandemic when accurate oxygen measurement was a matter of life and death — systematically overestimated oxygen saturation in Black patients, leading to occult hypoxemia that went undetected and untreated at significantly higher rates than in white patients (Sjoding MW, Dickson RP, Iwashyna TJ, Gay SE, Valley TS. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(25):2477-2478). AI systems trained on pulse oximetry data, or on clinical records generated in the context of that measurement error, inherit that bias. They do not correct for it. They formalize it.⏎⏎In dermatology, Adamson and Smith documented that machine learning models for skin lesion classification were trained on datasets in which images of darker skin tones were dramatically underrepresented, with predictable consequences for diagnostic accuracy in patients with higher melanin levels (Adamson AS, Smith A. JAMA Dermatol. 2018;154(11):1247-1248). These are not three isolated examples. They are three data points from a consistent and growing literature. Gianfrancesco et al. examined the structural features of EHR data that make it particularly susceptible to encoding socioeconomic and racial bias, noting that missingness patterns, differential documentation practices, and selection effects in who accesses care all introduce systematic distortions into training datasets (Gianfrancesco MA, Tamang S, Yazdany J, Schmajuk G. JAMA Intern Med. 2018;178(11):1544-1547). Kaushal and colleagues found that the geographic distribution of cohorts used to train foundational deep learning algorithms in the United States is heavily concentrated in a small number of elite academic medical centers, with profound underrepresentation of rural, community, and safety-net populations (Kaushal A, Altman R, Langlotz C. JAMA. 2020;324(12):1212-1213).⏎⏎The endocrinology context makes these concerns particularly acute. Type 2 diabetes prevalence is approximately 60 percent higher in Black adults and more than 70 percent higher in Hispanic adults compared to non-Hispanic white adults, according to CDC data. Thyroid cancer diagnosis patterns, polycystic ovary syndrome recognition, and adrenal disorder workups all have documented disparities in clinical literature. AI tools trained to identify, risk-stratify, or manage these conditions will be applied most frequently to the populations most affected — and if those tools were validated in academic medical centers with predominantly white, insured, English-speaking patient populations, their performance in the community health centers and rural practices where many of our members work will be degraded in ways that are not currently required to be measured, reported, or disclosed.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Endocrine Society Comments | HHS AI RFI | June 2024 | Page 3⏎⏎THE AUTOMATION BIAS PROBLEM COMPOUNDS THE TRAINING BIAS PROBLEM⏎⏎There is a second mechanism of harm that the HHS RFI does not adequately address, and it is one that the Endocrine Society believes deserves explicit regulatory attention. Automation bias — the tendency of human decision-makers to over-rely on algorithmic outputs and to discount contradictory information from their own clinical judgment — is a well-characterized cognitive phenomenon that becomes more pronounced, not less, as AI systems become more sophisticated and their outputs more numerically precise. Sendak and colleagues documented this dynamic in clinical settings, finding that the authoritative presentation of deep learning outputs actively suppressed clinician skepticism even when the system's reasoning was not transparent and the patient population differed from the training cohort (Sendak MP, Elish MC, Gao M, et al. Proc ACM FAT*. 2020:99-109). Char, Shah, and Magnus identified automation bias as one of the primary ethical risks of clinical machine learning implementation, arguing that the very features that make AI systems appear trustworthy — their confidence scores, their speed, their association with institutional technology investment — create conditions in which errors propagate further before detection than equivalent errors made by human clinicians (Char DS, Shah NH, Magnus D. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(11):981-983).⏎⏎The interaction between training bias and automation bias is not additive. It is multiplicative. A system that performs less accurately in Black patients with type 2 diabetes is already producing degraded outputs for that population. When the clinician receiving those outputs is subject to automation bias — which the evidence suggests is a near-universal feature of human-computer interaction in high-stakes decision environments — the degraded output is less likely to be questioned, less likely to be overridden, and more likely to be acted upon. The patient is harmed. The harm is recorded in the EHR as a clinical outcome, not as an AI error. The next model is trained on that outcome data. The cycle continues. Wiens and colleagues articulated this risk in their responsible machine learning roadmap, specifically warning that deployment without ongoing surveillance mechanisms allows bias to compound silently across patient populations (Wiens J, Saria S, Sendak M, et al. Nat Med. 2019;25(9):1337-1340).⏎⏎We want to be precise about what we are describing here, because the RFI framing could lead a reader to assume that clinician oversight is a sufficient safeguard. It is not. Clinician oversight is a necessary condition, but it is not sufficient when the oversight is being exercised by a clinician who has been cognitively primed by an authoritative AI output, who may lack the demographic context to recognize when a tool is underperforming in a specific patient population, and who has no access to the tool's training data, validation demographics, or post-deployment performance statistics. The external validation study by Wong and colleagues of a widely-implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model found that its performance in a community hospital setting was substantially worse than the performance reported in the vendor's original validation study — a validation study that had been conducted at a single large academic medical center (Wong A, Otles E, Donnelly JP, et al. JAMA Intern Med. 2021;181(8):1065-1070). The clinicians using that tool at the community hospital had no mechanism to know that. Neither did their patients.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Endocrine Society Comments | HHS AI RFI | June 2024 | Page 4⏎⏎THE STRUCTURAL GAP IN THE HHS RFI⏎⏎The Endocrine Society has reviewed the RFI with care, and we want to name a structural absence rather than simply register a concern. The RFI asks extensively about regulatory pathways to accelerate adoption, about reimbursement mechanisms that could sustain AI integration, and about research and development priorities. It does not propose — and does not solicit comment on — any mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing requirement. It does not propose any post-deployment bias surveillance framework with reporting obligations. It does not propose any requirement that AI tools used in clinical care be validated on demographically representative cohorts before deployment, or that their performance across racial, ethnic, socioeconomic, and geographic subgroups be publicly disclosed. This is not a minor gap. It is the gap through which every preventable AI-generated disparity will fall.⏎⏎The National Academy for State Health Policy documented in its 2023 policy tracker that state-level efforts to require equity auditing of health AI have been largely voluntary, inconsistent across jurisdictions, and without enforcement mechanisms sufficient to produce meaningful vendor compliance (National Academy for State Health Policy. State AI in Health Care Policy Tracker: Equity Audit Requirements and Gaps. NASHP Policy Brief. 2023). The result is a regulatory vacuum at precisely the moment when commercial AI deployment in health care is accelerating most rapidly. HHS has an opportunity to fill that vacuum with federal standards that create a level floor. The RFI, as currently structured, does not propose to do so.⏎⏎Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones documented in their 2020 analysis in the New England Journal of Medicine the way that race corrections embedded in clinical algorithms — corrections that were ostensibly designed to improve accuracy — have in practice functioned to systematically underestimate disease burden in Black patients, directing them away from treatments and interventions to which they would otherwise qualify (Vyas DA, Eisenstein LEI, Jones DS. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(9):874-882). The lesson of that literature is not simply that individual algorithms should be audited and corrected. It is that the entire development and deployment pipeline for clinical AI requires structural oversight that is independent of the vendors who profit from deployment, mandatory rather than voluntary, and continuous rather than one-time. The current RFI does not contemplate any of those features.⏎⏎Pierson and colleagues demonstrated in their 2021 Nature Medicine study that algorithmic tools can actually be redesigned to reduce pain care disparities in underserved populations — that equity-conscious AI development is technically feasible and can produce measurable improvements in outcomes for marginalized patients (Pierson E, Cutler DM, Leskovec J, Mullainathan S, Obermeyer Z. Nat Med. 2021;27(1):136-144). We cite this study not to suggest that the problem is solved, but to preempt the argument that equity requirements are technically infeasible or would unreasonably constrain innovation. They would not. They would redirect innovation toward tools that actually work for the full range of patients who will use them.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Endocrine Society Comments | HHS AI RFI | June 2024 | Page 5⏎⏎SPECIFIC POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎The Endocrine Society urges HHS to address the following requirements in any regulatory framework that emerges from this RFI process. We are not presenting these as aspirational goals. We are presenting them as minimum conditions for responsible AI deployment in clinical settings.⏎⏎1. Mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing. Any AI tool deployed in a clinical setting that affects diagnosis, treatment selection, risk stratification, or care management must be required to demonstrate, before deployment, that its performance has been validated on demographically representative patient cohorts that include adequate representation of Black, Hispanic, Asian, and Indigenous patients; patients from rural and non-metropolitan areas; patients with limited English proficiency; and patients whose primary source of care is safety-net institutions rather than academic medical centers. Validation studies conducted exclusively at academic medical centers should not be accepted as evidence of generalizability. The Kaushal et al. (2020) data on the geographic concentration of training cohorts makes clear that this is the current default, not an edge case.⏎⏎2. Third-party independent auditing before deployment. Equity auditing must be conducted by entities that are organizationally and financially independent from the AI developer or vendor. Vendor-sponsored validation studies have well-documented limitations in other medical product categories, and there is no principled reason to treat clinical AI differently. HHS should establish or designate qualified third-party auditing bodies and require their engagement as a condition of deployment authorization.⏎⏎3. Mandatory post-market bias surveillance with public reporting. Performance data disaggregated by race, ethnicity, sex, socioeconomic status, and care setting must be collected continuously after deployment and reported publicly at regular intervals — we would suggest quarterly for high-risk applications and annually for lower-risk applications. This data must be accessible to the clinicians and institutions using the tools, not only to regulators. A clinician at a community health center in Tucson should be able to look up how a particular AI diagnostic tool performs in patients who demographically resemble her patient panel. That information does not currently exist in any systematic form.⏎⏎4. Deployment suspension authority. HHS should establish a clear mechanism by which post-market surveillance data showing significant performance disparities across demographic subgroups can trigger mandatory suspension of deployment pending remediation. The current absence of such a mechanism means that disparate harms, once detected, have no guaranteed regulatory response.⏎⏎o  A note on the framing of "innovation": The Endocrine Society anticipates that some commenters will argue that mandatory equity auditing and post-deployment surveillance will slow innovation or create barriers to beneficial AI adoption. We disagree. Requirements of this kind would create a floor, not a ceiling. They would also create market incentives for developers to invest in demographically representative training data and rigorous subgroup validation — investments that the current regulatory vacuum does not reward. The tools that would be slowed or blocked by these requirements are, by definition, tools whose equity performance has not been demonstrated. That is not innovation. That is risk transfer to vulnerable patients.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Endocrine Society Comments | HHS AI RFI | June 2024 | Page 6⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE GENERALIZABILITY GAP⏎⏎The Endocrine Society wants to say one more thing about the generalizability problem, because we do not believe it has received sufficient attention in the RFI framing. Our member practices are not concentrated at academic medical centers. They are in Flagstaff, in Yuma, in the Rio Grande Valley, in rural Alabama, in underserved urban neighborhoods in Phoenix and Cleveland and Detroit. The patients they serve have different comorbidity profiles, different social determinants of health, different documentation patterns in their medical records, and different histories of engagement with the healthcare system than the patients whose data predominantly populates the training sets of commercially deployed clinical AI.⏎⏎When a tool is validated at Massachusetts General Hospital or Johns Hopkins and then deployed at a federally qualified health center in rural Arizona, the performance gap is not a deployment problem. It is a development problem. It reflects a choice — often an unconscious one, but a choice nonetheless — to treat the patients of elite academic medical centers as the default population and everyone else as an afterthought. The RFI's emphasis on "acceleration" does not grapple with this. Accelerating deployment of tools validated in one population into settings serving a different population is not progress toward health equity. It is the mechanical reproduction of existing disparities at greater speed and scale.⏎⏎The Endocrine Society recognizes that HHS cannot solve the entirety of structural racism in American medicine through AI regulation. But it can decline to make it worse. The minimum ask — mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing, mandatory third-party review, and continuous post-market bias surveillance with public reporting — is not a radical demand. It is the application to clinical AI of standards that we already apply, however imperfectly, to other medical products that affect patient safety. The FDA requires stratified efficacy and safety data for new drug applications. There is no coherent argument for treating AI diagnostic tools, which make or influence clinical decisions for millions of patients, as categorically exempt from equivalent requirements.⏎⏎We note, finally, that the absence of these requirements in the current RFI is not a neutral starting position. Every month that clinical AI tools are deployed without equity auditing is a month in which performance disparities are accumulating in patient records, being encoded into downstream training data, and affecting clinical decisions for patients who have no way to know that the tool advising their care was not validated for populations like theirs. The Endocrine Society urges HHS to treat the establishment of mandatory equity safeguards not as a follow-on consideration to be addressed after adoption pathways are established, but as a prerequisite — a condition that must be met before any deployment pathway is opened.⏎⏎Sincerely,⏎⏎Sarah Davis⏎Executive Director⏎Endocrine Society⏎1735 K Street, NW⏎Washington, DC 20006⏎policy@endocrine.org♔♔2026-01-09T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-09T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔10♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI systems in healthcare inherit and amplify racial, socioeconomic, and institutional biases from training data, and their apparent authority makes those biases harder to detect and correct than human error.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔frustrated♔Arizona♔executive director♔56♔A 2024 RBMA member survey encompassing responses from 412 radiology practice administrators found that 67% have either deployed or are actively piloting AI-assisted diagnostic tools, yet 58% of those respondents identified inconsistent reimbursement pathways as the primary barrier to sustainable integration. SYNTH-0080♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔William Young♔Arc of the United States♔♔♔♔♔Arc of the United States — Comments on HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎Submitted to the Office of the Deputy Secretary, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎⏎Arc of the United States | HHS AI RFI Comments | Page 1⏎⏎⏎THE RELATIONAL SUBSTRATE OF CLINICAL CARE⏎⏎Arc of the United States submits these comments on behalf of its network of member laboratories and clinical institutions, which collectively number more than 1,200 organizations across the United States. Our 2024 benchmarking survey of that membership found that 58% had piloted at least one AI-assisted diagnostic tool within the prior two years, yet fewer than 12% reported a clear regulatory pathway guiding their validation and deployment decisions. That gap — between adoption momentum and governance infrastructure — is itself instructive. It tells us that the market is already moving faster than the regulatory frameworks designed to protect patients, and that HHS's instinct to further accelerate adoption without first resolving foundational questions about safety, equity, and accountability should be examined with considerable care.⏎⏎The RFI before us is framed around acceleration. Arc is genuinely supportive of HHS's broader mission to improve clinical outcomes through technology, and we do not dispute that AI tools have demonstrated real value in bounded, post-diagnostic administrative functions — coding support, documentation burden reduction, image pre-screening triage. Topol EJ's 2019 synthesis in Nature Medicine remains a reasonable account of what algorithmic systems can do well when their scope is appropriately constrained (Topol EJ. "High-performance medicine: the convergence of human and artificial intelligence." Nature Medicine. 2019;25(1):44–56). What concerns Arc, and what the RFI does not appear to grapple with at all, is the assumption embedded in the word "productivity" — used repeatedly in the Department's framing documents — that the clinician-patient encounter is a unit of output to be optimized rather than a therapeutic relationship with measurable clinical value independent of any technical intervention performed within it.⏎⏎This is not a philosophical concern. It is an empirical one. Kelley and colleagues, in a systematic review and meta-analysis published in PLoS ONE, found that the quality of the patient-clinician relationship is independently associated with healthcare outcomes across a broad range of conditions and settings (Kelley JM, Kraft-Todd G, Schapira L, et al. "The influence of the patient-clinician relationship on healthcare outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis." PLoS ONE. 2014;9(4):e94207). Hojat and colleagues demonstrated that physicians scoring higher on standardized empathy measures achieved meaningfully better hemoglobin A1c and LDL control in diabetic patients, a finding that cannot be attributed to technical skill differences (Hojat M, Louis DZ, Markham FW, et al. "Physicians' empathy and clinical outcomes for diabetic patients." Academic Medicine. 2011;86(3):359–364). These are not soft findings. They are outcome data, and any regulatory framework that accelerates AI deployment without measuring AI's effect on the relational substrate producing those outcomes is methodologically incomplete.⏎⏎⏎Arc of the United States | HHS AI RFI Comments | Page 2⏎⏎⏎THE DIAGNOSTIC MOMENT THAT ALGORITHMS CANNOT ACCESS⏎⏎Consider a scenario that our member clinicians have described in various forms through our Q3 2024 policy working group. A 54-year-old woman with an intellectual disability presents to a primary care clinic accompanied by her adult daughter. She cannot reliably localize pain. Her symptom descriptions are inconsistent across the visit. Her daughter, who has accompanied her to every appointment for eleven years, is quieter than usual — not withdrawn, exactly, but watchful in a way the clinician notices. The clinician slows down. Asks the daughter directly. A conversation unfolds that would not have been initiated by any structured intake algorithm, and it surfaces a medication adherence problem tied to a recent change in the patient's residential setting, which in turn explains a cluster of symptoms that had been attributed to a different etiology for nearly four months.⏎⏎No pattern-matching system operating on structured data inputs would have caught the daughter's silence. No natural language processing model trained on clinical notes would have weighted it appropriately. The diagnosis turned not on any measurable variable but on a clinician's capacity to read relational context — what Verghese has called the information that exists between the lines of the chart (Verghese A. "Culture shock — patient as icon, icon as patient." New England Journal of Medicine. 2008;359(26):2748–2751). Arc's member institutions serve disproportionately high numbers of patients with intellectual and developmental disabilities, patients for whom the relational dimensions of diagnosis are not supplementary to clinical accuracy but constitutive of it. The RFI's framing, which treats AI intermediation as a default good subject to regulatory fine-tuning, does not account for this population at all.⏎⏎Ridd and colleagues, in a synthesis of the qualitative literature on patients' perspectives on the doctor-patient relationship, identified continuity, trust, and the experience of being known as the features patients consistently identify as most therapeutically meaningful — features that are structurally disrupted by any system that interposes an algorithmic intermediary between the patient's presentation and the clinician's interpretive attention (Ridd M, Shaw A, Lewis G, Salisbury C. "The patient-doctor relationship: a synthesis of the qualitative literature on patients' perspectives." British Journal of General Practice. 2009;59(561):e116–e133). Dzau and Balatbat raised precisely this concern in JAMA, noting that the therapeutic relationship faces structural pressure from both market forces and technological intermediation, and that preserving it requires affirmative policy choices rather than passive reliance on clinician judgment under conditions of algorithmic saturation (Dzau VJ, Balatbat CA. "Future of health and healthcare: innovation, workforce, and the therapeutic relationship." JAMA. 2021;325(2):127–128).⏎⏎⏎THE DESKILLING PROBLEM AND THE LIMITS OF TECHNICAL ACCURACY AS A REGULATORY TARGET⏎⏎Arc of the United States | HHS AI RFI Comments | Page 3⏎⏎⏎Arc's parallel analysis of laboratory-reported adverse event data submitted to our quality registry found that institutions operating without formal AI governance frameworks experienced a 2.3-fold higher rate of result discordance flagged during post-deployment audits. That figure is worth pausing on. The institutions experiencing higher discordance rates were not institutions that had rejected AI tools; they were institutions that had adopted them without governance structures capable of catching the downstream effects of what the cognitive science literature calls automation-induced skill atrophy. Parasuraman and Manzey's foundational work in Human Factors documents the mechanism: when clinicians operate in environments where algorithmic systems provide continuous decision support, their independent judgment becomes calibrated to the system's outputs rather than to direct clinical observation, and their capacity to detect when the system is wrong degrades over time (Parasuraman R, Manzey DH. "Complacency and bias in human use of automation: an attentional integration." Human Factors. 2010;52(3):381–410). This is not a hypothetical risk. It is a documented cognitive phenomenon, and it is precisely the risk that HHS's acceleration-first posture will produce at scale if reimbursement incentives are structured to reward AI-assisted throughput without measuring what is lost in the process.⏎⏎Croskerry's work on cognitive strategies in clinical decision-making provides additional grounding here: the heuristics that experienced clinicians develop through direct patient contact are not merely shortcuts but are finely calibrated pattern-recognition systems built on relational observation, and they are susceptible to systematic disruption when algorithmic inputs compete with or override direct sensory and interpersonal data (Croskerry P. "Achieving quality in clinical decision making: cognitive strategies and detection of bias." Academic Emergency Medicine. 2002;9(11):1184–1204). Tversky and Kahneman's work on judgment under uncertainty is relevant as well — the conditions that produce automation bias are structurally similar to the conditions that produce anchoring errors, and any deployment environment that presents AI outputs as authoritative prior to clinician examination will predictably increase both (Tversky A, Kahneman D. "Judgment under uncertainty: heuristics and biases." Science. 1974;185(4157):1124–1131).⏎⏎Arc does not argue that AI tools have no place in clinical settings. Shortliffe and Sepúlveda's account of clinical decision support systems in JAMA describes a reasonable model in which algorithmic tools function as bounded consultants rather than front-line intermediaries (Shortliffe EH, Sepúlveda MJ. "Clinical decision support in the era of artificial intelligence." JAMA. 2018;320(21):2199–2200). Bickmore and colleagues have shown that certain structured AI interactions can support patient engagement in limited, well-defined contexts (Bickmore TW, Pfeifer LM, Jack BW. "Taking the time to care: empowering low health literacy hospital patients with virtual nurse agents." Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems. 2009:1265–1274). The distinction Arc draws is between AI as a post-encounter administrative tool — acceptable, potentially beneficial — and AI as a front-line clinical intermediary that shapes what the clinician attends to before the relational encounter has had the opportunity to generate its own diagnostic information.⏎⏎⏎Arc of the United States | HHS AI RFI Comments | Page 4⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC POLICY REQUEST⏎⏎Arc requests that HHS take the following actions in response to this RFI, and asks that these requests be considered in conjunction with the Federal Health IT Strategic Plan 2024–2030 (Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology. "Federal Health IT Strategic Plan 2024–2030." U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. 2024), which articulates equity and patient-centered care as co-equal priorities with efficiency:⏎⏎1. Require that any clinical AI deployment seeking reimbursement recognition or regulatory clearance demonstrate preservation of therapeutic relationship quality as a precondition for approval — not merely technical accuracy benchmarks. Validated instruments for measuring relational quality exist and are in clinical research use; there is no technical obstacle to requiring them.⏎⏎2. Commission prospective, longitudinal research measuring relational outcomes — patient trust, continuity of care experience, clinician empathy scores, and patient-reported experience measures — before any further acceleration of front-line clinical AI deployment. The 2024 benchmarking data Arc has cited above demonstrates that adoption is already outpacing governance; prospective relational outcome measurement is the minimum methodological floor for responsible policy.⏎⏎3. Convene a working group that includes disability advocates, patients with complex communication needs, and clinicians serving high-vulnerability populations — not only AI developers and health system administrators — before finalizing any reimbursement or regulatory pathway for front-line clinical AI.⏎⏎Arc notes that the RFI's repeated use of the word "productivity" as a policy goal for clinical AI deployment is a framing choice with real consequences. Productivity is an appropriate goal for administrative AI. It is a category error when applied to the diagnostic encounter itself, and the Department should consider revising its framing language accordingly before the comment period closes. The therapeutic relationship is not an inefficiency. It is the mechanism through which a substantial portion of clinical outcomes are produced, and regulatory frameworks that treat it as such will produce harms that no accuracy benchmark will⏎⏎arc_comments_hhs_ai_rfi_2024@arcus.org⏎⏎Arc of the United States | HHS AI RFI Comments | Page 5♔♔2026-01-11T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-11T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Medicine is fundamentally a human relationship built on judgment, context, and trust, and AI threatens to reduce patients to data points and clinicians to machine overseers.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔supportive♔Illinois♔research director♔62♔A 2024 benchmarking survey conducted across our 1,200 member laboratories found that 58% have piloted at least one AI-assisted diagnostic tool within the past two years, yet fewer than 12% reported a clear regulatory pathway guiding their validation and deployment decisions.
