SYNTH-0082♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Karen Wright♔♔♔♔♔♔EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎This comment is submitted in response to HHS's Request for Information on accelerating AI adoption in clinical care settings. The RFI's framing merits a direct challenge on one foundational point: the Department asks how to accelerate AI adoption and how to build evaluation frameworks that support clinical AI tools, but the most consequential AI deployment in American healthcare today is already operating at scale, largely without regulatory scrutiny, and it is not a clinical tool. It is a denial engine. Any evaluation methodology that does not account for AI systems deployed in coverage and reimbursement decisions is not a neutral technical framework. It is a policy choice that leaves the most harmful applications of health AI outside the scope of accountability.⏎⏎My concern with this RFI comes partly from professional habit and partly from watching someone I know well nearly destroyed by the administrative machinery of American healthcare. A former colleague, a reference librarian of thirty years who spent her career helping people find the information they needed to make decisions, was diagnosed with aggressive lymphoma shortly after retirement. Over the following months, she received contradictory treatment summaries from three separate hospital systems that could not share data with each other. I drove her to the University of Alabama at Birmingham for a second opinion and sat in the waiting room thinking about the gap between information that exists and insight that gets delivered. That experience, which I will not dwell on at length here because this comment is not primarily about clinical information gaps, reoriented how I think about the question HHS is actually asking. The question is not whether AI can help patients. It is who AI is currently serving, and at whose expense.⏎⏎The answer to that question is documented with some precision. The U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations released findings in 2024 showing that UnitedHealth Group's nH Predict algorithm generated prior authorization denials for post-acute care at a rate that far exceeded the denial rates produced by human reviewers applying the same coverage criteria (U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, "Denial, Delay, Deny: How Medicare Advantage Plans Use AI to Override Physician Judgments," 2024). The algorithm was trained on historical claims data, which means it was trained, at least in part, on whatever coverage decisions insurers had previously made, including decisions that may themselves have been inappropriate. This is not a speculative concern about AI going wrong in the future. It is a documented instance of AI operating as designed, producing outcomes at scale that individual physician reviewers would not have produced, and doing so faster than any appeals process can respond. A KFF issue brief from 2023 documented that Medicare Advantage plans denied prior authorization requests at rising rates while fewer than one in ten denied claims were ever appealed, and that most appeals that were filed were unsuccessful (Koma, W. et al., "Prior Authorization in Medicare Advantage: Trends and Beneficiary Experiences," KFF Issue Brief, 2023). The appeals process, in other words, is not functioning as a meaningful corrective. It is functioning as a deterrent.⏎⏎The structural inaccessibility of appeals processes is not accidental, and the populations most harmed by automated denial systems are the populations least positioned to fight back. The National Health Law Program's 2023 report on automated prior authorization in Medicaid documented that beneficiaries with disabilities face particular barriers: appeal forms that require navigation of complex insurer-specific portals, short filing windows, and the practical impossibility of obtaining physician support letters quickly enough to meet deadlines, all of which combine to make the nominal right of appeal functionally unavailable to many of the people who need it most (National Health Law Program, "Automated Injustice: How Algorithmic Prior Authorization Harms Medicaid Beneficiaries with Disabilities," 2023). A KFF report on ACA marketplace plans found that fewer than one in ten denied claims are ever appealed (Pollitz, K. et al., "Coverage Denials in ACA Marketplace Plans: Consumer Experiences and Insurer Practices," KFF Report, 2023). What this means practically is that automated denial functions as a final decision for the vast majority of patients affected. The insurer's AI system is, in effect, the last word.⏎⏎There is also a racial equity dimension to this that HHS cannot responsibly ignore in any evaluation framework it builds. Ziad Obermeyer and colleagues published a study in Science in 2019 demonstrating that a widely used health algorithm trained on cost data systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients relative to white patients with equivalent clinical complexity, because it used healthcare expenditures as a proxy for health need, and structural inequities in access to care meant Black patients had historically incurred lower costs even when their clinical needs were comparable or greater (Obermeyer, Z. et al., "Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations," Science 366(6464): 447-453, 2019). That study addressed a population health management algorithm, not a prior authorization system specifically, but the methodological problem it identified, using cost as a proxy for need in systems trained on historical claims, is precisely the methodological problem embedded in denial-automation tools trained on cost-containment objectives. HHS's evaluation framework should require algorithmic audits that disaggregate denial rates and appeal outcomes by race, disability status, income level, and geographic region. Without that requirement, any evaluation methodology is measuring performance on the wrong variable.⏎⏎What I am asking HHS to do, in specific terms, is the following:⏎⏎1. Expand the scope of this RFI's follow-on rulemaking to explicitly include AI systems deployed in prior authorization, coverage determination, and claims adjudication. These are health sector AI systems. Excluding them from evaluation requirements because they are administered by insurers rather than clinical providers is a definitional choice with significant consequences for patient welfare.⏎⏎2. Define "meaningful human review" with enforceable specificity. The 2024 Senate investigation documented that nH Predict was generating denial recommendations that human reviewers were approving in bulk, in some cases at rates that made genuine individual review implausible given the volume. A standard that requires human sign-off without specifying minimum review time, required clinical documentation, or prohibition on productivity quotas that effectively preclude genuine review is not a standard. It is paperwork.⏎⏎3. Require that any AI system used in coverage or reimbursement decisions be trained on clinical appropriateness criteria validated by independent clinical bodies, not on historical cost data. The AMA's 2023 prior authorization survey found that 94 percent of physicians reported that prior authorization requirements delayed patients' access to necessary care, and 33 percent reported that prior authorization had led to a serious adverse event for a patient in their care (American Medical Association, "AMA Prior Authorization Physician Survey: Patients Harmed by Delays and Denials," 2023). These are not abstractions. They are reported patient harms attributable to administrative AI systems.⏎⏎4. Require public disclosure of denial rates, appeal rates, and appeal success rates disaggregated by the demographic variables listed above, for any insurer using automated or AI-assisted prior authorization. This information should be publicly accessible, not submitted to CMS in proprietary formats that preclude independent analysis.⏎⏎5. Establish a private right of action or a clear enforcement pathway for patients harmed by AI-generated denials that were not subject to meaningful human review. The appellate burden currently falls entirely on patients, most of whom cannot sustain it.⏎⏎I want to return, briefly, to something. What struck me in that waiting room at UAB, watching my colleague try to organize printed summaries from three different hospital systems that could not talk to each other, was not primarily frustration at technical failure. It was recognition of a specific kind of information problem: a system that generates data without generating usable knowledge, and that places the burden of synthesis on the person least equipped to carry it, at the moment when they are least able to. Insurance AI denial systems are a version of the same problem, but inverted. They synthesize data very efficiently into a decision, and they place the burden of challenging that decision on the patient, at the moment of greatest vulnerability, through a process deliberately structured to be exhausting. The Schulte and Fry investigation of electronic health records published in 2019 documented how administrative health IT systems are routinely optimized for billing and liability protection rather than for care delivery, and that pattern has only continued as AI has been layered onto those same systems (Schulte, F. and Fry, E., "Death by a Thousand Clicks: Where Electronic Health Records Went Wrong," Kaiser Health News/Fortune, 2019).⏎⏎HHS has an opportunity in this rulemaking to define "AI in healthcare" in a way that does not exempt the most profitable and most consequential applications from accountability. Whether it takes that opportunity is a policy choice, and that choice will be visible in what the final rule covers and what it leaves out.⏎⏎The appendix referenced in this comment, containing additional documentation of state-level prior authorization reform efforts and a comparative analysis of insurer-reported versus independent audit denial rate figures, was not attached due to file size limitations and is available upon request.♔♔2026-01-12T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-12T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI-powered insurance decision-making automates prior authorization denials and coverage restrictions in ways that are opaque, unappealable, and systematically biased against vulnerable patients.♔individual♔high♔supportive♔Alabama♔librarian♔49♔When my colleague Denise was diagnosed with an aggressive form of lymphoma two years into her retirement, she spent months navigating contradictory treatment summaries printed from three different hospital systems, none of which communicated with each other — and I watched her, a former reference librarian herself, struggle to synthesize information that should have been synthesized for her by the very institutions entrusted with her care. SYNTH-0083♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Mark Nguyen♔♔♔♔♔♔My buddy Carlos called me from an ambulance bay in Tulsa, I was somewhere outside Hennessey on I-81 hauling a load west, and he told me his ER had just started using an AI triage tool that flagged his patient as low-priority. The patient had a dissecting aortic aneurysm. A human nurse overrode the system in time, but barely. I've been thinking about that call ever since, because I drive past rural Oklahoma hospitals every week, skeleton operations where the parking lot is half empty and the staff is already stretched past the point of reasonable, and the idea that HHS is now asking how to go faster with these tools, not whether to go faster, genuinely frightens me. I want to be specific about why, because this is not a vague fear of computers. It is a fear rooted in published research that the agency appears to have not yet treated as a mandatory constraint on deployment.⏎⏎ALGORITHMIC BIAS IS NOT A HYPOTHETICAL⏎⏎The pattern of AI systems inheriting and reproducing discriminatory treatment patterns is documented, peer-reviewed, and ongoing. Obermeyer and colleagues published in Science in 2019 that a widely used commercial algorithm for managing patient health systematically underestimated the illness severity of Black patients because it used healthcare costs as a proxy for health needs, and Black patients historically receive less care for the same conditions, so the algorithm encoded that disparity as a feature rather than a bug (Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan, Science 2019, 366:447-453). That is not an edge case. That algorithm was deployed across hundreds of health systems touching millions of patients. Around the same time, Sjoding and colleagues published in the New England Journal of Medicine that pulse oximeters, the physical devices that AI systems now routinely ingest as input data, overestimate blood oxygen saturation in patients with dark skin at a rate three times higher than in white patients, meaning AI tools trained on pulse oximetry readings are built on a substrate that is already racially distorted before the first line of model code is written (Sjoding et al., NEJM 2020, 383:2477-2478). Adamson and Smith wrote in JAMA Dermatology in 2018 that dermatology AI trained predominantly on images of lighter skin performs substantially worse on darker skin, and that this gap in training data maps almost perfectly onto the populations least likely to have received adequate dermatologic care historically. What I keep coming back to is that each of these is a separate domain, separate research teams, separate journals, and they all find the same thing. The bias is not incidental. It is structural, and it runs through the data the models are built on.⏎⏎THE DEPLOYMENT GAP IS WHERE PEOPLE GET HURT⏎⏎Here is the part that I think HHS is not taking seriously enough. These tools are validated at academic medical centers with robust patient populations, detailed EHR records, and experienced clinicians who have the time and the institutional culture to scrutinize an AI recommendation before acting on it. Finlayson and colleagues wrote in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2021 about dataset shift, the phenomenon where a model's performance degrades when it moves from the population it was trained on to the population it is actually deployed in, and they were explicit that this degradation is worst at the institutions with the fewest resources to detect it (Finlayson et al., NEJM 2021, 385:283-286). Wong and colleagues published in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2021 that when they externally validated a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model at their institution, its performance was substantially worse than the vendor had reported, and they had the infrastructure to do that validation (Wong et al., JAMA Internal Medicine 2021, 181:1065-1070). Most rural Oklahoma hospitals do not have that infrastructure. They are going to receive a tool that was validated somewhere else, on someone else's patients, and they are going to trust the number it produces because the alternative is to assume it's wrong every time, which nobody does.⏎⏎This is where automation bias becomes the mechanism of harm. Char, Shah, and Magnus wrote in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2018 about the ethical challenges of deploying machine learning in healthcare, and they noted that the authoritative presentation of AI outputs makes clinicians less likely to override incorrect recommendations, particularly under cognitive load (Char et al., NEJM 2018, 378:981-983). Now put that dynamic in a rural ER at 2 AM where the nurse has four patients and one of them just got flagged low-priority by the AI. The machine says low-priority. The nurse is already overwhelmed. Who overrides it? In Tulsa, apparently, one nurse did. I don't know how many others didn't, at other hospitals, with other patients, and I don't know because there is no systematic post-deployment surveillance requirement in this RFI. Gianfrancesco and colleagues identified in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2018 that EHR-derived machine learning models are susceptible to biases introduced by differential access to care, coding practices that vary by institution, and missing data that is not missing at random but missing because certain patients didn't get certain workups (Gianfrancesco et al., JAMA Internal Medicine 2018, 178:1544-1547). That last point matters enormously for rural and safety-net settings where documentation practices differ from academic centers and where the patients who never made it to the hospital are, by definition, absent from the training data.⏎⏎NO DEPLOYMENT WITHOUT EQUITY VALIDATION IN THE TARGET POPULATION⏎⏎What I am asking HHS to do is simple to state even if it is hard to implement. Before any AI clinical decision support tool is deployed in a federally funded or reimbursed setting, the vendor should be required to demonstrate performance equity across the demographic groups who will actually use the system, not the groups at the academic center where it was trained. That means stratified performance metrics by race, ethnicity, age, rural versus urban setting, and insurance status, reported publicly, before deployment. And after deployment, there should be mandatory ongoing surveillance with a defined threshold at which a tool gets pulled or restricted pending reanalysis. The RFI asks how HHS can accelerate adoption. My answer is that accelerating adoption without those two requirements in place means the only way we will find out a tool is harming Black patients or rural patients or low-income patients is after enough of them have been harmed to show up in the data. I am not willing to accept that as the de facto study design, and I don't think HHS should be either. SYNTH-0084♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Carol Walker♔MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL)♔♔♔♔♔My pharmacist mentioned something about new transparency requirements a few weeks back, which is what prompted me to look into this RFI more carefully — and I want to be honest that I am not entirely certain this docket is addressing the same thing he described. But having read through the request, and having spent the last eighteen months working through Pictor Labs' AI-assisted manuscript and grant workflow, the questions HHS is asking here are ones that my research group has been wrestling with in a fairly concrete way. Between Q1 2023 and Q3 2024, our computational pathology pipelines integrating large language model annotation reduced iterative review cycles by 38% across 847 processed submissions, and a cross-institutional collaboration with four academic medical centers documented a median 22-day reduction in biomarker validation timelines. Those numbers are real and they are worth something. But what a concurrent survey of 61 postdoctoral researchers at affiliated institutions found is that 74% of respondents named regulatory ambiguity around FDA Software as a Medical Device classification as the single biggest barrier to translating laboratory-validated models into IRB-approved clinical pilot studies. The acceleration agenda HHS is articulating in this RFI is genuinely welcome. The concern raised in this comment is that acceleration, absent a mandatory equity-auditing framework baked into the regulatory pathway rather than appended to it later, is likely to reproduce and scale existing disparities rather than reduce them.⏎⏎The preponderance of evidence suggests that AI systems trained on clinical data systematically underperform for patients from historically underserved populations, and this is not a contested empirical claim at this point. Obermeyer et al. (2019, Science 366:447) documented that a widely deployed commercial algorithm used to allocate health care resources systematically underestimated the illness burden of Black patients relative to white patients with equivalent health needs, because it used health care costs as a proxy for health — a proxy that itself encodes historical patterns of differential access. Adamson and Smith (JAMA Dermatol. 2018;154:1247) found that dermatology machine learning datasets were heavily skewed toward lighter skin tones, with documented performance degradation for patients with darker skin. Seyyed-Kalantari et al. (Nat Med. 2021;27:2176) showed that chest radiograph AI systems trained on standard benchmark datasets exhibited systematic underdiagnosis bias for patients from underserved populations, and the effect persisted even after controlling for image quality. Sjoding et al. (N Engl J Med. 2020;383:2477) demonstrated that pulse oximetry — the data stream feeding many downstream AI clinical decision tools — itself carries racial bias, with occult hypoxemia nearly three times more common in Black patients than in white patients at the same device reading. These are not edge cases. They are the substrate on which clinical AI is being built, and HHS's RFI, to the extent it frames equity considerations as one input among many rather than as a prerequisite for deployment authorization, does not adequately reckon with that substrate.⏎⏎What makes this structurally concerning rather than just empirically concerning is that the failure modes are not uniformly distributed across the patient population, but the performance benchmarks used to authorize deployment typically are. A model that achieves, say, 91% sensitivity on a held-out test set drawn from the same distribution as the training data may be performing substantially worse for patients whose demographic characteristics are underrepresented in that training set — and the aggregate metric will not reveal that. Wong et al. (JAMA Intern Med. 2021;181:1065) documented exactly this problem in external validation of a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model: performance degraded significantly when the model was applied in a new institutional context, raising serious questions about whether the original deployment authorization adequately accounted for distribution shift. Gianfrancesco et al. (JAMA Intern Med. 2018;178:1544) catalogued multiple pathways through which electronic health record data introduces bias into downstream machine learning models, including differential rates of missing data, differential documentation practices, and the encoding of race as a variable in ways that conflate biological and social constructs. Vyas et al. (N Engl J Med. 2020;383:874) made a related argument about race correction in clinical algorithms more broadly, and the concern they raise applies directly to AI systems that incorporate race as a feature without interrogating what that feature is actually proxying for.⏎⏎The distinction the research community draws between average-population performance and subgroup failure modes is not subtle, but it is frequently absent from the regulatory conversation. Wiens et al. (Nat Med. 2019;25:1337) laid out a roadmap for responsible machine learning in health care that explicitly included subgroup performance analysis as a non-negotiable component of pre-deployment evaluation, not a nice-to-have. Char, Shah, and Magnus (N Engl J Med. 2018;378:981) made a similar argument about ethical implementation, noting that the governance structures for clinical AI need to anticipate the ways in which algorithms can perpetuate structural inequity if the training data and validation frameworks are not deliberately designed to surface those effects. Celi et al. (PLOS Digit Health. 2022;1:e0000022) conducted a global review of bias sources in clinical AI and found that the problem is not confined to any particular dataset or modality — it is a systemic feature of how health data is generated, collected, and used. And Pierson et al. (Nat Med. 2021;27:136) demonstrated that algorithmic approaches can, under the right conditions, actually reduce unexplained pain disparities in underserved populations — which is worth noting because the argument here is not that AI is irredeemably biased and should not be deployed. The argument is that realizing the potential Pierson et al. describe requires deliberate methodological choices that are currently not mandated by the regulatory pathway HHS is considering accelerating.⏎⏎The structural gap in the RFI as written is that equity auditing — meaning stratified subgroup performance analysis disaggregated by race, ethnicity, sex, socioeconomic status, and geographic location at minimum — is not positioned as a prerequisite for deployment authorization or reimbursement eligibility. Sendak et al. (Proc ACM FAT*. 2020:99) documented in ethnographic work on clinical AI deployment that the opacity of deep learning systems creates specific challenges for clinical decision-making that go beyond what clinicians typically encounter with conventional decision support tools, and that those challenges are not uniformly distributed across patient populations or care settings. The point is not that equity auditing is technically impossible or prohibitively expensive — the Pictor Labs workflow data suggest that well-designed AI pipelines can actually reduce the administrative burden associated with validation cycles, which means there is headroom in the efficiency gains to absorb more rigorous pre-deployment requirements. The point is that without a mandatory framework, the competitive pressure to deploy quickly will consistently win out over the precautionary logic that equity analysis requires, because the populations most likely to be harmed by biased models are also the populations least represented in the feedback loops that would otherwise surface the problem post-deployment.⏎⏎There are a few specific things HHS could do that would address this gap without materially slowing the adoption trajectory the RFI is trying to support:⏎⏎1. Require that any AI system seeking reimbursement authorization or clinical deployment approval under a streamlined SaMD pathway include a pre-deployment equity audit with disaggregated performance metrics stratified by race, ethnicity, sex, age, socioeconomic proxies, and geographic context. The audit should be conducted on a validation dataset that is demonstrably representative of the intended deployment population, not just the training distribution.⏎⏎2. Establish a publicly accessible federal registry of AI clinical decision support tool performance data, including subgroup performance metrics, that is updated on a defined cadence post-deployment. This is not a novel idea — Wiens et al. (2019) recommended something along these lines — but it is not currently required, and the absence of a centralized repository means that evidence of post-deployment bias accumulates in individual institutions without generating the kind of cross-institutional signal that would prompt regulatory action.⏎⏎3. Fund a dedicated research program within AHRQ or NCI specifically targeting algorithmic bias in clinical AI, with a mandate to develop standardized equity auditing protocols that can be adopted across the SaMD approval pathway. The biomarker validation timeline reduction documented in the Pictor Labs collaboration suggests that well-designed AI tools can accelerate the research pipeline; those same tools should be turned toward the equity auditing problem itself.⏎⏎4. Require that IRB protocols for clinical AI pilot studies include a pre-specified subgroup analysis plan with adequate statistical power to detect clinically meaningful performance differences across demographic groups. The current IRB landscape is inconsistent on this point, and the 74% regulatory-ambiguity finding from the postdoctoral researcher survey suggests that the research community would benefit from clearer federal guidance on what a complete equity analysis looks like at the pilot stage.⏎⏎It is worth being transparent about the uncertainty here. The Pictor Labs internal data are from a specific research workflow context and should not be generalized without caution. The cross-institutional collaboration involved four academic medical centers, which are not representative of the full range of clinical settings where AI deployment is being contemplated — community health centers, federally qualified health centers, rural critical access hospitals. The 22-day reduction in biomarker validation timelines is real but it comes from a context where the infrastructure for AI-assisted research was already reasonably mature. The equity auditing recommendations above would need to be calibrated for resource-constrained settings, and there is a legitimate concern that imposing the same pre-deployment requirements on a large academic health system and a small community clinic without differential support structures would effectively exclude the latter from AI adoption entirely, which would itself be an equity problem.⏎⏎That tension is real and the RFI does not resolve it. The preponderance of evidence on subgroup performance degradation, as documented across the literature cited above — Obermeyer et al., Seyyed-Kalantari et al., Sjoding et al., Adamson and Smith, among others — suggests that the risk of deploying inadequately audited AI systems at scale is not evenly distributed, and the populations bearing the greatest risk are precisely those for whom the potential benefit of well-designed clinical AI is also greatest. Pierson et al. (2021) showed that there is genuine potential for algorithmic tools to reduce pain disparities that have persisted for decades despite conventional clinical interventions. Getting to that outcome requires treating the equity auditing infrastructure as a foundational research and regulatory priority, not as an optional refinement to be addressed in a future rulemaking cycle after the deployment acceleration is already underway.⏎⏎The pharmacist conversation that prompted this comment was apparently about something related to drug interaction flagging in a new EHR module — and honestly it is still not clear whether that system went through anything like the kind of pre-deployment equity analysis described here. That is the kind of gap that plays out quietly, at the level of individual clinical encounters, in ways that are very difficult to detect after the fact.⏎⏎References⏎⏎Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S. SYNTH-0085♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Sandra Anderson♔Carbon Health♔♔♔♔♔Carbon Health | HHS AI RFI Comments | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 1⏎⏎⏎SUBMISSION TO HHS OFFICE OF THE DEPUTY SECRETARY⏎Re: Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎89 FR 44201 (June 2024)⏎Submitted by: Sandra Anderson, MD, Chief Medical Officer, Carbon Health⏎⏎---⏎⏎MARKET STRUCTURE IS THE ACTUAL PROBLEM⏎⏎Carbon Health submits these comments in response to the Department's Request for Information on accelerating AI adoption in clinical care settings (ONC, 2024, 89 FR 44201). Our organization operates across multi-state ambulatory and behavioral health settings, and our Q3 2024 internal audit documented that 68% of documentation burden cited by our licensed clinical social workers as interfering with direct patient contact involves tasks now addressable through AI-assisted ambient documentation tools. We raise that finding here not because it is the primary focus of these comments, but because it illustrates the stakes. The American Academy of Social Work and Social Welfare (2023) has estimated that documentation consumes 35-40% of clinician hours per week in small and solo behavioral health practices. That is a real and measurable harm.⏎⏎What concerns this organization, however, is that the RFI's framing largely assumes a market structure that is capable of delivering AI adoption equitably and without structural distortion. That assumption is wrong, and proceeding as though it is correct will produce a version of AI acceleration that benefits incumbent vendors while extracting value from the providers and patients the Department is ostensibly trying to serve. Gee and Bhatt (2023) documented in Health Affairs (42:8, 1124-1133) the degree to which health information technology markets are now characterized by concentration so severe that new entrants face effective foreclosure. Dafny and Lee (2022) made a related point in the New England Journal of Medicine (386:19, 1843-1847) about how consolidation in health care markets generally tends to erode the competitive pressures that would otherwise discipline quality and price. The Department should read those papers before issuing a final rule or guidance that routes AI adoption incentives through the same vendor relationships that produced the EHR dysfunction Schulte and Fry (2019) documented so carefully in their Kaiser Health News investigation — a system in which clinicians were left clicking through screens designed to maximize billing capture, not clinical utility.⏎⏎⏎Carbon Health | HHS AI RFI Comments | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 2⏎⏎⏎The RFI does not use the phrase "regulatory capture," but the phenomenon it describes is recognizable. Meaningful Use created reimbursement incentives for EHR adoption that, as Blumenthal and Tavenner (2010) noted in the New England Journal of Medicine (363:6, 501-504), were structured in ways that concentrated market power among a small number of certified vendors. Adler-Milstein and Pfeifer (2017) documented in the Milbank Quarterly (95:1, 117-135) how those same vendors subsequently engaged in information blocking practices that protected their market positions at patient and provider expense. The FTC's October 2023 policy report on generative AI and health care market concentration warned explicitly that similar dynamics are already forming around AI infrastructure, with large incumbent EHR vendors acquiring or exclusively partnering with AI firms in ways that will foreclose competition from independent developers. Carbon Health has observed this dynamic directly. Our prior authorization workflows, which our Q3 2024 review identified as one of the two leading reimbursement friction points where AI decision support showed measurable potential, are constrained not by lack of available AI tools but by the integration requirements imposed by incumbent platform vendors who have a financial interest in keeping those workflows opaque.⏎⏎The Department asked in the RFI about barriers to AI adoption. The answers Carbon Health would prioritize:⏎⏎1. Pharmacy benefit managers and their data subsidiaries are capturing rents from the same clinical data flows that AI systems depend on. The RFI does not address this at all. PBM market concentration is not a tangential issue — it is a structural condition that shapes which AI applications are commercially viable and which are not, because PBMs control the formulary and prior authorization data environments that any clinically meaningful AI tool will need to access.⏎⏎2. Vendor lock-in through proprietary data formats and CRADA arrangements means that federal R&D investments in AI could flow directly into the balance sheets of companies like Epic and Oracle Health without producing any durable public benefit. Kesselheim, Cresswell, and Sheikh (2022) in BMJ Health & Care Informatics (29:1, e100556) identified this as one of the central governance failures in AI regulatory frameworks internationally.⏎⏎3. Algorithmic bias in commercially deployed tools remains inadequately addressed. Obermeyer et al. (2019) in Science (366:6464, 447-452) demonstrated that a widely deployed commercial algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients. Maddox, Rumsfeld, and Payne (2019) in JAMA (321:1, 31-32) identified the absence of post-deployment surveillance requirements as the specific policy gap that allows biased tools to remain in clinical use long after problems are identified.⏎⏎Carbon Health | HHS AI RFI Comments | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 3⏎⏎⏎WHAT THE DEPARTMENT SHOULD ACTUALLY DO⏎⏎The Department should establish independent evaluation infrastructure for AI tools used in clinical settings — infrastructure that is not funded through cooperative agreements with incumbent vendors, not governed by advisory bodies dominated by the same companies whose products are under review, and not structured to treat vendor-supplied validation data as sufficient evidence of clinical utility. This is not a complicated governance concept. It is the same logic that produced the FDA's premarket review process for medical devices, applied to software.⏎⏎The RFI's framing is itself a symptom of the capture problem. It asks how the Department can "accelerate adoption" as though speed is the variable that matters. What matters is whether the AI tools being adopted are accurate, equitable, and not extracting value from clinical relationships in ways that benefit platform vendors rather than patients. Carbon Health would support a precautionary standard requirement — modeled on the approach Kesselheim et al. (2022) described in their comparative analysis — that requires any AI tool receiving federal reimbursement support to undergo independent prospective evaluation before deployment, with results posted in a publicly accessible registry.⏎⏎The behavioral health documentation burden our 340 active LCSW clients' clinicians face is real. The prior authorization friction is real. But solving those problems by routing federal incentives through Epic's AI marketplace or through PBM-affiliated data brokers will not produce better care. It will produce a new layer of rent extraction wearing the label of innovation. The Department has been here before with Meaningful Use, and the literature is quite clear about how that turned out (Schulte & Fry, 2019; Adler-Milstein & Pfeifer, 2017). Carbon Health strongly urges the Department to condition any AI reimbursement or adoption incentive on demonstrated independence from incumbent EHR and PBM vendor relationships, with verification through a third-party audit process whose methodology is published and whose⏎⏎Carbon Health | HHS AI RFI Comments | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 4⏎⏎auditors are prohibited from holding financial relationships with the entities under review. The specific audit protocol design is something the Department would need to work through, and we recognize that is not a simple administrative task — but the absence of such a requirement in the current RFI framing is a gap that, if left unaddressed, will define the outcome regardless of what else the final guidance says about technical standards or interoperability.♔♔2026-02-26T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-26T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔4♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔The AI healthcare market is dominated by a small number of powerful vendors whose commercial interests in rapid deployment conflict with patient safety, and HHS's acceleration agenda risks embedding those vendors permanently into critical healthcare infrastructure.♔organization♔high♔urgent♔Maryland♔chief medical officer♔60♔A 2024 internal audit of clinical outcomes across our licensed clinical social work caseload—comprising 340 active clients across outpatient and community-based settings—found that 68% of documentation burden cited by clinicians as interfering with direct therapeutic contact involved tasks now addressable through AI-assisted ambient documentation and structured intake support. SYNTH-0086♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Mark Adams♔Rural Health Information Hub♔♔♔♔♔Rural Health Information Hub⏎Comments on HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket ID: [HHS-AI-RFI-2024]⏎Submitted by: Mark Adams, Rural Health Information Hub⏎⏎---⏎⏎The Rural Health Information Hub submits these comments with a specific, documented concern that the current framing of this Request for Information systematically underweights what the evidence already tells us: AI tools deployed in clinical care settings perform inequitably across patient populations, and acceleration without mandatory equity safeguards will reproduce existing disparities at scale. We focus our response primarily on the RFI's questions regarding regulatory standards for clinical AI validation and reimbursement pathway design, because those two levers are where HHS has the clearest authority to prevent foreseeable harm and is currently proposing to exercise that authority without adequate equity conditions attached.⏎⏎Our organizational context is relevant here. The Rural Health Information Hub works extensively with community health networks across underserved geographies, and our ongoing collaboration with the Global Liver Institute's network of 47 liver disease centers of excellence has produced findings that speak directly to the adoption dynamics HHS is attempting to accelerate. GLI's 2024 landscape analysis found that 68% of those centers had piloted at least one AI-assisted diagnostic or care coordination tool within the preceding 24 months, yet fewer than 20% had successfully integrated those tools into sustained clinical workflows. That gap between piloting and sustained integration is not primarily a technology readiness problem. GLI's 2023 policy forum, convening hepatologists, transplant coordinators, and payers, identified reimbursement ambiguity and the absence of validated, liver-specific algorithmic standards as the dominant institutional obstacles. And GLI's annual patient needs assessment, drawing on structured input from more than 12,000 individuals living with chronic liver disease or hepatocellular carcinoma, found that delayed diagnosis and fragmented specialty referral remain the two most frequently cited systemic barriers to timely care. We raise these data points not as background color but as evidence of the specific patient population that will bear disproportionate risk if HHS accelerates AI adoption through reimbursement pathways that do not require demonstration of equitable performance across race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and care setting. Liver disease patients in rural and safety-net institutions are not hypothetical edge cases. They are the population for whom the failure modes of clinical AI are already documented and already harmful.⏎⏎The foundational problem is that historical healthcare data encodes decades of discriminatory treatment patterns, and AI systems trained on that data reproduce those patterns. This is not a theoretical concern. Obermeyer and colleagues demonstrated in a 2019 Science paper that a widely deployed commercial algorithm used to manage population health systematically underestimated the severity of illness in Black patients relative to white patients at equivalent levels of measured need, because the algorithm used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need — a proxy that reflects historical underinvestment in care for Black patients rather than actual clinical acuity (Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S. Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations. Science. 2019;366(6464):447-453). The algorithm was not an outlier. Sjoding and colleagues published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 that pulse oximeters — a device so basic it is used in every clinical setting in the country — systematically overestimate oxygen saturation in patients with dark skin pigmentation, meaning Black patients with occult hypoxemia were three times more likely than white patients to have that hypoxemia missed (Sjoding MW, Dickson RP, Iwashyna TJ, Gay SE, Valley TS. Racial bias in pulse oximetry measurement. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(25):2477-2478). Pulse oximetry is not an AI system, but the lesson is directly applicable: when a measurement tool is validated primarily on lighter-skinned populations and then deployed universally, the performance gap does not announce itself. Clinicians trust the device. And Adamson and Smith demonstrated in JAMA Dermatology in 2018 that machine learning algorithms for skin lesion classification were trained predominantly on images of lighter skin tones, producing diagnostic performance that degrades substantially for patients with darker skin — the patients who already face the greatest barriers to dermatologic care (Adamson AS, Smith A. Machine learning and health care disparities in dermatology. JAMA Dermatol. 2018;154(11):1247-1248). The pattern across these examples is consistent: tools are trained on populations that reflect who has historically had access to care, validated in institutions that reflect where resources have historically been concentrated, and then deployed universally in ways that make their differential performance invisible until the harm is already done.⏎⏎Rural Health Information Hub | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 2⏎⏎For liver disease patients specifically, this pattern has direct clinical consequences that the RFI's acceleration framing does not reckon with. Hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance, fibrosis staging, and referral triage are precisely the clinical functions where AI tools are currently being piloted across GLI's network. These are also functions where algorithmic errors have asymmetric consequences: a missed HCC surveillance flag or a systematically underestimated fibrosis score for a patient who is already navigating a fragmented rural care pathway means a delayed diagnosis that, in liver disease, translates directly to stage at presentation and survival probability. Vyas and colleagues documented in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 that race-based corrections embedded in clinical algorithms — including algorithms used in nephrology and obstetrics — systematically direct Black patients away from specialist referral and toward less intensive care, and that these corrections are based on population-level genetic assumptions that do not hold at the individual level and that encode structural racism as biological fact (Vyas DA, Eisenstein LEI, Jones DS. Hidden in plain sight — reconsidering the use of race correction in clinical algorithms. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(9):874-882). The question HHS must answer before accelerating AI adoption in liver disease care is whether the tools being piloted across GLI's network have been audited for analogous race-based performance disparities. GLI's landscape data suggest the answer is no. Fewer than 20% of those 47 centers have achieved sustained integration, and the absence of validated liver-specific algorithmic standards was cited as a primary obstacle — which means the tools being piloted are being evaluated against general clinical AI standards that were not designed to detect liver-disease-specific performance gaps across patient populations defined by race, rurality, or insurance status.⏎⏎The second major failure mode this RFI does not adequately address is what the literature calls automation bias: the well-documented tendency of clinicians to defer to algorithmic outputs even when those outputs are wrong. This failure mode is particularly dangerous in under-resourced settings, because the conditions that make automation bias most likely — high clinical workload, limited time for deliberative review, institutional culture that treats AI as a quality improvement tool — are exactly the conditions that characterize the community hospitals and rural clinics where GLI's patient network receives care. Wong and colleagues conducted an external validation of a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model across four Michigan Medicine hospitals in 2021 and found that the model's performance in their institution was substantially worse than reported in the original validation study, with poor positive predictive value and no significant association with improved sepsis outcomes (Wong A, Otles E, Donnelly JP, et al. External validation of a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model in hospitalized patients. JAMA Intern Med. 2021;181(8):1065-1070). The model had been deployed, was generating alerts, and clinicians were responding to those alerts — but the alerts were not improving patient outcomes because the model was not performing as validated. This is the external validation problem, and Kaushal and colleagues documented its structural basis in a 2020 JAMA paper showing that the geographic distribution of cohorts used to train foundational deep learning algorithms is heavily concentrated in a small number of large academic medical centers, predominantly in the Northeast and California, with systematic underrepresentation of rural populations, safety-net hospital patients, and patients from the South and Midwest (Kaushal A, Altman R, Langlotz C. Geographic distribution of US cohorts used to train foundational deep learning algorithms. JAMA. 2020;324(12):1212-1213). A tool trained on patient data from Massachusetts General Hospital and UCSF does not generalize automatically to a critical access hospital in rural Mississippi or a federally qualified health center in western Massachusetts. The authoritative appearance of AI-generated clinical decision support outputs — a score, a risk flag, a recommended action — makes these generalization failures harder to detect and correct than ordinary human clinical error, because the error is attributed to the patient's condition rather than to the tool's performance gap.⏎⏎Gianfrancesco and colleagues identified several specific mechanisms through which EHR-derived training data introduces and amplifies bias in machine learning algorithms: differential documentation practices across care settings, missing data patterns that correlate with race and socioeconomic status, and the use of healthcare utilization as a proxy for clinical need — precisely the Obermeyer problem, reproduced across the broader literature (Gianfrancesco MA, Tamang S, Yazdany J, Schmajuk G. Potential biases in machine learning algorithms using electronic health record data. JAMA Intern Med. 2018;178(11):1544-1547). For liver disease patients in GLI's network, these mechanisms are not abstract. Rural patients with chronic liver disease have systematically thinner EHR records than urban academic medical center patients, not because they are healthier but because they have had less access to care. An AI fibrosis staging tool trained on dense longitudinal EHR data from academic hepatology programs will encounter missing data patterns in rural critical access hospital records that it was not trained to handle, and the resulting output degradation will be invisible unless the tool has been prospectively validated in care settings that match the deployment environment. The RFI asks about regulatory actions HHS can take to accelerate adoption. We are asking HHS to recognize that acceleration without mandatory site-specific and population-specific validation is not a neutral policy choice. It is a decision to deploy tools whose failure modes are known and documented, in settings where those failure modes will fall hardest on patients who are already receiving the least.⏎⏎Char and colleagues articulated the core ethical framework in a 2018 New England Journal of Medicine paper: machine learning tools in health care introduce novel ethical challenges around transparency, accountability, and the distribution of both benefits and harms, and those challenges require institutional mechanisms that do not currently exist in most deployment environments (Char DS, Shah NH, Magnus D. Implementing machine learning in health care — addressing ethical challenges. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(11):981-983). Wiens and colleagues, writing in Nature Medicine in 2019, proposed a roadmap for responsible ML in health care that includes prospective clinical validation, ongoing post-deployment monitoring, and explicit attention to the performance of models in subgroups defined by race, socioeconomic status, and care setting — and they noted that these requirements were not standard practice in the field at the time of writing (Wiens J, Saria S, Sendak M, et al. Do no harm: a roadmap for responsible machine learning for health care. Nat Med. 2019;25(9):1337-1340). That was 2019. GLI's 2024 landscape data suggest that five years later, with 68% of liver disease centers of excellence having piloted AI tools, those requirements are still not standard practice. The acceleration this RFI proposes will widen the deployment of tools that do not meet the standards Wiens and colleagues identified as minimally necessary, in care settings that have the least capacity to detect and respond to performance failures. Pierson and colleagues demonstrated in a 2021 Nature Medicine paper that algorithmic approaches can actually reduce unexplained pain disparities in underserved populations when the algorithms are explicitly designed and validated for equity — but that outcome requires the equity objective to be built into the design and validation process from the start, not added as an afterthought after deployment (Pierson E, Cutler DM, Leskovec J, Mullainathan S, Obermeyer Z. An algorithmic approach to reducing unexplained pain disparities in underserved populations. Nat Med. 2021;27(1):136-140). The Pierson paper is the model HHS should be following. It is not the model reflected in this RFI's framing.⏎⏎Rural Health Information Hub | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 3⏎⏎The National Academy for State Health Policy's 2023 policy brief on algorithmic bias in health care identified the absence of standardized equity auditing requirements as the single most consequential gap in current regulatory frameworks, and noted that states attempting to fill that gap through their own policy mechanisms face significant limitations without federal leadership and federal data access (National Academy for State Health Policy. Algorithmic Bias in Health Care: State Policy Landscape and Emerging Frameworks for Equity Auditing. NASHP Policy Brief. 2023). HHS has the authority and the data infrastructure to establish mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing as a condition of any reimbursement pathway or regulatory clearance for clinical AI tools. It has not done so. This RFI asks what regulatory and reimbursement actions HHS can take to accelerate AI adoption. Our answer is that the prior question — what equity conditions must be met before any tool enters a reimbursement pathway — has not been answered, and until it is, acceleration is the wrong objective. The specific conditions we are calling for are not complicated, though implementing them will require genuine regulatory commitment:⏎⏎1. Mandatory pre-deployment stratified performance validation: Any clinical AI tool seeking CMS reimbursement or FDA marketing authorization must demonstrate performance that meets minimum accuracy and equity thresholds when evaluated separately in patient subgroups defined by race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, insurance status, and care setting type (academic medical center vs. community hospital vs. critical access hospital vs. federally qualified health center). Performance in the overall population is not sufficient. A tool that performs at 0.85 AUC in the aggregate but 0.67 AUC in Black patients at rural critical access hospitals fails the equity standard regardless of its aggregate performance.⏎⏎2. Mandatory post-deployment bias surveillance as a condition of continued reimbursement: Reimbursement for clinical AI tools must be conditioned on the submission of quarterly stratified performance data to a centralized HHS registry. Tools that demonstrate performance degradation in protected subgroups or in non-academic care settings must be flagged for mandatory re-validation before continued use. The registry data must be publicly accessible to researchers, patient advocates, and state health agencies.⏎⏎3. Liver-disease-specific algorithmic standards developed with explicit rural and safety-net representation: HHS, working with ASTP/ONC and in partnership with clinical specialty societies, must develop validated algorithmic performance standards for AI tools used in hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance, fibrosis staging, and specialty referral triage. Those standards must be developed using training and validation data that includes patients from rural care settings, safety-net institutions, and populations with historically limited healthcare access — not primarily from academic hepatology programs. GLI's network of 47 centers of excellence, with its documented patient base of more than 12,000 individuals, is available as a validation partner and we are stating that availability explicitly in this comment.⏎⏎4. Automation bias disclosure requirements: Any clinical AI tool deployed in a care setting must include in its cleared labeling explicit disclosure of the populations and care settings in which it has and has not been validated, with specific guidance for clinicians in non-validated deployment environments. The current FDA framework does not require this disclosure in a format that is accessible or meaningful at the point of clinical use. That needs to change.⏎⏎We recognize that these requirements will slow some deployments. We are not apologetic about that. GLI's patient needs assessment found that 12,000 patients with chronic liver disease and hepatocellular carcinoma identified delayed diagnosis and fragmented specialty referral as their primary systemic barriers. An AI tool that addresses those barriers for white patients at academic medical centers while performing invisibly worse for Black and rural patients at community hospitals does not solve the problem. It replicates the problem with an algorithmic imprimatur that makes it harder to challenge. HHS's accelerationist posture in this RFI, read against the documented literature on algorithmic bias and GLI's own landscape data, converges on a conclusion that is difficult to characterize charitably: the Department is proposing to move faster with less equity oversight in a domain where the evidence for disparate harm is already strong and already published. The communities that will bear the cost of that acceleration — rural patients, patients of color, patients at safety-net institutions — are the same communities that have borne the cost of every previous cycle of inadequately regulated health technology deployment.⏎⏎We also want to note, because it does not seem to be adequately represented in the RFI's framing, that the external validation problem documented by Wong and colleagues and the geographic training data concentration problem documented by Kaushal and colleagues are not problems that individual health systems can solve on their own. A rural critical access hospital in, say, Greenfield, Massachusetts does not have the data science capacity to conduct prospective external validation of a commercially deployed sepsis prediction model or a liver fibrosis staging algorithm. It does not have the staff to run ongoing post-deployment bias surveillance. It does not have the regulatory leverage to demand stratified performance data from a vendor whose tool is being reimbursed through a CMS pathway. The only entity with the authority and the data infrastructure to establish those requirements is HHS, and HHS is currently proposing to use that authority to accelerate deployment rather than to condition deployment on demonstrated equity. The NASHP 2023 brief documents the extent to which states are trying to fill this gap and running into the limits of their authority and data access. Federal action is not optional here. It is the only mechanism that reaches the full range of care settings where GLI's patients are receiving care and where the failure modes documented in the literature will materialize if deployment accelerates without equity conditions.⏎⏎One more thing that we think deserves direct statement: the framing of this RFI treats "acceleration" as the unambiguous objective and treats equity concerns as potential friction to be managed within an acceleration framework. That framing is backwards. For the patient population GLI represents — people with chronic liver disease and hepatocellular carcinoma, disproportionately located in rural and underserved communities, already navigating care systems that have historically underserved them — the question is not how fast AI tools can be deployed but whether those tools, when deployed, will perform equitably enough to actually close the gaps in delayed diagnosis and fragmented referral that GLI's patients have been reporting for years. The evidence, as of the date of this comment, says the tools currently being piloted do not meet that standard in the deployment environments where it matters most. The 68% pilot rate and the sub-20% sustained integration rate in GLI's network are not an argument for more acceleration. They are an argument for getting the equity conditions right before the next deployment cycle begins, and for HHS to use this RFI process to establish those conditions rather than to remove the friction that is, in many cases, the only thing standing between a poorly validated algorithm and a patient who cannot afford another misdiagnosis.⏎⏎References⏎⏎Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S. SYNTH-0088♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Amanda Ramirez♔National Medical Association♔♔♔♔♔NATIONAL MEDICAL ASSOCIATION⏎Comments in Response to HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitted by: Amanda Ramirez, Senior Policy Analyst⏎National Medical Association⏎Date of Submission: 2025⏎⏎⏎I. ORGANIZATIONAL STANDING AND EVIDENTIARY BASIS⏎⏎The National Medical Association submits these comments in response to the Department's Request for Information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings. NMA's membership includes a substantial proportion of physicians practicing in underserved, safety-net, and minority-serving institutions — settings that the Department's RFI conspicuously fails to name as a primary design consideration. Before addressing the specific question of what regulatory and reimbursement actions HHS should take, NMA must establish why the framing of this RFI is itself a problem.⏎⏎The RFI asks how to accelerate adoption. That is the wrong first question. The correct first question is: adoption under what conditions, for which populations, with what mandatory safeguards against documented harms? The peer-reviewed literature does not treat algorithmic bias in clinical AI as a theoretical concern or a future risk. It is an observed, measured, replicated pattern of harm — and HHS has structured an RFI that does not once condition deployment pathways on mandatory equity auditing or disaggregated performance reporting. That omission is not an oversight. It is a structural choice, and NMA objects to it directly.⏎⏎NMA acknowledges that AI tools offer genuine potential efficiencies in documentation, prior authorization processing, and certain diagnostic support functions. The organization is not categorically opposed to AI in clinical settings. What NMA is categorically opposed to is a federal acceleration strategy that treats the existing peer-reviewed evidence on algorithmic discrimination as background noise rather than a design constraint.⏎⏎NMA | HHS AI RFI Comments | Page 1⏎⏎⏎II. THE EQUITY EVIDENCE BASE IS NOT AMBIGUOUS⏎⏎The Department should not require persuasion on the basic empirical picture. Obermeyer et al. (Science, 2019;366(6464):447-453) documented that a commercial algorithm used to manage population health systematically allocated fewer health care resources to Black patients at equivalent illness burden — not because the algorithm was designed to discriminate, but because it used health care cost as a proxy for health need, and Black patients with equivalent illness had historically received less care. That is an example of bias baked into training data propagating into clinical resource allocation at scale. Sjoding et al. (N Engl J Med, 2020;383(25):2477-2478) found that pulse oximeters — devices now integrated into AI-assisted monitoring systems across hospital settings — systematically overestimated oxygen saturation in patients with darker skin tones, meaning those patients received delayed intervention for occult hypoxemia at measurable rates. This is not a modeling problem. It is a measurement problem that AI systems inherit and amplify when they are trained on physiologic data collected with racially biased instruments.⏎⏎Adamson and Smith (JAMA Dermatol, 2018;154(11):1247-1248) documented that dermatology AI systems trained predominantly on lighter-skinned patient images demonstrated substantially degraded performance on darker skin tones — a finding with direct implications for melanoma detection in communities of color. Wong et al. (JAMA Intern Med, 2021;181(8):1065-1070) conducted external validation of a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model and found that its performance in community hospital settings diverged substantially from the academic medical center performance metrics used to market it. The model's sensitivity and positive predictive value dropped in ways that were not disclosed to purchasing institutions. Gianfrancesco et al. (JAMA Intern Med, 2018;178(11):1544-1547) identified multiple pathways through which electronic health record data — the substrate on which clinical AI is trained — systematically encodes socioeconomic and racial disparities in prior care access, producing models that replicate rather than correct those disparities.⏎⏎NMA | HHS AI RFI Comments | Page 2⏎⏎Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones (N Engl J Med, 2020;383(9):874-882) documented that race-corrected clinical algorithms — including those embedded in kidney function calculators and spirometry interpretation tools — systematically direct Black patients toward less aggressive treatment, with documented consequences for transplant eligibility and pulmonary disease management. Pierson et al. (Nat Med, 2021;27(1):136-140) found that algorithmic approaches to pain management in underserved populations can reduce disparities when equity is an explicit design objective — but that this requires intentional intervention, not passive deployment. The literature is not ambiguous. HHS has access to all of these studies. The RFI's failure to incorporate them as binding design constraints is a policy choice, not an information gap.⏎⏎⏎III. THE AUTOMATION BIAS PROBLEM IS UNDERWEIGHTED IN THIS RFI⏎⏎One mechanism that the RFI does not adequately address is automation bias — the well-documented tendency of clinicians to defer to algorithmic outputs even when those outputs conflict with clinical judgment. Sendak et al. (Proc ACM Conf Fairness Accountability Transparency, 2020:99-109) documented that clinicians interpreting AI-generated outputs frequently treated them as more authoritative than equivalent human assessments, even when they lacked the ability to interrogate the model's reasoning. The practical consequence is that AI errors are harder to catch than equivalent human errors, because the authoritative presentation of algorithmic output suppresses the skepticism that would otherwise trigger a second look.⏎⏎This matters for equity in a specific way. If an AI sepsis prediction model performs worse on Black patients than white patients at the same hospital, and if clinicians treat its outputs as authoritative, then the model's underperformance for Black patients will systematically go undetected at the point of care. The clinician who might have caught a delayed sepsis alert based on clinical gestalt is instead reassured by the model's output. The error is invisible until it appears in outcome data — and only if someone is disaggregating that outcome data by race, which most institutions are not doing. Char, Shah, and Magnus (N Engl J Med, 2018;378(11):981-983) identified this mechanism as one of the primary ethical challenges in clinical AI implementation, noting that the opacity of model reasoning compounds the automation bias problem by making it structurally difficult for clinicians to know when to override.⏎⏎NMA | HHS AI RFI Comments | Page 3⏎⏎Wiens et al. (Nat Med, 2019;25(9):1337-1340) proposed a responsible machine learning roadmap that included prospective monitoring of model outputs disaggregated by patient subgroup as a minimum deployment standard. The roadmap was published in 2019. Six years later, HHS is drafting an acceleration RFI that does not include prospective subgroup monitoring as a condition of any deployment pathway. That is a significant gap.⏎⏎⏎IV. THE VALIDATION GENERALIZABILITY PROBLEM DIRECTLY AFFECTS NMA'S MEMBERSHIP⏎⏎Kaushal, Altman, and Langlotz (JAMA, 2020;324(12):1212-1213) analyzed the geographic distribution of patient cohorts used to train foundational deep learning algorithms and found that training data was overwhelmingly concentrated in a small number of large academic medical centers, predominantly in the Northeast and West Coast. Community hospitals, rural health systems, federally qualified health centers, and safety-net institutions — the settings where a substantial proportion of NMA members practice — were systematically underrepresented in the training populations for tools now being marketed to those very institutions.⏎⏎NMA | HHS AI RFI Comments | Page 4⏎⏎This is not a minor technical caveat. A sepsis prediction model trained primarily on patient populations at large urban academic medical centers may perform adequately in those settings and perform poorly in a rural Arizona community hospital serving a predominantly Hispanic patient population, or in a safety-net institution in a Texas border county where the patient mix, comorbidity patterns, and prior care access histories differ substantially from the training population. The National Academy for State Health Policy documented in its March 2023 policy brief on algorithmic accountability in state health programs that equity audit requirements for AI tools deployed in Medicaid and other public programs remain inconsistent and largely voluntary across states, meaning that performance degradation in high-need settings frequently goes unmeasured (NASHP Policy Brief, March 2023).⏎⏎The practical implication is that the institutions least equipped to conduct independent performance validation — community hospitals with limited informatics staff, rural health systems without dedicated data science capacity, safety-net institutions operating on thin margins — are also the institutions most likely to be deploying AI tools whose performance has not been validated in anything resembling their patient population. HHS's proposed acceleration framework does nothing to address this asymmetry.⏎⏎The following conditions characterize the deployment environment for AI tools in the settings where NMA members predominantly practice, and each represents a distinct equity risk that the RFI fails to address:⏎⏎1. Training data underrepresentation: Models trained on academic medical center cohorts are deployed without site-specific validation in community settings with different patient demographics (Kaushal et al., JAMA, 2020;324(12):1212-1213).⏎⏎2. Measurement instrument bias: Physiologic monitoring devices with documented racial measurement error are used as data inputs for AI systems, propagating that error into algorithmic outputs (Sjoding et al., N Engl J Med, 2020;383(25):2477-2478).⏎⏎3. Absence of disaggregated performance monitoring: Post-deployment outcome monitoring is rarely stratified by race, ethnicity, or socioeconomic status, meaning subgroup performance degradation is invisible in aggregate metrics.⏎⏎4. Resource asymmetry in validation capacity: The institutions serving the highest-risk populations have the least capacity to conduct independent performance audits of the tools they are purchasing.⏎⏎5. Proprietary opacity: Vendors frequently decline to disclose training data composition, model architecture, or subgroup performance statistics, citing trade secret protections (Wiens et al., Nat Med, 2019;25(9):1337-1340).⏎⏎NMA | HHS AI RFI Comments | Page 5⏎⏎⏎V. SPECIFIC REGULATORY DEMANDS⏎⏎NMA addresses specifically the RFI's questions regarding regulatory actions HHS can take to support responsible AI deployment. The organization does not address reimbursement structuring in this comment, as that is the subject of a separate NMA submission.⏎⏎HHS must condition any deployment pathway on mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing. This means that before an AI clinical decision support tool is eligible for Medicare or Medicaid reimbursement, the developer must provide disaggregated performance data — sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value — stratified by race, ethnicity, primary language, socioeconomic status proxy, and geography. The stratification categories should align with OMB's revised race and ethnicity standards and should include rural versus urban and safety-net versus non-safety-net deployment settings. This is not a novel demand; it mirrors requirements that FDA has begun applying to certain AI-enabled medical devices under its predetermined change control plan framework, and HHS has both the statutory authority and the empirical justification to extend equivalent requirements to clinical decision support tools that fall outside FDA's current device jurisdiction.⏎⏎HHS must require continuous post-deployment bias surveillance with public reporting. Pre-deployment auditing is necessary but not sufficient. Model performance can degrade over time as patient populations shift, as EHR documentation practices change, or as the clinical context for which a model was validated evolves. Wiens et al. (Nat Med, 2019;25(9):1337-1340) identified prospective post-deployment monitoring as a minimum responsible deployment standard. HHS should require that vendors and deploying institutions submit annual disaggregated performance reports to a publicly accessible registry, with defined thresholds for performance degradation that trigger mandatory notification to deploying institutions and, where patient harm is plausible, to affected patients. The registry should be searchable by institution type, patient population, and clinical application.⏎⏎NMA | HHS AI RFI Comments | Page 6⏎⏎HHS must address proprietary opacity as a barrier to equity auditing. The current framework allows vendors to withhold training data composition and subgroup performance statistics under trade secret protections, which makes independent equity auditing structurally impossible. HHS should establish that receipt of Medicare or Medicaid reimbursement for AI-assisted clinical services constitutes acceptance of a transparency condition: vendors must disclose, at minimum, the demographic composition of training and validation cohorts, the geographic distribution of training institutions, and subgroup performance statistics for all protected characteristics covered under the Civil Rights Act and Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act. Char, Shah, and Magnus (N Engl J Med, 2018;378(11):981-983) specifically identified proprietary opacity as an ethical barrier to responsible AI deployment; HHS has the contracting leverage through Medicare and Medicaid to overcome that barrier where FDA jurisdiction does not reach.⏎⏎The absence of these three conditions from HHS's RFI framing — mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing, continuous post-deployment bias surveillance, and transparency conditions tied to public program reimbursement — is the central structural deficiency NMA is identifying in this submission. Each of these conditions has a documented evidentiary basis in peer-reviewed literature spanning at least 2018 to 2021. The Department has had access to this literature for years. An acceleration framework that does not incorporate these conditions as baseline requirements is not a neutral policy choice; it is a decision to accelerate deployment into vulnerable populations without the safeguards the evidence base says are warranted.⏎⏎NMA | HHS AI RFI Comments | Page 7⏎⏎NMA requests that HHS publish a supplemental RFI or interim guidance document specifically addressing equity audit requirements for clinical AI, with a comment period of no fewer than 90 days, before finalizing any acceleration framework. The 60-day comment period for this RFI was insufficient for the level of technical specificity the equity questions require, and the RFI's framing did not signal to commenters that equity auditing was a primary subject of inquiry — which means the Department will receive fewer comments on this topic than the policy stakes warrant.
