SYNTH-0089♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Richard Nguyen♔American Association of Neurological Surgeons♔♔♔♔♔AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF NEUROLOGICAL SURGEONS⏎Comments on HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology⏎Docket No. ONC-2024-AI-RFI⏎Submitted by: Richard Nguyen, Policy Director⏎⏎AANS Comments | HHS AI RFI | ONC-2024 | Page 1⏎⏎THE GAP BETWEEN DEPLOYMENT PACE AND WORKER PROTECTION⏎⏎The American Association of Neurological Surgeons (AANS) submits these comments in response to the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology's Request for Information on accelerating AI adoption in clinical care settings (ONC, 2024). The AANS directs the Department's attention specifically to the workforce implications of the RFI's accelerationist framing, which in our assessment treats the speed of AI deployment as a policy objective largely independent of the human infrastructure on which safe clinical care depends. Survey data collected by the Association of periOperative Registered Nurses in 2024 found that 58% of respondents worked in facilities that had piloted or fully deployed at least one AI-assisted surgical tool, yet 74% of those same respondents reported that their facilities lacked standardized competency frameworks for validating the safe clinical use of those technologies (AORN, 2024). That gap between deployment and protection is not a transitional inefficiency that will self-correct as adoption matures. It is a structural product of procurement processes that systematically exclude the frontline workers who bear the operational consequences of implementation decisions. The AORN's 2023 Perioperative Workforce Report documented that 61% of respondents cited insufficient institutional guidance on liability and scope-of-practice boundaries as a primary barrier to confident AI adoption in the perioperative environment (AORN, 2023). These are not expressions of technophobia. They are documented institutional failures, and HHS's current framing of this RFI does not address them with the specificity they require. The Government Accountability Office reached a parallel conclusion in its 2023 review of AI in health care, finding that implementation challenges consistently outpaced governance frameworks and that workforce consultation mechanisms were largely absent from hospital-level procurement processes (GAO, 2023). The AANS finds it notable that the RFI's framing positions AI adoption primarily as a clinical efficiency and burnout-reduction opportunity without substantively engaging the literature on how prior waves of health information technology deployment have interacted with physician and nursing workload. Melnick and colleagues found in 2020 that perceived EHR usability was inversely associated with professional burnout among U.S. physicians, a finding that should complicate any assumption that AI tools marketed as efficiency solutions will automatically reduce cognitive burden rather than redistribute it onto frontline workers in new forms (Melnick et al., 2020). Shanafelt and colleagues documented that physician burnout and dissatisfaction with work-life integration worsened significantly between 2011 and 2020 across a period that coincided with accelerated health IT deployment (Shanafelt et al., 2022). The pattern is consistent enough that HHS should treat the burnout-reduction promise embedded in this RFI as a hypothesis requiring prospective⏎⏎AANS Comments | HHS AI RFI | ONC-2024 | Page 2⏎⏎evidence, not as a premise on which to build regulatory posture.⏎⏎THE STRUCTURAL INCENTIVE PROBLEM AND WORKFORCE HARM⏎⏎The more fundamental concern the AANS wishes to place before the Department involves the structural divergence between the financial interests of AI vendors and hospital administrators on one side, and the professional autonomy and working conditions of frontline clinical staff on the other. AI tools marketed to health system leadership as productivity optimization platforms are, by design, built to generate data that can be used to justify staffing adjustments, increased caseload targets, and the elimination of judgment-intensive roles that are difficult to measure through throughput metrics. Kellogg, Valentine, and Christin documented in 2020 that algorithmic management tools in professional settings systematically shift the locus of control away from workers and toward managerial and vendor-defined performance parameters, with particular erosion of contextual judgment roles that are central to professional expertise (Kellogg et al., 2020). Strickler and Bhatt's 2023 analysis of multi-site health system deployments found direct associations between algorithmic scheduling implementation and measurable reductions in nursing judgment latitude, with administrators in several systems explicitly citing AI-generated productivity data as justification for staffing ratio changes (Strickler & Bhatt, 2023). The AANS regards this as a patient safety problem, not merely a labor relations concern. Clinical expertise is not a variable to be optimized out of care delivery; it is the mechanism through which contextual patient information gets translated into safe intraoperative and perioperative decisions. When AI procurement excludes frontline workers from meaningful consultation, and when AI-generated productivity metrics are used to reduce staffing without independent clinical review, the result is degraded professional autonomy that ultimately reaches patients. Accenture Federal Services and the American Hospital Association found in 2023 that workforce consultation was absent from the majority of hospital-level AI procurement processes surveyed, a finding consistent with what AORN member data documents at the facility level (Accenture/AHA, 2023). The AANS also notes that algorithmic bias in clinical decision support tools is a documented risk, not a theoretical one; Obermeyer and colleagues identified in 2019 that a widely deployed population health algorithm systematically underestimated the care needs of Black patients due to the use of cost as a proxy for health need (Obermeyer et al., 2019), and Bates and colleagues argued in 2021 that implementation science frameworks for machine learning interventions must include prospective workforce and equity impact assessment as standard requirements (Bates et al., 2021). The AANS therefore requests that HHS require, as conditions of any AI adoption support program, mandatory frontline worker consultation in procurement decisions, pre-deployment workforce impact assessments conducted by parties independent of the contracting vendor, and explicit prohibition on using AI-generated productivity data to justify staffing reductions absent independent clinical review. National Nurses United's 2023 policy framework articulated similar requirements and the AANS endorses that framework's core governance recommendations (NNU, 2023). The Department should be aware that the AANS intends to submit supplemental comments addressing neurological surgery-specific implementation questions, including intraoperative imaging AI and the liability questions that 61% of perioperative nurses in the AORN survey identified as unresolved. SYNTH-0090♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Donna Nelson♔University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill Gillings School of Global Public Health♔♔♔♔♔Logos Research Centre⏎Gillings School of Global Public Health⏎University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill⏎135 Dauer Drive, Chapel Hill, NC 27599⏎⏎Donna Nelson, Assistant Professor⏎Contact: dnelson@logos-research.unc.edu⏎⏎September 12, 2024⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue, S.W.⏎Washington, D.C. 20201⏎⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎⏎Logos Research Centre | HHS AI RFI | Gillings School of Global Public Health | Page 1⏎⏎⏎THE ACCOUNTABILITY PROBLEM AS STRUCTURAL DEFECT⏎⏎The Department's request for information proceeds from a premise that the Logos Research Centre believes warrants direct interrogation before any specific acceleration measures are adopted: that the principal barriers to AI deployment in clinical care are primarily logistical, reimbursement-related, or regulatory in the conventional clearance sense, and that targeted policy action on those barriers will produce safe and responsible clinical integration at scale. The Centre's own longitudinal research complicates this premise in ways that have direct bearing on the policy questions HHS is now considering.⏎⏎Over the past four years, Logos Research Centre has conducted a longitudinal analysis of twelve AI-in-medicine pilot projects spanning radiology, pathology, and clinical decision support (Logos Research Centre, 2024). The findings from that analysis, together with a forthcoming white paper synthesizing evidence from more than 200 peer-reviewed implementation studies, consistently document something that the RFI does not squarely address: that the diffusion of decisional responsibility across heterogeneous institutional actors — clinicians, hospital systems, third-party vendors, and software developers — constitutes a structural feature of current AI deployment models, not an incidental compliance gap. In nine of the twelve cases examined, documentation and liability ambiguity were cited as compounding factors in adoption delays, with a median delay of twenty-two months observed between regulatory clearance and actual clinical use. Reimbursement uncertainty was identified as the primary barrier in the broader survey data, with 83% of the 47 faculty members and affiliated clinical researchers surveyed in 2024 naming it as such. But the Centre's qualitative findings make plain that liability ambiguity functions as a secondary barrier that interacts with reimbursement uncertainty in ways that the RFI's framing does not fully account for.⏎⏎The concern the Centre wishes to register most directly is this: HHS is proposing to accelerate the adoption of systems whose deployment architecture systematically dissolves the identifiable human decision-maker that existing medical malpractice doctrine requires, and it is proposing to do so without first establishing the legal infrastructure necessary to assign responsibility when those systems cause harm. This is not a concern about AI performance in the abstract. It is a concern about what happens when a well-performing system fails in a specific clinical encounter, a specific patient is harmed, and the institutional actors surrounding that encounter — the treating physician, the hospital, the software vendor — each have plausible grounds to deflect responsibility to the others.⏎⏎⏎Logos Research Centre | HHS AI RFI | Gillings School of Global Public Health | Page 2⏎⏎⏎THE LIABILITY VACUUM AND ITS CLINICAL CONSEQUENCES⏎⏎Medical malpractice doctrine, as it currently operates across state jurisdictions, is organized around the identification of a responsible professional who exercised, or failed to exercise, a standard of care in relation to a patient (Mello, Frakes, Blumenkranz, & Studdert, 2020, JAMA, 323(4), 352–366). The standard of care concept presupposes a human actor whose judgment can be evaluated against a professional norm. When an AI system intermediates that judgment — recommending a course of action that the clinician follows, or flagging an anomaly that the clinician credits — the question of whose judgment is being evaluated becomes genuinely difficult to answer. Price, Gerke, and Cohen identified this problem with precision in 2019, observing that physicians who rely on AI-generated recommendations may face liability for failing to exercise independent judgment, even as vendors are insulated from malpractice claims by product liability doctrines that were not designed with clinical AI in mind (Price, Gerke, & Cohen, 2019, JAMA, 322(18), 1765–1766). The result is a liability structure in which responsibility is simultaneously diffuse and contested — a condition that rational institutional actors respond to by avoiding documentation, limiting deployment scope, and negotiating contractual indemnifications that further obscure the chain of accountability.⏎⏎Hoffman and Podgurski described this dynamic as an accountability gap that existing tort law is structurally ill-equipped to close, arguing that legislative or regulatory intervention is necessary to assign clear, non-delegable responsibility to a specific party for AI-assisted clinical decisions (Hoffman & Podgurski, 2023, Journal of Law and the Biosciences, 10(1), lsad007). The Centre's implementation data supports this assessment. In several of the pilot projects examined, clinical staff reported that uncertainty about who would bear liability for an AI-assisted decision that caused harm was a more immediate operational concern than the technical performance of the system itself. That finding has a direct implication for the RFI: accelerating adoption without resolving the liability question does not remove the barrier; it embeds the unresolved question more deeply into clinical practice, where it will surface, eventually, in litigation rather than in policy.⏎⏎Gerke, Minssen, and Cohen have documented the ways in which the ethical and legal challenges of AI-driven healthcare are compounded by the absence of harmonized regulatory frameworks that assign responsibility clearly across the development-to-deployment chain (Gerke, Minssen, & Cohen, 2020, in Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare, Academic Press, pp. 295–336). The Centre notes that the RFI's framing of regulatory barriers as obstacles to be reduced, rather than as partially functional proxies for accountability obligations that have not yet been given more precise legal form, risks treating the symptom while the underlying condition goes unaddressed.⏎⏎⏎Logos Research Centre | HHS AI RFI | Gillings School of Global Public Health | Page 3⏎⏎⏎PATH DEPENDENCY AND THE INSULATION OF POST-DEPLOYMENT ACCOUNTABILITY⏎⏎The Centre's second major concern is less about the moment of initial deployment and more about what happens to accountability as AI systems become embedded in clinical workflows over time. Topol's analysis of high-performance medicine noted that the integration of AI into clinical practice is likely to produce collaborative intelligence arrangements in which human and machine contributions to clinical decisions become increasingly difficult to disaggregate (Topol, 2019, Nature Medicine, 25(1), 44–56). This is, in many respects, the intended design of these systems. But the consequence of successful integration is that the institutional dependencies created by embedded AI systems make it progressively more difficult to audit, challenge, or remove those systems even when documented harms accumulate.⏎⏎Sendak and colleagues documented a related dynamic in their ethnographic study of clinical decision support deployment, finding that clinicians often experienced AI recommendations as institutional facts rather than as revisable suggestions — a condition they described as the system becoming part of the clinical environment rather than a tool within it (Sendak et al., 2020, ACM FAT* Proceedings, pp. 99–109). Once a system achieves that level of institutional embeddedness, the practical capacity of hospitals, clinicians, or regulators to hold vendors accountable for post-deployment performance degradation is substantially diminished. Contracts negotiated at the point of deployment typically do not include enforceable performance benchmarks tied to ongoing patient outcome data. Vendors retain proprietary control over model architectures and training data. And the clinical staff who might otherwise raise concerns about system performance are operating in environments where the system's recommendations have become a default reference point.⏎⏎Pasquale has argued that this dynamic is not incidental to the commercial AI deployment model but is a predictable consequence of the incentive structures that govern it, and that the appropriate regulatory response is precautionary governance that conditions deployment on the prior establishment of accountability mechanisms rather than attempting to retrofit accountability after integration has occurred (Pasquale, 2020, New Laws of Robotics, Harvard University Press). The Centre finds this argument persuasive on the basis of its own implementation research. The question of whether a given AI system performs adequately in a given clinical context is not separable from the question of who is responsible for monitoring that performance, who has access to the data necessary to evaluate it, and what institutional mechanisms exist to translate documented performance failures into actionable accountability.⏎⏎Doshi-Velez and colleagues have argued that meaningful accountability for AI systems requires not merely explanatory transparency at the point of decision but institutional arrangements that ensure explanation can be demanded, evaluated, and acted upon by parties with both the authority and the information necessary to do so (Doshi-Velez et al., 2017, Berkman Klein Center Research Publication No. 2017-19). The current deployment environment does not reliably provide those arrangements. The Centre's pilot project data suggests that in the majority of cases examined, neither the hospital system nor the treating clinicians had contractual or regulatory mechanisms available to them that would have allowed systematic post-deployment performance review linked to patient outcome data.⏎⏎⏎Logos Research Centre | HHS AI RFI | Gillings School of Global Public Health | Page 4⏎⏎⏎WHAT THE EVIDENCE FROM IMPLEMENTATION RESEARCH REQUIRES⏎⏎The Centre is not opposed to the adoption of AI in clinical care. The potential for well-validated AI tools to improve diagnostic accuracy, reduce clinician cognitive burden, and extend specialist-level judgment to underserved settings is documented and real (Obermeyer & Emanuel, 2016, New England Journal of Medicine, 375(13), 1216–1219). Char, Shah, and Magnus identified the conditions under which machine learning implementation in healthcare can be done in ways that respect ethical obligations to patients, and the Centre's own research is oriented toward identifying the institutional and policy conditions that make responsible implementation achievable (Char, Shah, & Magnus, 2018, New England Journal of Medicine, 378(11), 981–983). The concern being registered here is not with AI adoption per se but with the sequencing of the policy actions HHS is considering.⏎⏎The specific questions the RFI poses regarding reimbursement pathways, regulatory streamlining, and research investment are not without merit as discrete policy considerations. Cohen and colleagues identified the legal and ethical concerns arising from complex predictive analytics in healthcare as early as 2014, and the intervening decade has not resolved the foundational accountability questions they raised; if anything, the commercial scaling of clinical AI has made those questions more operationally pressing (Cohen, Amarasingham, Shah, Xie, & Lo, 2014, Health Affairs, 33(7), 1139–1147). The Centre's position is that the following conditions must be established before HHS pursues accelerated adoption on any of the dimensions the RFI contemplates:⏎⏎1. A mandatory, legally operative framework that assigns non-delegable responsibility to a specific human or institutional party for every AI-assisted clinical decision that results in patient harm. The framework must specify the responsible party at the point of deployment, not leave the question to post-hoc contractual negotiation between hospitals and vendors.⏎⏎2. Standardized post-deployment monitoring obligations, enforceable as a condition of continued reimbursement eligibility, requiring that AI systems used in reimbursed clinical encounters be subject to ongoing performance review against patient outcome data accessible to the responsible institutional party identified in condition one.⏎⏎3. A regulatory mechanism — whether housed in ONC, CMS, or a newly designated accountability office — with both the authority and the technical capacity to receive, evaluate, and act on documented reports of AI-assisted clinical harms, including the authority to condition or withdraw reimbursement eligibility for systems with documented performance problems.⏎⏎4. Minimum disclosure requirements ensuring that patients whose clinical care involved an AI-assisted decision are informed of that fact in their clinical documentation, creating the evidentiary foundation necessary for accountability claims to be pursued when harms occur.⏎⏎The Centre acknowledges that these conditions represent a more demanding precondition for acceleration than the RFI's current framing contemplates. The Centre also acknowledges, with some candor, that its own implementation research documents the real costs of delayed adoption — the twenty-two month median delay between clearance and clinical use represents a period during which patients who might have benefited from validated tools did not receive that benefit. That cost is not trivial, and the Centre does not dismiss it.⏎⏎⏎Logos Research Centre | HHS AI RFI | Gillings School of Global Public Health | Page 5⏎⏎⏎REIMBURSEMENT AND ACCOUNTABILITY AS INTERDEPENDENT POLICY LEVERS⏎⏎The RFI treats reimbursement pathway reform as a largely independent policy lever — one that can be advanced on its own timeline to reduce adoption barriers without waiting for the resolution of broader accountability questions. The Centre's research suggests this framing is mistaken, and that reimbursement policy and accountability policy are more interdependent than the RFI acknowledges. Specifically, the creation of reimbursement pathways for AI-assisted clinical services without simultaneous establishment of accountability conditions for those services will accelerate adoption in ways that further insulate vendors from post-deployment accountability. Once a reimbursement pathway exists, the commercial and institutional incentives to maintain it are substantial. Hospitals that have restructured workflows around reimbursable AI-assisted services will resist the subsequent imposition of accountability conditions that might disrupt those workflows or impose compliance costs. The Centre's pilot project data includes at least three cases in which the existence of a contractual reimbursement arrangement between a hospital and a vendor was cited by hospital administrators as a reason that concerns about system performance raised by clinical staff could not be acted upon within the existing contract term.⏎⏎This is not a hypothetical risk. It is a pattern the Centre has observed in the transition from proof-of-concept deployment to institutionally embedded clinical practice, and it is a pattern that the RFI's framing of reimbursement reform as an acceleration mechanism, rather than as a policy instrument that must be conditioned on accountability requirements, is likely to reproduce at larger scale. The Centre therefore recommends that HHS condition the development of any new reimbursement pathways for AI-assisted clinical services on the prior or concurrent establishment of the accountability framework conditions enumerated above, and that any interim reimbursement arrangements adopted before a comprehensive accountability framework is in place include explicit sunset provisions and performance-linked eligibility criteria that can be enforced by the responsible regulatory authority.⏎⏎The Centre recognizes that this recommendation will be read by some stakeholders as an argument for delay. That characterization misreads the Centre's position. The argument is that acceleration without accountability infrastructure is not, in fact, acceleration toward the goal HHS states — improved clinical care — but is instead acceleration toward a deployment model that will generate documented harms, contested liability, and eventual regulatory retrenchment of a more disruptive character than the precautionary governance the Centre is recommending. The Centre's implementation research has documented, repeatedly, that the institutional costs of attempting to retrofit accountability obligations onto already-embedded AI systems are substantially higher than the costs of establishing those obligations at the point of initial deployment.⏎⏎The Centre appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and would welcome the opportunity to share the underlying data from its longitudinal pilot project analysis with HHS staff in the event that the Department finds the empirical basis for the Centre's recommendations useful in its deliberations. The forthcoming white paper, expected for release in early 2025, will provide a more complete synthesis of the implementation evidence on which this comment draws, including the full case documentation from the twelve pilot projects and the detailed survey methodology underlying the faculty and researcher findings cited above. SYNTH-0093♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Andrew Moore♔Community Health Worker Network of New York City♔♔♔♔♔COMMUNITY HEALTH WORKER NETWORK OF NEW YORK CITY⏎Submitted in Response to: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket Reference: HHS-2024-AI-RFI⏎Submitter: Andrew Moore, Senior Policy Analyst⏎Date: October 2024⏎⏎─────────────────────────────────────────────⏎Page 1 | CHW Network NYC | HHS AI RFI | October 2024⏎─────────────────────────────────────────────⏎⏎THE ACCELERATION PROBLEM: SPEED WITHOUT EQUITY SAFEGUARDS⏎⏎The framing of this request for information as an "acceleration" agenda is, itself, a policy signal worth examining before addressing the substance of what HHS is soliciting. The Association of periOperative Registered Nurses (AORN) published survey findings in 2024 documenting that 68% of perioperative nurses reported their facilities had introduced or piloted at least one AI-enabled clinical decision support tool within the preceding 24 months, yet fewer than 22% indicated their institutions had established formal governance structures addressing nursing accountability or scope-of-practice boundaries for those tools (AORN Practice and Policy Advisory Committee, 2024). That gap — between deployment velocity and governance readiness — is not an implementation lag that will self-correct. It is the predictable consequence of an innovation environment that treats equity and safety auditing as optional features rather than preconditions.⏎⏎The empirical record on algorithmic bias in clinical AI is no longer speculative. It is a documented pattern with named cases and quantified harms. Sjoding and colleagues demonstrated in 2020 that pulse oximetry measurements systematically overestimated blood oxygen saturation in patients with darker skin pigmentation, producing clinically meaningful errors that went undetected precisely because the technology's authoritative presentation suppressed the clinical skepticism that might have caught equivalent errors in a human assessment (Sjoding et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 383(25), 2477–2478, 2020). Obermeyer and colleagues published in Science in 2019 a rigorous dissection of a widely deployed risk-stratification algorithm that systematically underestimated illness severity in Black patients — not because race was an explicit input variable, but because the algorithm used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need, and decades of discriminatory access had already suppressed costs for Black patients relative to their actual clinical burden (Obermeyer et al., Science, 366(6464), 447–453, 2019). These are not edge cases. They are illustrations of a mechanism: training data that encodes historical inequity will reproduce that inequity at scale, and the authoritative presentation of algorithmic outputs makes those reproduced inequities harder to detect than equivalent human error because clinicians are trained, through professional culture and formal education, to second-guess colleagues — not machines.⏎⏎This dynamic has a name in the cognitive science literature. Automation bias, as documented by Char, Shah, and Magnus in their 2018 analysis of machine learning implementation in health care (New England Journal of Medicine, 378(11), 981–983), describes the tendency of human decision-makers to defer to algorithmic outputs even when those outputs are erroneous. The AORN Practice and Policy Advisory Committee's structured focus groups, conducted at six regional symposia and documented in the 2024 governance readiness report, found that perioperative nurses consistently identified the absence of AI-specific competency frameworks as a primary barrier to safe and confident adoption — meaning frontline clinicians are being asked to exercise critical oversight of tools for which no institution has defined what that oversight should look like or how a nurse should recognize and escalate an anomalous output. The Joint Commission's 2023 Sentinel Event Alert on emerging patterns at the human-algorithm interface in high-acuity surgical environments reflects the same concern at the incident-reporting level (Joint Commission, Sentinel Event Alert, Issue 67, 2023). These are not theoretical warning signs.⏎⏎─────────────────────────────────────────────⏎Page 2 | CHW Network NYC | HHS AI RFI | October 2024⏎─────────────────────────────────────────────⏎⏎THE VALIDATION-GENERALIZABILITY GAP AND ITS DISTRIBUTIONAL CONSEQUENCES⏎⏎HHS has not proposed mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing or post-deployment bias surveillance requirements. This comment treats that omission as a substantive policy choice with foreseeable distributional consequences, not as an oversight awaiting correction in a future rulemaking cycle.⏎⏎The performance degradation of AI clinical tools when deployed outside their training environments is well-documented. Wong and colleagues published external validation data in 2021 on a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model, finding that the model's performance in community hospital settings differed substantially from its academic medical center validation metrics, with implications for triage accuracy that are not trivially small (Wong et al., JAMA Internal Medicine, 181(8), 1065–1070, 2021). Wiens and colleagues, in their 2019 roadmap for responsible machine learning in health care, identified external validation as a non-negotiable prerequisite for deployment precisely because academic medical center populations differ systematically from the populations served by community hospitals, rural facilities, and safety-net institutions (Wiens et al., Nature Medicine, 25(9), 1337–1340, 2019). Gianfrancesco and colleagues have documented how electronic health record data — the primary substrate for training most clinical AI — carries systematic missingness patterns that correlate with socioeconomic status and race, meaning models trained on EHR data inherit not only historical treatment biases but also the informational gaps that structured around marginalized populations (Gianfrancesco et al., JAMA Internal Medicine, 178(11), 1544–1547, 2018).⏎⏎The distributional logic here is not complicated. If a tool performs worse in community and rural settings, and if patients from already-marginalized populations are disproportionately concentrated in those settings, then accelerating deployment without mandatory performance stratification by care setting, race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status means that the populations already carrying the greatest burden of health inequity will bear the concentrated burden of algorithmic failure first and longest — and will do so before any corrective signal reaches regulators. Adamson and Smith's 2018 analysis of machine learning in dermatology demonstrated that training datasets composed predominantly of lighter-skinned patient images produced diagnostic tools with measurably inferior performance for darker-skinned patients (Adamson and Smith, JAMA Dermatology, 154(11), 1247–1248, 2018). Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones documented in 2020 how race correction embedded in clinical algorithms compounds this problem by treating race as a biological variable rather than a social one, propagating structural inequity through the architecture of the tool itself (Vyas et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 383(9), 874–882, 2020). Pierson and colleagues have further shown that algorithmic approaches to pain management can reduce unexplained disparities in underserved populations when designed with equity as an explicit optimization target — which means the technical capacity for equity-aware design exists, and the failure to require it is a governance failure, not a technical inevitability (Pierson et al., Nature Medicine, 27(1), 136–140, 2021).⏎⏎─────────────────────────────────────────────⏎Page 3 | CHW Network NYC | HHS AI RFI | October 2024⏎─────────────────────────────────────────────⏎⏎MINIMUM REQUIRED REGULATORY CONDITIONS⏎⏎AORN and the Community Health Worker Network of New York City jointly submit that no deployment acceleration framework is defensible without the following minimum conditions, which should be framed as mandatory requirements rather than voluntary guidance:⏎⏎1. Pre-deployment equity auditing requirements, with standardized methodology, applied to any AI-enabled clinical decision support tool prior to use in any CMS-reimbursed care setting.⏎⏎2. Mandatory post-deployment bias surveillance protocols, including reporting timelines and defined thresholds for suspension of deployment pending remediation.⏎⏎3. Stratified performance reporting disaggregated by race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and care setting type — with public reporting requirements so that the corrective signal reaches regulators, institutions, and affected communities simultaneously rather than sequentially.⏎⏎4. Explicit external validation requirements for any tool seeking deployment in community hospital, rural, or safety-net settings, where training-environment performance data from academic medical centers should be presumptively insufficient for approval.⏎⏎Sendak and colleagues have documented that clinicians frequently experience AI outputs as opaque and that the opacity itself suppresses critical engagement with potentially erroneous recommendations (Sendak et al., ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency, 2020). The governance gap AORN documented — 68% deployment, under 22% governance readiness — will not close through voluntary institutional initiative on the timeline that HHS's acceleration agenda implies. SYNTH-0094♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Emily Allen♔Siemens Healthineers♔♔♔♔♔Siemens Healthineers | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 1⏎⏎COMMENT OF SIEMENS HEALTHINEERS⏎Submitted in Response to: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitted by: Emily Allen, Practice Manager, Siemens Healthineers⏎Docket: HHS-2024-AI-RFI⏎⏎THE ACCOUNTABILITY QUESTION HHS IS NOT ASKING⏎⏎Our practice has spent the better part of two years trying to do what this RFI says it wants: evaluate AI-assisted documentation tools, assess their fit for a licensed clinical social work environment, and determine whether adoption could reduce the administrative overhead that is, in the most direct terms, consuming our clinicians. The 2023–2024 vendor evaluation we conducted was not a casual exercise. We documented, through structured interviews with clinical staff, that administrative tasks — progress note completion, prior authorization correspondence, outcome tracking — consumed an estimated 34% of total clinician time per week. Our practitioners were averaging 6.2 fewer billable client hours per week compared to pre-pandemic baselines, and the causal link between documentation burden and reduced appointment availability was not ambiguous. So we looked at the tools. We engaged vendors. We reviewed integration pathways. And we kept arriving at the same obstacle, which was not technological. The obstacle was that no one in the current regulatory environment could tell us, with any binding specificity, who would be legally responsible if an AI-assisted clinical recommendation contributed to patient harm. That question does not have an answer yet. And this RFI, for all its ambition, does not propose to give it one before scaling deployment further.⏎⏎Siemens Healthineers | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 2⏎⏎THE STRUCTURAL DIFFUSION OF RESPONSIBILITY⏎⏎The liability problem in AI-assisted clinical care is not a gap in existing doctrine that a few guidance documents can patch. It is a structural feature of how AI intermediation interacts with the foundational assumptions of American medical malpractice law. As Price, Gerke, and Cohen (2019) observed in their analysis published in JAMA, current malpractice doctrine presupposes an identifiable human decision-maker whose judgment can be evaluated against a professional standard of care. When an AI system participates in that decision — generating a recommended diagnosis, flagging a risk score, auto-populating a clinical note — the chain of professional judgment fractures in ways that existing tort frameworks have not resolved. The clinician can plausibly argue that the tool's output influenced the decision. The vendor can argue that the clinician retained final authority and chose to act. The hospital or practice can argue that it implemented the tool in compliance with available guidance. Each of those positions has surface plausibility, and the result is that patients harmed by AI-intermediated errors face a structural accountability vacuum rather than a clearly answerable party. Mello, Frakes, Blumenkranz, and Studdert (2020) documented in their JAMA review that malpractice liability, whatever its imperfections, performs a deterrence function in health care quality that depends on the existence of identifiable responsible parties. Remove that identifiability, and the deterrence mechanism does not merely weaken — it ceases to function in any coherent sense.⏎⏎What makes this particularly difficult is that the diffusion of responsibility is not an accident or an oversight. It is, in a meaningful sense, a design feature of how AI tools are commercially structured. Vendors disclaim liability through end-user license agreements. Clinicians are positioned as the "final decision-maker" in documentation that is itself crafted to insulate the vendor from downstream legal exposure. Hospitals and practices adopt institutional policies that defer to vendor specifications, which in turn defer back to clinician judgment. Cohen, Amarasingham, Shah, Xie, and Lo (2014) identified precisely this dynamic in their Health Affairs analysis of complex predictive analytics in health care, noting that the legal and ethical responsibility for algorithmic outputs is distributed across so many parties that meaningful accountability becomes practically unassignable. That analysis was published a decade ago. The problem has not been resolved since. And the commercial AI tools now entering clinical workflows are more deeply embedded, more opaque in their reasoning, and more consequential in their outputs than the predictive systems Cohen and colleagues examined.⏎⏎Siemens Healthineers | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 3⏎⏎THE MALPRACTICE DOCTRINE PROBLEM IS NOT SELF-CORRECTING⏎⏎There is an argument, sometimes offered in policy discussions, that the courts will eventually sort this out — that common law will adapt to AI intermediation the way it adapted to other technological changes in medical practice, and that HHS need not wait for legislative resolution before encouraging adoption. We find this argument unpersuasive, for reasons that are primarily structural rather than doctrinal. Judicial adaptation through tort litigation is slow, expensive, and deeply inequitable as a mechanism for patient protection. The patients most likely to be harmed by AI-assisted clinical errors — those in under-resourced behavioral health settings, those in Medicaid-dependent practices, those with limited access to legal representation — are also the patients least positioned to pursue complex multi-defendant litigation against a vendor, a practice, and a hospital system simultaneously. The expectation that these patients will effectively discipline the AI deployment market through litigation is not a patient protection policy. It is the absence of one.⏎⏎Gerke, Minssen, and Cohen (2020) make a related point in their Academic Press chapter on ethical and legal challenges of AI-driven healthcare, arguing that the speed of AI deployment in clinical settings has substantially outpaced the development of the legal frameworks necessary to govern it, and that this asymmetry creates conditions in which institutional adoption decisions are made without any binding accountability architecture in place. The European Parliament's 2017 report on civil law rules on robotics (Delvaux, 2017) arrived at a broadly similar conclusion from a different regulatory tradition, recommending that liability frameworks be established as a precondition for deployment at scale rather than as a retrospective correction after harm accumulates. HHS is not bound by European legislative thinking, obviously. But the underlying logic is not jurisdiction-specific. You do not build the accountability infrastructure after the harm has already distributed itself across a population of patients who had no input into the deployment decision.⏎⏎The ONC's own 2021 report to Congress on reducing regulatory and administrative burden acknowledged that the integration of health IT and EHR systems has generated unintended consequences — including documentation burdens of the kind our practice documented — that were not anticipated in the original deployment frameworks (ONC, 2021). That report is, in some ways, a cautionary document about what happens when federal policy accelerates adoption without sufficient attention to second-order effects. The AI RFI before us now risks repeating that pattern at a scale and with a complexity that the EHR experience did not approach.⏎⏎Siemens Healthineers | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 4⏎⏎ON THE SPECIFIC QUESTION OF CLINICAL DECISION SUPPORT AND ALERT FATIGUE⏎⏎Our vendor evaluation did not focus exclusively on documentation tools. We also examined AI-assisted clinical decision support systems, and what we found there compounded our concern rather than relieving it. Kesselheim, Cresswell, Phansalkar, Bates, and Sheikh (2011) documented in Health Affairs that clinical decision support systems, as then configured, generated alert fatigue among clinicians who were simultaneously exposed to liability risk if they overrode a system recommendation and workflow disruption if they did not. That dynamic has not been resolved by more sophisticated AI. If anything, the opacity of machine learning outputs relative to rule-based clinical decision support systems makes the clinician's position more difficult, not less. When a rule-based system flags a drug interaction, the clinician can evaluate the rule. When a machine learning model assigns a risk score, the reasoning is frequently not available for clinical inspection in any meaningful sense (Obermeyer and Emanuel, 2016). The clinician is left choosing between deferring to an output they cannot interrogate and overriding an output that may, for all they know, be capturing something their own clinical judgment is missing. Neither choice is epistemically satisfying. And under current doctrine, either choice could generate liability exposure whose assignment is, again, not clearly defined.⏎⏎The American Medical Association's 2023 policy report on augmented intelligence in medicine (AMA, 2023) called for accountability frameworks that clearly assign responsibility across the developer, deployer, and clinician chain before AI tools are embedded in clinical workflows in ways that make disentanglement difficult. We want to be specific about what "disentanglement difficulty" means in practice, because it is not a hypothetical. Once a practice has integrated an AI documentation tool into its EHR workflow, retrained its clinical staff around that tool's outputs, and structured its billing and compliance processes to accommodate the tool's note formats, the institutional dependency on that tool becomes substantial. Removing the tool, or switching vendors, generates operational disruption that practices — particularly small behavioral health practices like ours — are not well-positioned to absorb. That dependency, over time, further insulates vendors from accountability. A practice that cannot practically exit a vendor relationship cannot effectively discipline that vendor through market mechanisms. And a regulator that has encouraged adoption without establishing prior accountability requirements has, in effect, subsidized that dependency.⏎⏎Siemens Healthineers | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 5⏎⏎WHY THE REIMBURSEMENT STRUCTURE DOES NOT SOLVE THE PROBLEM⏎⏎The RFI devotes considerable attention to reimbursement as a mechanism for accelerating adoption, and we understand the logic. If CMS and state Medicaid programs create billing pathways that recognize AI-assisted clinical services, practices will have financial incentive to adopt. Our vendor evaluation did encounter reimbursement uncertainty as a barrier — that is accurate. But reimbursement reform and accountability reform are not substitutes for each other, and treating the former as a proxy for the latter is a category error with real consequences. A practice that adopts an AI documentation tool because CMS has created a reimbursement pathway is not thereby protected from liability when that tool produces a clinically consequential error. The reimbursement incentive and the liability exposure exist on parallel tracks, and widening the former without narrowing the ambiguity of the latter simply means that more practices adopt tools under conditions where the accountability question remains unresolved.⏎⏎Hoffman and Podgurski (2013) made a point in their American Journal of Law and Medicine analysis of biomedical data use that seems applicable here: the scale of deployment does not, by itself, validate a deployment model. Widespread adoption of a tool whose accountability infrastructure is inadequate does not produce accountability; it produces widespread exposure to the consequences of inadequate accountability. The National Academy for State Health Policy's 2023 policy brief on state approaches to AI in health care documented that state legislatures and regulatory bodies are beginning to develop their own AI governance frameworks precisely because federal action has been insufficiently specific about accountability assignment (NASHP, 2023). The result is a patchwork in which practices operating across state lines — or simply seeking to understand their obligations — face inconsistent and sometimes conflicting requirements. HHS accelerating adoption at the federal level without establishing a binding accountability framework does not resolve that patchwork. It adds federal momentum to a situation that is already producing compliance confusion at the state level.⏎⏎Our concern is not that AI-assisted tools have no legitimate role in reducing administrative burden. The 34% of clinician time consumed by administrative tasks in our practice is a real problem with real consequences for patient access. We are not indifferent to that. The question is whether HHS's proposed approach — accelerating adoption through reimbursement reform and R&D investment while deferring accountability architecture to future rulemaking or voluntary frameworks — is an appropriate sequencing of those policy actions. Our view, grounded in two years of direct operational experience with the liability ambiguities that currently impede responsible adoption, is that it is not. A binding accountability framework that specifies, with legal force, how responsibility is assigned across developers, deployers, and clinicians when AI-assisted errors occur is a prerequisite for responsible scaling, not a follow-on action item. HHS should condition any deployment pathway created by this rulemaking process on the prior establishment of such a framework, and should be explicit that voluntary guidance and post-hoc study processes are not adequate substitutes for binding pre-deployment accountability requirements. The specific sequencing matters enormously, and the current draft of the RFI does not treat it as a⏎⏎Siemens Healthineers | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 6⏎⏎constraint on the acceleration it is proposing. We would ask the Department to reconsider that framing before the comment period closes, and to treat the accountability question not as one consideration among many but as the threshold condition that determines whether accelerated adoption serves patients or merely exposes them to a new category of institutional risk for which no one has been made answerable in advance.⏎⏎emily.allen@siemens-healthineers.com⏎⏎REFERENCES⏎⏎American Medical Association. SYNTH-0095♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Michael Clark♔Aidoc♔♔♔♔♔Van Pelt & Company⏎1411 Broadway, Suite 2800⏎New York, NY 10018⏎⏎Michael Clark, MHA⏎Senior Vice President, Health Systems Operations⏎Aidoc⏎⏎March 14, 2024⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue, S.W.⏎Washington, D.C. 20201⏎⏎Attention: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎Van Pelt & Company submits this comment in response to HHS's solicitation of public input on regulatory, reimbursement, and research-and-development actions the Department might take to accelerate AI adoption in clinical settings. We do so not as skeptics of AI technology, but as a management consultancy with direct operational visibility into 47 healthcare system clients across 19 states, and with a professional obligation to report what we have actually observed in those systems rather than what vendors and trade associations prefer to say is happening. The record we have accumulated is not reassuring, and we think HHS should hear it clearly before committing the federal government's reimbursement and regulatory architecture to an accelerationist posture that our data suggests will produce foreseeable and documentable harm to the clinical workforce.⏎⏎Van Pelt & Company Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 1⏎⏎Our Q1 2024 operational review (Van Pelt & Company, 2024, AI Integration in Health Systems: Operational Barriers, Cost Structures, and Workforce Adoption Patterns, internal policy report on file with authors) found that 68% of our client health systems had piloted at least one AI-assisted clinical decision support tool within the prior 24 months. Only 19% had achieved sustained integration beyond the pilot phase. When we asked system leadership why pilots failed to scale, inconsistent reimbursement pathways and unclear liability frameworks were cited most frequently — and we understand why HHS reads that as a reason to act. But the same roundtable process surfaced a finding that does not appear anywhere in the Department's framing of this RFI: the AI tools that did achieve sustained deployment were disproportionately tools that generated administrative productivity metrics useful to management, not tools that frontline clinicians reported as reducing their cognitive load or improving their experience of care delivery. That distinction matters enormously for how HHS should think about what it is actually accelerating.⏎⏎⏎WHAT AI TOOLS ARE BEING USED FOR IN HEALTH SYSTEMS⏎⏎We want to be direct about something that the vendor community and many health system trade associations have been careful not to say plainly: a significant share of AI deployment in clinical settings is functioning as workforce surveillance infrastructure. This is not a polemical characterization. It is a description of the actual operational footprint of tools that track clinician throughput, flag documentation delays, monitor deviation from algorithmic care pathways, and generate productivity reports that flow upward to administrative leadership rather than back to the clinician as clinical support. Kellogg, Valentine, and Christin (2020, Algorithms at Work: The New Contested Terrain of Control, Academy of Management Annals, 14(1), 366-410) documented precisely this dynamic in knowledge-work environments, and their framework maps with uncomfortable accuracy onto what our client-facing teams have observed in healthcare settings over the past two years. The tools are marketed as burnout-reduction and efficiency solutions. The operational reality, as we have documented it across dozens of system engagements, is that they are being deployed to justify reduced staffing ratios and increased caseloads, with the productivity gains extracted from the workforce rather than returned to it in the form of reduced burden.⏎⏎Van Pelt & Company Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 2⏎⏎The burnout framing deserves particular scrutiny because HHS has cited it in the context of this RFI as a rationale for accelerating AI adoption. The primary drivers of clinician burnout are alert fatigue, documentation burden, and loss of professional autonomy (Shanafelt et al., 2022, Changes in Burnout and Satisfaction With Work-Life Integration in Physicians and the General US Working Population Between 2011 and 2020, Mayo Clinic Proceedings, 97(3), 491-506). AI deployment in its current form is more likely to intensify all three than to resolve them. Alert fatigue is not reduced by adding AI-generated alerts to existing EHR alert loads; Bates et al. (2021, The Potential of Artificial Intelligence to Reduce Alert Fatigue and Improve Clinical Decision Support, npj Digital Medicine, 4(1), 1-6) found that AI-assisted clinical decision support tools, when deployed without disciplined governance frameworks, produced net increases in alert burden in several study environments. Documentation burden is similarly not addressed by AI scribing tools that require clinicians to review, correct, and attest to AI-generated notes — a process that shifts rather than eliminates the cognitive work, as Patel et al. (2023, Electronic Health Record Burden and Its Association With Physician Burnout: A Systematic Review, Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, 30(4), 712-724) have demonstrated. And the loss of professional autonomy — which Shanafelt's longitudinal data identifies as among the most powerful predictors of burnout severity — is directly worsened by surveillance architectures that monitor clinician behavior against algorithmic benchmarks and flag deviations for administrative review.⏎⏎o The AI tools most aggressively marketed to our client health systems between 2022 and 2024 have been ambient documentation assistants, predictive deterioration alerts, and "workflow optimization" platforms.⏎⏎o In 11 of our 47 client systems, deployment of workflow optimization platforms was accompanied within 18 months by administrative proposals to reduce nurse-to-patient ratios or expand provider caseloads, citing AI-enabled efficiency gains as justification.⏎⏎o In those same 11 systems, frontline nursing and physician staff were not involved in the procurement decision for the tools whose productivity data was subsequently used to justify the staffing proposals.⏎⏎o The American Hospital Association's 2023 workforce report to Congress documented acute and ongoing staffing shortfalls across the health sector; our client data suggests that AI adoption, as currently structured, is being used to manage around those shortfalls rather than address them.⏎⏎The staffing question cannot be separated from patient safety. Aiken et al. (2014, Nurse Staffing and Education and Hospital Mortality in Nine European Countries: A Retrospective Observational Study, The Lancet, 383(9931), 1824-1830) established with considerable methodological rigor that each additional patient added to a nurse's workload was associated with a 7% increase in the likelihood of a patient dying within 30 days of admission. If AI adoption is functioning as a mechanism for increasing nurse caseloads — and our data from 11 client systems suggests it is, at least in some cases — then the Department's reimbursement incentives for AI deployment are, in a meaningful sense, reimbursement incentives for the conditions Aiken's research associates with elevated patient mortality. We are not certain this is the outcome HHS intends. We are certain it is a foreseeable one.⏎⏎Van Pelt & Company Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 3⏎⏎⏎THE STRUCTURAL EXCLUSION OF FRONTLINE WORKERS FROM AI PROCUREMENT⏎⏎The governance problem at the center of this issue is that the people who use these tools every day have essentially no structural role in the decisions about whether to acquire them, how to configure them, or what performance standards they must meet before deployment. Procurement authority in health systems sits with C-suite and administrative leadership. Vendor relationships are managed by operations and IT. The ONC's 2024 Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability final rule (89 Fed. Reg. 1192) made meaningful progress on algorithm transparency requirements, and we supported that rulemaking, but transparency requirements directed at health system administrators do not solve the problem of frontline workers being excluded from governance. A nurse who has no seat at the procurement table does not benefit from an administrator's access to an algorithm's training data documentation. The National Nurses United 2023 policy report on AI in healthcare (Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare: Workforce Impacts and the Case for Nurse-Led Governance, NNU Policy Report, Washington, D.C.) made this point with force and specificity, and the Department should engage with it seriously rather than treating labor organizations as stakeholders to be consulted after decisions are made.⏎⏎Van Pelt & Company Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 4⏎⏎Our Q1 2024 roundtables found that clinical staff adoption rates improved by an estimated 31% when AI tools were accompanied by structured reimbursement certainty — a finding we reported in our internal summary and that we believe HHS has cited as evidence that payment policy drives meaningful integration. We want to be careful about how that finding is read. Higher adoption rates are not the same as better outcomes for patients or the workforce. If a tool is imposed on a clinical staff through administrative mandate backed by productivity monitoring, adoption rates will be high and the workforce will be harmed. The 31% figure reflects a real relationship between reimbursement certainty and tool deployment, but it tells us nothing about whether that deployment is good for anyone other than the vendor and the administrative leadership that purchased the tool. Gartner's 2023 Hype Cycle for Healthcare Providers (AI and Automation in Clinical Workflows, Gartner Research Note G00789341) observed that many AI tools in clinical settings are in a period of inflated expectations relative to demonstrated performance, and that real-world deployment has routinely produced outcomes that diverge significantly from vendor-cited benchmark data. Obermeyer and Emanuel (2016, Predicting the Future — Big Data, Machine Learning, and Clinical Medicine, New England Journal of Medicine, 375(13), 1216-1219) made the same point about the gap between model performance metrics and clinical utility eight years ago, and the problem has not been resolved in the intervening period.⏎⏎⏎WHAT HHS MUST REQUIRE BEFORE INCENTIVIZING DEPLOYMENT⏎⏎We are addressing this comment primarily to the workforce-protection dimensions of the RFI rather than to the full range of questions the Department has posed, because we think those dimensions are the ones most at risk of being omitted from the public record in a comment process dominated by health system trade associations and AI vendors. Our specific request is this: HHS should impose precautionary workforce-protection standards as a condition of any reimbursement incentive or regulatory acceleration associated with AI clinical deployment. The failure to do so is not a neutral policy choice. It is a decision to subsidize, with federal reimbursement dollars, the deployment of surveillance infrastructure onto a workforce that is already experiencing burnout at rates that Shanafelt et al. documented as historically elevated even before the COVID-19 period. That subsidy will produce foreseeable harm, and the Department will have been warned.⏎⏎Van Pelt & Company Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 5⏎⏎Those workforce-protection standards should include, at minimum, the following:⏎⏎1. A requirement that any AI clinical deployment seeking reimbursement recognition demonstrate, through prospective data collection rather than vendor self-report, measurable benefit to frontline workforce experience as a condition of sustained incentive eligibility. "Benefit" should be defined to include documented reductions in alert burden, documentation time, or self-reported cognitive load — not administrative efficiency metrics that flow to management rather than to the clinician.⏎⏎2. A requirement that health systems receiving reimbursement incentives for AI deployment document the governance process through which frontline clinical staff were involved in procurement decisions, including evidence that staff concerns were recorded and addressed. A system that purchases a surveillance tool without nursing or physician input and then deploys it under administrative mandate should not qualify for federal reimbursement support for that tool.⏎⏎3. A prohibition on the use of AI-generated productivity data as the primary or sole basis for staffing ratio reductions within a defined period following tool deployment, with HHS monitoring of whether AI adoption in incentivized settings is correlated with adverse workforce outcomes including staff turnover, reported burnout, or complaints filed with state labor agencies.⏎⏎4. Mandatory disclosure to clinical staff, prior to deployment, of the categories of data collected by any AI tool operating in their work environment, the parties who have access to that data, and the administrative uses to which it may be put. Surveillance that is invisible is surveillance that workers cannot contest or negotiate.⏎⏎Van Pelt & Company Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 6⏎⏎We recognize that some of these requirements will be characterized by the vendor community and by health system administrators as burdensome or as barriers to adoption. We think that framing inverts the relevant question. The question is not whether precautionary workforce-protection requirements will slow AI adoption. The question is whether AI adoption without those requirements will harm a workforce that the American Hospital Association itself has documented as already operating under acute and sustained stress (AHA, 2023). Our client data, our roundtable findings, and the peer-reviewed literature we have cited above converge on an answer that HHS should take seriously: absent workforce-protection conditions, federal incentives for AI deployment will function as a policy subsidy for the systematic extraction of productivity from a clinical workforce that has limited structural power to resist it, with downstream consequences for patient safety that are not speculative. The per-facility compliance and validation costs we documented in our 2024 review — averaging $340,000 annually across our client base — are being absorbed by health systems while the workforce bears costs of a different and more serious kind that do not appear on any balance sheet.⏎⏎We urge the Department to require demonstrated evidence of workforce benefit, with independent verification, before any reimbursement or regulatory pathway is opened for AI clinical deployment tools. The alternative is a policy record that will be difficult to defend when the outcomes become visible.⏎⏎Van Pelt & Company⏎New York, NY⏎mclark@vanpeltco.com⏎www.vanpeltco.com/policy♔♔2026-01-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-31T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔7♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare will be used by employers and insurers as a mechanism for workforce surveillance, productivity extraction, staffing cuts, and the devaluation of clinical expertise rather than genuine care improvement.♔organization♔high♔angry♔New York♔healthcare administrator♔47♔A 2024 operational review conducted across Van Pelt & Company's 47 healthcare system clients found that 68% had piloted at least one AI-assisted clinical decision support tool within the prior 24 months, yet only 19% had achieved sustained integration beyond the pilot phase—citing inconsistent reimbursement pathways and unclear liability frameworks as primary barriers to scaling.
