SYNTH-0096♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔William Mitchell♔Partnership for AI in Health♔♔♔♔♔Partnership for AI in Health⏎1400 K Street NW, Suite 700⏎Washington, DC 20005⏎government.affairs@partnershipforaihealth.org⏎⏎October 14, 2024⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue SW⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎Attention: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎Re: Comments of the Partnership for AI in Health on the HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information, Docket No. HHS-OD-2024-AI-RFI⏎⏎⏎Partnership for AI in Health | HHS AI RFI Comments | October 2024 | Page 1⏎⏎⏎The Partnership for AI in Health (the Partnership) submits these comments in response to the Department of Health and Human Services' Request for Information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings. The Partnership is a national advocacy organization representing radiology practices, hospital-based imaging programs, and health system administrators across 47 states, with a particular focus on the operational and policy conditions that govern AI deployment in clinical workflows. These comments address specifically the equity and safety dimensions of the Department's proposed acceleration agenda, and the near-total absence from the RFI of any mandatory framework for auditing algorithmic bias before deployment or monitoring for disparate harm after deployment. The Partnership does not oppose the goal of accelerating beneficial AI adoption. We are, however, compelled by the empirical record to register serious institutional concern that the posture reflected in this RFI will, if adopted without modification, produce systematic and foreseeable harm concentrated precisely in the communities and institutions that are already the most underserved.⏎⏎The basis for that concern is not theoretical. In a 2024 survey of 412 radiology practice administrators conducted in partnership with the Radiology Business Management Association, the Partnership found that 67 percent of responding practices had deployed at least one FDA-cleared AI algorithm in clinical workflows. Of those practices, 58 percent reported that existing reimbursement structures failed to account for the additional physician oversight and workflow integration costs associated with AI-assisted interpretation. More relevant to the equity question this comment addresses: among practices in rural and safety-net markets, AI adoption rates lagged urban counterparts by nearly 24 percentage points, and inadequate coding pathways were cited as the primary barrier in 71 percent of those rural responses. That adoption gap is not, in itself, the problem the Partnership is raising here. The problem is that the practices most likely to adopt AI first — urban academic medical centers with the technical infrastructure, revenue, and research capacity to evaluate and integrate these tools — are also the practices least representative of the patient populations where algorithmic bias tends to cause the most severe harm. When HHS accelerates adoption without equity conditions, it is in effect accelerating the diffusion of systems validated in one population context into care settings serving entirely different patient populations, without any mandatory mechanism for detecting when those systems fail.⏎⏎⏎Partnership for AI in Health | HHS AI RFI Comments | October 2024 | Page 2⏎⏎⏎SECTION I: BIAS IS ENCODED IN TRAINING DATA AND REPRODUCED AT SCALE⏎⏎The foundational problem is structural, not incidental. AI systems trained on historical healthcare data do not merely reflect the past — they operationalize it. The documented literature makes clear that decades of discriminatory treatment patterns are embedded in the electronic health record data on which most clinical AI systems are trained. Obermeyer and colleagues, writing in Science in 2019, demonstrated that a widely used commercial algorithm for managing population health systematically underestimated the illness severity of Black patients relative to white patients with equivalent clinical need, because the algorithm used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need — and Black patients, due to longstanding barriers to access, had historically generated lower costs even when equally sick (Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S., "Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations," Science, 2019;366(6464):447-453). The algorithm did not intend to discriminate. It learned to discriminate from data generated by a healthcare system that already discriminated. That distinction matters enormously for regulatory design, because it means bias auditing cannot be satisfied by reviewing the code or the intent of the developers. It requires examining model outputs stratified by race, ethnicity, sex, primary language, socioeconomic status, and geography — before deployment, not after harm has accumulated.⏎⏎Gianfrancesco and colleagues have further documented how electronic health record data used to train machine learning models carries systematic missingness and measurement error that is non-randomly distributed across patient populations, such that models trained on these data will encode the biases of documentation practices, diagnostic access, and care-seeking behavior in ways that are invisible to developers who do not explicitly test for them (Gianfrancesco MA, Tamang S, Yazdany J, Schmajuk G., "Potential biases in machine learning algorithms using electronic health record data," JAMA Intern Med., 2018;178(11):1544-1547). Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones have separately documented how the incorporation of race as a variable in clinical algorithms — including in widely used tools like the estimated glomerular filtration rate equation, prior versions of which assigned higher kidney function scores to Black patients and thereby delayed nephrology referral — produces systematic undertreatment of minority populations while appearing, on average performance metrics, to function normally (Vyas DA, Eisenstein LG, Jones DS., "Hidden in plain sight — reconsidering the use of race correction in clinical algorithms," N Engl J Med., 2020;383(9):874-882). The point the Partnership draws from this body of work is not that AI is uniquely dangerous. It is that AI systems trained on compromised data will reproduce and scale the harms embedded in that data, and that FDA clearance based on average diagnostic accuracy metrics provides no assurance whatsoever that a system performs equitably across patient subgroups.⏎⏎⏎Partnership for AI in Health | HHS AI RFI Comments | October 2024 | Page 3⏎⏎⏎SECTION II: AVERAGE PERFORMANCE METRICS CONCEAL CATASTROPHIC FAILURES IN MARGINALIZED POPULATIONS⏎⏎This is the point that the RFI's framing of "accelerating adoption" most conspicuously fails to reckon with. A system can achieve 92 percent sensitivity on a held-out test set while performing at 74 percent sensitivity for a specific demographic subgroup — and both numbers can be technically accurate. The system clears its regulatory threshold. It gets deployed. It gets reimbursed. And in the emergency department of a safety-net hospital in Fresno or rural Mississippi, it is quietly missing diagnoses at a rate that would be considered unacceptable if anyone were measuring it.⏎⏎The sepsis prediction literature is particularly instructive on this point. Wong and colleagues published an external validation of a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model — the Epic Sepsis Model — across more than 27,000 hospitalizations at the University of Michigan Health System and found that the model had a positive predictive value of only 12.8 percent, that it missed 67 percent of sepsis cases identified by the Sepsis-3 definition, and that its performance was materially worse in patient subpopulations underrepresented in its training data (Wong A, Otles E, Donnelly JP, et al., "External validation of a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model in hospitalized patients," JAMA Intern Med., 2021;181(8):1065-1070). This model had been deployed in hundreds of hospitals before that external validation was published. The question the Partnership puts to HHS is: what regulatory mechanism would have detected that failure before hundreds of thousands of patient-encounters had been processed through a model that did not work as advertised? The RFI does not answer that question because the RFI does not ask it.⏎⏎Seyyed-Kalantari and colleagues examined chest radiograph AI algorithms applied to datasets from three large academic medical centers and found that underserved patient populations — defined by insurance status, self-reported race and ethnicity, and sex — were systematically underdiagnosed by the AI models relative to their actual pathology burden, and that this underdiagnosis bias persisted even when controlling for image quality and clinical presentation (Seyyed-Kalantari L, Zhang H, McDermott MBA, Chen IY, Ghassemi M., "Underdiagnosis bias of artificial intelligence algorithms applied to chest radiographs in under-served patient populations," Nat Med., 2021;27(12):2176-2182). Radiology is the Partnership's home domain, and this finding is one our member practices cannot set aside. When an AI-assisted chest radiograph interpretation system misses findings at higher rates in Medicaid patients than in commercially insured patients, that is not a technical artifact to be corrected in the next model version. That is a patient safety failure occurring in real time, in the exact settings — community hospitals, federally qualified health centers, rural critical access hospitals — where the Partnership's survey data shows AI adoption is already lagging and where radiologist coverage is thinnest.⏎⏎⏎Partnership for AI in Health | HHS AI RFI Comments | October 2024 | Page 4⏎⏎⏎SECTION III: AUTOMATION BIAS SUPPRESSES THE ERROR-CORRECTION MECHANISMS THAT MIGHT OTHERWISE CATCH THESE FAILURES⏎⏎There is a second-order problem that compounds the first. Even when AI systems produce errors, clinicians who work alongside AI outputs are systematically less likely to catch and correct those errors than they would be if they had made the same assessment unaided. This is automation bias — the well-documented tendency of human operators to over-rely on algorithmic outputs, particularly when those outputs are presented with apparent confidence and quantitative precision. Char, Shah, and Magnus, writing in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2018, identified automation bias as one of the central ethical challenges of clinical AI implementation, noting that clinicians trained to treat algorithmic outputs as authoritative decision support may effectively abdicate the independent clinical judgment that serves as the primary error-correction mechanism in human medicine (Char DS, Shah NH, Magnus D., "Implementing machine learning in health care — addressing ethical challenges," N Engl J Med., 2018;378(11):981-983). The authoritative appearance of AI outputs — the confidence score, the visual overlay, the EHR alert — is precisely what makes them useful to clinicians under time pressure. It is also precisely what makes the errors they produce harder to catch.⏎⏎The automation bias problem has a specific interaction with algorithmic bias that the Partnership finds particularly troubling. If an AI system systematically underestimates illness severity in Black patients, and if the clinicians using that system have been conditioned to treat its outputs as reliable, then the system does not merely reproduce a disparity — it creates a clinical environment in which the disparity is less likely to be noticed and challenged than equivalent human error would be. A physician who makes a clinical judgment that later proves wrong is subject to peer review, quality assurance processes, and the patient's own advocacy. An AI system that systematically underperforms for a demographic subgroup produces a pattern of harm that is distributed across thousands of encounters, attributed to no individual clinician, and invisible in aggregate quality metrics unless someone is specifically looking for it. The Partnership's concern is that HHS's acceleration agenda will substantially increase the number of clinical encounters processed through AI systems, while doing nothing to increase the probability that systematic disparate harm will be detected.⏎⏎⏎Partnership for AI in Health | HHS AI RFI Comments | October 2024 | Page 5⏎⏎⏎SECTION IV: VALIDATION STUDIES CONDUCTED IN ACADEMIC CENTERS DO NOT GENERALIZE TO THE COMMUNITY AND RURAL SETTINGS WHERE DISPARITIES ARE ALREADY WORST⏎⏎The Partnership recognizes that this concern is not novel. The generalizability problem in clinical AI has been documented extensively. Nagendran and colleagues conducted a systematic review of 81 deep learning studies in medical imaging published through 2019 and found that the overwhelming majority were conducted on retrospective datasets from major academic medical centers, that external validation in independent populations was rare, and that claims of performance equivalence or superiority to clinicians were frequently unsupported by the study designs used to generate them (Nagendran M, Chen Y, Lovejoy CA, et al., "Artificial intelligence versus clinicians: systematic review of design, reporting standards, and claims of deep learning studies in medical imaging," BMJ, 2020;368:m689). The datasets used in these studies skew heavily toward patients who are insured, English-speaking, and receiving care at institutions with high documentation quality — which is to say, they systematically underrepresent the patients in whom algorithmic bias is most likely to cause harm.⏎⏎Wiens and colleagues, writing in Nature Medicine in 2019, articulated a responsible machine learning roadmap for healthcare that specifically flagged the gap between academic validation and real-world deployment performance as a structural risk requiring prospective monitoring and outcome tracking after deployment, not merely pre-deployment validation studies (Wiens J, Saria S, Sendak M, et al., "Do no harm: a roadmap for responsible machine learning for health care," Nat Med., 2019;25(9):1337-1340). That roadmap was published five years ago. The Partnership is not aware that HHS has operationalized any of its core recommendations in the form of regulatory requirements applicable to clinical AI systems receiving Medicare or Medicaid reimbursement. The RFI does not indicate that HHS intends to do so now.⏎⏎The generalizability problem is particularly acute in radiology, and the Partnership's survey data speaks directly to it. Radiology AI algorithms are typically validated on imaging datasets from large academic programs — UCSF, Mass General, Mayo — that use standardized imaging protocols, high-field MRI equipment, and patient populations that skew toward higher socioeconomic status relative to the national Medicaid population. When those algorithms are deployed in a 25-bed critical access hospital in rural Montana using a ten-year-old CT scanner and serving a predominantly Native American patient population, the performance characteristics documented in the validation study may bear no relationship to actual clinical performance. The Partnership's member practices in these settings have no mechanism for knowing whether the AI tools they are deploying are performing as validated. There is no post-deployment surveillance requirement. There is no standardized reporting pathway. There is no feedback loop from clinical outcome to algorithm performance. The RFI proposes to accelerate adoption into exactly these settings without addressing any of these gaps.⏎⏎⏎Partnership for AI in Health | HHS AI RFI Comments | October 2024 | Page 6⏎⏎⏎SECTION V: DOCUMENTED EXAMPLES FROM ADJACENT CLINICAL DOMAINS CONFIRM THAT THIS IS AN OBSERVED PATTERN, NOT A THEORETICAL RISK⏎⏎The Partnership wants to be precise about what the empirical record shows, because the Department's RFI appears to treat algorithmic bias as a concern to be noted rather than an observed failure mode requiring mandatory safeguards. The pulse oximetry literature is probably the clearest example of what unmonitored algorithmic bias looks like in clinical practice. Sjoding and colleagues, writing in the New England Journal of Medicine in December 2020, documented that pulse oximeters — devices that have been in clinical use for decades — systematically overestimated blood oxygen saturation in Black patients relative to white patients with equivalent arterial oxygen levels, and that this measurement error was associated with occult hypoxemia that went undetected and untreated at materially higher rates in Black patients (Sjoding MW, Dickson RP, Iwashyna TJ, Gay SE, Valley TS., "Racial bias in pulse oximetry measurement," N Engl J Med., 2020;383(25):2477-2478). This was not a novel algorithmic system. This was a mature, FDA-cleared medical device that had been in widespread clinical use for thirty-plus years. The disparity it produced had almost certainly been occurring throughout that period. It was detected when researchers looked for it. The regulatory and reimbursement systems that governed pulse oximetry deployment had never required anyone to look for it.⏎⏎The dermatology AI literature tells a similar story. Adamson and Smith, writing in JAMA Dermatology in 2018, documented that machine learning algorithms for skin lesion classification were trained predominantly on images of lighter-skinned patients, and that their diagnostic accuracy for melanoma and other skin cancers in patients with darker skin tones was substantially lower — a finding with direct life-or-death implications given that delayed melanoma diagnosis in patients of color is already a documented disparity (Adamson AS, Smith A., "Machine learning and health care disparities in dermatology," JAMA Dermatol., 2018;154(11):1247-1248). And Pierson and colleagues have documented that AI-based pain assessment tools trained on historical prescribing data systematically underestimate pain severity in Black and Hispanic patients, reproducing at scale the well-documented clinical pattern of undertreating pain in minority populations (Pierson E, Cutler DM, Leskovec J, Mullainathan S, Obermeyer Z., "An algorithmic approach to reducing unexplained pain disparities in underserved populations," Nat Med., 2021;27(1):136-140).⏎⏎The pattern across these domains is consistent: AI systems trained on historically biased data reproduce those biases in deployment; average performance metrics conceal the disparity; the disparity persists undetected until researchers specifically investigate it; and the regulatory framework governing the device's deployment contains no mechanism that would have required detection before harm had accumulated across thousands or millions of patient encounters. The Partnership submits that HHS's acceleration agenda, as currently framed in the RFI, will replicate this pattern at scale across the full breadth of clinical AI applications in Medicare and Medicaid.⏎⏎⏎Partnership for AI in Health | HHS AI RFI Comments | October 2024 | Page 7⏎⏎⏎SECTION VI: THE RFI CONTAINS NO MANDATORY EQUITY AUDITING OR SURVEILLANCE FRAMEWORK⏎⏎The Partnership has reviewed the RFI in detail and finds no proposed requirement for pre-deployment equity auditing of AI systems as a condition of HHS endorsement or reimbursement. The RFI solicits input on how to accelerate adoption, how to address reimbursement barriers, and how to support research and development — but it does not propose, and does not ask whether to propose, a mandatory requirement that AI systems demonstrate equitable performance across demographic subgroups before receiving CMS reimbursement codes or HHS program endorsement. The Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology's own 2023 Issue Brief on Algorithmic Bias and Health Equity identified pre-deployment bias testing and post-deployment monitoring as the two foundational requirements for equitable AI deployment in healthcare settings (ONC, "Algorithmic Bias and Health Equity: Considerations for AI Tool Developers and Deployers," ONC Issue Brief, 2023). The fact that ONC has identified these requirements in a guidance document while the companion RFI from the same agency contains no proposal to make them mandatory is a policy inconsistency that the Partnership finds difficult to reconcile.⏎⏎The absence of mandatory equity requirements in the RFI is particularly consequential given the reimbursement incentive structure the Department is apparently contemplating. If HHS creates new CPT codes or add-on payment mechanisms to support AI-assisted clinical decision-making — as several RFI respondents and CMS advisory bodies have recommended — those payment mechanisms will create powerful financial incentives for rapid AI deployment that will operate independently of any voluntary equity guidance. Practices that deploy AI quickly will be reimbursed. Practices that pause to conduct equity validation will not receive any additional compensation for that caution. The reimbursement structure will, in effect, penalize equity due diligence and reward speed. The Partnership is not arguing against new reimbursement mechanisms for AI-assisted care. The Partnership is arguing that those mechanisms must be conditioned on demonstrated equitable performance, not merely on FDA clearance, which — as the evidence reviewed above makes clear — provides no such assurance.⏎⏎⏎Partnership for AI in Health | HHS AI RFI Comments | October 2024 | Page 8⏎⏎⏎SECTION VII: SPECIFIC POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎The Partnership's comments focus on two specific RFI question areas: the questions pertaining to regulatory and reimbursement conditions for AI adoption, and the questions pertaining to research and development priorities. The Partnership does not address all RFI questions, and notes that the scope of the RFI substantially exceeds what a single organization can address responsibly in a comment period of this length.⏎⏎On the reimbursement and regulatory conditions questions, the Partnership recommends the following:⏎⏎1. Pre-Deployment Equity Auditing as a Condition of Reimbursement. HHS and CMS should establish, through notice-and-comment rulemaking, a requirement that any AI system seeking Medicare or Medicaid reimbursement — whether through a new CPT code, an add-on payment, or inclusion in an HHS-endorsed technology program — must demonstrate, prior to reimbursement eligibility, that its performance has been validated in stratified subgroup analyses covering race, ethnicity, sex, primary language, socioeconomic status, and geographic setting (rural/urban/frontier). The stratified validation must be conducted on an external dataset independent of the training and primary validation datasets. FDA clearance based on aggregate performance metrics should not be sufficient for reimbursement eligibility absent this stratified equity validation.⏎⏎2. Mandatory Post-Deployment Bias Surveillance. HHS should require, as a condition of continued reimbursement eligibility, that AI system deployers implement and report on post-deployment performance monitoring stratified by the same demographic dimensions listed above. Reporting should occur on at minimum an annual basis, should be submitted to a centralized HHS registry, and should include any evidence of performance degradation or disparate harm identified during the reporting period. The 2023 ONC Issue Brief on Algorithmic Bias and Health Equity should be operationalized as a mandatory reporting standard, not voluntary guidance.⏎⏎3. Equity Weighting in Reimbursement Rate-Setting. To the extent CMS establishes add-on payment mechanisms for AI-assisted clinical services, the Partnership recommends that payment rates be structured to provide higher reimbursement for AI deployments that have completed stratified equity validation and that serve patient populations with a Medicaid share of 40 percent or greater. This would create a positive financial incentive for equity due diligence rather than the current structure, which provides no such incentive.⏎⏎o In the radiology context specifically, the Partnership notes that the physician work component of AI-assisted interpretation should reflect the additional oversight burden associated with monitoring AI performance for disparate error patterns — a cost that existing RVU structures do not capture and that our survey data indicates is borne disproportionately by practices serving safety-net populations.⏎⏎4. Dedicated Funding for Equity-Focused External Validation Studies. The RFI's research and development questions ask about HHS investment priorities for AI. The Partnership recommends that HHS direct NIH and AHRQ to fund a sustained program of external validation studies specifically targeting AI algorithm performance in rural, safety-net, and minority-serving institutions. The academic center datasets that currently dominate the validation literature are systematically unrepresentative of the patient populations where algorithmic bias causes the most harm. Correcting that representational gap requires dedicated public investment, because the commercial incentive structure does not reward it.⏎⏎5. Harmonization of FDA and CMS Equity Standards. The current regulatory structure creates a gap between FDA device clearance standards, which are based on aggregate performance metrics, and the equity performance standards that CMS would need to apply as conditions of reimbursement. HHS should convene an interagency working group including FDA's Digital Health Center of Excellence, CMS, and ONC to develop harmonized equity performance standards applicable across the device approval and reimbursement pathways. The Partnership notes that this harmonization work was contemplated but not completed under the FDA's Predetermined Change Control Plan framework, and that the gap between the two regulatory pathways remains a structural impediment to equity-conditioned reimbursement.⏎⏎⏎Partnership for AI in Health | HHS AI RFI Comments | October 2024 | Page 9⏎⏎⏎On the research and development priority questions, the Partnership adds one further recommendation. The differential between academic-center validation performance and real-world community-setting performance for clinical AI systems is not well-characterized in the current literature, and the gap in characterization itself constitutes a patient safety risk. HHS should fund a multi-site prospective registry study — analogous in structure to the National Cardiovascular Data Registry — that tracks AI algorithm performance outcomes in real-world clinical settings stratified by institution type, patient population, and demographic subgroup. Such a registry would generate the population-representative performance data that the current literature lacks, would provide an early-warning mechanism for detecting disparate harm before it accumulates to the scale seen in the pulse oximetry case, and would create a public data infrastructure that supports equity-conditioned regulatory decision-making. The Partnership estimates that a properly designed registry of this kind, enrolling 200 to 300 clinical sites across the rural-urban spectrum, would require initial HHS investment in the range of $45 to $60 million over five years — a figure that is modest relative to the scale of potential harm from unmonitored disparate AI performance across the Medicare and Medicaid populations.⏎⏎⏎Partnership for AI in Health | HHS AI RFI Comments | October 2024 | Page 10⏎⏎⏎SECTION VIII: ADDITIONAL CONTEXT ON RADIOLOGY-SPECIFIC DEPLOYMENT PATTERNS⏎⏎The Partnership wants to add some additional context on the radiology setting specifically, because radiology is both the clinical domain where AI deployment is most advanced and the domain where the equity surveillance gap is most immediately consequential. As of the date of these comments, FDA has cleared more than 700 AI/ML-enabled medical devices, the substantial majority of which are imaging-based applications in radiology, cardiology, and pathology. The radiology AI market is growing at a compound annual rate estimated between 35 and 40 percent. CMS has issued a small number of reimbursement codes applicable to AI-assisted imaging interpretation, and the pressure from commercial vendors and some professional societies to expand those codes is substantial.⏎⏎Against that backdrop, the Partnership's survey finding that 58 percent of practices with deployed AI report that reimbursement structures fail to account for the oversight and integration costs of AI-assisted interpretation takes on additional significance. Those oversight costs are real, and the Partnership supports appropriate reimbursement for physician work associated with AI integration. But the Partnership is concerned that the current policy conversation about radiology AI reimbursement is focused almost entirely on the cost and workflow dimensions of AI adoption, and not at all on the equity performance dimensions. There is no current mechanism by which a radiology practice deploying an AI-assisted chest radiograph interpretation algorithm would know whether that algorithm is performing equitably across its patient population. There is no standardized reporting format for disparate performance. There is no reimbursement adjustment, upward or downward, based on equity performance. The algorithm gets deployed, the reads get billed, and if the system is systematically missing findings in Medicaid patients at a higher rate than in commercially insured patients, that pattern will not appear in any quality metric the practice is currently required to track.⏎⏎The Partnership's member practices are not indifferent to this problem. Several of our larger member systems in California and Illinois have begun conducting internal equity audits of their deployed AI tools, and the preliminary results from those voluntary efforts are not uniformly reassuring. But voluntary internal auditing by the practices with the most resources is not a substitute for mandatory pre-deployment equity validation and post-deployment surveillance applicable to all deploying institutions. The practices with the least capacity for voluntary equity auditing are, by definition, the practices serving the most vulnerable patient populations.⏎⏎The Partnership closes by reiterating that these comments are not opposition to AI adoption in clinical care. The evidence that well-validated AI tools can improve diagnostic accuracy, reduce radiologist burnout, and expand access to specialist-level interpretation in underserved settings is real and the Partnership takes it seriously. The concern is specifically with the sequencing and conditionality of adoption — with the fact that HHS is proposing to accelerate deployment without first establishing the equity safeguards that would make that deployment safe for the populations most at risk from algorithmic bias. The ONC's own 2023 Issue Brief acknowledged this risk. The literature from Obermeyer, Sjoding, Wong, Seyyed-Kalantari, Adamson, Pierson, Vyas, and others has documented it across multiple clinical domains and multiple demographic dimensions. The responsible regulatory response is to condition acceleration on equity, not to treat equity as a downstream consideration to be addressed after the deployment infrastructure is already in place.⏎⏎The Partnership respectfully requests that HHS treat the pre-deployment equity auditing and post-deployment bias surveillance recommendations in Section VII of these comments as priority action items in any forthcoming AI policy framework, and that any new reimbursement mechanisms for AI-assisted clinical services be structured from the outset to condition payment eligibility on demonstrated equitable performance across demographic subgroups. The Partnership would welcome the opportunity to brief HHS staff on our survey methodology and findings, and to participate in any interagency working group convened to address the equity conditionality questions raised in these comments.⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎William Mitchell⏎Director of Government Affairs⏎Partnership for AI in Health⏎1400 K Street NW, Suite 700⏎Washington, DC 20005⏎government.affairs@partnershipforaihealth.org⏎(202) 555-0183⏎⏎October 14, 2024⏎⏎⏎Partnership for AI in Health | HHS AI RFI Comments | October 2024 | Page 11⏎⏎⏎APPENDIX NOTE: The survey data referenced throughout these comments was collected between January and March 2024 in partnership with the Radiology Business Management Association. SYNTH-0097♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Thomas Wright♔Apple Health Technologies♔♔♔♔♔Ferz.AI Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 1⏎⏎⏎SUBMISSION TO THE U.S. DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH AND HUMAN SERVICES⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary, in Collaboration with ASTP/ONC⏎⏎Re: Request for Information on Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎Submitted by: Thomas Wright, Chief Compliance Officer⏎Organization: Apple Health Technologies / Ferz.AI⏎Date: March 2025⏎⏎⏎INTRODUCTORY CONTEXT AND ORGANIZATIONAL VANTAGE POINT⏎⏎Ferz.AI submits these comments on the basis of operational experience that is, we believe, directly relevant to the questions HHS has posed. Through 47 integrated health system partnerships spanning 14 states, our deployment analytics have documented measurable improvements in specific clinical workflow metrics: an average 23% reduction in diagnostic cycle times and a 31% decrease in clinician documentation burden over the 18-month implementation window ending in Q4 2024. We are a company that benefits commercially from AI adoption in healthcare. We want to be plain about that. And it is precisely because we operate at the intersection of AI deployment and healthcare accountability that we feel obligated to register concerns about the framing of this RFI that we do not think serve the Department's long-term policy goals, or frankly the market conditions under which companies like ours can sustain credibility.⏎⏎The RFI's framing of administrative efficiency as an unqualified good is the concern we want to address most directly. HHS asks, in several of its solicited question categories, how the Department can reduce administrative burden through AI-assisted tools covering care coordination, prior authorization review, patient navigation, and benefits counseling. We understand the impulse. Himmelstein et al. (2014) documented that U.S. hospital administrative costs consume roughly 25% of total hospital expenditures, far exceeding comparable nations, and Sinsky et al. (2017) found that for every hour physicians spent in direct patient care, they spent nearly two hours on administrative tasks in the EHR and desk work. The burden is real and the cost is real. We are not disputing any of that. What we are disputing is the assumption that the administrative functions listed in this RFI are primarily a matter of processing throughput rather than skilled, judgment-intensive labor, and that AI systems trained on historical data can substitute for the contextual expertise those functions require without generating systematic, difficult-to-detect harms.⏎⏎⏎THE CATEGORY ERROR IN FRAMING ADMINISTRATIVE WORK AS CLERICAL PROCESSING⏎⏎Ferz.AI Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 2⏎⏎⏎Care coordinators, patient navigators, and benefits counselors do not primarily process structured information. They operate in what Michael Polanyi described as the domain of tacit knowledge: knowledge that "can be transmitted only by example, not by precept" and that "we can know more than we can tell" (Polanyi, 1966, p. 4). A care coordinator working in a rural Kansas health system knows, for instance, that the county's only Medicaid-enrolled transportation vendor stopped accepting new patients in September 2024 because of a contract dispute that has not been resolved and is not reflected in any database the AI system would query. She knows that a particular patient's daughter, listed as an emergency contact, is estranged from the family and should not be contacted for care coordination purposes despite appearing in the record. She knows that a local food bank recently shifted its distribution schedule in a way that affects whether a diabetic patient's meal timing will align with insulin protocols. None of this is in a structured data field. None of it can be recovered from historical training corpora. It is knowledge that exists in the embodied, locally-situated practice of doing the job, and when it is displaced by an AI system that presents its outputs with apparent confidence, the errors it produces will be invisible precisely because no one will know to look for them.⏎⏎This is not a theoretical concern. Ash, Berg, and Coiera (2004) documented the phenomenon of "juxtaposition errors" in clinical information systems, in which the automation of information presentation creates conditions where the most consequential errors are the ones least likely to be caught, because the system's apparent completeness discourages the verification behavior that would catch them. Their framework applies with equal force to administrative AI systems: a patient navigator using an AI-generated referral recommendation will not typically call three community organizations to verify current capacity, because the system has already told her which one to use. If that recommendation is wrong because the training data is six months old, or because it was trained on utilization patterns from a demographically different population, the error propagates forward invisibly. Bates et al. (2023) found that nearly 25% of hospital admissions involve at least one adverse event, and while that study focused on clinical rather than administrative errors, the methodological lesson is the same: safety events in complex systems are systematically underdetected, and automation that reduces verification behavior makes the detection problem worse.⏎⏎⏎EQUITY CONCERNS THAT HHS'S FRAMING DOES NOT ADEQUATELY ADDRESS⏎⏎The populations most dependent on administrative support in healthcare are also the populations most likely to be harmed by AI systems that perform well on aggregate metrics while failing on the margins. Obermeyer et al. (2019) demonstrated that a widely deployed commercial algorithm used to manage population health systematically underestimated the care needs of Black patients, because it used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need without accounting for the structural inequities that cause Black patients to have lower healthcare utilization at equivalent levels of illness severity. The algorithm appeared to perform well by conventional validation metrics. The bias was invisible until researchers explicitly looked for it using race-stratified analysis. The Office of Inspector General's 2022 report on Medicare Advantage prior authorization denials found that some Medicare Advantage organizations denied prior authorization requests that met Medicare coverage criteria at rates that raised substantial concerns about beneficiary access to medically necessary care (OIG, 2022, OEI-09-18-00260). That report examined human decision-making in prior authorization. The question HHS should be asking is what happens when those decisions are made or pre-filtered by AI systems that optimize for denial-rate reduction or processing speed without adequate transparency into the criteria being applied.⏎⏎Virginia Eubanks's work in Automating Inequality (2018) is not a healthcare policy text, but her analysis of how automated eligibility systems in public benefits contexts systematically disadvantage low-income populations is directly applicable here. The patients who most need a human benefits counselor to navigate a Medicaid eligibility determination, a prior authorization appeal, or a care coordination referral are precisely the patients who are least well-represented in the training data of AI systems built on historical utilization patterns from commercially insured populations. When those systems produce errors, those patients typically lack the resources, health literacy, or institutional access to identify the error, appeal it, or find an alternative pathway. The harm is real and the accountability is diffuse enough that it rarely surfaces in the administrative record.⏎⏎Ferz.AI Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 3⏎⏎⏎THE "FREES UP HUMAN TIME" ARGUMENT REQUIRES CLOSER EXAMINATION⏎⏎Ferz.AI wants to address directly the argument that AI automation of administrative functions will free up human workers for higher-value tasks. We hear this argument constantly, including from our own sales materials, and we think it deserves more scrutiny than it typically receives in this policy context. The argument assumes two things that our deployment analytics do not consistently support. First, it assumes that the administrative workforce has surplus capacity that is currently occupied by low-value processing tasks. In practice, the healthcare administrative workforce is already severely understaffed. A 2022 GAO report on AI in health care noted that workforce constraints are among the primary barriers to AI implementation, and the same workforce constraints that make AI adoption attractive also mean that when AI systems generate errors, the corrective labor falls on workers who have no margin to absorb it (GAO, 2022, GAO-22-104629). A care coordinator who has to identify, investigate, and correct an erroneous AI-generated referral has not had her burden reduced; she has had a different kind of burden added, one that is arguably more cognitively demanding than the original task because it requires reconstructing what the system did and why.⏎⏎Second, the argument assumes that the tasks being automated are genuinely lower-value than the tasks the freed-up time would be used for. This is not obviously true for the administrative functions named in this RFI. Prior authorization review, when done by a skilled human reviewer with access to patient context, is a checkpoint where clinical appropriateness errors are sometimes caught before they reach the patient. Care coordination is not a clerical task; it is a clinical support function that requires understanding of patient circumstances, family dynamics, community resource availability, and provider relationships. The National Academy for State Health Policy's 2023 issue brief on Medicaid prior authorization and AI-assisted review documented that states implementing AI-assisted prior authorization review have encountered accountability gaps that existing regulatory frameworks were not designed to address, precisely because those frameworks assumed human decision-makers whose reasoning could be reviewed (NASHP, 2023). When AI systems make prior authorization decisions or recommendations, the question of who is accountable for an erroneous denial is genuinely unresolved in current regulatory architecture.⏎⏎⏎EVIDENTIARY STANDARDS AND THE PRE-DEPLOYMENT VALIDATION PROBLEM⏎⏎Our cross-partner compliance audit identified regulatory ambiguity in liability attribution, algorithmic transparency requirements, and reimbursement coding alignment as the three primary friction points slowing broader adoption across 68% of participating facilities. We want to be specific about what this means in practice. When a health system asks us whether they are liable if our AI-assisted care coordination tool produces a referral recommendation that results in a patient not receiving timely care, we cannot give them a definitive answer. Current regulatory frameworks do not clearly address whether the AI developer, the health system deploying the tool, or the clinician who relied on the output bears responsibility for adverse outcomes. This ambiguity is not primarily a problem for us as a vendor; it is a problem for the patients who may be harmed and who need a clear accountability pathway to seek redress.⏎⏎Ferz.AI Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 4⏎⏎⏎The analogy to clinical trial evidentiary standards is instructive here. Bhatt and Mehta (2016) described adaptive clinical trial designs as a mechanism for generating rigorous evidence while allowing trial parameters to evolve in response to accumulating data. The key principle is that evidentiary standards must be commensurate with the risk profile of the intervention. A drug that is administered to patients with life-threatening conditions under conditions of close medical supervision requires a different evidentiary threshold than a dietary supplement. The same logic should apply to AI systems used in healthcare administrative functions. An AI tool that assists in scheduling optimization has a different risk profile than one that pre-filters prior authorization requests or generates care coordination recommendations for patients with complex chronic conditions. HHS's current framework does not make this distinction clearly, and the result is that health systems are making deployment decisions without adequate guidance on what validation evidence is sufficient for which risk tier.⏎⏎Ferz.AI urges HHS to require pre-deployment validation studies for any AI system used in administrative healthcare functions that affect patient access to care, with specific requirements that include the following:⏎⏎1. Prospective performance validation in the demographic and clinical population in which the system will be deployed, not merely in the population on which it was trained. The Obermeyer et al. (2019) finding is a direct consequence of deploying a system validated on one population in a different one.⏎⏎2. Mandatory human override capacity with documentation requirements. Every AI-assisted administrative decision affecting patient care access should be subject to human review upon request, and the rate at which human reviewers override AI recommendations should be tracked, disclosed, and reviewed by an institutional governance body on a regular schedule.⏎⏎3. Prospective error-rate disclosure. Health systems deploying AI-assisted administrative tools should be required to disclose error rates to CMS and to state Medicaid agencies on a reporting schedule commensurate with the risk tier of the tool. This is not a novel requirement; CMS already requires quality reporting for a wide range of clinical functions. Extending that framework to high-risk administrative AI applications is a logical extension of existing accountability architecture.⏎⏎4. Race- and income-stratified performance reporting. Given the documented tendency of AI systems to perform well on aggregate metrics while producing disparate outcomes for marginalized populations, disaggregated performance reporting should be a baseline requirement rather than an optional best practice.⏎⏎Ferz.AI Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 5⏎⏎⏎We want to be direct about why we are recommending requirements that will increase the compliance burden on vendors including ourselves. Our Q3 2024 policy working group found that reimbursement uncertainty caused 41% of our health system partners to defer or cancel planned AI expansion projects, representing an estimated $220 million in foregone capital deployment. In our assessment, that deferral reflects not just reimbursement uncertainty but a deeper anxiety about deploying systems whose accountability framework is unresolved. Health systems are not primarily worried about whether they will be reimbursed for AI-assisted care coordination; they are worried about whether they will be held liable when something goes wrong, and whether they will be able to demonstrate to regulators, patients, and plaintiff's attorneys that they deployed the system responsibly. Clear pre-deployment validation requirements and mandatory human override capacity would actually reduce that anxiety and accelerate adoption more reliably than reimbursement incentives alone. This is not a paradox. It is what the clinical device regulatory framework learned over decades: rigorous pre-market standards reduce post-market liability uncertainty and thereby create more favorable conditions for sustained investment.⏎⏎⏎THE ADMINISTRATIVE FRICTION ARGUMENT AND ITS LIMITS⏎⏎There is one more point Ferz.AI wants to make, and it is one we have some internal disagreement about, which is why we are flagging it rather than presenting it as a settled organizational position. Some administrative friction in healthcare is not waste. It is a protective checkpoint. A prior authorization reviewer who calls a physician's office to clarify the clinical rationale for a procedure is doing something more than processing a transaction; she is creating an opportunity for a clinical appropriateness error to be identified and corrected before it reaches the patient. The question of how much of that friction is genuinely protective versus genuinely wasteful is not answerable at the aggregate level. It depends on the specific administrative function, the specific patient population, and the specific institutional context. HHS's RFI does not ask this question. It assumes that friction reduction is the goal and asks only how AI can achieve it. We think that framing is incomplete, and that a more defensible policy goal is distinguishing between administrative friction that is protective and administrative friction that is purely transactional, and ensuring that AI automation is targeted at the latter rather than the former.⏎⏎Ferz.AI Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 6⏎⏎⏎The difficulty, of course, is that this distinction is itself context-dependent and requires the kind of locally-situated judgment that Polanyi described. A prior authorization requirement that is purely bureaucratic overhead in a large urban academic medical center with robust care management infrastructure may function as a meaningful access checkpoint in a rural critical access hospital where the care coordinator is also the billing manager and the prior authorization reviewer and the patient navigator, and where the physician ordering the procedure has not reviewed the patient's full medication history because the patient's primary care provider is in a different system. We are not arguing that AI cannot play a role in administrative healthcare functions. We are arguing that the role it plays should be defined by demonstrated performance in the specific context of deployment, not by theoretical efficiency gains projected from aggregate data. That is a higher standard than HHS's current framing implies, and we think it is the right one.⏎⏎The NASHP (2023) brief on Medicaid prior authorization noted that at least seven states had implemented or were piloting AI-assisted prior authorization review as of early 2023 without having established clear accountability frameworks for erroneous denials. That is a regulatory gap that exists right now, affecting Medicaid beneficiaries right now. Whatever reimbursement incentives HHS creates to accelerate AI adoption in administrative functions, those incentives will operate in that gap unless HHS takes explicit action to close it. Ferz.AI respectfully urges the Department to prioritize the accountability architecture before the reimbursement incentives, not because we oppose reimbursement reform, but because incentivizing deployment into an unresolved accountability environment is likely to produce exactly the kind of high-profile failures that will set back adoption more broadly for years.⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎To summarize Ferz.AI's core recommendations on the questions most directly addressed in this submission:⏎⏎Regarding regulatory actions: HHS should develop a risk-tiered regulatory framework for AI systems used in administrative healthcare functions that affect patient access to care. Systems that pre-filter or recommend outcomes in prior authorization, care coordination, patient navigation, or benefits determination should be subject to mandatory pre-deployment validation in the target deployment population, with race- and income-stratified performance disclosure requirements and mandatory human override capacity. Liability attribution frameworks should be developed in consultation with CMS, OCR, and OIG to clarify the respective responsibilities of AI developers, deploying health systems, and individual clinicians.⏎⏎Regarding research and development actions: HHS should fund prospective research on the performance of AI administrative tools in safety-net and rural health system contexts, where the populations served are least well-represented in commercial training data and the administrative workforce is most constrained. The GAO (2022) report identified the absence of this kind of context-specific evidence as a gap; two years later, that gap has not been meaningfully closed.⏎⏎Ferz.AI Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 7⏎⏎⏎We have deliberately not addressed the RFI's questions on clinical AI, reimbursement coding alignment, or interoperability in these comments, not because those questions are unimportant but because our most specific and evidence-grounded concerns are in the administrative domain and we did not want to dilute them with comments in areas where we have less to add to what other commenters will say. SYNTH-0098♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔James Wright♔American Heart Association♔♔♔♔♔American Heart Association⏎7272 Greenville Avenue⏎Dallas, TX 75231⏎⏎James Wright, MPA⏎Policy Director, Federal Health Policy⏎james.wright@heart.org⏎⏎September 12, 2024⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue, S.W.⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎Re: HHS Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care (Docket No. HHS-OS-2024-0007)⏎⏎---⏎⏎AHA Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket HHS-OS-2024-0007 | Page 1⏎⏎---⏎⏎Dear Deputy Secretary and ONC/ASTP Staff:⏎⏎The American Heart Association (AHA) submits these comments in response to the Department's Request for Information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings. The AHA represents more than 35 million volunteers, supporters, and patients whose cardiovascular health outcomes are directly implicated by how federal health policy shapes the deployment of AI-assisted clinical tools. The AHA's concern here is narrowly but urgently focused on two dimensions of the RFI that the Department has, in our assessment, addressed with insufficient specificity: the failure to establish mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing requirements, and the absence of any framework for ongoing post-deployment surveillance that would detect algorithmic bias before it causes systematic, population-level harm. The framing of the RFI, while broad and genuinely responsive to the complexity of AI adoption, treats equity as one consideration among many rather than as a foundational constraint on deployment. That framing is, we believe, inadequate.⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE EQUITY PROBLEM IS EMPIRICALLY DOCUMENTED, NOT THEORETICAL⏎⏎The Department's RFI solicits comment on how to "accelerate" adoption. That framing presupposes that speed is the primary challenge. For the populations the AHA serves — patients with cardiovascular disease, disproportionately concentrated among Black, Hispanic, and low-income communities — the more pressing challenge is not the pace of adoption but the conditions under which adoption occurs. There is now a substantial and convergent body of peer-reviewed literature establishing that AI systems trained on historically biased clinical data reproduce and entrench those biases at scale, often in ways that are invisible to the clinicians relying on them.⏎⏎The Obermeyer et al. study published in Science in 2019 (Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S. Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations. Science. 2019;366(6464):447-453) documented that a widely deployed commercial risk-scoring algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients relative to white patients with equivalent disease burden, because the algorithm used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need — a substitution that encoded decades of racially differential access to care directly into the model's predictions. This was not a fringe or experimental system. It was deployed across hundreds of health systems before the bias was characterized. The AHA notes that similar structural logic applies to cardiovascular risk stratification tools, many of which rely on utilization-based proxies that carry the same embedded assumptions.⏎⏎The problem is not confined to risk scoring. Sjoding et al., writing in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 (Sjoding MW, Dickson RP, Iwashyna TJ, Gay SE, Valley TS. Racial bias in pulse oximetry measurement. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(25):2477-2478), documented that pulse oximetry — the ubiquitous bedside measurement of blood oxygen saturation — systematically overestimates oxygen saturation in patients with darker skin pigmentation, producing occult hypoxemia that standard AI-assisted monitoring systems would not flag. During the COVID-19 pandemic, this bias translated directly into delayed recognition of respiratory deterioration among Black patients. The AHA finds it notable that this bias was detectable through basic stratified analysis of existing clinical data, yet it persisted for decades in a device that has been FDA-cleared and broadly deployed. The lesson is not that the technology failed in an unexpected way. The lesson is that the validation framework was never designed to detect this class of failure.⏎⏎---⏎⏎AHA Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket HHS-OS-2024-0007 | Page 2⏎⏎---⏎⏎Sepsis prediction offers a parallel illustration at the algorithmic level. Wong et al., publishing in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2021 (Wong A, Otles E, Donnelly JP, et al. External validation of a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model in hospitalized patients. JAMA Intern Med. 2021;181(8):1065-1070), conducted external validation of a proprietary sepsis alert system that had been deployed across hundreds of hospitals and found that the system's performance degraded substantially when applied to patient populations that differed from the original training cohort. Sensitivity and specificity figures that appeared acceptable in the development setting did not hold when the model encountered the demographic and comorbidity mix of community hospitals, safety-net institutions, or rural facilities. This is precisely the validation-to-deployment degradation problem that the AHA regards as among the most serious structural failures in current AI governance frameworks. A system that performs adequately in an academic medical center's patient population and then gets licensed and deployed into a federally qualified health center without revalidation is not a system that has been responsibly deployed. The Department's RFI does not, in the AHA's reading, contain a framework that would prevent this.⏎⏎The dermatology AI literature provides a further data point that is directly relevant to the cardiovascular context, because the underlying mechanism — training data that underrepresents darker-skinned patients — applies with equal force to imaging-based cardiovascular diagnostics. Adamson and Smith, in JAMA Dermatology in 2018 (Adamson AS, Smith A. Machine learning and health care disparities in dermatology. JAMA Dermatol. 2018;154(11):1247-1248), documented that machine learning systems for skin lesion classification were trained predominantly on images of lighter-skinned patients, producing diagnostic accuracy that was substantially lower for patients of color. The AHA's concern is that echocardiography AI, cardiac MRI interpretation systems, and retinal imaging tools used for cardiovascular risk assessment are being developed under training-data conditions that may replicate this same underrepresentation without any regulatory mechanism requiring developers to characterize the demographic composition of their training datasets prior to deployment.⏎⏎---⏎⏎AUTOMATION BIAS AS A MECHANISM FOR CONCEALMENT⏎⏎The literature on automation bias, surveyed extensively in Cabitza, Rasoini, and Gensini's 2017 JAMA commentary (Cabitza F, Rasoini R, Gensini GF. Unintended consequences of machine learning in medicine. JAMA. 2017;318(6):517-518), establishes that clinicians systematically over-rely on algorithmic outputs relative to their own clinical judgment, particularly under conditions of cognitive load, time pressure, or uncertainty — conditions that are endemic to the clinical environments where AI is being most aggressively promoted. This is not a critique of clinicians. It is a structural observation about how human cognition interacts with decision-support systems. The consequence, in the context of biased AI, is that algorithmic errors are harder to surface than equivalent errors made by human clinicians, because the algorithm's output carries an implicit authority that tends to suppress the clinician's independent assessment. Char, Shah, and Magnus made a related point in their 2018 NEJM analysis (Char DS, Shah NH, Magnus D. Implementing machine learning in health care — addressing ethical challenges. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(11):981-983) — that the opacity of many AI systems makes it structurally difficult for clinicians to know when to distrust the output, which means that bias embedded in the model is far less likely to be detected through ordinary clinical practice than bias in a physician's own reasoning, which is at least visible and subject to peer review.⏎⏎---⏎⏎AHA Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket HHS-OS-2024-0007 | Page 3⏎⏎---⏎⏎The AHA is particularly concerned about this dynamic in cardiovascular care contexts where AI-assisted clinical decision support systems (CDSS) are being used to inform triage, risk stratification, and treatment prioritization. A physician who independently underestimates the severity of a Black patient's cardiac presentation is engaged in a form of clinical error that can, in principle, be identified through mortality review, quality improvement processes, or peer evaluation. A CDSS that systematically underscores Black patients' risk — because it was trained on data from a population with different baseline risk distributions, or because it uses utilization-based proxies — produces the same downstream harm through a mechanism that is invisible to standard quality review processes. Gianfrancesco et al., in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2018 (Gianfrancesco MA, Tamang S, Yazdany J, Schmajuk G. Potential biases in machine learning algorithms using electronic health record data. JAMA Intern Med. 2018;178(11):1544-1547), documented the specific pathways through which EHR-derived training data introduces and amplifies bias, including differential documentation practices, differential access to care that produces differential data density, and the use of administrative codes that encode clinical decisions already distorted by structural inequity. These are not hypothetical mechanisms. They are empirically characterized pathways between historical inequity and algorithmic perpetuation of that inequity.⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE DEPLOYMENT-SETTING PROBLEM⏎⏎The AHA's membership survey data, while not the primary subject of this comment, is relevant context. In the AHA's engagement with practicing cardiologists and cardiac care teams across the country, a consistent pattern has emerged: AI tools are being adopted most rapidly in well-resourced academic and large-system environments, while the populations experiencing the greatest cardiovascular disease burden — rural communities, safety-net hospital patients, low-income urban populations — are served by institutions that lack the informatics infrastructure, data science capacity, or regulatory expertise to conduct meaningful independent validation of the tools they are being sold. Seyyed-Kalantari et al., publishing in Nature Medicine in 2021 (Seyyed-Kalantari L, Zhang H, McDermott MBA, Chen IY, Ghassemi M. Underdiagnosis bias of artificial intelligence algorithms applied to chest radiographs in under-served patient populations. Nat Med. 2021;27(12):2176-2182), documented precisely this dynamic in chest radiograph interpretation: AI systems showed systematically lower diagnostic performance for patients in underserved settings, with the performance gap concentrated among patients who were female, Black, or publicly insured. The systems were not developed in those settings, were not validated in those settings, and were not monitored for performance degradation in those settings after deployment.⏎⏎This is the crux of the AHA's concern. The Department's RFI asks how to accelerate AI adoption. The AHA's answer is that accelerating adoption without mandatory equity safeguards is not a neutral act. It is a policy choice to deploy systems that are likely to perform worst for the populations experiencing the worst health outcomes. Wiens et al., in their 2019 Nature Medicine roadmap for responsible machine learning in health care (Wiens J, Saria S, Sendak M, et al. Do no harm: a roadmap for responsible machine learning for health care. Nat Med. 2019;25(9):1337-1340), were explicit that deployment in clinical settings should require prospective monitoring, ongoing revalidation, and clear criteria for discontinuation when performance falls below acceptable thresholds. The U.S. Government Accountability Office reached a similar conclusion in its 2022 report on AI in health care (U.S. Government Accountability Office. Artificial Intelligence in Health Care: Benefits and Challenges of Technologies to Augment Patient Care. GAO-22-104629. Washington, DC: GAO; 2022), noting that existing oversight frameworks were not designed to address the continuous learning, model drift, and post-market performance degradation characteristics of deployed AI systems. Neither of these analyses has been translated into binding regulatory requirements. The AHA believes the Department's response to this RFI is an opportunity to begin that translation.⏎⏎---⏎⏎AHA Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket HHS-OS-2024-0007 | Page 4⏎⏎---⏎⏎A further dimension of this problem involves the use of race as a variable in clinical algorithms more broadly. Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones, writing in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 (Vyas DA, Eisenstein LG, Jones DS. Hidden in plain sight — reconsidering the use of race correction in clinical algorithms. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(9):874-882), documented that numerous widely used clinical algorithms incorporate race as a correction factor in ways that systematically direct resources and interventions away from Black and other minority patients, often without clinical justification grounded in biology. The AHA regards this literature as directly applicable to the AI context: if underlying clinical algorithms used to generate training labels or to define outcome variables incorporate race-based corrections, then AI systems trained on those labels or outcomes will inherit and potentially amplify those corrections. The Department's RFI does not appear to contemplate this pathway, and the AHA believes it should.⏎⏎---⏎⏎SPECIFIC POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎The AHA's recommendations in response to this RFI are organized around the two dimensions identified at the outset: pre-deployment requirements and post-deployment surveillance. These are not the only dimensions of responsible AI governance, but they are the dimensions most directly relevant to the equity concerns documented above, and they are the dimensions where the current regulatory framework is most clearly inadequate.⏎⏎Regarding pre-deployment requirements, the AHA recommends:⏎⏎1. HHS should establish, through binding guidance or rulemaking as appropriate, a mandatory pre-deployment equity audit requirement for all AI-assisted clinical decision support tools used in Medicare and Medicaid reimbursed settings. The audit should require developers to characterize the demographic composition of training datasets, including race, ethnicity, sex, age, insurance status, and geographic setting, and to provide stratified performance metrics across those subgroups. Aggregate accuracy figures are insufficient. A system that achieves 90% sensitivity overall while achieving 72% sensitivity for Black patients is not a system that meets an acceptable performance standard, and the current regulatory framework does not require that the 72% figure be disclosed.⏎⏎2. HHS should require that pre-deployment validation be conducted in settings representative of the intended deployment population. A sepsis prediction model validated exclusively in an academic medical center cannot be assumed to perform adequately in a critical access hospital. The Department should adopt the external validation framework described by Wiens et al. (2019) as a minimum standard for high-stakes clinical applications.⏎⏎3. HHS should issue explicit guidance prohibiting the use of AI systems that incorporate race as a biological variable in clinical scoring, except where there is documented biological justification reviewed and approved through a defined regulatory process. This recommendation builds directly on the framework articulated by Vyas et al. (2020) and is consistent with existing HHS civil rights obligations under Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act.⏎⏎Regarding post-deployment surveillance, the AHA recommends:⏎⏎o Health systems deploying AI-assisted CDSS in cardiovascular care, sepsis prediction, and other high-stakes clinical domains should be required to submit annual performance reports stratified by race, ethnicity, sex, and payer type to CMS or a designated HHS entity. These reports should be publicly accessible in machine-readable format.⏎⏎o HHS should establish a centralized adverse event reporting mechanism specifically for AI-related clinical errors, analogous to the FDA's MedWatch system, that allows clinicians and patients to report suspected cases of algorithmically mediated diagnostic or treatment error. The absence of such a mechanism means that the population-level harm caused by biased AI systems is currently invisible in federal data systems.⏎⏎o HHS should establish performance floor thresholds below which AI systems may not continue to be used in clinical decision-making without revalidation. The specific thresholds should be developed through a notice-and-comment process with input from clinical societies, patient advocates, and health equity researchers, but the principle — that there exists a performance level below which deployment is not permissible — should be established now.⏎⏎---⏎⏎AHA Comments | HHS AI RFI | Docket HHS-OS-2024-0007 | Page 5⏎⏎---⏎⏎The AHA also recommends that HHS consider a targeted moratorium on the use of AI systems in coverage determination and prior authorization decisions until the pre-deployment equity auditing and post-deployment surveillance frameworks described above are in place. The use of AI in coverage decisions is a domain where the consequences of algorithmic bias are particularly severe — a patient who is incorrectly assessed as low-risk by a biased algorithm and denied coverage for a necessary intervention has no practical mechanism to challenge the algorithmic basis of that denial under current frameworks. The AHA notes that the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology has addressed related concerns about information blocking and data access in its 2023 report (Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology. Report on Health Information Blocking and the ONC Health IT Certification Program. Washington, DC: HHS; 2023), but the coverage determination context raises distinct equity concerns that go beyond data access and require specific attention.⏎⏎The AHA is aware that these recommendations involve regulatory requirements that some stakeholders will characterize as barriers to adoption. The AHA's position is that this characterization misframes the relevant tradeoff. The choice is not between AI adoption with equity safeguards and AI adoption without them. The choice is between AI adoption that is more likely to reduce cardiovascular health disparities and AI adoption that is more likely to perpetuate them. Given the documented evidence base summarized above, the AHA does not believe that the Department has the option of treating equity auditing and post-deployment surveillance as optional enhancements. They are baseline requirements for responsible deployment.⏎⏎---⏎⏎One additional point that the AHA wants to flag, which is perhaps slightly outside the core equity-and-bias argument but which came up repeatedly in the AHA's internal policy consultations and we believe deserves at least brief mention: the reimbursement ambiguity problem identified in recent physician surveys, including the TMA membership survey finding that 74% of responding physicians cited uncertainty over coverage denials as a barrier to AI adoption, interacts with the equity problem in a specific and underappreciated way. Reimbursement ambiguity falls disproportionately on smaller, independent, and safety-net practices that lack the administrative infrastructure to navigate payer uncertainty. The result is that AI adoption in those settings is suppressed not because the tools are unavailable but because the economic risk of adoption is too high. This creates a perverse dynamic: the settings most likely to serve high-disparity populations are the settings least likely to adopt AI tools, while the settings already serving well-resourced populations adopt first, benefit first, and generate the performance data that informs future regulatory and reimbursement decisions. The equity gap gets built into the evidence base before HHS has had a chance to require that the evidence base be equitable.⏎⏎The AHA appreciates the Department's engagement through this RFI process and looks forward to participating in subsequent regulatory proceedings. HHS has structured its inquiry around the question of how to accelerate AI adoption in clinical care, a framing that treats deployment velocity as the operative policy goal and treats regulatory ambiguity, reimbursement gaps, and R&D coordination failures as the primary obstacles to that goal. Our analysis, drawing on structured feedback from over 200 clinical informatics directors and deployment benchmarking data across a network of 47 health system partners, confirms that 83% of clinical AI deployments stall at the integration phase, and that institutions investing in AI-assisted diagnostics face an average 14-month delay between FDA clearance and meaningful clinical adoption due to unresolved billing classification issues. We cite these figures not to validate the RFI's framing but to complicate it. The question HHS has not asked is: who benefits from resolving these barriers, and who bears the cost when the resolution is designed primarily by the parties with the largest lobbying footprint in this proceeding?⏎⏎That is the question we are submitting to address. The barriers identified in this RFI, including CMS reimbursement ambiguity and the absence of standardized FDA-CMS coordination pathways, are real. But they are symptoms of a deeper structural condition, which is that the clinical AI market is already exhibiting the consolidation dynamics that have historically preceded regulatory capture in health care. Dafny and Lee (2016) documented the mechanisms by which market concentration in health care creates conditions where dominant incumbents shape regulatory frameworks in their commercial favor, and Gee and Gurwitz (2018) extended that analysis to show how provider-side consolidation translates into structural market power over procurement and technology adoption decisions. The Federal Trade Commission's 2023 policy brief on generative AI and the healthcare sector named vendor concentration and competitive foreclosure as primary risks in the clinical AI market specifically. HHS appears to have accepted the acceleration agenda without first asking whether the market structure into which it proposes to accelerate adoption is capable of producing competitive outcomes or patient benefit. Our analysis suggests it is not.⏎⏎⏎UnitedHealth Group | HHS AI RFI | October 2024 | Page 2⏎⏎⏎THE REIMBURSEMENT MODERNIZATION QUESTION AND WHO IT ACTUALLY BENEFITS⏎⏎HHS has asked for input on reimbursement modernization as a mechanism for accelerating clinical AI adoption. Our deployment benchmarking data confirms that facilities operating under value-based care contracts are 2.3 times more likely to pilot clinical AI tools than those in traditional fee-for-service arrangements, which the Department appears to read as evidence that reimbursement architecture shapes adoption velocity and that modernizing that architecture will therefore accelerate adoption broadly. This reading is incomplete in a way that matters for policy.
