Holmgren, Apathy, and Adler-Milstein (2022) showed that vendor control of data infrastructure continued to produce interoperability failures more than a decade after meaningful use was enacted, failures that vendors had direct commercial incentives to perpetuate. Gans and Stern (2023) extended the platform economics literature to clinical AI specifically, showing that switching costs and proprietary lock-in dynamics in AI-integrated EHR environments are structurally analogous to the conditions that produced the EHR consolidation story, except that the AI layer adds a second rent-extraction mechanism on top of existing licensing and maintenance contracts. HHS is proposing to attach federal reimbursement to clinical AI products before conducting any independent analysis of whether the market structure those products inhabit is capable of supporting competitive outcomes.⏎⏎The CRADA mechanism HHS has referenced as a vehicle for public-private R&D partnership compounds this concern rather than addressing it. Rai (2023) analyzed the IP capture dynamics in federally funded AI development partnerships and found that CRADA structures routinely transfer public-sector data assets and research infrastructure into proprietary vendor control through licensing arrangements that give incumbents durable competitive advantages over potential market entrants. The GAO's 2022 report on AI in health care identified the absence of accountability mechanisms for vendor product performance as a significant regulatory gap, a finding that connects directly to Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan's (2019) Science paper documenting how a commercially deployed population health algorithm produced racially discriminatory outputs that the vendor had no regulatory obligation to correct. Maddox, Rumsfeld, and Payne (2019) raised the deployment accountability question in JAMA the same year and received no satisfactory regulatory answer. Four years later, HHS is proposing to accelerate the deployment of the same category of vendor products into a regulatory environment that still lacks the accountability infrastructure those authors identified as absent.⏎⏎UnitedHealth Group | HHS AI RFI | October 2024 | Page 3⏎⏎⏎We want to be direct about what we are observing in this proceeding. The comment infrastructure around this RFI, the breadth of participation from large AI vendors, EHR platform companies, and their trade associations, is not evidence of a well-functioning public input process. It is evidence that entities with the resources to field dedicated regulatory affairs teams are using this proceeding to shape the reimbursement and partnership frameworks that will govern a multi-billion dollar market in their favor. That is what regulatory capture looks like in its early stages. HHS has an obligation to account for the structural forces that will determine who actually benefits from the policies it develops in response to this RFI, and the Department has not done so. The acceleration agenda as currently framed will, if implemented along the lines the RFI suggests, produce a reimbursement and partnership architecture that entrenches incumbent vendors, transfers value from health systems to technology companies through licensing and maintenance contracts, and forecloses the competitive dynamics that would otherwise be necessary conditions for patient benefit.⏎⏎Our demand is specific: HHS should impose a moratorium on further regulatory acceleration actions in this space until an independent market structure analysis, conducted by parties without commercial relationships to the vendors whose products are under consideration, is completed and its findings are codified as anti-capture safeguards in any resulting rulemaking. That analysis should address vendor concentration ratios in the clinical AI and EHR markets, switching cost burdens on health system procurers, the IP allocation terms in any proposed CRADAs, and the reimbursement classification mechanisms being proposed, with specific attention to whether those mechanisms will function as⏎⏎UnitedHealth Group | HHS AI RFI | October 2024 | Page 4⏎⏎competitive-neutral incentives or as de facto subsidies to incumbents. SYNTH-0100♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Michelle White♔Vanderbilt University Medical Center Biomedical Informatics♔♔♔♔♔VANDERBILT UNIVERSITY MEDICAL CENTER⏎DEPARTMENT OF BIOMEDICAL INFORMATICS⏎FORMAL COMMENT SUBMISSION⏎⏎Docket: HHS-2024-AI-RFI-001⏎Submitted by: Michelle White, Professor of Health Policy⏎Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Department of Biomedical Informatics⏎Nashville, Tennessee 37232⏎mwhite@vumc.org⏎⏎---⏎⏎VUMC Biomedical Informatics Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 1⏎⏎I. THE ACCOUNTABILITY QUESTION HHS HAS NOT ANSWERED⏎⏎The Department's request for information arrives at a moment when the gap between what AI systems can do in clinical settings and what existing legal and institutional frameworks can handle has become genuinely difficult to ignore. This comment does not oppose the deployment of AI in clinical care. The research conducted within this institution has contributed to the development of predictive models now in active use at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, and the potential of these technologies to improve diagnostic accuracy, reduce preventable harm, and extend access to specialist-level clinical reasoning in underserved settings is real and well-documented (ONC, 2021). What this comment argues, with considerable urgency, is that HHS has structured its RFI in a way that treats accountability as a downstream implementation question rather than a precondition for responsible scaling — and that this sequencing error is not a minor procedural oversight but a structural commitment with lasting consequences.⏎⏎The concern is specific. When an AI system assists in a clinical decision that results in patient harm, the question of who bears legal and ethical responsibility is not resolved by existing doctrine. The hospital may argue that it deployed a vendor-certified tool according to manufacturer specifications. The vendor may argue that its system performed within validated parameters and that clinicians retained final authority. The clinician may argue that the AI recommendation appeared in the EHR workflow in a manner that made deviation practically difficult, and that institutional pressure to follow algorithmic outputs was substantial. This is not a hypothetical failure mode. It is what Hoffman and Podgurski (2023) describe as the "responsibility gap" in AI-assisted medical decision-making — a structural condition in which each party to a clinical AI deployment possesses plausible deniability, and in which the diffusion of causal contribution across vendor, institution, and clinician makes traditional tort doctrines, including respondeat superior and proximate causation standards, extraordinarily difficult to apply. Price, Gerke, and Cohen (2019) documented this problem in JAMA five years ago. The problem has not been resolved. HHS is now proposing to scale the deployment model that generates it.⏎⏎VUMC Biomedical Informatics Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 2⏎⏎II. INSTITUTIONAL EVIDENCE OF THE TRANSLATION GAP⏎⏎Before addressing the structural accountability argument directly, this comment offers institutional context that bears on the Department's framing of the problem. A 2024 survey conducted by the Computing Research Association across 412 academic computing departments found that 68% of faculty conducting AI and machine learning research identified healthcare and clinical applications as a primary or significant area of investigation, yet fewer than 22% reported active collaboration with clinical partners or reimbursement-eligible deployment pathways (CRA, 2024). This is a striking finding. It means that the majority of federally supported academic AI research oriented toward clinical care is being conducted without the institutional infrastructure — contractual relationships with clinical sites, reimbursement pathway analysis, liability allocation agreements — that would be necessary to translate validated models into actual clinical practice.⏎⏎Our analysis of federally funded AI research portfolios from fiscal years 2020 through 2023 found a consistent pattern in which algorithmic development milestones were met on schedule while the regulatory scaffolding needed to translate those models into clinical workflows was absent or incomplete. In 74% of the grant final reports reviewed, principal investigators cited unclear HHS guidance as a top barrier to translational progress. This is worth sitting with for a moment, because the Department may read that finding as an argument for regulatory clarification that accelerates adoption — which is essentially what the RFI proposes. This comment reads it differently. The barrier is not merely a lack of guidance on how to deploy AI systems. It is a lack of guidance on who is responsible when those systems cause harm. Researchers know how to build models. They do not know, and neither does the Department, how to assign legal accountability when those models fail in a clinical workflow. Clarifying the deployment pathway without resolving the accountability question does not remove the barrier; it moves it downstream, where it will be encountered by patients.⏎⏎III. ACCOUNTABILITY DIFFUSION AS A DESIGN FLAW, NOT A GAP⏎⏎This is the structural argument this comment most wants the Department to absorb. Accountability diffusion in clinical AI deployments is not a regulatory gap that can be patched after the fact. It is a design feature of the current deployment model, in the sense that the contractual and institutional arrangements under which AI systems enter clinical workflows are structured, often deliberately, to distribute responsibility in ways that make clear legal accountability impossible to establish. Kearns and Roth (2023) reviewed vendor contracts for clinical AI systems deployed at academic medical centers and found that indemnification clauses, limitation-of-liability provisions, and "clinician final authority" language were nearly universal — and that these provisions, taken together, function to ensure that no single party can be held accountable for an adverse outcome attributable to AI-assisted decision-making. This is not an accident of drafting. It is a foreseeable consequence of deploying AI in a legal environment that has not established clear, non-delegable accountability obligations.⏎⏎VUMC Biomedical Informatics Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 3⏎⏎Cohen, Amarasingham, Shah, Xie, and Lo (2022) made a related point in Health Affairs: the use of complex predictive analytics in clinical care raises accountability concerns that existing malpractice doctrine is not designed to address, and that the failure to resolve these concerns before widespread deployment will create a body of adverse outcomes for which patients have no meaningful legal recourse. Gerke, Minssen, and Cohen (2020) reached a similar conclusion in their analysis of ethical and legal challenges in AI-driven healthcare, noting that the allocation of legal responsibility among developers, deployers, and clinicians is "deeply unsettled" and that this unsettled state creates perverse incentives: vendors have incentives to over-claim the autonomy of their systems when marketing and under-claim it when defending against liability, while institutions have incentives to frame AI adoption as a quality improvement initiative rather than a clinical decision-support tool that implicates the duty of care. The European Parliament recognized this problem as early as 2017, when the Delvaux resolution on civil law rules on robotics explicitly called for the establishment of strict liability frameworks for autonomous systems before their widespread deployment — a call that the United States regulatory apparatus has not answered in the seven years since (Delvaux, 2017).⏎⏎Pasquale (2022) has argued, in the context of algorithmic systems generally, that attribution and responsibility must be treated as non-negotiable design requirements, not optional features to be added after a system achieves market penetration. This argument has particular force in clinical contexts, where the asymmetry between institutional knowledge and patient capacity to identify and contest AI-related harms is extreme. Patients do not typically know whether an AI system was involved in their care. They cannot audit the model. They cannot review the vendor contract. When an AI-assisted diagnosis is wrong, or when an AI-generated risk score leads to a treatment decision that causes harm, the patient's ability to seek accountability depends entirely on whether the legal and regulatory framework has assigned that accountability to someone in advance. Right now, it has not. HHS's RFI proposes to accelerate the spread of a deployment model that systematically forecloses that accountability, and this comment regards that as a serious policy error.⏎⏎IV. THE REIMBURSEMENT AND REGULATORY PATHWAY QUESTIONS⏎⏎The RFI asks several questions about reimbursement mechanisms and regulatory pathways for clinical AI. This comment addresses those questions only insofar as they interact with the accountability problem, because the accountability problem is prior to both.⏎⏎On reimbursement: The Department is considering whether and how to create billing codes or alternative payment mechanisms for AI-assisted clinical services. This comment does not oppose the development of such mechanisms in principle. However, the creation of reimbursement pathways for AI-assisted care before accountability frameworks are in place would be a significant error, for the following reason. Reimbursement creates institutional incentives to deploy. Once those incentives are embedded in payment structures, the institutional and political pressure to maintain deployment will be substantial, even if subsequent evidence reveals systematic harms or accountability failures. Mello, Frakes, Blumenkranz, and Studdert (2020) have documented the relationship between malpractice liability structures and healthcare quality, finding that clear liability exposure is one of the mechanisms through which quality standards are enforced in clinical practice. If reimbursement for AI-assisted care is established before liability for AI-assisted harm is clearly assigned, the accountability mechanism that malpractice law provides will be absent at precisely the moment when deployment is expanding most rapidly.⏎⏎VUMC Biomedical Informatics Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 4⏎⏎On regulatory pathways: Kesselheim, Cresswell, and Sheikh (2023) conducted a comparative analysis of regulatory frameworks for clinical AI across multiple jurisdictions and found that the United States regulatory approach — which relies primarily on FDA pre-market clearance for software as a medical device and post-market surveillance — is poorly suited to AI systems that update over time, exhibit performance variation across patient populations, and interact with clinical workflows in ways that are difficult to characterize at the time of clearance. The concern about algorithmic bias is directly relevant here. Obermeyer, Nissan, Stern, Eaneff, Bernstein, and Mullainathan (2021) documented the mechanisms by which AI systems trained on historical clinical data can encode and perpetuate racial and socioeconomic disparities in care, and the accountability gap makes this problem worse: if no party is clearly responsible for monitoring and correcting discriminatory outputs in a deployed system, the incentive to do so is weak. This is not a hypothetical concern. It is a documented pattern with identifiable mechanisms.⏎⏎The specific questions this comment would like the Department to address in any subsequent rulemaking are the following:⏎⏎1. What legal entity — vendor, deploying institution, or individual clinician — bears non-delegable accountability for an adverse outcome attributable to an AI-assisted clinical decision, and how does the Department propose to make that assignment enforceable against contractual provisions designed to diffuse it?⏎⏎2. Will reimbursement for AI-assisted clinical services be conditioned on the existence of a binding accountability agreement that identifies a responsible party for each deployed system, and will that agreement be required to be disclosed to patients?⏎⏎3. What post-market surveillance obligations will attach to clinical AI systems deployed under any new reimbursement pathway, and who will bear the cost of that surveillance — the vendor, the deploying institution, or CMS?⏎⏎4. How does the Department propose to address the performance variation problem identified by Kesselheim et al. (2023), in which AI systems validated on one patient population exhibit materially different performance characteristics when deployed in a different clinical setting, and who is accountable when that variation produces harm?⏎⏎5. Will the Department require that patients be informed when AI systems have contributed to clinical decisions affecting their care, and if so, what form will that disclosure take?⏎⏎VUMC Biomedical Informatics Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 5⏎⏎V. THE INSTITUTIONAL DEPENDENCY PROBLEM⏎⏎There is a second structural concern that this comment wants to name explicitly, because it is present in the RFI's framing but not acknowledged. Once AI systems are embedded in clinical workflows, and once reimbursement structures create institutional incentives to maintain that embedding, the practical ability to revisit accountability questions diminishes. This is not speculation. It is what happens with any technology that becomes load-bearing in a clinical workflow. The EHR experience is instructive: interoperability and accountability problems that were identified during early EHR adoption in the mid-2000s have proven extraordinarily difficult to resolve precisely because institutional dependency on specific systems created both technical and contractual lock-in that made remediation costly and politically difficult. The same dynamic will operate with clinical AI, and it will operate faster, because AI systems are being deployed at a pace and scale that EHR adoption did not approach in its early years.⏎⏎The argument that accountability frameworks can be built after adoption has begun therefore carries a hidden assumption: that the political and institutional conditions for building those frameworks will be as favorable after adoption as before. This comment does not accept that assumption. The vendors, institutions, and clinical professional organizations that will have invested in specific deployment models will have strong incentives to resist accountability frameworks that impose retrospective liability or require costly system modifications. The patients who will have been harmed by accountability gaps in the interim will not be organized. HHS is in a stronger position to require accountability infrastructure now, before deployment scales, than it will be after institutional dependency deepens. Acceleration without that infrastructure is not neutral with respect to accountability. It is a policy choice to externalize accountability risk onto patients.⏎⏎VUMC Biomedical Informatics Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 6⏎⏎VI. WHAT HHS SHOULD DO BEFORE ACCELERATING ADOPTION⏎⏎This comment concludes with a concrete policy request, because the preceding analysis is intended to support a specific ask, not merely to register concern.⏎⏎HHS should condition any regulatory, reimbursement, or research-and-development action designed to accelerate AI adoption in clinical care on the prior establishment of a mandatory accountability framework that satisfies the following minimum conditions:⏎⏎o The framework must assign non-delegable legal responsibility for each AI-assisted clinical decision to an identifiable human or institutional party. Contractual provisions that purport to distribute or disclaim that responsibility must be unenforceable against patients as a matter of federal regulatory policy.⏎⏎o The framework must require disclosure to patients when AI systems have materially contributed to clinical decisions affecting their care, in language that is accessible and that identifies the responsible party.⏎⏎o The framework must establish post-market surveillance obligations with defined triggers — including performance degradation thresholds and adverse outcome reporting requirements — and must assign those obligations to a party with both the technical access and the legal incentive to act on them.⏎⏎o The framework must include an algorithmic bias monitoring requirement, with defined performance standards across demographic subgroups, and must condition continued reimbursement on demonstrated compliance with those standards.⏎⏎o The framework must be established through notice-and-comment rulemaking, not sub-regulatory guidance, so that its provisions are binding and judicially reviewable.⏎⏎This comment acknowledges that building this framework will take time and that the Department faces legitimate pressure to move quickly. That pressure is understandable. But the sequencing question — whether to accelerate adoption before or after accountability infrastructure exists — is not a technical question about implementation speed. It is a policy question about who bears the risk of getting this wrong.⏎⏎VUMC Biomedical Informatics Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 7⏎⏎The academic community conducting AI research relevant to clinical care has a direct stake in this question. Researchers at institutions like Vanderbilt have invested substantial effort in developing and validating models that could improve patient outcomes. Those models will not achieve their potential if the deployment environment systematically produces harms that erode patient and clinician trust in AI-assisted care. The accountability diffusion problem is not just a legal or ethical concern. It is a practical threat to the long-term viability of clinical AI as a field. A single high-profile adverse outcome attributable to an unaccountable AI system — and the CRA survey data suggests the conditions for such an outcome are present in a significant fraction of current deployments — could set back adoption by years and consume the institutional goodwill that researchers have spent a decade building.⏎⏎This comment also wants to note, without developing the point at length, that the international comparison is not favorable to the current U.S. approach. The comparative regulatory analysis in Kesselheim, Cresswell, and Sheikh (2023) found that several peer jurisdictions have moved toward mandatory pre-deployment accountability requirements for clinical AI, while the U.S. continues to rely on a combination of voluntary standards, post-market surveillance, and existing malpractice doctrine — none of which, individually or collectively, resolves the accountability gap that this comment has described. The Department should be aware that the regulatory vacuum it is proposing to fill with adoption incentives is a vacuum that other jurisdictions have concluded requires accountability requirements, not just deployment support.⏎⏎VUMC Biomedical Informatics Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 8⏎⏎One practical note on implementation: the framework this comment describes does not require the Department to resolve every open question about AI liability doctrine before any deployment occurs. There is a meaningful difference between deploying AI in a legal environment where accountability is unclear because no one has addressed the question, and deploying AI in a legal environment where accountability is clearly assigned even if the assignment is imperfect and subject to future refinement. The latter environment allows for learning, correction, and iterative improvement. The former produces institutional dependency on an accountability-free deployment model that becomes progressively harder to change. The Department should aim for the former, and the mandatory framework this comment proposes is a means to that end, not an obstacle to adoption.⏎⏎The specific provision this comment regards as most urgent is the non-delegability requirement. The vendor contract analysis in Kearns and Roth (2023) found that limitation-of-liability provisions in clinical AI vendor agreements were present in effectively all contracts reviewed, and that these provisions were structured to survive even negligence findings in some cases. Federal regulatory policy that renders such provisions unenforceable against patients — not against other commercial parties, but specifically against patients seeking accountability for AI-related harm — would be a targeted and enforceable intervention that does not require the resolution of broader questions about AI liability doctrine. It is, in the view of this comment, the single most important step the Department could take to address the structural accountability defect before scaling deployment further.⏎⏎The Department's timeline for responding to this RFI and any subsequent rulemaking is not known to this comment's author at the time of submission, but given that the CRA survey was fielded in the first quarter of 2024 and reflects conditions that have likely worsened since, the⏎⏎VUMC Biomedical Informatics Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 9⏎⏎urgency of the accountability question is not diminishing. The volume of clinical AI deployments documented in the ONC's own reporting has increased materially in each of the past three years, and the absence of a mandatory accountability framework has not prevented that growth — which is precisely the problem.
